en: Durveka’s *Dharmottarapradīpa*: the *Nyāyabindu* composed by the teacher Dharmakīrti.
The First Chapter: Direct Perception (Pratyakṣapariccheda).
Oṃ, homage to the One Free from Passion.
Oṃ, homage to the Omniscient One. *Note: This title and salutation do not appear in manuscript AP.*
The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge; therefore, that [right knowledge] is here explained.
— Nyāyabinduṭīkā composed by Ācārya Dharmottara.

Victorious are the words of the Sugata, the enemy of passion and its like, who conquers the world that is the cause for the continuous production of the calamity of birth; they bring about the thinning away of the darkness of the mind.
The *Dharottarapradīpa*, composed by Ācārya Durveka Miśra:
The Sūtras, Abhidharma, and Vinaya— the words of the Sugata— constantly triumph through their marvelous nature, being free from contradiction.
[2] The leaf here is torn— wherein all the principles (tattvas) of the entire aggregate of objects appear like reflections in a mirror.

Having correctly elucidated these vast words of Dharmottara, which are directed toward the illustrious Dharmakīrti and are for the benefit of the world, I acquire merit; by means of that merit, may I deliver the world from the ocean of suffering.
Those possessed of stains such as stinginess are unable to perceive virtue; for in this matter, the honest are indeed the touchstones for testing gold. (The leaf here is torn.
[End of *Hemaparīkṣā*]. The virtuous are truly the touchstones.

Desiring to compose this *Nyāyabinduṭīkā*, Dharmottara— having understood from scripture (*āgama*) the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) regarding the merit of worshipping the Blessed One as something beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) because there is no other way of knowing such a subject, and having accepted its authority—
and since merit is the opposite of demerit, the absence of obstacles to the fruit of merit is possible through the application of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhavidhi*).
Therefore, for the purpose of composing the treatise without obstacles and for its completion— [the leaf here is missing]— saṃ- [DhPr p.

Furthermore, by studying that [text], one who has acquired merit through the extraordinary excellence born from hearing the multitude of the Lord’s qualities will likewise attain an understanding of the true meaning of the treatise he seeks to know without obstacle;

and the conduct of the learned, as observed in the world, will also be maintained. With this intention, he begins a worship of the Lord consisting of praise, by means of the narrative known as *Vāgvijaya*.

It might be argued: since the purpose of worship is merely to generate merit, one should first perform the physical worship of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) prior to beginning the work one intends to undertake.
Why is that [work] not undertaken?
If it is argued that even in an undertaking preceded by that [work], the objection would arise: "Why was praise and worship itself not made the precursor to the undertaking?
In that case, this [objection] would be like the objection regarding the Aśoka grove; thus, it is not even worth repeating before the wise.
This is incorrect;

for if one were to employ words of praise while arranging the bodily worship, it would follow that this verse—which does not constitute an explanation of that [worship]—is being composed out of context.

However, bodily worship, because it occupies the place of the preparatory ritual acts such as providing a comfortable seat and instruction, is not troubled by the objection regarding the composition of something irrelevant.
[5] The leaf is missing here—this is what is said: This would indeed be the case if such praise and worship were prescribed for the sake of one's own interest.

What then? Even when the glorification of the Blessed One’s qualities is performed for the sake of the audience, the verse must necessarily be understood by the listeners, at the very least, out of a desire to know the qualities of the poem.
Through that knowledge, the qualities of the Tathāgata reside within the mental continuum of the listener for that duration.

Among them, those who already possess minds of extreme faith toward the Blessed One, perceiving that their own minds are rightly settled in one who possesses such a preeminent excellence of qualities, attain stability of mind.
Furthermore, for those who are neutral, the minds of those intent on their own welfare find it appropriate to turn toward one who is so greatly exalted and adorned with such jewels of qualities;
thus, the mind of those who become disillusioned, thinking, "For so long we have remained indifferent while being negligent," becomes established [in faith].
And even for those who are not particularly well-disposed, [the thought arises]: "Why should we suddenly harbor hostility toward one who is such an abode of virtues?"
Thus, from such reflection, there may arise either a slight turning away [from unwholesome states] or equanimity.
Consequently, through the production of clarity of mind in one who is exceedingly serene and of stability of mental clarity in one who is equanimous, an excellence of merit arises.
Even for a third person, though there is only a slight turning away, there is still the generation of merit.
However, by maintaining neutrality, one avoids falling into the hells brought about by the intensification of hatred for the Blessed One; this occurs through the pacification of that hatred.

But in the absence of worship consisting of praise, the threefold purpose of the audience would not be accomplished—therefore, it is established that worship consisting of praise is prescribed with the aim of benefiting both oneself and others.

[6] The leaf is broken here— where the manuscript *saṃ* reads "duḥkhāni" (sufferings)— in that context, by this verse, the Blessed One is praised for his perfection of his own welfare, his perfection of the means for the welfare of others, and his perfection of the welfare of others.
Because all three of these perfections must necessarily be discussed:
for you, whose great compassion has been made habitual through long-term practice, the perfection of the welfare of others is the primary purpose,
while the other is secondary.
Since the Tathāgata-nature is likewise an incidental [subject], it must certainly be discussed.
Thus said Bhaṭṭa Varāhasvāmin: "He for whom the Tathāgata-nature is incidental, having directly realized the nature of the entire world."

And since that [attainment of one's own welfare] is impossible without the perfection of means, its exposition is also necessary. Furthermore, this [perfection of means] is not established for one who has not attained the perfection of one's own welfare; thus, its exposition also necessarily follows. As she (the Goddess) said:

“Having himself crossed over, he leads the entire world; for the Protector is authorized in the teaching of the path. In this regard, for one who has achieved his own welfare (*svārthasampatti*), there is the perfection of the means for accomplishing the welfare of others (*parārthasampādanopāyasampat*), and the perfection of the accomplishment of the welfare of others which is to be achieved by those means. First, the perfection of his own welfare is stated by the passage beginning with “by birth” and ending with “of the Sugata.”
By the statement, "The accomplishment of the welfare of others is not achieved for one who lacks skillful means," the perfection of the means for the welfare of others is expressed.
"Such is the nature of reality,

and this is what must be practiced"— instruction on the Dharma in such a form is indeed the Blessed One’s perfection of the means for accomplishing the welfare of others, characterized by his understanding of the benefit of the world;
it is like the excellence of a supreme physician’s means for effecting the alleviation of disease, consisting of the diagnosis of the nature of the illness and the prescription of medicine.
Immediately following that, the perfection of the welfare of others—which is to be accomplished through the perfection of those means—is expressed by the next word.
In this context, the connection is with the phrase "vāco jayanti" (the words triumph).
It is considered intransitive because the object is not intended to be expressed.
The words characterized by the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya triumph;
that is, they excel and become preeminent.
Since excellence is relative to its own kind, the implicit meaning is that they become superior to the words of Īśvara and others.
Alternatively, "they conquer" means they overcome;
and since overcoming has as its object a rival,
the meaning is that they effect the overcoming of the treatises of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika).

Because these [scriptures] establish meanings that are established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas those [other scriptures] are the opposite of that; this has been stated here merely on the basis of what is established by the intellect. However, in the *Viniścayaṭīkā*, this qualification is employed as a reason, beginning with the words "by the power of reasoning" (*yuktiprabhāva*).

When the question arises as to whose these [qualities] are, he says: "of the Sugata. This word *su* should be understood as functioning with three meanings: he has gone to what is excellent (*praśastaṃ gataḥ*), thus he is the Sugata.
He has gone in such a way that it is praiseworthy;
he has departed from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
How is his going in that manner?
Because one transcends cyclic existence through the vision of selflessness,
and because that [vision] relies upon wisdom (*prajñā*).
Alternatively, since roots meaning "to go" also mean "to know," "gone" (*gata*) in the sense of "praiseworthy" means "having known."
And that reality is praised, characterized by selflessness;
its nature as reality is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, this word "su" is observed to function in the sense of being praised.
Just as those who live by their beauty are called "surūpa" (possessing beautiful form),
so too the Sugata has gone such that there is no returning;
he has gone, meaning he has departed from saṃsāra.
Furthermore, because the Blessed One has struck down birth and its defects— which are denoted by the term "return"— by utterly destroying their seed, which is the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*),
the word *su-* is used here in this sense as well;
just as in the expression "a well-tended fever" (*sunayo jvaraḥ*).
Or, the Sugata has gone without remainder;
he has gone as far as it is possible to go, having reached that state.

This is because the Sage has attained that state through the abandonment of all characteristics of remainder, characterized by the absence of afflictions and the perfection of body, speech, and intellect.
The word *su* is also seen used as an adverbial prefix (*vṛtti*), as in the expression "a well-filled jar" (*supūrṇo ghaṭaḥ*).
To the question "Of what kind is that Sugata?", he says: "of the Victor," that is, the conqueror.
To whom does this victory belong? He says: it belongs to the world, that is, the realm of living beings.
And this victory should be understood as the world's excellence resulting from the attainment of the supreme state (paramapada) in relation to the world;
for this very reason, the world becomes transcended.

Because it is the opposite of that [worldly power], "overpowering" (abhibhava) should not be understood as the disparagement of the body and so forth in relation to another king, like a king's victory over another king. Of what kind of world?

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called "birth" (*jāti*) because by means of it one is born and wanders through cyclic existence (*saṃsarati*). It is called "casting away" (*vyasana*) because by means of it one is scattered, cast about, and thrown here and there in various ways.
Or, *vyasana* means "that which one casts away.
A compound should be formed with the restrictive sense (*antarnīta-niyama*) implied, such that birth itself is the calamity (*vyasana*).
For a living being, while still thirsting, performs various actions by which it wanders through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, since that very [craving] scatters and casts him about here and there by way of producing [birth], it is logical that craving itself is "misfortune" (*vyasana*).

Alternatively, "misfortune" refers to attachment— that is, the dogmatic insistence (*abhiniveśa*) in the form of "May I become a *vidyādhara*," "May I become a god," and so forth— regarding birth, which is production within a specific class of beings.
Or rather, it refers to the calamities and sufferings— such as disease, grief, and so forth— which are based on dullness (*jāḍya*);
in the former explanation, it refers to that [dullness], while in the latter explanation, it refers to their continuous succession or flow (*prabandha*).
Or rather, that itself is the preeminent bondage;
in the sense of a stream, it is by way of continuity;
in the sense of bondage, it is of the continuity.
[This refers to] the cause of production.
And thus, by employing the term "cause" (*hetu*) together with the phrase "continuous production" (*prabandha-prasūti*), he intends to refute the views of others.
For when it is stated in this manner, this...

[In the manuscript, the word] *duḥkhāni* occurs; this is the intended meaning: being dull-witted and led by no other sentient being, he himself performs various such actions by which he wanders thus in saṃsāra.
But it is not impelled by another, as others think:
"This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by God, it goes to heaven or to hell."
Or it is indeed an error.
"[Mahābhāvana- 30,28] Thus it is said.
Otherwise, he would have stated [the term] "of one who has taken recourse to the destruction of birth" together with its other qualifying attributes.
Of what kind of Sugata [is this said]?"
Because of the disappearance of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there is enmity toward the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as passion;
for by that [disappearance], they have been uprooted along with their very roots from within one's own continuum.
Precisely because you, O Blessed One, are the enemy of passion and the other afflictions, [you are called the Victor].
And the world is the cause for the continuous production of the calamity of birth;
therefore, he is superior to it and its conqueror. Alternatively, "because of his enmity toward passion and the like" is an epithet of the world.
This is because he is one for whom passion and the other enemies are constant adversaries and perpetual harmers;

therefore, you should be understood as a "Victor" (*vijetā*) precisely because of your state as a Sugata. As for the explanation that you are the enemy of the passion and so forth belonging to the world, it has not been stated here because it is [merely] afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
He asks what kind of speech it is and says: "The mind," and so forth.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is nescience (*avidyā*), is like darkness because it obstructs the discernment between real and unreal objects;
and that [nescience] is described as if it were a distinct property (*dharma*) of the mind—that is, of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*)—due to a certain perspective.
In reality, however, ignorance is simply afflicted knowledge;
or rather, it is the afflicted mind itself, which is "darkness" (tamas) just as previously explained.
Some, however, declare that the compound term *manastamas* denotes the meaning of "non-knowledge."
"Tānava" means thinness, attenuation, or the state of becoming weak;
"ādadhānāḥ" means producing or effecting that [attenuation].
By the mention of "tānava-grahaṇa" (the grasping of attenuation), he declares this: your words do not entirely eradicate the ignorance of the world.

Because one would be liberated merely by hearing it, resulting in the absurdity that the cultivation of the path (*mārgabhāvanā*) is useless; rather, when reflected upon for a long time, they attenuate delusion (*moha*) by causing its manifestation to become weak. Alternatively, it is explained in another way: those words conquer—that is, they overcome—*tamas*, [and thus] the activity of delusion.
They establish [the fires];
the remainder is the same as before.
Here, the inscription is rubbed away.
Alternatively, one who has darkness (*tamas*) in the mind is "mind-darkness" (*manastamā*), meaning a fool; the state of being that is "mind-darkness-ness" (*manastamastā*);
its end (*anava*) is its cessation.
For instance— *nūti* means new;
those [factors] which, by being opposed to that, produce it, [operate] through the production of delusion (*mūḍhatva*),
because they set it in motion.
"The remainder is the same as before"—thus the verse has been explained.
[10] The inscription here is rubbed away. [11] The inscription here is rubbed away.
Let this alone be considered: when Dharmottara was praising the Tathāgata, why did he not state that victory belongs primarily to this very [treatise] itself?
Why, instead, did he establish it only as a secondary consequence by way of a qualification of the Dharma? To this, the following response is given.

By the venerable master Dharmakīrti, for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the Blessed One’s teaching... [omitted] ...since that is the subject at hand, victory is primarily set forth here. The manuscript has been rubbed [and corrected] in this place.
Alternatively, for one whose very words are victorious in such a manner, victory through the rod is established as being superior according to the principle of victory;
and this has been indicated by the term "conqueror."
By the words "preceded by right knowledge" (*samyagjñānapūrvikā*) and so forth, the subject matter and purpose of this treatise are stated.

Alternatively, according to the view of the followers of scripture (*āgamika*), the Blessed One has entered final nirvana (*parinirvṛta*) in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).
Since this very [treatise] exists as his body once he has entered final nirvana, the follower of scripture has thus set forth the victory of speech alone.

By the words beginning with "samyagjñāna," that which is the purpose of this treatise— the thorough understanding of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)— is stated, along with its own purpose, which consists in the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Nor can it be asserted that the purpose of the thorough understanding of right knowledge is merely the complete comprehension of right knowledge itself, rather than the accomplishment of the goals of human life.
For the cultivation of right knowledge consists precisely in the realization of its own nature through the removal of misconceptions;
with the intention of showing how that [cultivation] could serve as a purpose for the self itself, Vinītadeva and Śāntabhadra have provided this explanation.
Disregarding that explanation, [the author] explains [it] by stating "the subject matter and the purpose are being stated.
And this is the intention behind such disregard: indeed, that "this is the purpose of this" is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and not otherwise.
And this well-known accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārthasiddhi*),
which occurs even for cowherds, women, and others without the cultivation of right knowledge, exists when there is right knowledge;

whereas it does not occur for the wise even when that cultivation of right knowledge is present, it therefore does not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that cultivation.
What then? It is the purpose of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) itself that ought to be its utility.

By the sentence beginning with "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*), the author of the *Vārttika*—by means of this instrumental statement—states the observed purpose of the subject matter of the treatise, which is characterized by right knowledge; that is, the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha-siddhi*).
This is understood from the context as being [stated] by the author.

But surely, that wherein the operation of denotation (abhidhā-vyāpāra) comes to rest is the meaning of a sentence; yet this does not find its finality in the accomplishment of a human goal. What then? It finds its finality in the hearer’s cultivation of correct knowledge.
How, then, is that [correct knowledge] said to be the meaning of the sentence? It is explained as follows:

although that correct knowledge is taught to the disciple with respect to the verbal denotative function (*śabdābhidhāvyāpāra*), and thus the act of teaching—which has the disciple’s correct knowledge as its object—is the primary meaning of the sentence, nevertheless, since this [knowledge] is possible as the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), it is stated here by way of defining that [intended meaning].
For indeed, why does he exert himself so much toward its very production?

Because it is said that "the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge" (*samyagjñānapūrvikā sarvapuruṣārthasiddhiḥ*). Furthermore, in cases where the object is possible only as the literal denotation (*abhidhāviṣaya*) and not as the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), [it is not considered a valid source of knowledge].

In that case, that very [sentence-meaning] is postulated. However, when two possibilities exist, since the sentence is directed toward the latter, its meaning is such; thus, by the principle of the "implied" (ārthena nyāyena), the purpose of the denotation—namely, the accomplishment of human goals—is stated as the sentence-meaning, and this is how it is explained.
[13] By the passage beginning with "all preceded by..."—
APE [14]— the writing here has been rubbed away.
However, some others explain this statement of Dharmottara differently.

In this context, by the word *prayojana* (purpose), the result (*phala*) is not intended; rather, it is that by which one is impelled (*prayujyate*) or set in motion, or that which causes one to act (*prayojayati*).
And that consists in being the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
For a person is impelled to engage [with this work] because the subject matter—right knowledge—is the cause for the accomplishment of human goals.
This same purpose is intended even in what follows.
Therefore, it is appropriate to clarify that in the passage beginning with "And here," the purpose that impels engagement is stated to be the cause for the accomplishment of all human goals.
And we perceive that this is not very well-connected;

for here, the purpose (*prayojana*)—namely, that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise, is the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—has been stated, as it will be made explicit by what follows. Therefore, even in this case, a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the purpose of the subject matter" must necessarily be employed.
And thus, this rule regarding compound words would be inapplicable;
for that status of being the cause for the accomplishment of human goals belongs not to the subject matter—namely, correct knowledge—but rather to the person.
How then could the word expressing the purpose be compounded with the word expressing the subject matter?
Nor is its connection with the denotatum established in any form whatsoever;
for it is only when two capable words undergo "integration into a single meaning" (ekārthībhāva) that such a relation occurs.

For a son of Yajñadatta, by virtue of being related to Devadatta through a status such as servitude, cannot become the object of a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) such as "Devadatta’s son" (*devadattaputra*).
Now, if it is argued that because the expression emphasizes the state (*bhāva*), the meaning is "the state of being a motivator" (*prayojakatva*);
and since that [state] exists as a relation through the motivatorship of the one who has taken refuge [in him], then the rule regarding semantic competency (*samarthavidhi*) is postulated.

Now, if the state of being the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal residing in right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) constitutes the "purpose" (*prayojana*)—in the sense of being the motivator—then it follows that right knowledge itself is the purpose.
For it is not the case that the state of being a purpose can itself be the purpose;
nor does a person, impelled by right knowledge, engage in the act of [attaining] right knowledge.
However, it is by virtue of being the cause for the accomplishment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). How, then, could that [mere sound] be the purpose?
Furthermore, the linguistic usage of elders is indeed the ground for the usage of words and their meanings.

Furthermore, an elder who prompts [others] should not be called the "prompter" (prayojaka) merely because he possesses the status of a prompter; rather, the purpose of the prompter is said to be the production of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Otherwise, one might as well say that the teacher—who acts to bring about the production of correct knowledge in those being instructed—is the prompter, or even that one who urges another who is making a mat to continue making it is the prompter for that act. One who speaks in such a manner is neither a worldly person nor an investigator, and thus should simply be disregarded.
Moreover, why would this [logical reason] not be established otherwise, such that one would have to die and be reborn after perishing?
It is not so, for it is easily established in another way as well.
And in his explanation of "being the motivator" (*prayojakatva*), what weight does Dharmottara see that he would express such an unexpressive [term]?
And how could one employ [the term] *prakaraṇa* (context) in a way that is difficult to justify?
Furthermore, when a person acts out of a desire to obtain or avoid something, he is impelled by the acts of appropriation and rejection.
As Akṣapāda said: "That object with reference to which one acts is the purpose (*prayojana*)" [NSū 1.1.28].
"Concerning" (adhikṛtya) means "with reference to" (uddiśya).
Furthermore, one does not engage in activity desiring or wishing to avoid a cause for the accomplishment of human goals that is distinct from right knowledge.
What then? One engages with reference to the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; therefore, those two alone are the appropriate purposes.

For one who has nothing to abandon, nothing to acquire, and who is free from desire for objects—even though [the means] may be a cause for achieving the goals of human life—one does not engage [with them].

Since worldly activity proceeds from memory accompanied by desire, enough with this blind adherence to the words of one who lacks insight into the true nature of things and whose view is limited to merely justifying the verbal expression.
Now, it is argued that the purpose of the subject matter (*abhidheya-prayojana*) is the motivator.
If it is argued that therefore this fault does not apply, that is untenable.

For a person, being impelled by the desire to achieve a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), does not engage with the subject matter characterized as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); rather, he engages with the treatise—namely, with the act of listening to the text.
It functions [toward the whole].
Now, because the treatise has the nature of both word and meaning,
it likewise functions toward the aggregate consisting of both the word and the object denoted.
How then is the genitive case used in the phrase "of the book" (*granthasya*) or "of the treatise" (*prakaraṇasya*)?

If, on the other hand, this meaning [is intended]: "the purpose is that which sets in motion [activity] toward the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise"—that is, toward the collection of both the expression and the expressed—then it would be incoherent to say that "it sets in motion [activity] toward the treatise."

Furthermore, if by the aforementioned etymology the word "purpose" (prayojana) were intended to signify that which prompts [the composition], such that what is desired to be communicated would be its prompter, then it would have been said that the purpose of the subject matter is stated by the words "preceded by right knowledge" and so forth;
and the person who is the primary related party would have been shown by the expression "of the person."
But this is not the case; therefore, by the word "purpose" (*prayojana*), it is the result (*phala*) itself that is intended here and in what follows.
Now, it might be argued: "If the practitioner is one who seeks a result, why does he not simply engage with the result itself? Why exert effort for the sake of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?"

It is precisely the desire for the fruit characterized by the abandonment of what is to be discarded (*heya*) and the acquisition of what is to be adopted (*upādeya*) that seeks the knowledge which is the basis for those two.
Otherwise, what harm is there in [the author] fearing his own potential for contradiction?
However, regarding the position of the fruit, it is shown that its subject matter (*abhidheya*) is useful for the engagement of persons.
For the body of a treatise is twofold: word and meaning.
Among these, the purpose of the word is solely the communication of its own denotation.
It is nothing else;
therefore, it is not further analyzed.
However, if the subject matter were devoid of purpose, then the composition of words intended for its comprehension would likewise not be undertaken.

But is it not the case that this technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) does not have its constituent meanings obliterated? Rather, through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "that by which one employs [an action]" or "that which causes one to employ [an action]," it also applies to the result (*phala*).
If it is asked, "How then is this explained?"—
it is true;
however, the fact that right knowledge is the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal is not prompted by the Self alone, but rather by the Person (puruṣa).
Furthermore, the measure of the fault has been stated therein;

and in the analysis of the compound as "the purpose regarding the subject matter" (*abhidheye prayojanam*), a great many faults have been shown. Therefore, even by one who possesses such an understanding, neither a purpose of that kind nor a motivator of that kind should be expressed here by the word "purpose" (*prayojana*).

"Rather, it is the result itself"—thus everything is clear. Now, one might object: "In this treatise (*prakaraṇa*), wishing to engage the listeners, the author states the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*); therefore, it would be more appropriate for him to state those very two for this [work] itself. And since those two are characterized by the communication of their respective subject matters," anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is twofold," and so forth.
For this reason, the nature of the body of this treatise is twofold.
As it is stated in the *Kāvyālaṅkāra*: "Poetry consists of word and meaning together" [1.16].
Therefore, the subject matter and the purpose are now being stated.
In the *Kāvyālaṅkāravṛtti*: "This word *kāvya* (poetry) applies to both sound (*śabda*) and meaning (*artha*) when they are refined by qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
To the question of how there is this twofold division, he says:
"Sound," etc.
By the word "ca" (and), he conjoins the sense of "together with," as it constitutes the body of the treatise (*prakaraṇa*).

This is what is meant: since word and meaning exist in a relationship of the delimiting and the delimited, the nature of a treatise does not belong otherwise; thus, because the treatise possesses this dual nature, when the subject matter and the purpose are stated, the treatise itself is thereby stated.

If this is so, then since there is no difference in their being bodies, why is it not said that [the purpose belongs] to the signifier itself, just as it does to the signified? Furthermore, a person does not engage with the signified in its abstract form, but rather engages with the text itself through the activity of listening for the sake of knowing the signified. Seeing these two positions, he says "therein" (*tatra*), which serves here to specify.

The intention here is that this [investigation] is useful for human activity in the sense that it is nothing other than [the inquiry into the purpose]. For a composition of words is not undertaken or heard merely because the word has the result of communicating its own meaning; for that would be considered no more significant than an examination of a crow’s teeth.
What then? It is because that meaning possesses a practical purpose.
Therefore, what is the point of saying this? If so, one might ask: "Why then is the denotable object (abhidheya) also mentioned? To this he says: "But the denotable object," and so forth.
The word "but" (tu) shows that the denotable object is distinct from the denotation (abhidhāna).
The word "api" (even/also) is to be understood as following after the phrase "is not to be commenced.
Thus, the meaning is this: even the composition of words for the sake of understanding that [reality] might not be undertaken, let alone its being heard.
Just as an investigation into the teeth of a crow need not be undertaken by a discerning person because it serves no purpose, so too,
by demonstrating that this treatise ought to be undertaken, its subject matter and purpose are stated by this [opening verse].
Since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge, this treatise is commenced for the sake of its realization; such is the meaning of the sentence here.
And in this context, the purpose of right knowledge—which is the subject matter of the treatise—is stated to be the cause of the accomplishment of all human goals.

The word "yathā" (as/how) is used to indicate the scope of a meaning that has been stated in general; its sense is: "just as this has been shown, so should everything else be viewed. "Tat parīkṣeta" (one should examine that) is an instruction regarding the object [of examination], specifying that one should examine it in such and such a manner.
The term "collection of words" (padasaṃhati) refers to what exists in the intellect;

or, "examination" (parīkṣā) means the determination [of a matter] after deliberation, and because it has that as its purpose, the treatise (śāstra) is also so designated. [Objection: But surely, one should not undertake [this work] if its subject matter is devoid of purpose?
He states what is accomplished by this statement with the words "Therefore," and so forth.

Since that which lacks a purpose or a subject matter is not undertaken, therefore—by demonstrating its fitness for undertaking and thereby making it clear that "this very thing, being worthy of being commenced, is now commenced by me"—and since the fitness for undertaking has been demonstrated, the fitness for being heard is also demonstrated by virtue of the same underlying cause; thus, they are induced to proceed.

But surely, by the phrase "the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge," only a single part—the subject matter and the purpose—has been stated, not the whole; so how can it be said that "it is expressed by this sentence"? It is replied: It is said: [The whole is expressed] because the connection between the subject matter and the purpose is indicated by the mention of their respective parts. For when one says, "There is honey in this well," the person who desires honey understands the connection between the well and the honey, even though the word "well" does not directly denote the honey. Similarly, here too, although the words do not directly denote the connection between the subject matter and the purpose, the connection is understood through the indication of the two related parts. Furthermore, since the subject matter and the purpose are not established without a connection, the statement of the connection is necessarily implied. Therefore, it is correct to say that the entire meaning is expressed by this sentence. Moreover, the connection is not merely the mere coexistence of the two; rather, it is the relationship of means and end (sādhyasādhanabhāva). And that is indeed expressed by this sentence. Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, the word "all" (sarva) is used to indicate that the accomplishment of every human goal whatsoever is preceded by right knowledge, and not just some specific goal. This is because the word "all" is employed to exclude other things. For example, when one says, "All food has been eaten by him," it is understood that he has eaten everything except poison and such things. Likewise, here too, the word "all" excludes the accomplishment of goals such as heaven, which are achieved through ritual action (*karma*), thereby indicating that the accomplishment of the goal of liberation (*mokṣa*) is preceded by right knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is that the accomplishment of the goal of liberation is preceded by right knowledge. Consequently, the subject matter and the purpose are indeed expressed by this sentence. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the word "all" is used to indicate that the accomplishment of every human goal whatsoever is preceded by right knowledge, and not just some specific goal. A sentence, indeed, is defined as a collection of connected words that, while mutually dependent through their meanings, experience the relationship of primary and secondary (guṇa-guṇibhāva) with respect to a single meaning intended to be expressed as the principal one.

In this regard, if all the word-meanings were equally primary, there would be no mutual assistance; consequently, there would be no connection between the words at all, and thus the very nature of a sentence would be lost. Therefore, what has been stated by him is well-said.

He explicitly states, by means of the words "yathā," "tathā," and "yasmāt," exactly how and why the statement of the subject matter and the purpose of this work—which consists of the collection of words beginning with "samyagjñāna"—is made;

that is, for the sake of the student's comprehension of that right knowledge (implied by the word "arthāt"). Furthermore, this should be understood as an explanation of the meaning established by the force of the phrase "and that [right knowledge] is being explained."

By the word *iti*, the intrinsic nature of the sentence-meaning is indicated; and by the word *idam*, because it is established in the intellect, that very meaning is shown as if it were fit for designation by a finger.
And by this [word *iti*], the primacy [of the sentence-meaning] is established, since it is the means (*upeya*) for the accomplishment of human goals.
Furthermore, because correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) being imparted is merely a means to that [liberation], it lacks primacy.
For this very reason, according to the logic of the purpose, the attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

However, by way of verbal function (*śābdī vṛtti*), it has been shown that the act of producing proficiency (*vyutpatti*) regarding the object of the student's correct knowledge is the sentence-meaning.

But surely, by the statement beginning with "samyagjñāna" (right knowledge), only the status of right knowledge as a cause for the attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) has been demonstrated, and not that this [work] is its purpose.
Yet it was also stated that the purpose of that very [knowledge] is expressed by this [work].
How, then, is this consistent? Or rather, is it not [the case]?
Even by that much, it is not known what its subject matter is, nor what its purpose; anticipating this doubt, he says: "And here," and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that the purpose is that right knowledge is the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), that is untenable, because it contradicts the root [text] and contradicts reason.

For indeed, the statement of the Teacher beginning with "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*) and so forth acknowledges the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārthasiddhi*) itself as the purpose (*prayojana*), but not its status as the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal.
In the explanation of the meaning of the individual parts, he will clarify that very [accomplishment] as the purpose.
Nor is it accepted or logical that the state of being a cause is distinct from the cause itself.
In that case, how is it that by stating the purpose (*prayojana*) of this very right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*),
the relationship (*sambandha*), the purpose, and the subject matter (*abhidheya*) all become stated when this meaning is being explained?
It will exist; and in this case, no purpose or motivating cause need be stated,
according to the principle already explained.
For here too, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the word] "purpose" being understood as the material cause (*upādāna*) related to the activity.
Furthermore, there is no general royal edict by which the word "purpose" could be assumed to have the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning;
if that were accepted, the previously mentioned objection would recur.
True. It is not intended that the purpose (*prayojana*) of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is its being the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
What then? It is the accomplishment of the human goal itself.
If it is asked, "How can this be called [the purpose] if it is not expressed by words? [the answer follows].
The word "ca" (and) here has the sense of "because.

Therefore, since it has been stated that right knowledge— the subject matter of this treatise— is the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal, the phrase "therefore the purpose has been stated" must be repeated twice.
And here, by implication, it remains that the accomplishment of the human goal itself [is established].

Since the statement that right knowledge is the cause with respect to that [goal] has already stated its purpose, the point is: what further could be done by an explicit expressive word? By this much alone, this is sufficiently proven; however, many others will yet come forward on this matter.
Because all success regarding the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) arises from it as their cause, it is "the accomplishment of all human goals" (sarvapuruṣārthasiddhi).
That which has such a causal nature as its purpose is likewise [designated].
And that is indeed the accomplishment of the goals of human life.
By this etymological derivation, that very [knowledge] is expressed by this word.
When the expectation arises as to "whose is such [knowledge]?", some understand this to refer to "the right knowledge (samyagjñāna) which is the subject matter of this treatise.
Others, however, [hold it refers to] the Sage (arṣa).

[16] Having formed the possessive suffix *mat* in the sense that "this [treatise] has a purpose in its beginning," and intending to indicate it as a primary factor, they assert that it possesses a purpose (*prayojanavattva*).
Thus they justify the point: since the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is achieved through right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), for that very reason, that [knowledge] is the purpose.
Furthermore, the fact that this [treatise] serves as the cause for that [knowledge] is precisely what constitutes its "having a purpose."

Since it is established that when correct knowledge exists, it is the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), they consider that this has been stated by relying on the relationship between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*)— namely, the state of being established and the act of establishing— and thus there is no fault whatsoever.
Others, however, by shifting the position of the word "ca" (and), interpret the passage as meaning that the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal has been stated,

and the purpose has also been stated. Still others, by applying the term "cause of the accomplishment of the human goal" metaphorically to the effect, denote the accomplishment of the human goal itself.
They justify the use of this figurative expression for the purpose of showing that [the goal] cannot be accomplished by any other means.
However, some commentators, being unable to justify this in any way whatsoever, describe it as merely a faulty reading resulting from the occurrence of the word "sahita.
In this matter, only those who are wise will distinguish between what is essential and what is trivial.

It might be argued: "Just as the subject matter and the purpose are stated as being auxiliary to the engagement [with the treatise], why are the connection and so forth not also stated? To this he says: "And in this...
The word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of "because."

For instance, by stating that "correct knowledge (samyagjñāna), which is useful for human goals, is to be explained by means of this treatise," it is established that correct knowledge is the subject matter (abhidheya) of this composition of words,
and its explanation is the purpose (prayojana).
And it has been stated that this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) is for the purpose of explaining [the three] misfortunes (*apāya*).
Therefore, by the power of stating the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), the connection (*sambandha*) and other elements are implicitly stated;
however, this is not a single sentence [that explicitly states] the connection.
It is capable of directly stating both the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*);
however, by stating one, it indicates the other three through implication. In this regard:
But how is it that what was stated for one thing becomes stated for another? He says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*).

This collection of particles (*nipātasamudāya*) occurs everywhere in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). The "human purpose" (*puruṣārtha*) is the application (*upayoga*), that is, the activity (*vyāpāra*), characterized by the rejection of what is to be abandoned and the adoption of what is to be accepted.
That which possesses this [nature] is "thus" (*tathā*).
This being the case, he asks what is established and says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
By the word "that" (*tat*), the meaning of the sentence just mentioned should be understood as being referred back.
The "subject matter" (*abhidheya*) is one limb, that is, one part,
in relation to the other parts such as the connection (*sambandha*) and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the connection and so forth," the subject matter and the purpose (*prayojana*) are both subsumed.
"Stated" means stated as it were; they have been revealed, yet a direct denotation of this [meaning] is not possible therein.
Now, as for the purpose of the subject matter, just as it is directly expressed by the sentence, [so too is it here].
To the question, "In that case, why are the relation (*sambandha*) and so forth not also mentioned?", he says: "But not...
The particle *tu* (but) either emphasizes or distinguishes.
This is the intention: if all categories (*padārtha*) were to attain primacy, [then they would have been mentioned].
In that case, the sentence itself would fall apart, because, due to the absence of mutual dependence, it would fail to convey a single meaning.
Therefore, a sentence is postulated as having a single meaning to be expressed, rather than many;
for if it were not directly capable [of such expression], it would be ineffective.
How is it not incapable?
If it is indeed incapable, then one should not say that it is "not directly capable. Therefore, this [objection] is not to be stated.
He says: "But one" (*ekaṃ tu*).

Here, the particle *tu* (but) should be understood as excluding [the other two meanings] by virtue of being the direct denotation (*vācyatva*). It excludes the single [meaning] from being [the primary object].
It shows and illuminates,
because in that case the denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) of the sentence is impossible;
for this very reason it was said "the [meanings] have been explained," and thus it has been explained by us.
It would not contradict this [position].
Now, even if it is granted that the denotable object and so forth are what is manifested by the sentence,
they are not its denotation.
Nevertheless, that object must necessarily exist.
Anticipating the question, "In that case, which word expresses what?", he says: "Therein," and so forth—meaning, among those things such as the denotable object and the rest.
The word "that" (*tad*) refers to the subject matter (*abhidheya*);
"is explained" (*vyutpādyate*) refers to the purpose (*prayojana*).
And here, the purpose is considered in relation to the speaker's activity of composing the treatise.
And [this concerns] the listener’s act of hearing.
For instance: all discerning persons engage in an activity only after investigating its purpose.
Consequently, one might ask: for what purpose has this treatise been composed by the Teacher?

When there arises the doubt as to why the listeners should listen, "instruction" (vyutpādana) is stated as the purpose. This treatise was composed so that those who are being instructed might bring about right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) within themselves as instructors; and since the students, desiring instruction for themselves as directed by the teacher, listen to this treatise, the purpose of both the composition and the listening of the treatise is instruction.
The word *tat* here ends in the accusative case.

This is because in the phrase "from which it is derived" (*vyutpādyate*), the suffix *-la* is prescribed for the object of the causal agent (*prayojya-karman*), not for the object of the action of the causal agent itself (*prayojya-kriyā-karman*).
Furthermore, even in common worldly usage, the term *pada* is observed to be employed according to the etymology: "that by which a meaning is stepped upon (*padyate*) or understood (*gamyate*)."
Therefore, he says that the term "purpose" (*prayojana*) means "that by which [the subject] is explained.
Otherwise, this would not be a single word (*pada*), but rather a collection of words (*padavṛnda*). Alternatively, it should be understood as: "in this [treatise], [the subject] is explained."
Now, it was indeed stated that "the purpose is the accomplishment of the human goal. Why, then, is this considered again?
And how is it said to be something else? To this he says: "And the purpose here..."
This is intended as a conjunction with another point to be stated;

the meaning is this: it is not that the purpose [of the treatise] has not been stated, but rather that the purpose of the statement "the word which brings about the meaning as a subordinate element (guṇabhūta) is being etymologically analyzed" is now being considered.

That is to say, when the question is asked, "What is the purpose of the causative suffix (ṇic) in the phrase 'its analysis is performed'?", it is the purpose of that [causative suffix] which is being considered.
In this context, regarding the determination of the meaning as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), the very composition of the treatise (*prakaraṇa*) constitutes its function.
Now, one might ask: why is this doubt raised—namely, "for what purpose is it composed by the speaker, and for what purpose is it heard by the listeners"?
Anticipating the objection that "those two would indeed proceed in exactly this way," he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*), meaning "because.
Now, how is the purpose of the exposition of both stated?
For that from which one gains proficiency is the purpose of that proficiency.

As for the claim that "the instruction belongs to him who instructs," this is not so; for since the purpose is intended to be the instruction characterized by the activity of the instructor, the purpose for both [instructor and instructed] is indeed the instruction itself.
Only one [teacher] proceeds in one way and another in a different way;
how indeed might the linguistic proficiency residing in the mental continuum of the listener arise through the power of my activity? Thinking thus, the teacher proceeds.

For this very reason, the purpose of the agent is the production of that linguistic proficiency which resides in the mental continuum of the listener and is governed by the activity of the one who prompts him.
In this very way, he becomes the one who brings about proficiency;
as for the listener, however, he proceeds with the thought: "How indeed, by means of the teacher's activity, may proficiency arise within my own mental continuum?"
For this very reason, the listener’s proficiency, which is presided over by the activity of the teacher, is also the purpose;
in this very way, he is the one to be instructed by that [teacher].

However, there is no explicit word indicating the relationship [between the treatise and its purpose]; rather, that relationship is to be understood through implication alone. For when a discerning person begins this treatise for the sake of explaining right knowledge, he has already demonstrated that this alone—and nothing else—is the means; thus, the relationship between the means and the end (upāyopeyabhāva) of the treatise and its purpose is indeed shown.

Regarding the word "sambandha" (connection): it exists. Therefore, the exposition [of the treatise] is dependent upon the activity of the author; thus, the exposition serves as the purpose for both [the author and the listener].
Concluding with the word "iti," which functions here as a causal term, he says: "The purpose of both the composition of the treatise and its hearing is exposition."
Now, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has been applied, how can the derivation serve the purpose of both? In this way, there would be both a question and its answer.
What, then, is the purpose of merely showing that much?

The purpose is to demonstrate that the teacher possesses an uncommon causal status (*asādhāraṇakāraṇatā*) regarding the acquisition of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), even though he is merely an instrumental cause (*nimittamātra*) in some respect, such as through the consumption of curd and so forth.

This is the meaning: in demonstrating the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), it might be shown that the teacher is similar [to other causes] by virtue of being merely useful for the acquisition of right knowledge, such as through his own health and so on;
however, he also possesses a specific activity characterized by instruction (*upadeśa*) toward that acquisition.
He has provided the instruction with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) so that one might understand the word "discourse" (*kathā*).

If it is argued that, since a direct operation [of the teacher] toward the derivation of words such as "food" (*bhojana*) is impossible, the operation of the Teacher is therefore understood [as being directed toward that],
this is not so.
For it would be more logical to indicate [the agent] with the causative suffix (ṇic) that this skill of exposition belongs to the commentators and not to the author.
Now, was it not said that "the purpose of the designation is not being examined"? Is that very point now being examined under another pretext? True.

With the intention that [the object] is not defined merely as the meaning of a sentence, it was said, "That is not defined"; however, there is no contradiction in its being defined even as the meaning of a word. Regarding the statement "samyagjñānaṃ vyutpadyamānām," the author of the *Bhāgavṛtti* maintains that this expression is ungrammatical because the root *pad*, in the sense of "to learn" (*vyutpatti*), is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

That is not very convincing, because we frequently observe the use of the transitive verb *pad* (to know) with an object in expressions such as "the convention is established" (*vyutpannaḥ saṅketaḥ*).
For example, the author of the *Vārttika* used it in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: [as follows].
"The mind (*manas*) has arisen with the intention [to denote it]; therefore, if that [mind] is considered [to be the referent], then [the following applies]:
if the categories of meaning, such as the denotable object (*abhidheya*) and so forth,"
If that is so, then of which word is the relation the meaning? He says: "In the relation," and so forth.
"By implication" means not by the function of denotation (*abhidhā*).
By the particle *eva*, he excludes the denotation of the word.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "only. He asks, "How [is this] by implication? and replies: "By one who is discerning. "Upāya" means the cause.
The arising of right knowledge is that which is to be attained;
it is the state of those two [means and end],
by virtue of which there occurs the designation of both the means and the object to be attained.
The particle *eva* should be understood as following the word *upāya*,
because it is precisely the non-connection with the means (*upāya*) that is suspected as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
whereas connection with anything other than that will be suspected later.

However, when it is necessary to exclude other possible connections that have been raised by the suspicion of being purposeless, another restriction must be understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*);
yet this alone is not what is explicitly stated.
Furthermore, "not another" should be understood as "not exclusively another."

[Objection: But surely, even though the subject matter and so forth have been stated prior to hearing the treatise, they are not accepted by discerning persons because of the lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
So what is the purpose of stating these at the beginning of the work?

True. Even when things are mentioned within a specific context, they are not definitively established. However, even regarding the subject matter and so forth that have been stated, doubt arises when there is no means of valid cognition;
and from doubt, people proceed to act.
For even a doubt regarding the purpose is a factor for the engagement of discerning persons.

That the relationship of such a work is to be explained is shown by the very statement of the purpose. As it has been said: "The treatise and the purpose are not understood from the basis of the relationship. [17]
[17] Since it is included within the statement of those [other categories] that have been mentioned, it is not stated separately because there is no purpose [for doing so].

[Ślokavārttika 1.18] Not accepting the view that the opening statement functions as an incentive by means of revealing the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth, he says: "But surely... (*nanu ca*).
This is a collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) meaning "I object" (*codayāmi*).
The phrase "be present" (abhimukho bhava) is an indicator of this meaning.

Immediately after hearing [the word], an inference—or some other means—proceeding by means of the prior locus of the sound is capable of establishing the invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatā) of the word with its object;
for the validity of the cognition of an imperceptible object based on a lack of connection is impossible.
Furthermore, that [reliability] is impossible for the word;

and the status of the teacher as a trustworthy person (āpta) is difficult to ascertain, such that the word might cause one to understand the true nature of an object by virtue of being the instruction of a trustworthy person.
"Is undertaken" (ārabhyate) means the undertaking (ārambha), namely, the treatise (prakaraṇa).
A "portion" (pradeśa) of that is a "single part" (ekadeśa); by implication, this refers to the beginning of that [text]. To the objection that this is not true, he says: "It is true."

If this is true, for what purpose then are they stated? [The word] "in the case of those that have been stated" (*ukteṣu*)—the particle *tu* indicates the distinction of the stated position from the unstated position. By this he means the following: in the absence of a proving or a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a connection restricted to a specific locus can only be logical by virtue of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, it indicates either a possibility based on reasoning or an excellence;
otherwise, how could doubt arise even regarding things that possess valid means of cognition, such that the use of the particle *api* would be appropriate?

[Objection: Is it not the case that the opening statement has activity as its fruit? And if there is no such activity, what is the use of even generating a doubt? [The author] says: "And from doubt" (*saṃśayāc ca*).
Here, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*ādarthe*).
Now, first of all, those who have approached the teacher with faith act after having ascertained the matter from his words; they do not act out of doubt.

Nor does even those who, being the opposite of that, entertain doubt, act out of doubt. Anticipating the objection that "if they were to act, their status as discerning persons would be lost," he says: "Even a doubt regarding the matter... [is a cause for action].
By the word "also" (api), he indicates that this is not merely the case regarding the ascertainment of the object.

For if those who act without ascertainment toward what is capable of being ascertained were to do so, they would forfeit their status as prudent persons. However, where one acts out of desire due to doubt regarding the object, [there is no such loss].
The meaning is that they do not deserve censure.
Furthermore, if one who doubts due to the lack of entry into the second mode [of cognition] through reasoning were never to act,
then no one would ever act upon anyone's word, and thus much worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be lost.
Is it not the case that cessation is based on the certainty of harm, and that certainty of harm arises from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
yet such a means does not exist here?
But there is no mode other than cessation that is distinct from activity; therefore, activity is established without effort. Why then [is there] this beginningless [desire for it]?
Even doubt regarding the lack of purpose is a factor for desisting; for this very reason, the author of the treatise himself ought to state the relationship and other elements at the outset.
For the speech of commentators might otherwise be suspected of being for the sake of mere play or some other motive.

Regarding the authors of treatises (*śāstrakṛt*), we perceive no purpose nor even any engagement in stating a subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth that is contrary [to what is actually intended] at the commencement of their work;
therefore, doubt is appropriate in their case.
However, when [these elements] are not stated, listeners might imagine the subject matter of this treatise to be purposeless, like an examination of a crow’s teeth.
Either the practice is impossible to perform, like the instruction to adorn oneself with the crest-jewel of the serpent Takṣaka as a means to cure fever;
or the purpose is undesirable, like the instruction on the sequence of one's mother's marriage;

Or rather, it is possible that the entire context is indeed without a means [to its end].
To this he says: "The useless," and so forth.
The word "also" (api) indicates that not only is there no determination of the purpose, but [the opposite is the case as well].
If it must necessarily be stated that the subject matter and so forth exist, then the commentators themselves will state them;

Now, it may be argued: they do explain them because such explanation is a factor for engaging [with the work].

But if the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth were not stated, activity itself would be impossible; how then could there be commentators who exist [only] because of that, such that this [text] might be suspected of refuting their discourse?
To this it is said:
the objection raised is not that the elucidation of the subject matter and so forth should never be performed by anyone at all.

However, with the intention that the initial statement need not be composed for that purpose, those who have directly approached the Teacher can achieve both comprehension and engagement through his very words; thus, their capacity as commentators is possible. In the first [meditative state], an aspect of disadvantage is experienced in abundance,
whereas through reasoning, there is an entry into a second aspect;
in the other [state], however—
Since the aspect of the object is experienced by perception (*dṛk*),
whereas according to reasoning (*yukti*) there is an entry into the absence of objective aspects, how can there be no contradiction given that both are experienced as mutually contradictory?
Let it be so.
If it is asked, "Even so, how is the suspicion of uselessness (*anarthāśaṅkā*) dispelled by the statement of this [work]?

it is replied: By the statement of the purpose (*prayojana*) of the subject matter (*abhidheya*), which consists in the accomplishment of the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), the first suspicion of uselessness is dispelled;
and by the detailed determination of both the subject matter and its purpose, the second and third suspicions are dispelled.
The third [alternative] is also refuted by the demonstration of the connection through the understanding of capacity (*sāmarthya*).
As for the fourth, however, it is refuted by the force of the commencement of this treatise on the part of the Teacher, who possesses supreme discernment (*viveka*).
For, even though other means were possible, this most eminent person of great foresight would not have undertaken such a treatise [if they had not seen its necessity].

Now, it might be argued: suppose there were some other "light" method (*upāya*) composed by someone else, existing in another location and arising at the same time [as this work]. How, then, could there be a refutation of that other light method composed by him?
In this case as well, his very state of being a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*) is the great basis [for the composition].

Precisely because he acts with prior deliberation, one must consider in many ways that this treatise was not composed for this purpose by him either here in Āryāvarta or elsewhere in the world at the present time; rather, having investigated and observed [the situation], and having determined that this is a concise means (*laghu-upāya*), it was appropriate for him to compose this, and not otherwise.
In every case within this treatise, when the opening statement exists, this very method [of refuting other easy means] is the course to be followed.

For is it not accepted that even elsewhere there is no statement refuting other easy means without first revealing the subject matter, its purpose, and so forth? If this is so, then let the refutation of other possible misconceptions regarding the lack of purpose be done in this very same way; what then is the need for the opening statement? This is not so.
For the entry of a mouse is not the same as the entry of a needle.

Since people act because of the expectation of a result, [the author] says this in order to establish that expectation of a result.
Of what nature is it? It is a "limb" (*aṅga*), meaning the cause (*nimitta*) of activity.

non-contradictory cognition is right cognition (*samyagjñāna*).

Furthermore, the very capacity to induce activity toward the indicated object is what constitutes the capacity to cause attainment;
it is nothing else. For instance: not...

[18] *svayam eva*. ______________________________________________ Having thus explained the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) of the passage beginning with "correct knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*) through this continuous exposition, he now explains the meaning of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*) starting with the words "non-contradictory" (*avisamvādaka*).
Herein is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):

What is intended by this "correctness" (*samyaktva*) of knowledge— that through connection with which it is called "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*)? If correctness is simply the grasping of the true nature of things (*vastutattva*), [then...]

Furthermore, if it is argued that inference is the attainment of an object already grasped, then in either case, inference would be an incorrect cognition (*asamyagjñāna*) because it does not grasp a real entity (*avastu*).

Alternatively, if it were considered a correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) because it attains what was not previously grasped, then even the cognition of water would be a correct cognition since it attains the mirages that were displayed; thus, there would be no such thing as an incorrect cognition at all.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin), considering that these positions are refuted by their very non-acceptance, demonstrates [at 8a] that "correctness" (samyaktva) is intended to mean "non-contradictory" (avisaṃvādakatva). That which is non-contradictory is called "consistent" (saṃvādaka); for the prefix *vi-* functions here as a negation of consistency.

Since the negation of that [non-correspondence] is of a positive nature, it remains as correspondence itself; thus, the word *avisamvādaka* (non-contradictory) has the meaning of "corresponding. This is the sense: valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is that which is non-contradictory and which brings about the attainment of the object that is the target of purposeful action.
It might be argued: indeed, the linguistic usage of elders is the ground for determining the meaning of words.
And in that context, the term "conformity" (saṃvāda) does not apply to that which causes one to attain the object as it was presented;
rather, it applies to truthfulness and so forth.
Furthermore, cognition does not possess such a nature [of being a means of attainment].
To the question, "Whence then does the word 'corresponding' (saṃvādaka) apply there?", he says: "And in the world" (*loke ca*).
The particle *ca* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*) or the sense of "also" (*api*).
"In the world" refers to people who engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahartṛ-jana*).

This is the intention: just as in the world the term "reliable" (*saṃvādaka*) is applied to a person because it is possible for him to bring about the attainment of the object indicated by the cause for the application of words such as "truth," so too it is applied to cognition because that possibility exists there as well.
Now, it might be argued: the term "reliable" applied to a person is not caused by the bringing about of the indicated object, but rather by the bringing about of the promised object.
How then could there be the occurrence of a sign (nimitta) here?

That very same demonstration, however, occurs in some cases by means of verbal expression, in some cases by means of ascertainment, [19] ... in some cases preceded by the appearance of an object, and in some cases through a different mode of operation; this is the distinction.
It is the word "concordant" (*saṃvādaka*).
However, the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the same in all cases. [19] Here, a reading appears to have been added later, but because it is subtle, it is not recited.
Regarding "causing to reach" (*prāpayan*), since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*) by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*, the meaning is "because of causing to reach. [20]
In this way, it should be understood in subsequent cases as well;
[this is according to] Pāṇini 3.2.126.

Knowledge does not bring about the object by producing it;

rather, it brings about the object by inciting the person toward that object. Furthermore, this capacity to incite is nothing other than the capacity to point out the object that is the focus of the activity. Indeed, one cannot forcibly incite a person [to act].

Thus, by stating that "it is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it makes one attain the object pointed out," the author asserts that a single cognition possesses both the quality of pointing it out and the quality of making it attained.
Since attainment is impossible without activity, it follows by implication that [the means of knowledge] also possesses the quality of being an instigator of action.
Furthermore, these two functions cannot belong to a single entity;
for one [part] reveals the object, while by the other [part] one knows it.
Fearing the objection that "it causes one thing to proceed, which is to say, it initiates an activity immediately thereafter;

and it causes another thing to be reached, since by means of that attainment the person becomes connected [to the result]," he says: "And when [the object] has been shown"—the word "and" (ca) being used in the sense of "because."

The intention of one who asserts that "the state of being a prompter" (*pravarttakatva*) is itself "the state of being a bringer" (*prāpakatva*) is as follows: although something may be a "demonstrator" (*pradarśaka*) by directly perceiving an object and generating a corresponding ascertainment (*niścaya*), or another [cognition] may become a cause for external activity by demonstrating [the object], the former is designated a "prompter," while the latter is designated a "bringer" because it becomes the instrumental cause for the attainment of the external object through the mediation of prompting.

Nevertheless, that very state of being a cause for external activity—which consists in the mediating operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) such as "inciting to act"—is the only one that is useful, because it is through the incitement of the person and the production of the object by cognition that "inciting" and "causing to reach" are possible; no other [operation] serves this purpose.
Thus, in reality, since every cognition accompanied by ascertainment brings about comprehension, there are no two further operations of "inciting" and "causing to reach."
For this very reason, it is established that only the first cognition in that case is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Consequently, there is no difference between [the cognition] and the qualities of "actually indicating" the object and so forth;
however, a difference based on conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) certainly exists.

For this very reason, these terms—*pradarśaka* (indicator), *pravarttaka* (instigator), and *prāpaka* (attainer)—are not synonyms, just as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) are not.

It might be thought: what, then, is the purpose [of this distinction], such that there is no activity of attainment (*prāpaṇa-vyāpāra*) for knowledge other than instigation (*pravarttana*), and no effort to be accomplished through instigation other than comprehension (*adhigama*)?

If [the objection is raised that] the purpose [of the subsequent cognition] is to negate the validity of the subsequent knowledge, then since that would be negated simply by the fact that it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitā*), what is the point of such an effort? To this it is replied:

if, because of its being a demonstrator, the state of being a prompter (*pravarttayitṛtva*) and the state of being a bringer-about (*prāpayitṛtva*) were in reality different [from the state of being a demonstrator], [then there would be a problem].
In that case, since it cannot be established that [the cognition] apprehends what has already been apprehended, by whom could its validity be denied?
For instance—that cognition does not apprehend what has already been apprehended;
rather, it prompts action toward what has been apprehended.
Furthermore, that which has been grasped leads to attainment;
and since those who act accordingly have distinct modes of engagement (*upayoga*), how can their validity be set aside?
For when there is no operation of leading to attainment other than the instigation (*pravartanā*) of the cognition, and no instigation other than its manifestation (*pradarśana*).

Furthermore, by the very first moment of perception or inference, the continuum of a real entity (*vastu-santāna*) capable of causal efficiency can be determined as the object of purposeful action; therefore, since the subsequent moments occurring within that same continuum share an identical state of acquisition and preservation (*abhinnayogakṣema*), their status as valid cognitions is set aside.
By this, that which was stated by someone regarding Dharmottara is also refuted: "If [the cognition] possesses the quality of indicating [the object]..."

If that is so, then the statement that "that which causes one to attain the object already indicated is a corroborative [cognition]" would have this meaning: "that which indicates what has already been indicated.
But this is not tenable, because there is no difference in the object [between the two cognitions].
For instance, if it is said that there is no difference between objects from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then there is nothing objectionable.
However, even then, one should not speak in such a manner;
for what has been said is far too little.
Nor should it be said that "being produced" (kṛtakatva) establishes "impermanence" (anityatva),

for why not also say this is because there is no difference in meaning? If, on the other hand, the absence of difference in meaning is asserted with respect to the application of words, then that is unestablished, since a difference in exclusion (vyāvṛtti) has been demonstrated.

Therefore, the meaning is this: that which, having directly indicated an object and produced a corresponding ascertainment, becomes the cause for external attainment—either by way of prompting activity or through direct connection—is "concordant" (*saṃvādaka*). However, in reality, there is no operation of the prompter or the attainer other than the operation of indication, characterized by the comprehension of the object of cognition; thus, neither the state of being a prompter nor the state of being an attainer constitutes a distinct causal operation.
"these two are distinct.

For this very reason, the apprehension of the object itself is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). And once the object has been apprehended, the person is set in motion and brought to its attainment.

And such is the purpose. This being the case, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is completed through the apprehension of the object. For this very reason, a means of valid cognition has as its object that which has not yet been apprehended. For by whichever cognition an object is first apprehended, by that same [cognition] the person is impelled and the object is attained. In that very instance, what further task remains to be done by another cognition?
Therefore, that which has already apprehended its object is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

It might be thought: "If the apprehension itself were the fruit for subsequent [cognitions] as well, then, due to the absence of any further utility, they would indeed be invalid; however, since the fruit of the impelling [cognition] is activity (*pravṛtti*) and the fruit of the procuring [cognition] is attainment (*prāpti*), their functions are distinct because their fruits are produced differently. To this he says: "For this very reason."
