Since the attainment of an object by cognition does not occur through the production of that object,
and since there is no engagement [of the person] by means of forceful impulsion,
for this very reason, the result is the apprehension— that is, the determination— of the object.
It is not [defined by] the activity (pravṛtti) and so forth.
But surely that is established as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since it is when that [fruit] exists that its operation is completed?

And even when there is comprehension, [the inquiry] is not concluded in the absence of activity and attainment; thus he says: "And when [the object] is comprehended. The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "because" (yasmāt).

Because, by that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) which has revealed the object, the person—though not yet set in motion toward it—is [considered to have attained it] due to the presentation of what is suitable for activity.
And because there is no other operation belonging to that [cognition], it is said to be "set in motion.
When it possesses an object, its very nature is to set [the person] in motion;
that is to say, by means of cognition, the object is rendered fit for purposeful activity.
"Let it be that the person is thus impelled, yet the object is not attained;
and thus there exists another operation depending on something else," he says: "is attained. The word "ca" (and) is as before.
Even though this object has not yet been attained, it is shown to be capable of being attained; thus, it is said to have been "caused to be attained.
For this very reason, the capacity for attainment is the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of cognition.
And that [capacity] is based on the fact that [the cognition] derives its own existence from the object to be attained.
For that by which one proceeds must also be considered as being for the sake of attainment.
However, the ascertainment of capacity belongs to every inference in which purposeful action appears, and it is intrinsic;
likewise, for certain perceptual cognitions that induce activity, it is intrinsic when, through repeated practice, all suspicion of error has been completely dispelled.

When a cognition apprehends an object that is not impaired by sleep or other such factors, which is located nearby, and whose manifestation is not dependent on anything else— provided its manifestation is not otherwise—

it determines the object to be real precisely through the awareness of that form (*tadrūpasaṃvedana*). However, for some [cognitions], this determination occurs through the removal of doubt regarding a potential error existing at a later time, based either on a subsequent cognition consisting of the appearance of purposeful action (*arthakriyānirbhāsa*), or from itself as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from some other source, namely, the perception of an object that is invariably concomitant with it.
"It is determined" (*niścīyate*). There is also a reading in some places as "the object has been brought [to the person]" (*prāpitaś cārthaḥ*).

That, however, is more appropriate, because they are presented as a single syntactical unit: [the cognition] is "set in motion" (*pravartita*) by making one fit for action, and it "brings the object" (*prāpita artham*) by pointing out the object to be attained. Thus, they are shown to be one and the same.
Thus, even further on, this very reading is considered correct;
and that being so, and such being the case, it is "completed," having reached its conclusion.
Therefore, the sense is that it is logical for realization to be the fruit;
for no fruit other than realization is tenable,
and once it has arisen, the activity is completed.

Therefore, for this reason, that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is one whose object—its referent—is not yet attained, meaning it has not been delimited by another cognition. [Objection: But surely a subsequent cognition whose object has already been attained will be a *pramāṇa* with respect to that object, since it contributes something additional to it. For the distinction between *pramāṇas* does not arise solely from a difference in objects, but also from a difference in utility; to this he says: "by which very... (*yenaiva*).

For this reason: since it was stated that [the object] is "set in motion" or "attained" by the preceding [cognition] through its suitability, what further or additional task remains to be performed once it has already been apprehended by that prior cognition?
[DhPr p. 20]

In this regard, that object which is known as something seen is made the objective domain of activity by perception. For perception is the indicator of that object in respect to which its operation of direct manifestation is followed by conceptual thought.

Therefore, that which is known as something already seen is what is shown by perception. Inference, however, having ascertained through the observation of a mark (*liṅga*), indicates an object of activity; it does not [reveal] anything new. The sense is that by the very first [cognition], that which was to be accomplished has already been accomplished.

For this reason, a cognition whose object has already been apprehended—whether it belongs to the same class as the apprehending cognition or a different class—is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By this, it has been demonstrated that what is called the "convergence of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasaṃplava*) simply does not exist. Now,
has it not been shown by this continuous argument that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is that which indicates the object of activity?
According to the principle that will be stated later, perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) are two forms of valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*).

In that regard, if the presentation of their respective spheres of operation were identical, there would be no distinction between them such that "this is perception, a valid means of knowledge" and "this is inference, a valid means of knowledge."
Therefore, one must state that these two have entirely different objects of cognition.
And since this is so, one must explain what [is known] by which [means]; thus he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
Among those two—perception and inference—that which is known through being seen is ascertained.

If one were to act simply on the grounds that something is "known," then even an object of inference, being ascertained, would result in being made the object of activity by perception; therefore, the phrase "as having been seen" is employed.

Now, why is it not said that "that which is seen"? It is not so stated because, since momentariness and other such properties are also objects of perception by virtue of being "seen," this would entail the impossibility of the application of inference.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that perception does not grasp [an object] through ascertainment (*niścaya*), but rather through appearance (*pratibhāsa*)?
Why then is it said that it is 'known' and 'ascertained'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because... [The object] is followed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), pursued, and determined in the form "I see."
Therefore, it is said that [the object] is "known by seeing.
By the term "by conceptualization," it should be understood as being by a subsequent conceptualization that conforms [to the perception].
This is because an operation accompanied by a non-conforming conceptualization lacks validity with respect to that [object], just as in the case of [the cognition of] momentariness.
The intention of one who speaks thus is as follows: this is stated to be the definition of conventional valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*).

Therefore, even though something is manifest according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛttyā*), if it is not made an object by a corresponding conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it does not differ from that which is not manifesting, because it is unfit for conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*).

In this way, that grasper as well—being incapable of being employed in conventional discourse because its activity is not apprehended by a corresponding conceptualization—is unable even to bend a blade of grass; thus it does not transcend the state of being a non-grasper. Therefore, what was said—that "the very nature of being a demonstrator is identity because of its capacity for instigation," and what was also said—that "the result is simply the comprehension"—should be understood as referring to those [cognitions] whose activities are followed by a corresponding ascertainment, and which are themselves followed by a corresponding ascertainment.

Thus, wherever it is stated by such expressions as "perception indicates the object" or "perception grasps the object," in all such cases, it should be understood that its function is necessarily accompanied by a corresponding ascertainment (*niścaya*).

If it is argued that, this being the case, it would follow that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) also possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*), Dharmottara himself will raise this objection and refute it; therefore, it is not discussed here.

If perception thus indicates the object of engagement, then inference does so as well. In that case, perception shows a restricted object as it appears; and inference shows a restricted object as connected with the logical mark (liṅga). For this very reason, regarding a restricted object—
They are the indicators; therefore, they are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not any other cognition. (Dharmottara’s *Pramāṇaviniścayaṭīkā*, p. 21, l.
That which indicates an object capable of being attained is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it leads to attainment. And because it leads to attainment, it is a *pramāṇa*.
How, then, is the distinction [between the two types of *pramāṇa*] established?
He says: "But inference...
The word "but" (tu) indicates the difference between inference and perception.
Perception does not, while itself determining [an object], point out the object of activity; rather, it causes one to determine it.

But as for inference, since it determines [its object] by itself, how is it able to determine that which does not appear [directly]? To this he says: "from the observation of the mark" (*liṅgadarśanāt*).
That is, from the observation of a mark such as smoke, which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with the probandum (*sādhya*).

And "perception" (darśana) here is intended to mean either the grasping of the specific form [of the sign] preceded by the knowledge that "in all cases this is inseparably connected with the probandum," or the grasping of the specific form in some instance preceded by the recollection that "in all cases it is inseparably connected with the probandum.
Now, one might ask: why is the presentation of the object of engagement not shown for other types of cognition as well, just as it is for perceptual and inferential cognitions?
Now, if it is argued that [the scripture] is not presented because it lacks authority, how again is there a lack of authority for the other [scripture]?
If you say: "Because it indicates an object of engagement that is not fixed," [we reply:]...

In that case, one might object that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) would likewise lack validity due to being of such a nature; anticipating this, [the author] states "And thus" (*tathā ca*), demonstrating the distinction between those two and other types of cognition.
And in that regard, because direct perception brings about certainty by generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows its own operation...

Regarding the manner of indicating the object of activity [at a time other than when there is a sign]: at another time, through the observation of a logical mark (*liṅga*), one proceeds by means of one's own certainty regarding the manner of indicating the object of activity.

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—appearing as it manifests and shining forth in its own nature—demonstrates that which is restricted to being an entity (*bhāva*) alone, capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).
By this, the intention is that it does not demonstrate what is non-existent, nor what is indeterminate.
And inference demonstrates a restricted object;
the word "and" (ca) conjoins inference with perception by way of their being equal in demonstrating what is restricted.
The phrase "connected with the mark" (liṅgasambaddha) is a qualification [of the object] by way of its being the logical reason (hetu).

This is the meaning: because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is connected—either through identity (*tādātmya*) or through origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—to an object that is excluded from what is of a different class and which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), therefore inference, which arises from that [mark], necessarily indicates and determines it.
By this, it is demonstrated that even inference does not indicate an unreal object, nor is it indeterminate with respect to whether the object is of the nature of existence or non-existence.

However, this is the distinction: while inference arises by relying on a form perceived at the time of grasping the relation—which is common [to many instances]—and although it determines the particular (svalakṣaṇa), it does not determine that which is unique to another continuum; thus, even though it depends on the object of purposeful activity, its object is indeed the universal (sāmānya).
Perception, however, even while depending on an object of engagement, has exclusively an uncommon object as its domain;
for it determines the object precisely through a form that is uncommon to other mental continua.
It is not explicitly stated because of its subtlety.
Now, there is this intention of someone: "Let it be that perception reveals a restricted object because it directly perceives the object;
but how does inference, which does not directly perceive an imperceptible object, reveal it as restricted?"
"Therefore, it is not the case that both [scriptures] demonstrate a fixed meaning, but rather only one.
Addressing that proponent who denies the validity of the whole, he concludes by saying "ataḥ" (therefore).
Because perception demonstrates with certainty that which is manifested as a real entity;

and although the imperceptible is not directly manifest in the interval, inference— born from effect or essence— demonstrates a state of existence strictly determined by its connection to that [entity],
while inference born from non-perception demonstrates a corresponding non-existence strictly determined.
Therefore, for this reason, both of these are of such a nature;
thus, by this [statement], the negation of the negation of the totality is concluded.
However, if it were explained otherwise, then—let it be so—[the following would apply].
The meaning would be that since they demonstrate a fixed object, these two are "those that demonstrate a fixed object";
furthermore, the clarification of what is already perfectly clear would result in being purposeless.
[DhPr p. 22]

By these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and by another [means], some object is shown to be utterly erroneous, such as water in a mirage; and because it is non-existent, it cannot be attained. Some [object] is indeterminate with respect to existence and non-existence, such as an object of doubt. Furthermore, there is no object in the world that is endowed with both existence and non-existence; therefore, such an object cannot be attained.

And since all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—whether affirmative or negative—proceed without perceiving a determining factor, they remain indeterminate with respect to existence and non-existence;
[the author asks] how, then, these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be shown to have a determinate object, and thus he says: "by that" (*tena*).
By that [term], "demonstrating a determinate object" is meant.
For it is alleged that these two lack validity because they do not demonstrate a determinate object;
the sense is: even if that [lack of demonstration] were present, how could validity arise?

By demonstrating the manner in which these two [perception and inference] reveal their respective objects of operation, and by showing that other forms of knowledge do not so reveal them, he clarifies— through the words "that which was present in the intellect is now not otherwise," and so forth—
that no other cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is to be connected with the statement by modifying the word order to "no other cognition is a valid means of knowledge."

If this is so, then since there is no difference in their being cognitions, these two [inference and verbal testimony] should also not be considered valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To this he says: "to attain" (*prāptum*).
Because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), this is a causal phrase.
Therefore, the meaning is this: because it reveals an object that is capable of being attained, perception and the other [means of knowledge] are "attainers" (*prāpaka*).
"Let it be that which brings [the object] about;
but why is it a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? To this he says: "And because it is a bringer-about"—the word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis.

[Objection: But surely, even other things besides these two indicate an object that is capable of being attained; therefore, why would that which indicates it not also be an "attainer" (*prāpaka*), and why, by virtue of being an attainer, would it not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? [Response: To this he says: "By the two means of valid cognition.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
By the inclusion of the term "absolutely" (*atyanta*), he shows the distinction from the object of doubtful cognition.
To the question, "Why would such [an object] not be attained? he says: "And that" (*sa ca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Even though it presents [an object] with certainty, its lack of validity has been demonstrated because it presents what is not beneficial.

If someone were to argue that while this [object] is of such a kind, the object of another's cognition will be otherwise, and that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) presenting that [other object] will therefore be valid—for this reason he says: "someone."

The meaning of doubt is that which has doubt as its objective support (*ālambana*). For the cognition "Is it a post or a person?"—having delineated the post, while taking "or a person" as its objective support—delineates the absence of that [post]. Therefore, it [doubt] is non-deviant with respect to the person, who is the non-existence of the post. Thus, the person...

And while determining the post to be non-deviating from existence, he does not show it as necessarily non-existent; nor does he show it as necessarily a post or a man in the case of its non-existence. Thus, he shows it as indeterminate with respect to both existence and non-existence.
Precisely because he is unable to show it as determined to one side, he wavers.
"Therefore, doubt is justified.
Now, [the opponent might argue: "If the opposite meaning is not attained because of non-existence, why is this [other meaning] not attained? To this he says: "And not..."
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because.
Now, one might object: "Granted that doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*) are non-valid cognitions (*aprāmāṇya*), what is lost for us?
There will be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And by all," and so forth.
Because it is included within everything.

Thus, the object must be shown; yet that [object in question] is impossible to attain. Therefore, a cognition that shows an object which is unattainable, utterly contrary [to reality], and determined as either existent or non-existent is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, those who seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) seek a cognition that serves as the cause for attaining an entity capable of purposeful action. And precisely that which they seek is what is investigated in this treatise. Consequently, right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is that which demonstrates an entity capable of purposeful action.
He says "by that which is not a logical mark" (*aliṅgena*) because [inference] would likewise be such [i.e., non-inferential].
It is called "non-marked" (*aliṅga*) because no logical mark exists for it as its producer.

If that were to be produced by everything that is not a logical mark, then it would follow that even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises subsequent to perception would be so; thus he says "the regulator" (*niyāmaka*).
For the apprehension of a determined object by cognition is dependent upon the object; thus, the object is the regulator.
Without seeing that [object], one might ask:
does [the cognition] indeed proceed even after having seen the object that serves as the regulator, which occurs subsequent to the perception?
Since other conceptual constructions lack that nature, one might suspect they possess suchness;
it is said in response:
in the term "pravarttayet," the sense of the causative suffix (ṇic) is to be understood as being included within it.

Therefore, this point is as follows: [the objection that] "it proceeds without seeing a determiner" is thus refuted by the fact that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in the wake of perception proceeds by means of the perceptual cognition only after having seen a determiner. However, as for other conceptual constructions lacking a logical mark (*aliṅgavikalpa*), since they arise and proceed by means of something other than that [perception], the determiner is not directly seen by them; consequently, the undesirable consequence (*anuṣaṅga*) follows that those [constructions] would likewise [lack a determiner].

Others, however, connect the term "non-indicative" (*aliṅga*) for the purpose of excluding inference; having raised the doubt, "But how can such a thing be done by that very [cognition], even though it consists of a determinate judgment (*avasāya*) and is non-indicative?", they explain that the phrase "without seeing a regulator" functions as a qualifier of the causal state, meaning: "because it has proceeded without seeing a regulator."
Having thus explained [the literal meaning], they also demonstrate the intended sense (*tātparyārtha*):

although conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising from words and so forth do not waver by touching upon both sides [of a dichotomy], nevertheless, when they proceed without relying on a regulating factor (*niyāmaka*), they are not logical (*yauktika*).
They transcend the state of being doubt;
this is precisely the intended meaning even in the previous explanation.

Although both contradictory aspects are not manifest for that [cognition] as a whole, because it enters into a second aspect through reasoning, it possesses the quality of indicating an object determined as either existent or non-existent by way of having the nature of doubt.
Thus [they say].
Some, however, construe it as follows: "one who has acted without having seen a thing that is invariably concomitant with the object, which must be determined by conceptualization.
And they state that the phrase "without a logical mark" (*aliṅgena*) is a qualification of this very same point by way of providing its reason.

However, both [schools] refute the over-extension [of the definition] by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pṛṣṭhabhāvin*), under the heading of an inquiry into the validity of a conceptual construction that apprehends an object not previously apprehended.
Therefore, the meaning is this: because all of that [conceptual content] has not been previously apprehended...
"By virtue of being intended as that which leads to the goal, it must necessarily be performed.

[The author] says "And that" (*sa ca*) to show that even though it indicates an indefinite object, it may nonetheless lead to its attainment; the word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Immediately after the word "impossible" (aśakya), that [particle] should be understood as having the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa).
The meaning is that such an indefinite object cannot be attained because it is impossible [to attain]. Now, one might object: let all such things not be attainers (prāpaka).
Anticipating the objection as to why it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he concludes what was previously stated with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since it is a means of valid cognition precisely because it brings about attainment, therefore, when an object cannot be attained— due to its being utterly contrary [to reality], its impermanence, or its indeterminacy— [it is not a means of valid cognition].
These two are causes because they serve as qualifiers for the other two by way of their causal nature;
the word "ca" (and) signifies a conjunction of meanings that have not [otherwise] been reached.
Someone might be utterly deluded.

The conclusion follows the respective order starting from "some are indeterminate" and so forth: for the statements "knowledge is other" and "knowledge is not other," that which has been demonstrated by him [is the following].
That alone is what must be attained. For it has been stated that that which brings about attainment consists in the realization of the object.

This might be argued: "Only that which indicates an object capable of being attained is right cognition (*samyagjñāna*), and nothing else"—this [definition] is groundless; and if so, why is something else not also examined? To this he says: "by those seeking purposeful action" (*arthakriyārthibhiḥ*).
Because of which:
the accomplishment of the action, such as burning and so forth, is the purpose (*artha*).

They are "tathā" because they seek that [object]. By means of these [cognitions], that which is the cause for the attainment of a real entity capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is sought—that is, it is investigated. Furthermore, this investigation by them is to be understood as arising precisely from the desire for causal efficiency.
And by the phrase "by those who possess discernment," it should be understood from the context [of the discussion].

Otherwise, since even those discerning persons who seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) might observe false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), the investigation of that [false cognition] would also follow as a consequence.
Even if that [true cognition] is indeed sought by them, he says "and which... to address why other cognitions are not also investigated.
The word "ca" is used for emphasis.
It is being deliberated upon, that is, examined.
This right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) which prompts action is explained by way of analysis as that which you follow.
This is his intention: the Teacher does not investigate knowledge out of mere habit;
rather, it is out of consideration for those who require it for effective action (*arthakriyā*).
Since they seek only such knowledge and nothing else, that alone is investigated.

The phrase "that very [thing]" is stated with the intention of referring to the primary sense; however, it is not the case that false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is not investigated at all in this treatise.
For, by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), an investigation of it is possible within the section beginning with "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*).

Now, one might ask: "Why is right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) established as being precisely that which demonstrates an object capable of being attained? To the question, "Why is this irrelevant matter being mentioned? he says:
"— Regarding the word *tataḥ*:
since nothing other than that [which is sought] is to be sought by discerning persons who desire purposeful action (*arthakriyā*),
that alone is what must be investigated."
Because investigation is impossible due to being preoccupied with worldly attachments,
it follows by implication that right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is nothing other than that which reveals a real entity capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsamartha*).
Let it be that right cognition is exactly of this nature.

Furthermore, even if it presents one thing while causing another to be attained, why would that not be right cognition (*samyagjñāna*), and why would it not be conventionally designated as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
In that case, even the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like would not lose its status as valid knowledge.
He says: "And that which...
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis;
by this, [the phrase] "pītaśaṃ(-śaṅ)"...

As for the view held by some that even a false cognition (*khādijñāna*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) insofar as it accords with reality in some respect, he shows that this too is to be excluded from the category of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). [Objection: But is this not equivalent to what has not been stated? For we observe that even a white conch shell, which was not presented by the cognition of a yellow conch, and even a mass of mirage-rays, which was not presented by the cognition of water, are nonetheless reached.
This is not so;
for that attainment is not preceded by knowledge of it,
because its object is a thing that has not been known.
And by that [initial cognition], the object—whether it be a white conch or a mirage—is not known;

rather, the attainment of such an object occurs only through a subsequent cognition. This has been thoroughly examined in the investigation of validity (*prāmāṇya*) by this very [author] and is therefore not stated here.

In that regard, the object other than what has been shown possesses a different form, a different location, and a different time; for an object is distinct due to its association with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*). And this association with contradictory properties consists precisely in the difference of location, time, and form.

Therefore, a cognition that apprehends an object as having one form is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an object possessing another form, just as a cognition apprehending a yellow conch is not valid with respect to a white conch. Furthermore, a cognition that apprehends something located in another place is not a valid means of knowledge with respect to what is located in that other place, just as the cognition apprehending a gem in the light of a gem situated at the opening of a keyhole is not valid with respect to the gem located inside the room. And a cognition that apprehends something connected with another time is not a valid means of knowledge with respect to an object existing at that other time.

Just as a dream-cognition apprehending an object at midnight or at midday is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object at that time—on what grounds could it be said that "that very object must be attained by it"? To this he says: "Because of the comprehension of the object" (*arthādhigama*). For (*hi*) means "because."

By stating "it has been said," the non-difference of [the means of knowledge] from its result—such as demonstration and so forth—is established in reality; for it has been revealed by this very [statement] that the fruit of the means of knowledge is simply the apprehension of the object, though it was not explicitly stated [as such].
For if one thing were apprehended and another were attained, [there would be a discrepancy].
The point is that in that case there would be a distinction between the manifestation and the attainment,
whereas non-distinction has been established. But how is it stated by the phrase "the very realization is the fruit" that its nature is such?
For validity consists in being a means of attainment (*prāpakatva*),
and the result is not distinct from that;
or rather, it is stated thus because it is a "means of attainment" by virtue of revealing an object that is capable of being attained.
For it means that it determines by presenting such an object;
and since determination does not differ from being a means of attainment (*prāpakatva*),
let it be that right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is precisely the state of attaining the object presented.

As for the objection that if one perceives that very object, such as a conch-shell, as having a yellow form, how can that be incorrect knowledge? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). Here, *tatra* introduces the statement; the predicate to be established is "otherness" (*anyatvam*), meaning that the real object is something else, possessing a different form and so forth, from the form that is being displayed.

He says "viruddha" (contradictory), meaning that although [the object] is differentiated by its aspects and so forth, it is not other than that [reality], because of the determination that "this is that very same thing.
The word "hi" means "because."
If difference [between things] were due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, then it would not be due to the difference of place and so forth; thus he says:
"Place," etc.
As for why this is so:

"Let it be thus; nevertheless, why is a cognition that apprehends an object as distinct in its aspects and so forth not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding an entity endowed with other aspects and so forth? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). For whatever is indeed shown by correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), that alone is what must be attained.

And since that [object] is different from that [cognition] because it is distinguished by its form and so forth, he asks: "What, like what, would not be a means of valid cognition? To which he replies: "Just as... He asks: "What is the status of that which perceives a different location? To which he replies: "In another location..."
To the question "Why is this not a valid means of knowledge?", he says: "Just as...
By the word *apavaraka*, a specific location such as the interior of a cave or the like is expressed, because the word *apavaraka* also possesses this meaning.

Even if the reading were *apavarakadeśastha* ("situated in a corner of the room"), there would be no fault. To address the question of what the status is for that which perceives objects at different times, he says: *kālāntara*.

This means that which perceives an object associated with—i.e., connected to—a conventional time other than the time of its presentation; in other words, that which perceives an object belonging to a different time.
The particle *ca* (and), as before, conjoins this with the preceding [example] by way of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
Illustrating that, he says: "For example" (*yathā*).

This is its meaning: for one who is sleeping during the latter part of the night and experiences a manifestation of midday, the hair on whose body stands on end at the sight of goods belonging to a son involved in trade.
Thus, even if a son is perceived instantaneously through a chance occurrence (*kākatālīyanyāya*), that cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For that [cognition] is indeed related to the time of midnight in ultimate reality, yet it is perceived as being connected with the time of midday; and precisely because it appears as the time of midday, it is [taken to be] the time of midday.

But is it not the case that while [an object] can be made to reach [the cognition] as restricted by place and restricted by form, it cannot be made to reach [the cognition] at the very time it is delimited? No, it is not said so; for at the very same time it is delimited, [it is reached].

"It must be reached at that very same time. For the time of seeing is one thing, and the time of reaching is another. However, whatever time is delimited, that alone is what must be reached by it. And because of the determination of non-difference, the unity belonging to the continuum is to be understood.
There is no fixed rule regarding that time at which midnight is the hour of arrival.

Alternatively, one who has slept at midnight might see his son arrive when the sun has risen in the middle of the day; and when the night has turned to dawn and midday has arrived, he sees that very same son in that very same place.
Even one who is awake sees what has already occurred;
his cognition, though it possesses the quality of mere correspondence, is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because [for him] midnight is [perceived as] midday.
At that time, although his son had not yet arrived, he perceived him as having arrived;
for [the son] was restricted by the specific place and time of midnight.
And that time does indeed exist;
however, one should understand that from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), it is midnight—the time of appearance—for that object which is associated with the time of midday.
By this, the cognition of one who is asleep and hears a text being recited by someone else is explained as having an unreal object (*asatyārtha*). This is how it should be understood.
For one who is overcome by sleep perceives the listener— whose self is distinct in place and time— and the text to be heard;
yet those two [the listener and the text] are not connected to that [dreamer's] place and time,
nor does he perceive them as they actually exist in their own place and time.
And by this very same method, the dream of the horse should also be explained;

for even there, in the dream of the horse, those things which appear as objects of perception at a certain time do not exist in that manner, and those things which do exist at a certain time are not perceived at that time.
For dreams are seen during the middle of the night and other such times, yet those objects are perceived as being connected with sunrise and so forth;
therefore, because certain things experienced in a dream are absolutely non-existent, they lack existence by virtue of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

However, the meaning of the treatise is this: those objects which are intended to be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) do not exist at all, even in a true dream, since they are subject to the deviation of temporal differences observed [in waking].
This is the intention of Dharmottara in citing such a specific dream-cognition:
"Some proponents of true dreams maintain that a dream-cognition of this kind has a real object; therefore, I have cited this example in order to quell that misconception."
However, there is no distinction whatsoever between this [dream cognition] and any other dream cognition,

because all dream cognitions are false cognitions due to their lack of an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*). Now, considering that one who says, "The attainment of what is being attained occurs at the very same time as the determination of what is being determined," intends to show the untenability of this point:
He raises an objection with "But surely... and so forth.
By stating that what is restricted to a specific place and restricted to a specific form can be brought about [as a result], he expresses his lack of disagreement regarding these two points.
However, he says "But as for the time... to indicate that this [other point] is not possible.
By means of these two modes just mentioned, he states the dissimilarity (vaidharmya):
that time which constitutes its delimitation is delimited accordingly;
that attainment which possesses that time occurs accordingly.
In that way, it cannot be reached;
the meaning is that at the very time it is delimited, it cannot be reached.
And by speaking thus, he has shown that what was said—namely, that [the sense organ] grasps at a different time—is untenable.
"Because all knowledge has such a nature"—
with these words beginning with "it is not said," the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) states that the challenger's objection is an attack on what was not even mentioned.
By this [objection], nothing at all [is gained].
That which has right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) as its preceding cause is described as such;
that which exists prior to the effect is called the "preceding" cause.
If the word "cause" (kāraṇa) were employed, it would be understood that the accomplishment of the human goal has its direct cause [in this]; however,
by using the word "prior" (pūrva), only that which is prior is stated as the cause.
He clarifies the intention of this [author] toward someone standing nearby who asks, "Why is it not stated by you in this way? with the words "For another... (*anyo hi*).
The word "iti" means "because.
He asks, "If it is not stated in this way, then what indeed is stated? and answers with "But rather... (*kin tu*).
This collection of particles and non-particles is used solely in the sense of "only.
But surely this statement is inconsistent,
for there is no such thing as that which is already delimited, by virtue of which one could say this.
However, it is more appropriate to say that it is the time at which [the action] was cut off,
rather than saying it is that very same [time]; this is indeed so.
Effort should be made solely for awakening.
By the phrase "at which time" (*yatkālam*), the form *tatkālam* is obtained;
by the word *tat*, the relative pronoun *yat*—which has the entity as its object—is drawn forward.

From this, the meaning is as follows: at whatever time a particular object is delimited, that very same object must be reached at that same time. Alas! While intending to insert a goitre, the eyeball has come out. In this way, indeed, the statement would be justified.
Furthermore, it follows that this [position] is no different from the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
There is indeed a great difference;
it is simply that you have not analyzed it correctly.

For instance, in the state of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), by the compound *yatkālaṃ tatkālam*, the action characterized by delimitation and the action characterized by attainment are expressed through the *bahuvrīhi* [compound].
However, now, in reality, this is not the meaning:
that an object which is connected to and delimited by a certain time must be attained in its own nature as being connected to that very same time, whether then or at another time.
The meaning is that whatever exists at the very time when the determination [of an object] occurs, that alone is what must be attained.
Consequently, it is established that a cognition which apprehends something non-existent at the time of the determination is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the statement beginning with "at which time" and so forth should be understood as being intended with reference to the attainment of an external object.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, there is no activity of attaining other than the manifestation of cognition; thus, at the very moment the object is determined, it is attained.
This has been explained in detail immediately following by this very [author], so otherwise there would be a contradiction with his own words. [Objection:
Even so, attainment of that which exists at the time of determination is simply not possible.

Since every object is indeed momentary, there would be no cognition whatsoever that could attain the object as it was presented; thus, the definition of "right cognition" (samyagjñāna) would be impossible. Anticipating this objection, he says: "by non-difference"—that is, by way of a single form, through the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) in the manner of "this is that very same thing."
The continuum (*santāna*) is the series of moments consisting of the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*); it is that which is dependent upon these.
This is its nature: here, the definition of conventional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being stated.
Therefore, the actual ontological status of things is not absolutely required [for this purpose].

In this regard, although in the actual state of things there is a difference between the determined [object] and the attained [object], nevertheless, due to the force of ignorance and because of the arising of one thing after another in immediate succession, practitioners of conventional discourse adhere to the collection of moments in the form of cause and effect as being "this very same thing," perceiving them as a unity. Consequently,
the attainment [of the object] by means of that which exists at the time of determination is indeed possible.

The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the explanation of the term "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*). Having thus explained the term "right knowledge" through this treatise, he now wishes to explain the preceding word; therefore, he states the analysis of its grammatical compound as "right knowledge."
And right cognition (samyagjñāna) is of two kinds: that which manifests as purposeful action (arthakriyānirbhāsa), and that which prompts one toward what is capable of purposeful action.
Of these two, that which prompts [action]—
This is now examined here. And that [prior perception] is merely a prior [condition]; it is not the direct cause. For when correct knowledge exists, there is recollection of what was previously seen;
from recollection comes desire; from desire comes purposeful activity.
And since [the attainment of the goal] arises from activity (*pravṛtti*), it is therefore not a direct cause.

Now, one might object: "The accomplishment of the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is the *prayojana* (purpose) of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) in the sense of being its effect; thus, it would be more appropriate to say that [the attainment] has right knowledge as its cause. Why, then, was it stated in this way? To this he replies: "Because of the effect" (*kāryāt*).
By this, he shows that the word *pūrva* (prior), which denotes a state of being established (*vyavasthāvācin*), indeed functions in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).
The term *bhavat* is a word expressing a cause, because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.126].
If this is so, one might suggest that the word *kāraṇa* itself should be used; to this he replies with the word *kāraṇa*.
The meaning is this: that which acts is called a "cause" (kāraṇa), but not that which is of a non-acting nature.
Furthermore, the designation "cause" applied to that which does not act is merely figurative, based on its being the cause of a cause.
And when a primary sense is possible, a cognition based on a secondary sense is not appropriate.

Therefore, that very knowledge which is the immediate basis for the accomplishment of the human goal should be understood by the word "cause. If such a cognition occurs even when the word "prior" (pūrva) is used, then what is the distinction? To this he says: "the word 'prior'."
The word *tu* expresses its distinction from the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*): [it means] "only the preceding," namely the immediate cause, while the other is [the mediate cause].
Now, if both were possible, the word "preceding" would be appropriate for the purpose of excluding the immediate cause and grasping the other;
however, this is not the case.
He says "and twofold" because it is the direct cause for the accomplishment of every human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because.

He asks how there is twofoldness and replies: "efficient action" (*arthakriyā*). It is called *nirbhāsa* because [the object] appears therein (*nirbhāsate asmin*). That from which there is the appearance of efficient action is thus [described]. Because immediately after the knowledge of the means (*sādhana*), [the result follows].
A cognition in which burning and so forth appear arises;
it is described in this way.

However, some maintain that because an ordinary person (arvāgdarśana) is unable to establish the conventional relationship of cause and effect within a single moment, they describe the cognition itself as being the very appearance of burning and so forth.
This is because it appears as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) therein;
furthermore, it is that which induces activity toward what is capable of purposeful action.
That which has as its objective domain the purposeful action to be attained through engagement is described in this way.
Regarding the conjunction [of the two] with respect to the appearance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), he asks: "What is being examined of the other two? and answers: "Of those two.
Even though it is the direct cause that prompts activity, why is there such hostility toward anything else that this alone is investigated?

Or rather, what is the point of the word "prior"? He says: "And that" (*tac ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) means "because. This is the intended meaning: since that from which [actions] proceed is the cause of the attainment of the object mediated by everything [intervening], and therefore, being a constituent part of that activity, it is merely "prior" (*pūrvamātra*), provided there is no obstacle.
"But it is not the immediately preceding cause. By mentioning only the "prior" [cause], it is understood as being separated by an interval.
Strengthening this very point, he says: "But not... and so forth.
The word "tu" has the sense of a distinction.
Why is this so? He says: "because of right knowledge"; for (hi) means because.
When that right knowledge— by virtue of the context, appearing as the means— is present,
there occurs the recollection of the burning and so forth known through a cognition capable of producing the seed of memory;
from that follows desire, which is the wish for its attainment.
From that [cognition], there arises "activity" (*pravṛtti*), which is the intellect (*buddhi*) accompanied by effort and desiring to attain the object presented by the motivating cognition.
And its "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the acquisition of what was intended to be acquired.

Since there is an intervention by means of recollection and so forth, it follows from the context that [the initial cognition] is not the direct cause for the attainment of the means to the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Although there is direct attainment of that which appears as causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*),
nevertheless, that is not to be examined. For it is precisely regarding those things where seekers who possess discernment have doubts that [examination is required].

That is now examined. When there is a cognition in which purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) appears, the human goal is accomplished; therefore, seekers have no doubt regarding that [cognition], and thus it need not be examined. Consequently, in order to indicate that right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) which is the cause of non-perception [of the object] and is worthy of examination, the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) was set aside and the term "prior" (*pūrva*) was employed.
[24] But according to ACPHN, it is "due to the appearance" (*-nirbhāsāt*);
according to BED, it is "in the appearance" (*-nirbhāse*).
If even an indirect cause of attainment is examined, then a direct cause must be examined all the more so; thus he says: "the appearance of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyānirbhāsam*).

The particle *tu* indicates that [the cognition] presents as distinct from the perceptual awareness that initiates action (*pravarttaka-adhyakṣa*) a manifestation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyānirbhāsa*).

When the reading is *yadā prāptihetuḥ*, then—according to the final interpretive position regarding the phrase "manifestation of causal efficiency"—it is the cause of that attainment of satisfaction and so forth which, though distinct, is established by worldly determination (*lokādhyavasāya*).
However, in the reading *prāpti*, there is no fault in that interpretation.
In the previous explanation, however, the cause of attainment must be expressed by the word "attainment" (*prāpti*) through metaphorical usage;
or else, the word "attainment" should be understood as having an instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*).
To the question, "Why is that not examined? he says: "For in whichever [case]... and so forth.
For this reason:
"possessing apprehension" means possessing doubt; since the mention of "apprehension" is illustrative, it should also be understood as meaning "possessing error."

The intention of one who speaks thus is this: it is not out of some addiction that the author of the treatise examines [the subject] without first investigating knowledge or failing to attain composure; rather, this undertaking is for the sake of the purpose of those to be instructed.
And the removal of doubt and error is the purpose of those to be instructed.
Therefore, one should examine precisely those [cognitions] which function in such a manner.
He says "in the manifestation of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*) to show that even when there is a manifestation of causal efficiency, they function in that way;
the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of the word *tu* (but).
Why do they not function in that way?
Because when this direct cause is present, the human goal is accomplished; for immediately thereafter, the fruit is experienced.
Or rather, it is due to the attainment of contentment and so forth.

In both of these two explanations, while the two things denoted by the term "appearance of causal efficiency" remain present, these two constitute the cause of doubt: either the non-perception of an immediate result, or the absence of the attainment of a distinct object established by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
The sense is: "But in the absence of that [proximity], how could they have doubts?"—meaning, let them not have doubts in that regard; what is established by this? He says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

If that which is separated [from the result] is the instigator and not the cause for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then why was it said: "That which exists prior to the effect is called the cause"?
Fearing that the qualification "directly" (*sākṣāt*) would be meaningless if applied to a non-direct cause—which is not a cause at all—he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since a direct cause is beyond suspicion and thus does not require investigation, therefore I shall demonstrate correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—which is the motivator, which is precisely because it is not a direct cause, and for that very reason is worthy and fit for investigation.
— Thus, it follows that the Teacher has used the term "prior" (*pūrva*) instead of the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

This is what is meant: this word "cause," which refers to a remote cause-of-a-cause, does not function there as a direct denoter; for its etymological derivation is "that which acts" (*karoti*) is a "cause" (*kāraṇa*).
Rather, it applies by way of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) because of its being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*).

The "purpose of man" (*puruṣārtha*) is the object for man. An "object" (*artha*) is that which is sought; that is to say, it is desired. It is either an object to be abandoned (*heya*) or an object to be acquired (*upādeya*). For an object to be abandoned is desired for the sake of being abandoned, and an object to be acquired is desired for the sake of being acquired. There is no third category other than those to be abandoned and those to be acquired; for that which is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*), because it is not to be acquired, is indeed to be abandoned. Its "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) consists of abandonment and acquisition. This is based upon causes (*hetunibandhanā*).

For "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is said to be origination; however, accomplishment based on knowledge is practice (*anuṣṭhāna*). Practice consists of the abandoning of that which is to be abandoned and the acquisition of that which is to be acquired. Therefore, the performance characterized by the abandonment of what is to be abandoned and the acquisition of what is to be acquired is called "accomplishment."
It might be argued as follows: even though the cause has been grasped, it is precisely right knowledge that will be understood as the object of investigation;
for the meaning is that it is being expounded because it is yet to be established.
But the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), being a factor (*kāraka*), is subordinate and follows the principal;

therefore, in accordance with the principal, that word—by the principle already described—is applied through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on proximity, since it is untenable for the primary cause, which is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), to be the object of the act of production (*vyutpatti-karman*). Thus, by abandoning [the primary sense] through its being for the sake of that [knowledge].
One will indeed act only toward that which is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Just as in the expression "the beds cry out," because the primary meaning of the word "bed" is incompatible with being the agent of the act of crying, the word "bed" abandons its primary referent and, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refers to the persons [lying] upon them by virtue of their proximity (*pratyāsatti*)— namely, their being situated thereon.
This is true;
however, this being the case, such skill would belong to the commentators and not to the author of the treatise—thus everything remains faultless.
Now, wishing to explain the term *puruṣārthasiddhi*, [the author] provides the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *artha* together with the word *puruṣa*.
And he explains the nature of the object (*artha*) and of the person (*puruṣa*) with the words "and [the nature] of the object," and so forth.

By stating that "it is sought after" (*arthyate*), he shows the suffix *-ac* in the sense of the object derived from the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root *arth* in the sense of "to beg" (*yācñā*). He clarifies the meaning of "it is sought after" (*arthyate*) by means of the words "it is desired" (*kāmyate*) and "it is wished for" (*iṣyate*); the meaning of the word "as much as" (*yāvat*) is that the extent of the object expressed by "it is desired" is exactly the same as the extent expressed by "it is sought after."
[25] *Artha* is used in the sense of "requesting"—according to the *Dhātupāṭha* (10.373;
according to the edition by Böthlingk, it is at 10.357).
To the question "What is this *artha*? he says: "That which is to be abandoned (*heya*)."
The word "vā" has the sense of "and.
An "artha" (object) is that which is sought or desired. [An objection: "In that case, the object is not something to be abandoned. To this he says: "to be abandoned" (*heya*).
"Hir" means "because. Since that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) is desired to be abandoned—that is, relinquished—it is therefore an object (*artha*).
This is the intended meaning: indeed, an object is that which is desired.
In this context, although there is no desire for acceptance, there is nevertheless a desire for rejection.
If one asks, "If an object is desired to be abandoned, how can it be an object to be accepted?", he says: "Even that which is to be accepted is merely desired for the sake of being taken up.
The word "even" (api) indicates that it is not only that which is to be rejected that is desired.
But is it not the case that the object is neither something to be abandoned nor something to be adopted, but rather something else?
If so, why is that [other thing] not also demonstrated? To this he says: "And not...
Here, the particle *ca* functions as an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or signifies the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
"But surely there is also a category of things to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*), wherein there is neither engagement nor cessation.
How then can that which is established by experience be denied? To this he says: "Because [it is] disregarded" (*upekṣaṇīya iti*). The word *hi* means "because."
On this point, someone says: "Just as it is not to be accepted (*anupādeya*), so too it is not to be rejected (*aheya*).
In that regard, if it is to be rejected because it is not to be accepted, then why is it not to be accepted because it is not to be rejected?
What that venerable one has said is well-stated; however, his mind was not directed toward investigating the meaning of the word "to be rejected" (*heya*).

"And all this is the accomplishment of the goals of man. Here, the word "all" (*sarva*) is used in the sense of the totality of *substances* (*dravya*), not in the sense of the totality of *types* (*prakāra*). Therefore, the meaning is not that even the two types of accomplishment are based solely on right knowledge; rather, the meaning is: whatever accomplishment there may be, [it is based on right knowledge].

All of that, in its entirety, is based upon right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). For from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), there is no accomplishment of the object, even by chance (*kākatālīya*). To explain: if it causes one to obtain the object exactly as it was presented, then the accomplishment of the object occurs;
[this is] what was intended.
For it is thus:
that which is abandoned, relinquished, and not accepted is called "to be abandoned" (*heya*).
And "abandonment" (hāna) means non-acceptance;
it is not the discarding of something after having taken it up.
Therefore, even in the case of snakes, poison, thorns, and so forth, "abandonment" is simply the absence of engagement with them.
And that [equanimity] exists even toward what is to be disregarded;
thus, if it were accepted as such, it would then incur the status of being something not to be abandoned.
And since that [reason] is not accepted by him, it is clear that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) for him;
however, it is not unestablished for us,
because the state of being unacceptable— that is, the state of not being to be accepted— is established.

If it is argued that it is improper to establish the identity of the "to be abandoned" (*heya*) with [the "to be cultivated"] merely by disregarding the third category— the "to be equanimously regarded" (*upekṣaṇīya*)— which is established through experience,
then you have said something agreeable.
For we too do not maintain that the two well-known objects, the "to be abandoned" and the "to be equanimously regarded," possess a single nature.

However, what is the fault in designating indifference by the word *heya* (to be abandoned) through its connection with action, and likewise designating it by the word *hāna* (abandoning) through its sense of non-acceptance?
Furthermore, this status of being "to be abandoned" or "to be accepted" is to be understood in relation to a single person at a single time.
Now, stating the analysis of the compound *siddhi* with the word *artha*, he states its meaning: "of that"—and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in common usage "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) means "completion," as in the expression "the accomplishment of rice"? How then can it be described in this way? [The author] says: "dependent upon a cause" (*hetunibandhanā*). "Cause" (*hetu*) means the reason (*kāraṇa*). "Dependent" (*nibandhana*) is so called because the cause is bound (*nibadhyate*) within it; it refers to the domain of connection (*pratibandha-viṣaya*).
Having analyzed the compound as "that which has a cause as its dependent" (*hetur nibandhanam asyāḥ*), the meaning to be stated is "dependent upon a cause" (*hetu-pratibaddhā*).
If such is the nature of accomplishment based on the object (*janaka*), then what will it be like when based on cognition (*jñāna*)? To this he says: "In cognition...
The particle *tu* indicates the difference between this accomplishment and the previous one.
And explaining it in this way, [the author] states in his commentary on the word *artha*: "The *artha* is the purpose (*prayojana*), such as burning, and so forth."

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the term *siddhi*, both Vinītadeva and Śāntabhadra—who commented that "there is the accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) of burning and so forth for that [fire]"—will be refuted.

This is because the accomplishment of burning and so forth belongs to the fire and such things themselves from their own causes, and not to the cognition, since the cognition does not produce that [effect].
Now, if *siddhi* means performance (*anuṣṭhāna*),...

In that case, he says "the abandonment, the acquisition, and the accomplishment" with the words "and of that which is to be abandoned. The word "ca" (and) indicates either a reason or an emphasis, and it should be understood as following after the word "hānam" (abandonment). The second "ca" has the sense of conjunction.
To show what is established when this is so, he says "tataḥ" (from that).

Since such an accomplishment (*siddhi*) is based upon knowledge, for that reason, having explained the analysis and meaning of the words *puruṣārthasiddhi*, [the author] now states the analysis in order to explain the word *sarva*: "And all... By analyzing it in this way, he confirms what was explained by Vinītadeva: "It is both 'all'—meaning worldly and supramundane—and 'proximate' and 'remote,' as well as the 'human goal' (*puruṣārtha*)."
"Thus his success [is achieved]," he refutes that as follows: for in this way [DhPr p.32]:

And that which makes known what has been shown leads precisely to right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). That which makes known what has been shown but does not lead [to attainment] is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). And how could that which does not lead to attainment be the cause for the accomplishment of an object? Therefore, that from which the accomplishment of an object does not arise is not right knowledge; whereas that from which the accomplishment of an object does arise is indeed right knowledge. For this very reason, right knowledge must be explained with effort, since it alone is the cause for the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

When [the sūtra] is explained by means of the word "all" (*sarva*), because there is no qualification regarding the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha-siddhi*), the accidental attainment of a goal through false knowledge would be precluded;
yet such an attainment is not possible.
And as to how it is not possible:
This will be demonstrated immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, as for Śāntabhadra, who explains [the term] as: "It is both 'all' and 'human purpose,' or the purpose of all persons; its accomplishment," [that too is addressed].
That [objection] too is refuted by this very same door.

Now, since the word "all" (*sarva*) is observed to function both in the sense of "every kind" (*prakārakārtsnya*) and in the sense of "entirety" (*niḥśeṣatā*), it is not known which function is intended here; therefore, he says: "The word 'all'. It functions—that is, operates—as a denotative term (*vācaka-bhāvena*) in the sense of the entirety of a substance (*dravya*).

As in the statement, "God is the efficient cause of all things that have an origin," the term *dravya* (substance) here should be understood as that which is fit to be designated by the pronoun "this" (*tad*), and not as earth and so forth as established in the Vaiśeṣika system. Thus it has been said:
“Where all names are applicable as the characterization of a thing,
that object which is intended to be differentiated is called a ‘substance’ (dravya).
Thus, even the accomplishment of human goals (puruṣārtha-siddhi) is capable of being designated by the expression “this is that.”
Therefore, that too is a substance;
because it is apprehended as occurring in such a manner, [the author] explicitly states a negation even of that which is established as occurring elsewhere.
"Vṛtta" means "it occurs."
Just as former [commentators] explain: "This mendicant is a consumer of all flavors," and just as this word "all" (sarva) denotes the entirety of types (*prakārakārtsnya*), so it is here as well.
To the question, "What is the benefit if one does not accept its application as the entirety of types? he says: "Therefore... (*tataḥ*).
Therefore, because there is no apprehension of a partial or complete occurrence [of the means], one might ask: "Even so, how does this meaning follow?

It follows indeed; for when the word *sarva* (all) expresses both modality (*prakāra*) and totality (*kārtsnya*), this is the meaning: there is no mode of accomplishing the goals of man (*puruṣārtha*), whether characterized as a result or otherwise, that is not based upon right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Thus,
since this is the case, the meaning is that both types of accomplishment are preceded by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Now, even in this sense, because both modes have been included, what indeed remains uncomprised such that this meaning would be lost through such great effort?

How could it be that no particular instance of a loss, which falls within the category [of "loss"], is lost? For indeed, one who consumes all six types of tastes does not consume every single individual instance of sweet, sour, and other tastes;
nor, by not doing so, does he fail to be a consumer of all tastes.
[26] It is not correctly read [as such].
If this is not the meaning, then what is it? He says: "But rather" (*api tu*).
This is a collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) which occurs everywhere in the sense of "but rather" (*kin tu*).

Now, if it is asserted that this [attainment] is entirely based upon right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it would follow that there is no accomplishment of an object even by chance (*kākatālīya*) through false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*);
yet this is not tenable.
For although the accomplishment of an object is not invariably determined by false knowledge, [it does occur].
Nevertheless, it does indeed exist occasionally;
for example, if someone, having ascertained smoke from a mosquito-lamp situated above a fire, infers the fire, and then reaches that fire through purposeful activity.
And for this very reason, false cognition possesses an occasional object.
Because it is the basis for accomplishment,
and because right knowledge is invariably the cause that serves as the basis for the accomplishment of an object, it is right knowledge alone that is explained with diligent effort.
However, it is not the case that the accomplishment of the object does not occur at all because of false cognition;
rather, this fault arises only when there is a grasping of the occurrence of all its aspects.
For in this way, by means of correct cognition, any other mode that cannot be established is excluded.
However, it is not the case that any particular instance of attainment (*siddhi*) included within those modes is produced by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
Nor can individual instances of rejection (*hāna*) and acquisition (*upādāna*) be denoted by the word "mode" (*prakāra*), for that would entail the consequence of an infinite number of modes.

Therefore, the word "all" (*sarva*) must be understood as functioning to denote the entirety of the modes—this being the view of the predecessors, which he anticipates and addresses with the word "false" (*mithyā*).
The term *kākatālīya* refers to something accidental, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says: "For thus... (*tathā hi*). From that [he means] from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
He says "it has been shown" (*pradarśitam*) to show that even that [cognition] indeed causes one to reach [the object]. The word "and" (*ca*) means "because.
He says "it has been shown" to state that since even a false cognition might cause one to reach [the object], the restriction that [only] right cognition [does so] is untenable.
The particle *eva* (co) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*) and should be understood as following the word "aprāpayat" (not having reached),
because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*) by Pāṇini’s rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ* (3.2.126).
The meaning is that it is precisely because it does not lead to the attainment of the object it has displayed that it is called "false cognition" (*mithyājñāna*).
For this alone is the true nature of false cognition: namely, its failure to reach the object it has displayed.
The point is that the designation "false cognition" would only be superimposed upon that which *does* lead to attainment.

One might object: "Let it not be a means of attainment; why should it not nonetheless be the basis for the establishment of that object? To this he says: "non-attaining" (*aprāpaka*). The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of "because."
With the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he provides a summary of the point already stated:
since false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is precisely that which does not lead to the attainment of the object shown, therefore, from whatever is false cognition, no establishment of the object follows.
Furthermore, one who, by chance, perceives the smoke of a mosquito-wick above a fire and infers the fire [to be present there]...

Even he, prior to the time of inference, having ascertained and distinguished the smoke-form— the effect of fire— which is restricted and excluded from things such as mosquitoes and wicks, does not attend to it at the time of inference; for if he were to attend to it then, error would be impossible, provided that the cause of doubt has not yet been removed.
Let alone the case of observing a swarm of gnats;
even when smoke is observed, since its being an effect of fire is still subject to doubt, how could a conscious person truly be free from suspicion?
Therefore, the ascertainment of fire arises only from smoke whose form is ascertained and restricted.
However, when there is apprehension of only one side from another source, yet the cause for suspicion has not been removed, that is indeed doubt (*saṃśaya*).
And doubt, which reveals an object that is indeterminate as either existent or non-existent and impossible to attain, is not the basis for the accomplishment of the object;
rather, its intention is that such attainment comes only from another cognition.
Thus, in other cases of false cognition as well, validity is not tenable;

and just as that attainment [of validity] occurs only through another cognition, so it has been explained in detail by Dharmottara himself in the *Viniścayaṭīkā*, and therefore it is not elaborated upon here.
He says "and because... in order to show that the establishment of the object might also occur from some [source].

He demonstrates by implication that even the Master does not accept false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) as the basis for establishing an object, since it presents a form as if it were distinct from something else.
This is shown when he says: "For this very reason."
Since the accomplishment of an object does not occur from false knowledge,
but certainly does occur from correct knowledge,
it is for this very reason [that the former is abandoned].
The inclusion of the word "effort" (*yatna*) indicates that the exposition of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) follows as a necessary consequence.
It has already been stated that this is because there is indeed an exposition of a certain kind of false cognition.
By the phrase "for this very reason," he explicitly states—using words such as "since" (*yataḥ*)—that very thing which was required as the logical reason, for the sake of easy comprehension.

This is the intention: if the Teacher had intended that the accomplishment of an object could result even from false knowledge, then he would not have explained right knowledge alone through its systematic elaboration.
Yet, he has explained precisely that [right knowledge] in such a manner.
Therefore, it is concluded that this was certainly not his intention.

[Objection: Is it not the case that when there is the restriction "only preceded by right knowledge" (*samyagjñānapūrvikaiva*), it follows that the accomplishment of an object does not occur from false knowledge? And yet, this restriction has not been explicitly stated; so how is this meaning obtained? [The author] says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). Because, in the word "all" (*sarva*), there is a totality of objects...
Then, as far as he might say: "Whatever accomplishment of the goals of human life there may be, it is based solely upon right knowledge."

Thus it has been stated that "all that [is accomplished] is preceded by right knowledge. The word *iti* is used here in the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Furthermore, there is a constant syntactic connection between the pronouns *yat* (that which) and *tat* (that). Therefore, this is the meaning: since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge, therefore that right knowledge is being expounded.

And although right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is subordinate within the compound, it is nevertheless the primary element in this treatise because it is that which is to be explained. Therefore, it alone is connected with the word "that" (*tat*).
It is said to be "explained" (*vyutpādyate*) in the sense that it is established through the removal of misconceptions.

When the commentary exists, the following meaning is obtained: the accomplishment of all goals of the person (*puruṣārtha*) without exception is preceded by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); there is no manifestation whatsoever that is not preceded by it.
For that reason, the sentence "the accomplishment of the goals of the person is based solely on right knowledge" is an emphatic statement (*sāvadhāraṇa*).
Whatever measure of subject matter one is able to state, that much has been stated by this [saying]: "All [activity] is preceded by right knowledge.
Therefore, the word *iti* should be understood in the sense of *tasmāt* (therefore).
But where is the word *yat* by which there is a connection with the meaning that is about to be stated? To this he says: *yad*.
The particle *ca* has the sense of "it is clear that this is so.
Since there is no direct mutual dependence between the two words themselves, it should be understood as referring to the meanings of *yat* and *tat*.
Connection (*abhisambandha*) is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*).
This being so, he asks what kind of meaning is established [by this] and says: "that" (*tat*).
But surely, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*).
How, then, could there be a reference by that word (*tacchabda*) to that which is non-primary, through a reflection upon the primary? To this he says: "Even though...

(*yady api ca*). The collection of particles *yady api ca* functions in the acceptance of a statement intended to express a specific distinction. And this [usage] is frequently seen in the Mahābhāṣya.

The term "compound" (samāsa) means the meaning of the compound; this is the intended sense. For one who asserts that [the object] is primary because it is what must be explained, the intention is as follows: primacy is twofold, namely, verbal and objective.
In that regard, although there is no primacy in the verbal sense, since right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is what must be explained, it is presented by another cognition [as the primary object].

Who could deny the primacy of that which is independent by virtue of its own intrinsic logic? Thus, one who explains that there is no contradiction in referring to it with the word "that" (tat) disregards the commentary of Vinītadeva. For he explains it thus: "Because it is indicated in the neuter gender, it refers to right knowledge (samyagjñāna)."
