The intention is this: since a reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*) of right knowledge is untenable if that knowledge is not predominant, it would be impossible even to grasp its logical mark (*liṅga*); how then could that which is unestablished be proven?
Therefore, because of its predominance, it is precisely that right knowledge [which is the object].
And here, there is a fourfold misconception concerning number, definition, object-sphere, and result. Among these, in order to refute the misconception regarding number, he says:
"Right cognition is twofold" (NB I.2).

"Twofold" (*dvividham*) means that it has two kinds or modes (*dvau vidhau*); thus it is twofold. Furthermore, by way of demonstrating the number, the distinction between its individual instances is shown.
Connection (*sambandha*) means the linking with that word, which is to say, its acceptance.

Therefore, this is the meaning: that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), acting as the instrument, is established—that is, it is made understood by the disciples—by means of the refutation of misconceptions; this is the sense.
For this very reason, he states "that" (*tat*) in the accusative case, referring to it as "this" (*etat*) along with its supporting reasoning.

As it is said: "[27] 'The other is correctly reminded of what is his own' (PV IV 267)," there is no contradiction with the definition when one states that [the object] is established by means of the removal of misconceptions.
Statements such as "the means of valid cognition are well-known" [cf. PSṬ Ms A 12b1;
NA k.2;
PVṬ 96a7f] should be understood as having been set aside.
[27] “[The opponent] is reminded of the convention” (PV IV 267).

Now, one might ask: since valid cognition has already been thoroughly explained by means of the *Vārttika* and other such works, how is this treatise not redundant? There is no fault here, because this treatise was composed for those of sharp intellect who take delight in concise presentations.
Now, what is the misconception here that is being refuted so that this [point] may be established? He says: "fourfold" (*caturvidha*). The word "and" (*ca*) means "because.
It is fourfold, meaning of four kinds.
In this context, *vipratipatti* (disagreement) is a contrary understanding regarding right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). To what object does it refer?
He says: "Number" (*saṃkhyā*).

By this, the fourfold nature of conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) has been shown due to the difference in their objects. To explain: first, there is the conflict regarding number; for instance, the Lokāyatikas maintain that perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the Sāṃkhyas maintain that there are exactly three means of valid cognition: perception, inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*).

Regarding the ṛṣi-knowledge known as *pratibhā* (intuition) which occasionally arises here among worldly people, since it is not shown to be included within either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), the ancient Vaiśeṣikas maintain that there are only three: perception, inference, and ṛṣi-knowledge;
whereas the Naiyāyikas maintain that there are four: perception, inference, comparison (*upamāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*).
According to the Prabhākaras, [the means of valid cognition] are perception, inference, analogy, verbal testimony, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone.
According to the followers of Kumārila (the Kaumārilas), they are perception, inference, analogy, verbal testimony, presumptive testimony, and non-existence (*abhāva*).
There is also disagreement regarding their definitions—for instance, the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the Bārhaspatyas, and others maintain that perception is exclusively conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
According to the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others, [perception] is both conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
According to those who maintain the doctrine of partial validity (*aṃśavāda*), even erroneous cognitions such as that of a yellow conch-shell are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
According to the Ahrīkas (Nirgranthas), inference is produced by a cause characterized by a single mark (*ekalakṣaṇahetuja*).
"Arising from a cause characterized by six features" refers to the followers of Pūrvayoga;
"arising from a cause characterized by five features" and "arising from a cause characterized by four features" refers to the Naiyāyikas.

There is also disagreement regarding the object: the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others maintain that perception and inference have universals (*sāmānya*) as their objects. There is also disagreement regarding the result (*phala*): [some hold] that the nature of valid cognition (*pramārūpa*) is indeed distinct from all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the fruit is fivefold" (*pañca-phalam*):
therein, among those [five], the number is distinguished by means of its non-genus (*ajāti*).
Thus, by analyzing the compound as "that which has two kinds or modes (*vidha*) of determination," he demonstrates that the word *vidha* also signifies "mode" (*prakāra*).
For even Adharmapāla, the author of the *Prakīrṇavṛtti*,

states that there are only two manifestations of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). And since a distinction between these manifestations has been demonstrated, the definition of correct cognition is restricted to each individual manifestation.

It can be explained. However, as long as the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*) is not demonstrated, it is impossible to state a single definition of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) that conforms to all its instances. Therefore, the statement regarding the numerical distinction is an integral part of the statement of the definition itself; for if the numerical distinction consisting of the difference between instances is not demonstrated, it is impossible to demonstrate the difference in their definitions. This is because [the numerical distinction] is a subordinate element of the instruction of the definition.
And thus, first, the distinction of numbers has been stated.
[28] The word *vidha* has been shown to denote a "manner" (*prakāra*).
Furthermore, his intention is not that the word *vidhā*—because it denotes a genus (*jāti*)—cannot denote a mode (*prakāra*).
For since it has multiple meanings, its usage as denoting a mode is frequently observed in such passages as: "In these four [categories], reality (*tattva*) is fully encompassed" (Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 2).

Now, one who intends to act, thinking "How indeed might I act based on valid cognition alone and not on what is not valid cognition?", first desires to know the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of valid cognition itself, not its number (*saṅkhyā*). Therefore, it is the definition alone that must be explained, not the number. And if that definition belongs to only one [cognition], then there is only one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But if it belongs to many, [then there are many].

In that case, a plurality of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would indeed be unavoidable. Now, if that definition belongs neither to a single [means] nor to many, then by the very power of explaining the definition, the disagreement regarding number is already refuted; so what is the point of a separate refutation of the disagreement regarding number? To this he says: "Number" (*saṃkhyā*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because. "Door" (*dvāra*) means "means" (*upāya*).

He asks, "In what form is it shown? and replies: "Two. By the word *iti*, he states the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*). He asks, "What is the purpose of showing this very distinction between individual instances? and replies: "And when there is a distinction between individual instances" (*vyaktibhede ca*). The particle *ca* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). [He means: if the description of the definition (*lakṣaṇākhyāna*) were possible even when the distinction between individual instances is not shown, [then there would be no need for it].

Nevertheless, what is shown by this? Since comprehension does not arise from mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, he says "if it is not shown" in order to demonstrate negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well. The particle *tu* indicates the distinction between the position of showing [the example] and the position of not showing it. By saying "that which follows all individuals," his intention is this: if the differences between individuals are not displayed, it is impossible to state a definition that is restricted to each individual.
Because it is impossible. A definition being stated must be expressed as a single entity that follows after all individual instances;
and it is not possible to state such a thing, precisely because it is impossible.

Now, one might object: why is it said that [the universal] which follows all individuals is impossible to express, when there exists a single, easily stated definition, namely, "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge"? True. However, that which is the specific, individual form of cognitions is what is useful for those desiring action in their engagement with the world.

There is no fault [in our position], because the intention is that such a defining characteristic does not exist. Alternatively, there exists no common defining characteristic that is capable of refuting misconceptions; and as for the defining characteristic of non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*), misconceptions are not thereby refuted, since others also accept non-contradiction in other cases as well.

With this intention it was said: "It is not possible to state only one [characteristic]. Since the injunction of the remainder is established by the force of the negation of the specific, and because such a common characteristic is indeed possible, this word *sakala* (all) must be applied in the sense of totality (*kārtsnya*) regarding what has been employed.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), which conforms to the fourfold types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) whose distinctions between individual instances have been demonstrated.

It can be said that [inference] follows two kinds of inference characterized by the distinction between the demonstrated (*pradarśita*) and the individual (*vyakti*), because it is born from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*). If this is indeed the case, one might ask: "What follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). Since it is impossible to demonstrate a single such [mark] without having first demonstrated [the general rule], "therefore" means for that reason. It should be understood that "an auxiliary member for stating the definition" (*lakṣaṇakathanāṅga*) means an auxiliary member for stating a definition restricted to each individual instance (*prativyaktiniyata*).
What, then, is this twofold nature? He says:
"Perception and inference. (NB I.3)

Now, even if it were granted that it is impossible to state a single definition of such a kind, what of it? For even if the distinction in number is not shown, the distinction in definitions can certainly be demonstrated. Anticipating the objection as to why the statement of the distinction in number is a necessary part of stating that [definition], he speaks by way of negative concomitance (*vyatirekamukhena*) to reinforce the point already stated by way of positive concomitance (*anvayamukhena*), beginning with the words "lakṣaṇa" (definition).

When there arises the expectation— "At what time is it impossible to show the difference in characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*), which is observed to be distinct for each individual [instance]?"— the phrase "not shown" (*apradarśita*) is to be supplied later [in the sentence].
The particle *tu* (but) serves to emphasize.
Or [the author] distinguishes [the number] from what has been shown.
If it is asked: "But surely the difference in number is not itself the difference in individuals;

so how can it be said to consist of a difference in individuals?"—[the answer is that] because, in reality, there is no such thing as a number existing apart from the things numbered, the number and the things numbered are intended here to be one.
And it is said thus:
previously, however, it was stated by way of demonstrating number, relying on the distinctions among those whose natures are constructed by conceptualization.
Furthermore, by intending to express the identity of the number and the numbered object, the very misconception regarding the numbered object is refuted.

Alternatively, it is said that the distinction of numbers belongs to that whose nature is a distinction of entities (individuals)— a distinction of such a kind constructed by the artisan of conceptual construction (kalpanā).

Since a distinction in number is postulated only when things are distinct in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), what fault is there in stating this as a descriptive restatement of their actual nature? Furthermore, all of this has been said for the following reason: it is appropriate to state only the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) because it is useful for those desiring to engage [with the subject]; however, that very characteristic cannot be explained otherwise than by demonstrating the distinction in number. Thus, the demonstration of the distinction in number is intended.

If it is argued: "Surely, even if the number were not explicitly stated as 'twofold,' once it is said that 'it is correct knowledge,' the distinction between its two manifestations is already shown; and this being the case, it would be easy to explain the difference in their definitions. Therefore, what is the purpose of the word 'twofold'? We reply: This statement is made for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that once [the categories] are established, it is intended to show that they are *exclusively* twofold.

Otherwise, since only this much has been introduced here by way of defining [the means of valid cognition], the suspicion that elsewhere there might be yet another correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) to be defined would not have been eliminated.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that "by the definition itself, the disagreement regarding the number [of means of valid cognition] is thereby refuted"—that is utterly incoherent;
for if this were stated with the specific definitions in mind, [it would not suffice].

In that case, since the distinctions between individual instances have not been demonstrated, it was stated that it is impossible to describe that [universal] as restricted to each individual instance;
and since it has not been so described, one is not able to act accordingly.
Because this [definition] is capable of establishing that such is perception and inference,
and that there is no other valid cognition besides these two.
Now, as for the definition of the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa):
Even that [distinction], being of such a common nature, cannot be stated; by whom, then, could it be so established?
And it has already been said that even if it were so stated, such a misconception would not be refuted.
Nevertheless, one might argue: "Even when it is said that [knowledge] is of two kinds, how is it that anything other than these two is excluded from being incorrect knowledge?"
What is the purpose [of this work]? It is said: first, those learners who take the teacher as their authority are made to understand the intended meaning by the mere words of that teacher alone;
furthermore, for those who follow reasoning, logical justifications have been cited in other treatises.
Since this treatise begins with the authority of wise people, the proof has been stated by them themselves; therefore, the mention of their number is not something that need not be accepted.
[The author] says "in the definition" to explain why it is stated at the very beginning, even though it is a subordinate part of the instruction on the definition.
In this way, he brings together the fact that the means are equal.
Since the two-fold nature could exist in some manner or other, he asks— "What, moreover?"—
where "what" is used in a general sense and "moreover" [indicates a specific inquiry].

*Pratyakṣam* means that which has gone toward (*prati-gatam*) or relies upon (*āśritam*) the sense-organ (*akṣam*). The compound is formed according to the rule: "Words such as *ati* and others, when used in the sense of 'transcending' and so forth, form a compound with a word in the second case" (Vārttika 4 on Pāṇini 2.2.18).

Because the rule regarding the gender of the final member is prohibited in compounds involving *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alaṃ*, and *gati*, the gender of the resulting term follows that of the expressed object (*abhidheya*).

When the defining characteristic (*liṅga*) exists, the word "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*), which applies to all things possessing that characteristic, is established. Furthermore, the dependence upon the sense-faculties (*akṣāśritatva*) is the etymological basis (*vyutpattinimitta*) of the word, but not its functional basis (*pravṛttinimitta*). By means of this dependence on the sense-faculties, however, the quality of being a direct manifestation of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*), which inheres in the same substrate as that [dependence], is indicated. That alone is the functional basis of the word. Consequently, whatever directly manifests an object—
That cognition is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[29] Now, one might object that according to this etymological derivation, only sensory cognition would be denoted by the term *pratyakṣa*, and not the cognition of yogis and so forth; to this he says—[the commentary states]:
"Specifically," and expresses what is intended: "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

Anticipating the question, "What is the compound in the term *pratyakṣa*, and by which rule [is it formed]?"— for the sake of easy comprehension and to dispel misconceptions— he says, "gone toward," and so forth.
The sense-faculty (*akṣa*) is "gone to" (*gata*), meaning it has resorted to [the cognition] as its producer.
But it is not by way of being something to be contained (*ādheyabhāvena*).

And by analyzing [the compound] in this manner—namely, that it "occurs with respect to each sense-organ" (*akṣam akṣaṃ prati vartate*)—he rejects the *avyayībhāva* formation according to its etymological derivation.
In a compound, there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).
And this compound should be understood as being designated a *tatpuruṣa*.
To the question "By which rule is this [formed]?", he says: "The words beginning with *ati*," and so forth.
He says "it has all genders" (*sarvaliṅga*) to show that this manner was displayed by him out of self-importance (*āhopuruṣikayā*), and that there is no merit whatsoever in it.

The intention is that, if it were an *avyayībhāva* compound, forms such as *pratyakṣo vṛkṣaḥ* (the tree is perceptible) and *pratyakṣā mṛgāḥ* (the deer are perceptible) would not occur, nor would the genitive form *pratyakṣasya* be possible. To the question, "How then does this [term] possess all genders?", he says: "Like the thing denoted" (*abhidheyavat*).
"Like the denoted object" means as if it possessed the denoted object.
That which has the gender (*liṅga*) of the denoted object is "like that. And when that is the case, this word *pratyakṣa* possesses all genders.
[29*] A cf. NBh ...

Now, one might object: since the rule *paraval liṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.26) prescribes that in a compound, the gender of the final member prevails, and because the word *akṣa-*—standing in the position of the subsequent member in relation to the word *prati-* within the compound *pratyakṣa-*—is thus adopted as the indicator (*liṅga*), how can it be said that its gender is determined by its denotation (*abhidheya*)? To this he says: "prāpta... (it has been obtained).
Now, by what means is the negation of its being a *liṅga* (gender-marker) in the subsequent word established?

It cannot be by the compound *prāptāpanna-gati-samāsa*, because in that rule the terms are understood in their own forms (*svarūpa*), whereas here that is not the case. If it is argued that it follows from the *gati-samāsa* rule, that too is incorrect.

Since the rule *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge* (Pāṇini 1.4.59) [establishes that prefixes are called *upasargas* when connected with an action], and the subsequent rule *gatiś ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.60) prescribes the designation *gati* specifically when there is a connection with an action, one might object: "The word *prati* is not [an action], nor is there a connection with the action of going here; therefore, this [designation of *gati*] is incorrect. This objection is not valid, because it is the word *prati* itself that occurs in that sense [of "toward" or "in relation to"]. Thus, there is no fault.
By the inclusion of the term "gati" (course), those for whom the designation "gati" is observed therein are honored;
since that [designation] is observed in the case of *prati* and so forth, they too are included as being of such a nature.
If this is so, then how is it that the Master Dignāga stated, "it occurs with respect to each sense-organ (*akṣam akṣaṃ prati*)," thus [defining] perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
Therefore, since it was stated merely for that purpose, there is no fault.

However, if being dependent on the sense-faculties (*akṣāśritatva*) alone were the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), then only sensory cognition (*indriyavijñāna*) would be called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
It is not based on pride and so forth.

Just as the word "cow" (*go*), although derived from the act of going—as in "the cow goes"—takes as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the "cowness" (*gotva*) inherent in a single object, which is characterized by the act of going;
thus, the word "cow" is established whether the cow is moving or not moving.
That by which something is measured is "māna" (the instrument of measurement).

By the word *māna*, used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), the means of valid cognition characterized as similarity (*sārūpya-lakṣaṇa*) is denoted. Following the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of its relationship [with the object], that which is the measurement is inference (*anumāna*).

"Inference proceeds when the property of the subject has been grasped and the relationship between the probandum and the probans has been remembered"; thus, [inference] is said to occur at a later time.

Now, if one adopts the etymological derivation "that which has gone toward" or "that which rests upon" the sense-organ (*akṣa*), then mental perception, self-awareness, and the perception of yogins would not be denotable by the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). To this, he says: "resting upon the sense-organs."
Because:
"derivation" (vyutpatti) is the formation of a word through the division of its base (prakṛti) and so forth;
"functioning" (pravṛtti) is the denotation of meaning by the word—referring here to the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) which is the subject under discussion.
The particle *tu* is used for emphasis.
What, then, is the ground for its application? He says: "by this.

By the particle *tu*, he shows the distinction between this [ground for application] and the ground for etymological derivation (*vyutpattinimitta*). This is because there is an obligatory connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.

That very quality which is characterized as the direct realization of an object—the immediate presentation of an object by virtue of its dependence upon a sense faculty—is indeed the basis for the application of the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

But how can one thing be characterized by another that is unrelated to it? Lest there be an over-extension [of the definition], he says: "Inhering in the same object," because it is specified as being the cause [of the perception].
The meaning is that it is characterized by that which is inherent in the same object.
In a single object characterized as cognition, the quality of directly manifesting the object is inherently present together with the state of being dependent on the sense organs (*akṣa*).
Although, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), neither inherence nor the inherent substrate exist, [they are so designated conventionally].

Nevertheless, since it is possible for the co-inherence (*ekārthasamavāya*)—which is itself conceptualized—to exist between "dependence on the sense-faculties" and "direct perception of the object," both of which are based on real entities and are themselves conceptualized as being grounded in the exclusion of those [other] things;
what contradiction is there in such a designation?
Or, if this was stated merely according to what is accepted by others (*paraprasiddhyā*), what harm is done?
Even so, how does this overcome the previous fault? To this he says: "And therefore" (*tataś ca*).
Since the state of being a direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*) is the basis for the application [of the term], the word "and" (*ca*) indicates the meaning: "for this reason, this is said."

Anticipating the objection of a bystander who has not heard the injunctive statement—asking, "What fault is there if the basis for the application [of the term] is its dependence on the sense organs (*akṣāśritatva*)?"—the author says: "If... The particle *tu* indicates that this is a distinct position. Now, it might be argued: "That very direct perception of an object which is inherent (*samaveta*) by virtue of its dependence on the sense organs is what should be indicated by this [term]; thus, the situation remains as before."
[Objection: "This would result in the non-inclusion of mental perception (*mānasa*) and so forth. [Reply: No;

because being produced by a sense organ (*akṣajatva*) is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) and thus not primary, while the direct manifestation of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*), which is what is being characterized, is primary. Since the secondary characteristic ceases once that which is to be characterized has been identified, there is no fault at all.
This is just as in the case of the expression, "Let the curd be protected from crows."

Otherwise, even in this case, because the quality of being harmful— which is inherent in the same object as the nature of being a crow— is used as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there would be no protection of the curd from dogs and other animals.
Now, if [it is argued that] only that which is harmful...
That [quality] which is inherent in crows is the very same in other things as well;
and since it is characterized [by that quality], it is called "the protector of the curd" even when referring to something else.
Since this is the same even in the case of direct perception of an object, why should the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) not be applied to mental cognition and the like?
"What is this that is observed: that a word, even though its derivation is established elsewhere, makes that [other thing] the object of its application? To this he says: "Just as...
This is easy to understand; however, the particle *api* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), [referring to] "cowness" (*gotvam*).
Therefore, [the object] beyond that is to be seen.
Since inference has perception as its basis, perception is presented first; this is how it should be understood. For, in order to show another cause (nimitta) therein—
The word "and" (ca) conjoins perception and inference as being equal in their force.
Just as perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about the attainment of an object due to its inseparable connection with that object, so too is inference.

In the same way, inference (*anumāna*) is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about the attainment of an object that has been determined, owing to its inseparable connection with that object.
Regarding this, [the definition of] perception (*pratyakṣa*) is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpodha*) and "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*).
Here, the locative case in the word *tatra* functions as a specification within the context of the locative sense.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence: "therein" (*tatra*) refers to those two, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), which is a reference to the whole;
"perception" (*pratyakṣam*) is a reference to a single part.
Therein, the separation of the single part—the universal of perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva-jāti*)—from the whole is "selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*).
In this context, having referred to perception (*pratyakṣa*), its quality of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) and its non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*) are prescribed.

That well-known cognition which is directly manifest with respect to objects for both you and us should be regarded as endowed with the qualities of being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous;
it is impossible to express [these qualities] there because speech functions sequentially.

It is said that the sequence follows from logical necessity (*nyāyaprāptatva*), but it does not mean that even when other causes are present, an explanation must necessarily follow the order in which the terms were listed.
Having explained the term *pratyakṣa*, he now wishes to explain the term *anumāna* and first states the meaning of the word *māna*: "it is measured" (*mīyate*).
What is expressed by this word, thus etymologically derived? It is "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

By means of the instrument—that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the accomplishment of the action characterized as inference—or rather, by its designator, there is similarity (*sārūpya*).
That whose characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is its own-nature (svabhāva) is "tathā" [i.e., of such a nature].
This qualification is made by way of its being the cause (hetubhāva).
If this is so, then how is it that in some places it is said: "Inference is the cognition of the object of inference arising from a mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics"?
What contradiction is there in saying that cognition itself, characterized by similarity (*sārūpya*), will be designated in that way?
Such, then, is the means of valid cognition (*māna*).
But how is it inference (*anumāna*)? To this he says: "subsequently" (*paścāt*).
By this subsequent verse on the meaning, he demonstrates that the word *anu* forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the word *māna* according to the rule "gati-prādayaḥ.
Furthermore, it is not intended to mean "after the measure" (*mānasya paścāt*), which would have resulted in an *avyayībhāva* compound like *anuratha* and so forth.

For here, it is the means of valid cognition (*māna*) itself that is intended as occurring after the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth; it is not something that occurs after the means of valid cognition. Moreover, under the interpretation of this as an *avyayībhāva* compound, there is not only a loss of the intended meaning, but also [other defects].
However, the genitive case in the phrase "of inference" (anumānasya) would not be heard;

to the question "after what? he says: "of the mark" (liṅga). This genitive is used in connection with the word "paścāt" according to Pāṇini’s rule 2.3.30: "The sixth case ending is used with a word ending in a suffix having the sense of 'atas'."
To explain how this inference occurs subsequent to the pair [of cognitions], he says: "having been apprehended.
"Equal strength" means equal capacity.
"For the sake of attaining validity" is understood from the context of the discussion.
With the words "Just as... and so forth, he establishes this very point.
However, the fact that inference is invariably concomitant with its object should be understood as being through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).
And thus, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the capacity to lead one to the attainment [of the object], which constitutes its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).
"Delimited" means determined (*adhyavasita*).
For one who speaks thus, even perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only insofar as it brings about the apprehension of a continuum that has been determined;
since this [other cognition] is likewise [determined], how could it not be so? This is the sense.
This is also the point being demonstrated regarding their equal strength:
even for perception, its state of being invariably concomitant with the object is caused solely by the fact of its arising from that object;
and since this is the same for inference as well, there must also be equality in the cause, namely, the non-deviation from the object.
And it should not be thought: "If being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneousness is unestablished,
what other nature of perceptual cognition remains that could be restated as the referent of the word 'perception'?"

Since it is well known to everyone that a direct perceptual cognition (*sākṣātkārijñāna*) regarding objects— which conforms to the presence and absence of the sense faculties— is denoted by the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*),
this [definition] is a prescription of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) with reference to that [already established] fact.
"Free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) means that which is devoid of, or separated from, conceptual construction.

The meaning is that it is devoid of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). By this term [“non-erroneous”], the Cārvāka— who asserts that "perception alone is the single means of valid cognition" and that "the ascertainment of an object through inference is difficult to obtain"— is refuted.
And by stating that "the smallest [unit] has that same measure," the Mīmāṃsaka is also refuted.
Everywhere, this particle *iti* marks the completion of the sentence's meaning;
however, where it refers to a specific object, that very object is explicitly mentioned.
The passage beginning with "tatra" and ending with "nirdhāraṇam" is easy to understand.

It should be understood as follows: "by that" refers to the universal (jāti) called "perceptuality" (pratyakṣatva), which is established in common usage because it follows after sensory perception and the like.
The word "tatra" is used here to introduce the statement, meaning "this being the case."

Thus, by way of this sequence of restatement and injunction, whatever else has been explained by others— namely, that "the designation ‘perception’ is itself the designated object because it is free from conceptual construction, and thereby the relationship between the designation and the designated is established"— that is irrelevant to the present task of refuting misconceptions; therefore, he demonstrates that such an explanation is a misinterpretation.

As for the explanation offered by another, namely, "that direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is enjoined by way of restating (*anuvāda*) the two qualities—freedom from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*)—which are already established in other passages," that too is not tenable;

this is demonstrated as follows: for when the relationship between the definiendum (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is already established, the definiendum is to be enjoined by way of restating the definition.

However, when [the object] is not already established, the logical principle is that by means of a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), it is the definition itself that must be enjoined, not the object to be defined (*lākṣya*). Furthermore, whatever methods of support and refutation exist for the other two positions have been analyzed by the author himself in this very *Viniścayaṭīkā*, and thus are not discussed here.
He asks: how can there be a prescription of "freedom from conceptual construction" and so forth by way of restating [the property of] being direct perception?
He says: "well-known. By this, he shows that a restatement (anuvāda) is the subsequent verbal designation of something already previously established.
By prescribing that "it should be viewed in this way," he demonstrates that an injunction (*vidhi*) is the making known of what was previously unknown by means of a word.
The passage beginning with "And this is not... up to the word "iti" is easy to understand.

Furthermore, although the apprehension that conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs is not fit to be cited because it is not common to mental perception and other types of cognition, [the author] nevertheless mentions it.

It should be understood that this [definition] has been set forth for the purpose of demonstrating that which characterizes "direct perception" (pratyakṣa)— namely, the state of being a direct realization of an object—
or else for the purpose of showing its well-known status according to the traditional sequence.
For instance, first it is established that what is well-known as perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which conforms to the presence and absence of the sense faculties (*indriya*).

Subsequently, it is demonstrated that even regarding this cognition dependent on the sense faculties— which is well-known as perception for you— the sole ground for the application of the term "perception" is the direct realization of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of restating that":

since that which is "removed from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*)—meaning it is devoid of, or has departed from, conceptual construction—the term *kalpanāyā apoḍham* expresses the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), considering there to be no difference in meaning.
However, in the expression *kalpanāpoḍham*, it is not merely the past passive participle in the sense of the agent.
For if it were devoid of that [nature], there would be a contradiction with the Master’s commentary;
[rather,] it is said to be non-erroneous with respect to the nature of the thing capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).
The nature of a real entity (*vastu*) is that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*), consisting of color and the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of configuration.
In this regard, that which does not err is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
Now, is there the possibility of another cognition within a single cognition, such that this prohibition would be appropriate?

Seeing an opening for the objection that "even in conceptual cognition there is no further conceptualization, and thus it too would follow as being free from conceptualization (*kalpanāpoḍha*)," [the author] clarifies the intended meaning of this [definition] with the words "by its nature of conceptualization" (*kalpanāsvabhāvena*) and so forth. In all manuscripts of Dharmottara’s commentary, the reading found is *kalpanāsvabhāvarahitam* ("devoid of the nature of conceptualization"), and not *kalpanāsvabhāvena rahitam* ("devoid by means of the nature of conceptualization").

And by speaking thus, he shows that in the definition-statement of the Teacher, "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), this word *kalpanā* has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning; therefore, the sense is "devoid of the nature of conceptual construction" (*kalpanātvena rahitam*).

Alternatively, he shows that by means of the property (*dharmin*) called "conceptual construction," there is an indication of the property (*dharma*) known as "the appearance being capable of association with verbal expression."

This is because it coheres with the clarification that "the meaning is 'devoid of the nature of conceptual construction' (kalpanāsvabhāvarahita)" in both ways; and "conceptual construction" (kalpanā) is to be understood as that which is about to be described.

Thus, while clarifying the meaning of the word [pratyakṣa], he [Dharmottara]—on the occasion of critiquing the definition of perception according to Ācārya Dignāga, namely: "Conceptual construction is the association with name, genus, and so forth"—[proceeds as follows].

Having postulated the meaning: "That cognition which is not designated by a name, nor expressed through a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and which conforms to the distinction of its object—that is perception" (Nyāyavārttika, p. 41), [the author asks]: "Now, what meaning is denoted by the word *pratyakṣa*?"
If it is perceptible, how can it be inexpressible?
On the other hand, if it is not perceptible, then the word "perceptible" is non-denotative.
Even if it denotes the universal of perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva-sāmānya*), if it is distinct from that [particular];
It has not been stated as perception.
Now, if it is non-different [from perception],
why has it not been stated [as such]?
If that [perception] is expressed by the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), how is there no contradiction?
Or, if it is not so expressed, then its utterance is useless?
And yet, perception is designated as "free from conceptual construction."

And as for what Uddyotakara said, beginning with, "Who else besides the Venerable One is capable of making that which is not denotable [denotable]? (Nyāyavārttika, p. 41), all of that has been indicated as the mere manifestation of his poor intellect's failure to understand the meaning of words as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Here, "non-erroneousness" (*abhrāntatva*) is intended to mean non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*).

Disregarding the previous explanation that "by this, the cognition of two moons and the like is excluded, and the Yogācāra view is also included," he states the meaning of the term *abhrānta* (non-erroneous): "Non-erroneous" refers to that which is not mistaken regarding an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*). That is what is called non-erroneous.
However, one should not understand that "non-contradictory" is what is intended here; this will be clarified later.
Even a non-object is determined as being an object in reality; therefore, the qualification "capable of causal efficiency" is added.
[Objection: Then let it simply be "capable of causal efficiency. [Response: No.
This is because it is intended to make known that only that which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyākṣama) possesses the nature of a real entity (vastutva).
What is that which is capable of causal efficiency? Is it the particular (svalakṣaṇa)? Or is it the universal (sāmānya)?
Then he says, "It is something else entirely," namely: "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*).
"Configuration" (*sanniveśa*) refers to qualities such as squareness, which are properties of appearance.

That [configuration] is the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*), the qualifier, of that color—which is denoted by the word "entity"—consisting of an aggregate of atoms such as white, which has arisen in that manner; it is thus [described].

Because it is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that only a phoneme (*varṇa*) characterized by its specific arrangement (*sanniveśa*) is effective in causal action (*arthakriyā*), he says this:
"that which has that very thing as its essence" (*ātman*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is expressed as such.
And this should be understood as stated with reference to the object of visual cognition (*cākṣuṣajñāna*).
"Otherwise, there would be much that is inconsistent.
By this it is indicated that only the accumulation of atoms possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and not the whole (*avayavin*), because the latter does not exist.
It does not wander, it does not err—that is, it does not apprehend things in a manner other than they are.
It might be argued as follows: in your view, the external object is nothing other than the atom itself;
and all cognition is directed toward those most subtle atoms.
A coarse appearance arises.
How, then, can it be said that anything is non-erroneous? To this it is replied:

among atoms produced by a single causal complex, which possess distinct spatial natures, there exists no intervening space characterized by the nature of atoms of shadow or light, due to the absence of such causes.
Because [atoms] are devoid of intervals, their mere appearance as having spatial extension and as a manifestation of magnitude is nothing other than grossness itself.
In that case, how could non-conceptual consciousness—which is based on an aggregate of such atoms—be erroneous?
[It would not be erroneous] if it were to perceive each individual atom as occupying multiple locations; however, it does not perceive many [atoms] as occupying multiple locations.
One might also be mistaken in this regard if one were to perceive atoms located in different places as occupying a single location;
but this is not the case,
because there is no appearance of a mass that is even the size of a single atom.
For if only a single part were perceived, the object would appear as a mere atom and not as something occupying an extended space;
nor is the perception of many [atoms] an error,
because the cognition "that is this" arises from their identity (*tādātmya*).
This is the meaning: many such atoms, which are apprehended by a single cognition, are what is meant by "gross" (*sthūla*).
However, the notion that "this is one gross [object]" is called a property of appearance (*pratibhāsa-dharma*), because it is established on the basis of such an appearance;
it is not a property of the real entity (*vastu-dharma*).
Since [the argument] is not established for each [atom] individually, enough with this prolixity here.
But even so, how can consciousness—which perceives atoms that are mutually unconnected by nature as being connected—not be called erroneous?
To this also it is said:
What is this "non-mixture" (asaṃsṛṣṭatva) intended by you,
on account of the apprehension of which cognition is described as erroneous due to a contrary grasping?
Is it the state of having diverse forms?
Now, is it the state of being in different locations, or rather being separated by a dissimilar form, or perhaps being intermingled with an object perceivable by another sense organ?

In that case, if manifoldness is intended to mean non-conjunction, then no such thing as the apprehension of conjunction is possible, because atoms would always be apprehended as being exclusively non-conjoined,
since they appear only as having the nature of occupying distinct locations.
For if they were to appear as having a single form, [they would necessarily be conjoined].
Only a minute particle would appear;
there would not be an appearance of an extended location.

If it is intended that "occupying different locations" means being unconnected, that is even less possible, because since the blue atoms occupy different locations, they are perceived exactly as occupying different locations.
For it has been stated that if only a single part were to appear, the whole object would appear as a mere atom.

Now, if what is intended by "separated" or "unmixed" is that it is intervened by a dissimilar form (rūpa) itself, then, because that [intervention] is impossible, there can be no apprehension of the opposite.
Since blue atoms are indeed contiguous, being devoid of any intervention by other types of matter,
and they appear in such a state— because no heterogeneous atoms, such as those of light, arise in the intervening space and because none are perceived— how can there be an illusion?
Furthermore, when a shadow-atom or a light-atom is about to arise, by what is it obstructed such that it does not arise?
Nor can it be said that there is no space for another atom between two atoms,
because an atom is partless and thus has space everywhere.
This is true;
however, it is not because of a lack of opportunity that it does not arise, but rather because of the absence of its cause.
Why is there no cause?
Because there is no such thing as "svahetutva" (being its own cause), this is not even a valid objection.
Now, if "non-mixture" (*asaṃsṛṣṭatva*) is intended to mean being interspersed with tangibility and so forth, which are perceivable by different sense faculties,
then the statement that "consciousness perceives atoms in a state of mixture" would effectively mean that it perceives them as devoid of what is perceivable by other sense faculties.
And thus, there is nothing undesirable.

For even if the touch and other qualities perceivable by other sense faculties are not apprehended, the blue form itself is nonetheless apprehended as it exists in its own location and with its own nature.
Furthermore, when the intrinsic nature of things that are devoid of what is perceivable by different sense faculties is being apprehended, it does not become apprehended erroneously.
Because there is no error regarding even one of the [three factors of] place, time, or form,
and because non-apprehension is not an illusion.
But surely, there exist intervals between the atoms that consist of space?
And yet they do not appear as having intervals;
how then can this be non-perversion?
Furthermore, what is this so-called "space"?
If it is said that there is no such thing as a nature consisting of a different form,
even so, it has already been stated regarding its nature as contact and so forth; furthermore,
it is the absence of any substance possessing resistance.
Thus, space is likewise a non-entity;
consequently, when it is said that "space is the interval," there is no other distinct entity whatsoever.
And these two characteristics are for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions,
not for the purpose of excluding inference;
for [otherwise] it would have been said that there is "an interval" (antara).
Thus, it is said that atoms are without interval;
therefore, atoms that are without interval appear as being indeed without interval.
Why, then, is it said that the interval is space?
And yet, that does not appear.
For how could that which is absolutely non-existent, like the horn of a hare, ever manifest?
[Objection: But surely, even if there were no internal space (*ākāśātman*), it would follow that atoms would come into contact with one another.
This is not a fault.

We do not say that the form of atoms is one while their location is not one; rather, those [atoms] arise with distinct forms and locations, devoid of any heterogeneous form in between, and thus appear exactly in that way. So how could there be the consequence of a commingling of forms?

But surely, the color blue appears in the location of taste and so forth; therefore, how can consciousness that perceives what is not in that location as being in that location be called non-erroneous?
To this, it is said:
When a location appears, then the object that appears within that appearing location is said to be "qualified by that location.
If taste and so forth were to appear in visual consciousness, then when blue—which pervades that location—is being apprehended, the consciousness would be erroneous.
Yet, taste and so forth do not appear there.
Because it is impossible for that which is perceivable by one sense organ to appear in the cognition of another sense organ, how could there be a perception of the location of that [blue]?
For it is the blue itself appearing that constitutes the location; no other location whatsoever appears.
And when there is no appearance of what is perceivable by other sense-faculties, there is the appearance of a pure form.
Furthermore, the appearance of a pure form is itself the appearance of something continuous.
Therefore, blue atoms are perceived as being without intervals.
Therefore, blue atoms situated in their own location are apprehended by their very own nature.
Consequently, because not even one of the [three]—location, time, or form—is abandoned, the consciousness appearing as blue is indeed non-erroneous.
All of this reality of the apprehended object has been explained in detail by Dharmottara himself in the *Viniścaya*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

But if this were so, would it not follow that the Yogācāra position is not included [in the definition of non-erroneousness], since all consciousness belonging to one who is not omniscient is erroneous with respect to its object because it proceeds in the form of apprehended and apprehender?
If you ask, "In that case, why is the previous explanation not disregarded? [the answer follows].
It is said:
this definition does not belong to the Yogācāra system,
but rather to the Sautrāntika system alone.
Furthermore, it is not possible to apply everything [from the Abhidharma] to the Vijñānavāda,
because it is impossible to apply such statements as "its object is the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If one asks, "What then is the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) in that system?"
It is simply the state of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*).

If it is asked how the exclusion of [erroneous perceptions such as] a double moon is achieved, there is no fault, because the intention is that correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is precisely what is thus [free from conceptual construction].
Why would this not also be the case in the Sautrāntika system?
If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) is therefore redundant,
this is true;
however, it will be explained solely for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions.

Regarding what was explained by previous [scholars]—namely, that "the term 'non-erroneous' (abhrānta) is for the purpose of excluding the cognition of those with ophthalmia and the like, while the phrase 'free from conceptual construction' (kalpanāpoḍha) is for the purpose of excluding inference"—he speaks [in the following verse], clearly setting aside that [explanation]: "And this...
The particle "ca" (and) is used here for emphasis.
It should be understood that what follows is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions;
it negates the intention of the predecessors.
The word "but" (na tu) serves to distinguish [the author's view from theirs].
Now, why is it said that [the statement] "it is not for the purpose of excluding inference" is made,
given that each [of the three marks] individually excludes inference? To this,
it is replied:
"The two characteristics" refers to the inclusion of both for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions;
since the exclusion of [other means of knowledge] such as inference is established by each one individually, this is the collective result.
Therefore, the phrase "not for the sake of excluding inference" is negated with emphasis, meaning it is not *only* for the sake of excluding inference.
If, however, the inference being formulated is intended to exclude [the definition] due to a desire to refute misconceptions, then the two [conditions] are not for that purpose alone.
But surely, these two characteristics were not explained by the predecessors as being for the purpose of excluding inference;
rather, it was only the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) [that was so explained].
The inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), however, is for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as that of two moons;
how then could it be for the purpose of excluding inference? Thus [it is said].
(DhPr p. 45)
By the very inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), inference is already excluded.

In that case, if the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) were not included, then the perception of a tree while walking and so forth would be [considered] direct perception because it is free from conceptual construction. Since one who acts based on that obtains the tree itself, it would be valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*) due to its correspondence with reality.
Furthermore, there might be the suspicion that [the definition] "perception is free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) is insufficient;
to exclude that, the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) is included.
For that [cognition], being erroneous, is not perception.
Furthermore, because it lacks being produced by a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*), it is not inference (*anumāna*);
nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is stated that the perception of trees moving and so forth is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
If it is argued that "inference is established by the very inclusion of the term 'free from conceptual construction' (*kalpanāpoḍha*)," this is true;
however, if the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) were solely for the purpose of exclusion, then it would logically serve only to exclude inference.
But it is not for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as that of two moons,
since their exclusion is established by the very fact that this [definition] occurs within the context of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*).
For, having introduced that "correct cognition is of two kinds," this definition being prescribed is indeed prescribed within that specific context.

"Now, this being the case, since [the definition] is already fulfilled by the phrase 'free from conceptual construction' (*kalpanāpoḍha*) alone, the inclusion of the term 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*) is superfluous.
This is another fault they find;
however, Dharmottara’s intention is that it is not appropriate [to claim] that this [term] is intended for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as those of a double moon.
If this term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) were not included, one might ask: "What is the purpose of it? To this he says: "In that case...

[referring to the verse]. Now, one might object: since even the perception of trees while moving is excluded from being "correct cognition" precisely because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādaka*) despite being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), its exclusion is already established; so what is the point of the word "non-erroneous"?
To this he replies: "For from that... [referring to the following verse].
"Merely a tree" is [an example of] being undetermined by movement;
"iti" is used here in the sense of a reason.
Let there be right knowledge (samyagjñāna).
But how can there be the possibility of its being perception?

For one might suspect that what is right knowledge is not necessarily perception; anticipating this, he states what was previously mentioned by way of a further application: "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*).
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction with respect to its quality of being non-contradictory (*saṃvādakatva*).
This shows the nature of the doubt regarding the particle *iti*;
and this doubt should be understood as being based on reasoning.
Alternatively, the word *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*ādare*).
This suspicion would arise if the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) were not included;

for if it were included even though [the term "non-erroneous"] is already present, one might ask, "What is the use of this? To which he replies: "For the purpose of excluding that" (*tannivṛttyarthaṃ*), meaning solely for the purpose of removing that suspicion.
By this, he shows that although, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), such cognitions are already excluded by virtue of the context being correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Nevertheless, for the sake of directly refuting the disagreement of those who maintain that there is partial correspondence (*aṃśasaṃvāda*), the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) must indeed be made.

One might object: "What is added by the inclusion of 'non-erroneous,' such that it serves to refute this disagreement? To address this doubt, it should be understood that even [cognitions] such as the perception of moving trees while standing at a distance are stated to be false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*).
By the word *iti*, he expresses the manner [in which something was] stated;
it means "stated" or "revealed" by virtue of the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous," according to the context.
When there is the expectation of the question, "From what [source] was that false cognition stated?", one should connect it with the word "that" (*tat*) mentioned first.
Since this is so, the meaning is as follows: because that [cognition] is erroneous due to seeing a moving tree and so forth, it is not perception;
therefore, by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), it is stated that it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
Let it be that it is not perception because of its erroneous nature; [but what of it?]

If, however, it were of the nature of inference (*anumāna*), then how could its being such [i.e., direct perception] not be precluded? To this doubt, the word "and" (*ca*) should be applied, meaning "because it is not inference.
Why is it not inference?
Because it does not arise from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*).

If one should object: "Even if this is so, it will still be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); how then can it be false knowledge?"—then the following must be stated in response to that doubt.
Since there is no other means of valid cognition for that [object] than the navel (the central channel),
it lacks the intrinsic nature of being perceptible and so forth;
or rather, the meaning is "because of the inclusion of the term 'non-erroneous' (abhrānta)" in this context.

Now, if the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) were to function in the refutation of [the validity of] inference and the like, then it would indeed possess the capacity to designate them as false cognitions; however,
since the existence of inference and so forth has already been excluded by their own internal logical inconsistency, how could they be "non-erroneous"?
If it is asked, "If it is false cognition, how is it that a tree is obtained from it?",
[the answer is: no tree is obtained from it.
For a tree is delimited by its movement across various locations, and yet a tree is apprehended as restricted to a single location; therefore,
the tree is seen exactly as it was observed while moving.
That which is seen is not obtained; and that place which is obtained has not been seen. Therefore, no object whatsoever is obtained from that [perception].
Rather, an object such as a tree is obtained only through another cognition.
Thus, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is for the purpose of eliminating misconceptions.

Likewise, by means of the inclusion of "non-erroneous," the inclusion of "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is also excluded from inference; this is stated for the purpose of refuting misconceptions.
By this inclusion, it is said that [perception] is knowledge that is non-conceptual.
True;

however, it should be understood that by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), which provides assistance through the refutation of the nature [of perception as being] inference and so forth, it is stated that such [cognition] is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
Now, one might object: should not the non-perceptual status of that which lacks the definition of perception be demonstrated?

If it is asked, "Why has the refutation of its being of the nature of inference and so forth been made when it is irrelevant to the present topic?"—the answer is: what harm is there in having done so as a secondary consequence (*prasaṅga*) in demonstrating that it is not perception?
The passage beginning with "yadi" and so forth is easy to understand.
It is said that "only from that" [the tree] is perceived as delimited by a false cognition consisting in the sight of a tree passing by;
it is called a "tree" because it appears as a tree, yet even while appearing thus, it is not actually a tree.
The phrase "restricted to one part" is stated with reference to the ultimate tree that is to be reached.
"For what reason? means: for that reason just mentioned above.
[Objection: But even from that [reason], there is the attainment of a tree which possesses a form capable of performing causal functions such as providing shade; so how can this be denied?
He says: "From another cognition"—that is, from another cognition consisting of the appearance of a stationary tree, which arises from approaching that location.
In this context, the false cognition is merely the cause for the activity of the seeker, but it does not bring about the attainment of the tree; such is the summary meaning.

If the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is for the purpose of establishing that [perception] is not false cognition, then it is not for the purpose of refuting conflicting views; thus he says: "In this way" (*evam*).
By the word "in this way," the form of the method of reasoning just mentioned is indicated.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: "in this way," by means of the method of reasoning just stated.
The term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is included for the purpose of excluding the contradictory cognition that [perception] is of such a nature [as conceptual].
If this is so, then it is the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" alone that serves to refute the misconception,
and not the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
And having raised the doubt that these two [terms] were stated for the purpose of excluding those [two types of error], he says: "In the same way" (*tathā*).
The meaning is: just as the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) was used, so too is this [term "conceptual"] used.

This is for the purpose of refuting a misconception; for some maintain that even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises subsequent to perception is a form of perception, on the grounds that it is non-erroneous according to the conventional determination of worldly people.
It should be understood that this is for the purpose of refuting that [view].

In that regard, if the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) were not included, then cognitions such as "this is a jar" would be perception because they are non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).

For one who acts based on such [cognition], an object such as a jar is attained; thus, because it is consistent (*saṃvādaka*), it would be correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), and because it is non-erroneous, it would follow that it is perception—this is the objection.
To exclude that [possibility],
it is not perception because its nature is conceptual construction,
and it is not inference because it lacks being produced from a logical mark possessing the three characteristics.
Inference is indeed non-erroneous because it functions by determining its own appearance— which is not an external object— to be an object;
perception, however, is not mistaken regarding the form that is its apprehended object.
However, it is not the case that "non-contradictory" and "non-erroneous" must be understood here [as separate qualifiers];
for in this context, perception is precisely right cognition (*samyagjñāna*), and nothing else.
Since non-contradiction is already established by the very fact of being right cognition, the further inclusion of the term "non-contradictory" would indeed be purposeless.
For the meaning of the sentence would be this: that cognition called "perception" which is non-contradictory is [both] free from conceptual construction and non-contradictory.
And there is no purpose served by this double mention of "non-contradictory.

Therefore, it should be understood here that "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) refers to that which is not mistaken regarding the nature of the real thing (vastu-rūpa) in its apprehended form, which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā-kṣama).

Furthermore, as to what kind of conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is intended here, he says: "Conceptualization is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with a verbal expression" (I-5). [This begins with] the words "verbal expression," etc.

That by which something is expressed is "expression" (*abhilāpa*), meaning the expressive word. The "association with expression" (*abhilāpasaṃsarga*) is the association within a single cognition between the form of the signified object and the form of the signifier, both existing as objective aspects (*grāhyākāra*).
[31] *Abhilāpe*ti—[Note: the phrase "abhilāpetyādi" does not exist in E.P.; it is found in A.B.H.N.]
And there is no other means of valid cognition [to confirm it];
therefore, it must be stated and applied, as before, that the cognition "this is a jar" and so forth is an incorrect cognition (*asamyagjñāna*).
But how can this [cognition] be an incorrect cognition when it is consistent with reality (*saṃvādin*)?

Even if it lacks the status of incorrect cognition characterized by non-conformity [with reality], why is its status as incorrect cognition—not consisting in the absence of the function of an instrument due to the lack of apprehension of a previously unknown object—not admitted, as is the case with memory and the like?
If it is argued that this [cognition] which grasps an object qualified by universals (jāti) and so forth does possess the apprehension of a previously unknown object; [we reply:]...
Since this has been refuted at length elsewhere, let it rest for now.
However, we shall analyze the true meaning of the passage beginning with "its own appearance" (*svapratibhāsa*), as we intend to explain the words that refute misconceptions regarding the object.
For the moment, having disregarded the interpretations of previous [commentators] due to seeing their flaws, he explains the meaning of "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in another way.

In order to perform that which was stated [by the Teacher] word-for-word, which is their intended meaning and possesses an unerring sense, he says "but not" (na tu), explicitly prohibiting what had previously been prohibited by implication; here,
"but" (tu) denotes an emphasis.
The passage beginning with "yataḥ" and ending with "veditavyam" is easy to understand.
If conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consists in the association of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, then that [construction] is impossible precisely because universals and the like do not exist.

Now, if cognition proceeding by way of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then all cognition of one who is not omniscient proceeds in that manner;
what, then, remains that could be non-conceptual? With this intention, he asks about the nature of conceptual construction: "Of what kind?"—he asks this in general terms.
"Punar" means specifically;
"iha" refers to the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Abhilāpa" is that by which something is expressed or spoken; it is the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*).
And that "conjoining" (saṅkenta) means meeting.
Therefore, when the forms of both the signifier and the signified are present together within a single cognition, then the signifier and the signified become conjoined.
That cognition in which there appears an image of the denotable object that is capable of being associated with verbal expression is described as such.
In that regard, some cognition possesses an appearance conjoined with verbal expression;
for example, the conceptualization of the object "jar" by one who has mastered linguistic conventions has an appearance conjoined with the word "jar."
However, there is a certain [cognition] which, although not actually conjoined with verbal expression, possesses an appearance capable of being conjoined with verbal expression;
this is the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of a child who has not yet mastered linguistic conventions.

In that case, if conceptualization were defined merely as "an appearance conjoined with verbal expression," the conceptualization of one who has not mastered linguistic conventions would not be included.
However, when "fitness" (*yogya*) is included in the definition, that [conceptualization] is also subsumed;
for although the conceptualization of a newborn infant on that very day does not have an appearance mixed with verbal expression,
it certainly has an appearance that is fit for association with verbal expression.
And that which is associated with verbal expression is also capable;

therefore, both are included by the term "capable" (*yogya*). The object of expression (*vācya*) is the form of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*), which has been brought to a state of identity with the color seen at a particular time, or which appears as such [a representation].
He states the analysis (*vigraha*) of this term together with the word *saṃsarga*: "by means of expression" (*abhilāpena*).
Connection (*saṃsarga*) is the relation (*sambandha*) with the speaker (*vādaka*). The compound is formed by the rule of separation (*yogavibhāga*) in Pāṇini 2.1.30, which governs the third case.
Alternatively, this has been provided as an explanation of the meaning;
however, the compound should be understood as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*).
To the question, "How, moreover, is a connection between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) possible?", he says: "In one [thing]."
It must be stated that "meeting by way of the form of the apprehended" means "abiding as the form of the apprehended within a single cognition.

That is to say, if the form of the object (*artha*) becomes mounted upon a single cognition together with the form of the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*), then there is a conjunction between the signified and the signifier.
Let it be granted, then, that the forms of the expression and the expressed are mounted upon a single cognition.

Anticipating the objection— "To what extent do the signifier and the signified become connected as the denoter and the denoted, such that the cognition grasping them would be conceptual (savikalpaka)?"— the author states "tataḥ" by way of a conclusion:
when two things appear as having such-and-such forms and are presented [to consciousness], then they are "intermingled," meaning they are connected as being of that nature.

The point is that the apprehension of the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakatva*) for these two occurs precisely through the manifestation of their forms as the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) within a single cognition.
This [definition], "capable of being associated with a verbal expression" (*abhilāpasaṃsargayogya*), has been provided as an explanation of the meaning;
however, the compound should rather be understood as "capable of association with a verbal expression."

Since a compound involving a dative of purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*) occurs only when there is a relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*), one might object: "If that is so, let it simply be 'an appearance associated with verbal expression' (*abhilāpa-saṃsṛṣṭa-pratibhāsa*); what is the use of including the term 'capable' (*yogya*)? Anticipating this criticism, he begins to demonstrate how [the term] is effective: "In that case" (*tatra*) serves as an introductory phrase for the sentence.
That which has an appearance mixed with verbal expression is "thus" (tathā).
To the question "Of what [is this] like?", he says: "Just as" (yathā).
This refers to the cognition that relies upon both aspects: "This is the denotable (vācya) of this," and "This is the denoter (vācaka) of this."
If it is asked, "In the absence of a connection with verbal expression, how is fitness determined? [the answer is:
because its manifestation is not restricted.
Furthermore, there is no fixed appearance because of the absence of a cause for the restriction of appearance.
For an apprehended object, in producing consciousness, would produce it with a restricted appearance;
just as form, in producing visual consciousness, produces it with a restricted appearance.
The conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*), however, does not arise from external objects;
therefore, because it lacks a cause for the restriction of its appearance, its appearance is unrestricted.
Conventional designation (*saṅketa*) consists either in the application of words to objects or in the nature of the causal relationship between the understanding [of a word] and its employment.
One by whom the convention (*saṃketa*) has been mastered and understood is "one who has mastered the convention" (*vyutpannasaṃketa*).

If for such a person every [word] were of that nature, then one could not say "some [particular one]"; furthermore, if the term "capable" (*yogya*) were used, nothing would be gained. Therefore, he says "some" (*kācid*).
The particle *tu* indicates that the cognition of one who has mastered linguistic convention is distinct from the cognition of a child;
he states this by saying "like what" (*yathā*) to show with what [cognition] it is comparable.
The suffix *-kan* in the word *bālaka* is used in the sense of smallness (*alpa*).

If it is argued that even by defining [cognition] as "that which appears as conjoined with verbal expression," cognitions of such a kind are included, then what is the point of including the term "capable" (*yogya*)? To this he says: "In that case.
Between those two, that cognition of one for whom the linguistic convention has not yet arisen is not included.
He states when it is indeed subsumed: "abhilāpa... (by verbal expression).

Since this [conceptualization] consists in the manifestation of an object, it is said that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is a cognition whose appearance is conjoined with verbal expression; the meaning is that this occurs when there is speech.
By the statement "iti" (thus), its formal aspect (*ākāra*) is described.
First, this fault exists even if [the object] is absent;
but if, even when there is a capable apprehension, it is not included therein, then what is the use of that? To this he says: "capable" (*yogya*).
The particle *tu* indicates the distinction from the state of non-production.
The word "also" (api) implies that it is not only [the cognition] appearing as mixed with that [object];
for such an ordinary person, conceptual construction is established by inference.
Therefore, the point is that it must necessarily be apprehended.

But how, then, is she included by the mention of "the fit" (yogya)? He says: "Even though... This collection of particles (*nipātasamudāya*) is used everywhere to signify the acceptance of a specific qualification.
It is likewise [to be understood] as "one whose birth (*janman*) occurred during the day."

Just as one says "born on the day" or "produced on the day," so too should it be understood as "of one born this very day" (*aharjātasya*). If this is so, how is that [convention] included for one who has mastered linguistic conventions? To this he says: "And which... (*yā ca*).
And [the word] "ca" (and) is used for conjunction with respect to what precedes;
the sense is: if it were not capable of contact with that, how could it experience contact with it?
Since this is so, therefore...

Is it not the case that, since the appearance is already perceived, one must postulate a capacity (*yogyatā*) on the grounds that the experience of its association [with a word] would otherwise be inexplicable?
