And yet, there is no association with verbal expression in the conceptualization of an infant, because of their lack of proficiency in linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
With the intention of asking how capacity (*yogyatā*) could be postulated, he raises the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "non-existent" (*asatī*) and so forth.
Having thus raised the objection, thinking that it is established through inference (*anumāna*), he states the proof: "unrestricted" (*aniyata*).
The meaning is: because of the absence of a specifically determined form (*pratiniyatākāra*).

Since the subject under discussion (*prakaraṇāpanna*) is established and the reason (*hetu*) has been stated, the formulation of the proof (*sādhanaprayoga*) is easily accomplished; therefore, he did not state the formal argument (*prayoga*).

This same intention should be understood to apply to the subsequent cases as well when only the reason is mentioned. However, the formal argument should be formulated here in this way: "That conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which has an indeterminate appearance..."
That [conceptualization] is capable of being associated with words, just like the conceptualization of a student.
But how is the conceptualization of an infant established, such that these subsequent [arguments] and their constituent proofs would not be unestablished in their locus (*āśrayāsiddha*)?
This is not a fault.

Having taken as the subject (*dharmin*) the conceptual construction established by inference—because it is intended as the appropriation of these [elements]—it should be understood that this inference was not explicitly set forth because it is easily known. It should be viewed in this way: whatever purposeful activity of a living being occurs in a particular instance, [is preceded by a cognition].
That [activity] is preceded by conceptual construction (vikalpa),

just as the activity of one who has mastered linguistic convention regarding objects such as food is. Furthermore, the child’s activity directed toward the breast and so forth— characterized by a restriction that excludes everything else— is a logical reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).
And since such an activity is apprehended through perception, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required for its own establishment.
Why, then, does conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) not arise from objects? Because it is independent of the presence of objects.
For even an infant, as long as it does not recognize the breast currently being seen as "this is that very same one" by means of its prior perception, will not cease crying; however,
one should not think that a proof for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has been set forth here by the phrase "even an infant" and so forth.

As explained by others, this is because that treatise is intent on demonstrating the establishment of independence from the proximity of external objects. But is it not the case that, due to its being beyond direct perception, there is a doubt regarding its having an indefinite manifestation; thus, this reason is "unestablished through doubt" (sandigdhāsiddha)?
He says: "And [there is] the state of having an indefinite appearance"—here, *ca* (and) has the sense of *yasmāt* (because).
The restriction (*niyama*) of the appearance—that is, of the form of cognition—is that this must be either the form of an object or the form of a word.
Whether its nature consists solely in the form of color (*rūpa*) or solely in the form of taste (*rasa*), its cause—that which produces it—is absent;
because of that absence, there is no arising.
"Existence" (*bhāva*) means arising (*utpāda*); by negating that, "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*).

If one were to explain [the phrase] "due to the absence of a cause for the restriction of appearance" as "because it does not exist," then, according to the literal text, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*).

On the other hand, if the statement of the reason were formulated otherwise, the reason would remain unexpressed with respect to that object. Furthermore, Dharmottara’s style is observed here to consist merely in stating the essential nature of the proof (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, how could the prima facie argument—that conceptual construction does not arise from objects—not be well-founded? And if one were to justify all of this by saying that [the object] dies and is reborn in some way or another, it would indicate a lack of skill on the part of the speaker.
[Objection: Surely there will be some cause for the restriction of the appearance in that case.
Now, [the opponent] objects that this [definition] is too narrow;
therefore, he says "grāhya" (to be grasped) so that it may be understood from what source its non-arising constitutes suchness (*tathātva*).
For if it were simply stated as "an object" (*artha*), then since the sense faculty (*indriya*) also produces cognition, it too would possess the capacity to determine the form [of the cognition].
Nor has its status as the cause of a specific form been established by way of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*);

rather, it is established as the cause for the specific determination of the apprehension of the object. Thus, there is the "apprehension of the graspable" (*grāhya-grahaṇa*). The graspable is the objective support (*ālambana*).
If this is so, let it simply be "the apprehendable" (grāhya). Even for an exclusion (apoha), there is the status of being apprehendable;
yet it is not the cause for the restriction of appearance.
Therefore, in order to exclude that [non-existent], it is established that "an object is that which is capable of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāsamartha*).
It "would act" means it is able to act;
for, by way of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), its capacity is ascertained to reside in that very [object].
An illustration of this is as follows:

"having a determinate appearance" means that, while setting aside the form of the word, it maintains only the form of the object—just as, while setting aside the form of taste, it maintains only the form of visible matter.
If this is so, then even the conceptual construction of a child will arise from the object itself.

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, there will be a determinate manifestation," he recalls what was stated previously by way of a logical consequence (prasaṅga), beginning with the words "vikalpa" (conceptual construction).
The particle *tu* distinguishes this from the cognition previously cited.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) should be formulated as follows: whatever cognition does not arise from an object does not possess a determinate manifestation.
Just as there is recollection of the past and so forth for one who is proficient in linguistic convention, or a synthetic cognition of color, taste, and so on; yet,
no conceptual construction arises in an infant from the object itself— this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Now, since the conceptual construction of a fool is imperceptible, its arising or non-arising cannot be ascertained; therefore,

intending to object that this reason is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*), he asks "Whence?"— this is a question regarding the general reason— and again [he asks], "How?"— this is regarding the specific [reason].
And this use of *kim* in the sense of reproach (*kṣepa*) occurs through the expression *vidarbhya*.
Therefore, the meaning is: "this [is not so] for any reason whatsoever.
He states the reason: "because of the object" (*arthāt*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) should be stated as follows: That cognition which, in its own production, is independent of the presence of an object, does not arise from that object;

for example, the consciousness of one who has mastered linguistic conventions regarding an object that perished long ago. And the conceptualizing consciousness of a child is independent of the presence of an object. This is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
In order to refute this lack of proof (*asiddhi*), he composes an introductory section and says: "For even a child... and so forth;
[he] applies his mouth to the breast.
A cognition that unifies an object previously seen with one seen later has a non-present object, because the state of having been previously seen is not present;
and that which has a non-present object is independent of the actual object.
Furthermore, because there is no cause for a restriction in its appearance, it has an unrestricted appearance;
and such [an appearance] is capable of being associated with verbal expression.
The word "also" (api) indicates that this is not only the case for one who is proficient [in language].
"Since" (hir) means "because.
"Yāvat" is a particle used in the sense of a limit.
"The state of having been previously seen" (pūrvadṛṣṭatva) means being an object of previous perception.
By this, he describes the nature of the reflective recognition (*pratyavamarṣa*) that "this very thing is that which was previously apprehended by me as the cause for the cessation of hunger.
He does not merely reflect; he recognizes (*pratyabhijānāti*).
The word *tāvat* is used here to indicate a limit.
Because weeping has ceased, he, being such [a person], does not cry;
for it is understood that by all people, within their own mental continuum, this and other such linguistic conventions arise due to the cause of unifying the past and present perceptions.
Moreover, this is because such [unification] is not observed even when a clod of earth or similar object is presented elsewhere.
But surely, because the organs of a child are not yet mature and because he has not grasped linguistic conventions, even a word in the form of internal discourse is impossible for him;
or, if it were possible, the apprehension of the object would be useless.
So how can it be said that "as long as he does not reflect thus"? It is replied: it is so said.
For indeed, there exists a certain distinct state of unification between that which has been seen and that which is being seen, which is presented as the cause in that context;
and when this state is communicated by means of a word, it is communicated by that very word through repeated practice,
yet it is not said that one reflects upon it in that very same way [as the word itself].

Now, it may be granted that at the time of seeing [the breast] for the second time and so forth, there is the "offering of the face" (*mukhārpaṇa*) through the unification of what was previously seen and what is now being seen; but how can this be after falling to the ground?
For he certainly did not see the breast before, such that he could unify it with what is currently being seen by means of that prior vision and thus offer it.
In that case, we say it is due to experience in another birth;
even in that birth, it is by the power of experience in yet another birth.
And since saṃsāra has no beginning, what loss is there?
If it is argued: "The form of sound also certainly exists there; so what is the use of this effort to make the apprehension of the capable [object] effective? [We reply:
Let it be that the form of sound is latent there due to practice in another life.
Furthermore, let it not be that there is a manifestation of an object conjoined with a distinct word for one who will later acquire proficiency;
such [a cognition] is not called a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*).
Let him then recognize the breast as "this is that very same [breast]" by way of its having been previously perceived.
He asks, "What follows from this? and replies: "The previously seen and the subsequently seen. This is a dvandva compound treated as a singular.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis and should be understood as following the word *kurvan*.
Alternatively, the suffix *śatṛ* is used in the sense of a causal reason (*hetau*).
Thus, the meaning is this: because it unifies [the present object] with that which was previously perceived, it therefore has an object that is not present.
To the question, "Even while performing [this unification], how can it have an object that is not present?", he says: "[Because of] the state of having been previously perceived."
This is the intended meaning: being the object of a previous perception is what is called "having been previously perceived.
Once that previous perception has ceased, the thing no longer possesses the status of being the object of that previous perception.

Thus, by means of a cognition occurring at a later time, the thing is seen as having the status of being the object of a previous cognition, even though that status is not actually present [at that later time].
"Let it be that [the cognition] has a non-proximate object; however, how is it established that it is independent of the proximity of the object? To this he says: "asannihita... (non-proximate).
The word "ca" (and) means "because."
"Having a non-proximate object" means being independent of the proximity of an object. By this, he states the reason for its independence from the proximity of an object.
Such a formal argument (*prayoga*) should be understood as follows: whatever cognition has a non-proximate object is independent of the proximity of an object.
Just as the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of people like us has the past and future as its objects;
and because it is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) by virtue of having been previously seen, the cognition of a child has an object that is not present—this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In all editions of Dharmottara’s work, the reading is "of what was previously seen" (*pūrvadṛṣṭasya*).
However, the reading following the *Pradīpa* has been adopted here.

Now, for the sake of the students' easy comprehension, he demonstrates how the establishment of each preceding reason occurs upon the establishment of each subsequent reason: "and independent" (*anapekṣam*).
Sensory consciousness, however, depends upon the object because it grasps only that object which is present;
and because the object is the cause for the restriction of its appearance, it possesses a restricted appearance.
Therefore, it is not capable of being associated with verbal expression.
For this very reason, even though one might admit that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is both the signified and the signifier, this [perception] is said to be non-conceptual.
For even if the particular characteristic alone were both the signified and the signifier, a cognition of an object associated with verbal expression would still be conceptual.
Furthermore, sensory consciousness is non-conceptual because its appearance is restricted by the object and thus does not possess an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression.

In that case, auditory cognition— which grasps the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound— would have an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression, since some specific characteristics of sound are the signified and others are the signifier.
And thus it would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
This is not a fault;

for even though there exists a relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is apprehended as having been perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).

Now, if "having an indeterminate appearance" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), why is "independence from the object" the reason (*hetu*), such that it is said, "being thus real, it has an indeterminate appearance"? And how is the intermediate passage, beginning with "because of the cause for the restriction of appearance," to be understood? It is replied:
this [passage] beginning with "not independent" is not to be understood as a single syntactical unit.
What then? A split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) must be made here.

And in that context, "since" (*yataḥ*) means "because. [The term] *anapekṣam* means being independent of the proximity of an object. [The phrase] "not arisen because of the cause for the restriction of appearance" means "due to the absence of the cause for the restriction of appearance"; having made this split in the sentence by the force of this implication, [the meaning follows].
Therefore, since there is no cause for a restriction of manifestation and because [the object] does not arise, it should be construed as having an unrestricted manifestation (*aniyata-pratibhāsa*).
The word "such" (*tādṛśam*) means "non-manifestation" (*apratibhāsa*); and the particle "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "moreover" (*vaktavyam*) or "this is so."
Since someone might occasionally suspect that all of this [applies] even to sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), he says "sensory... in order to refute that;
the particle *tu* distinguishes conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) from it, because the latter possesses a determinate manifestation.

Here, previous commentators have explained: "Because it is impossible to apply a convention to a particular (svalakṣaṇa) due to its lack of causal capacity and its uniqueness, there is no relationship between the denotable and the denoter; and because it apprehends a particular that is neither denotable nor denoter, sensory cognition is non-conceptual.
This [explanation], however, is flawed.

Thinking that the state of being non-conceptual can be easily established even otherwise, so what is the use of introducing the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which is irrelevant to the present context, he says: "For this very reason.
Because sensory cognition has a restricted manifestation—for this very reason, for this cause alone—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) will have its definition stated later.
The word *api* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
To explain how it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) when there is the apprehension of an object of expression (*vācyagrahaṇa*), he says: "Even though... (*yady api hi*).
The collection of particles *yady api hi* functions in the sense of the word "even if" (*yadi nāma*).
Or rather, "hi" is a mere rhetorical ornament.
Consciousness, when associated with verbal expression, becomes conceptual (*vikalpaka*).

By speaking thus, the intention is this: even if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to exist as a denotable object through the purification of the internal organ (*koṣṭha*), nevertheless, that sensory cognition reflects only the particular characteristic within itself.
But since it does not grasp the signifier either, how could it appropriate for itself the nature of conceptualization, which consists in the appearance of an object conjoined with verbal expression?
For the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) would have to be grasped as both the signified and the signifier.
Furthermore, the state of being an object of perception existing at the time of the convention does not belong to the entity now;
for just as the perception existing at the time of the convention is incompatible with the present, so too the status of being its object no longer belongs to the thing now.

Therefore, auditory cognition, not perceiving the state of having been seen at a prior time, does not grasp the relationship between the signifier and the signified; rather, it grasps the relationship between the expressed and the expresser.

By this very same logic, even the cognition of a yogi, despite being illuminated by all words and their objects, is non-conceptual because it does not grasp [the object] as having been produced at the time of linguistic convention.
Let it be that sensory cognition has form and so forth as its objective support.
Because the denoter does not appear [in sensory cognition] while only the denoted appears, it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).

However, intending to object that the sensory cognition in which both of these appear would necessarily be conceptual (*vikalpaka*) because both appear, he asks: "The auditory... and so forth. [This refers to] the case where there is no impairment of the sense organ.
The meaning is that this [position]—that all sensory cognition is non-conceptual—is not acceptable.
The connection is as follows: auditory cognition would have an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Of what nature is it? It is that which grasps the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound.
The meaning is that because this [cognition] is qualified by being the cause [of the cognition of the object], it grasps the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the word.

To the question, "Even for one who grasps the word, if the denoted object is not grasped, how can it be so [i.e., a means of valid cognition]? he says: "[It is] with regard to the word" (*śabda-*)—the particle *ca* (and) is used in the sense of "because."
Something is the signifier (*vācaka*) and something is the signified (*vācya*).
For example, [the rule] "The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.22) and so forth exists in the mind.
*Iti* means "therefore."
"Let there be such an appearance; what follows from this? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

This being so—that is, when that aforementioned state exists—it should be viewed as follows: when by one [word] the two technical terms *tarap* and *tamap* are uttered as the designata (*saṃjñin*), at that very time another [word], namely *ghaḥ*, is somehow uttered as the designation (*saṃjñā*).

In that case, for a person perceiving those two [the past convention and the present object] through a single auditory cognition, it would follow that the auditory intellect is conceptual (*vikalpikā*).

How, then, is this fault avoided? He says: "Even though... The word "and" (*ca*) means "because"; for that very thing which was grasped at the time of the linguistic convention is what is grasped here in this manner.
If it is argued that "let it be so," and that [the word] is apprehended as having been seen at the time of the convention, he says: "And not...
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis or to indicate a reason.
By stating "being an object of perception," he explains the meaning of the term "having been previously seen."
He asks, "How is it that it does not exist? and replies with the word "yathā" (just as).
The particle "hi" is used in the sense of "because.
The word "arthasya" refers to that which is currently being perceived.

The sense is that, in the absence of that [subsequent cognition], the persistence of the previous perception would follow by the logic of being dragged along by a fetter. Anticipating the objection—"Let us grant that those two words being apprehended were seen at the time of the convention; nevertheless, why does that cognition not grasp the relationship between the signifier and the signified?"—the author concludes by saying "tataḥ" (therefore).
Since the denoted and the denoter are grasped as being the very time of the convention, for that reason auditory cognition does not grasp the relationship between the denoted and the denoter.
Let it be so for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) being grasped in that way;
what follows from this? [The opponent] says "previously," meaning: "This [cognition] will again grasp this [object] in exactly that same way."
The meaning is that because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), there is no apprehension of [the object] as having been seen at a prior time.
This might be argued: "Neither the object nor the word will be apprehended as being something previously seen through convention;
nevertheless, they will be apprehended as denoting a qualified [object] and as being the denotator of a qualified object."
This is incorrect.

For those who speak thus intend this: that object which was perceived at the time of the convention by a cognition and is not identified with the form associated with a particular word is not grasped by that [cognition] as being denotable by that word.

Likewise, when a cow is not perceived as being identical with the form of a horse—which was associated with the word "horse" at the time of the convention and is apprehended by the cognition of a cow—the cow is not grasped as being denotable by the word "horse. Furthermore, it is not made one with that form which was associated with the sound "gha" at the time of the convention and is apprehended by auditory cognition. In that case, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) regarding [the suffixes] *tarap* and *tamap*.
Similarly, by whichever cognition a given word [is apprehended],...

Perception is that cognition which is devoid of that [conceptual construction], and which is not affected by delusions caused by cataracts, rapid motion, spinning, traveling in a boat, or physical agitation.

(I-6) The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: that cognition which is devoid of—that is, empty of—that conceptual construction, being of the nature of conceptualization, and which is non-erroneous, is perception.

To show that "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) and "non-erroneousness" (*abhrāntatva*) constitute the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) only when they are mutually dependent, and not individually, it is stated: "that [cognition] devoid of those two is perception. Thus, it is shown that the two definitions, being mutually dependent, have perception as their common object. It is not identified with the form associated with an object perceived at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*).
It is not by that [auditory cognition] that the word is apprehended as denoting that object.

Just as the word "cow" (go-śabda), which is not perceived as being identical with the word "horse" (aśva-śabda)—which was perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) and is associated with the object "horse"—is not apprehended as denoting the object "horse"; and just as it is not made one with the phonetic form associated with the meanings of the suffixes *-tarap* and *-tamap* through auditory cognition, then the word "gha" is likewise [not so apprehended]. Thus, that very same lack of proof is refuted by experience.
And since a real relationship has been refuted, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

When there is a grasping [of an object] as having been previously perceived, that cognition—being a manifestation of an object associated with verbal expression—is indeed of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus everything is clear.

Just as it was argued that auditory cognition possesses a manifestation capable of being associated with verbal expression, so too can this be argued for the cognition of a yogin; therefore, extending (*atidiśan*) this very same rebuttal to that case as well:
He says: "By this.

According to this principle—that a cognition which does not grasp the fact that the object being perceived belongs to the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) does not grasp the relationship between signifier and signified—the cognition of a yogi, even while manifesting all words and objects as will be described, is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) by virtue of this reasoning.

[Objection: "Granted that the cognition which grasps the relationship between the signifier and the signified may be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), but how can this [cognition] which grasps all words and their objects be so? To this he says: "By convention" (*saṃketa*).
The sense is that, according to the reasoning already stated, even for a yogin, there is no existence of being an object of prior perception.
He explains the Master’s commentary, "devoid of that," with the words "by that.
[Objection: But even in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no other conceptual construction;
therefore, why does it not also possess the quality of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*)?

Now, if it is argued that "being devoid of conceptual construction" is not itself conceptualized, then even that is conceptualized by way of this very form, namely, "as being devoid of conceptual construction. Seeing how this could be so, he states the intended meaning of "devoid of conceptual construction":
"by the nature of conceptual construction"—the nature of conceptual construction is the state of appearing as capable of being associated with verbal expression; [it is devoid] by means of that.

Just as in the case of [the definition] "horned, humped, with a tail at the end," the very horns and so forth— which possess the horns and other features— are designated as the marks (liṅga) of "cowness"; in the same way, he shows that the property called "being a conceptual construction" (kalpanā), which consists in appearing as capable of being associated with verbal expression, is indicated by means of the subject (dharmin) known as "conceptual construction."

For this very reason, it is established that the objection raised by Uddyotakara against Ācārya Dignāga’s definition of perception— namely, that which is called "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*)— is indeed similar to the objection raised by Dharmakīrti.
By the word "by another" (*pareṇa*), it refers to one situated in another place, [referring] to that cognition which is free from error (*anāhitavibhrama*) as being perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) here is precisely its own elaboration; [the author] asks, "What is the purpose of establishing a connection with that which stands at a distance? and replies: "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
Since these two taken together constitute the definition of that [perception], they are indicated by a singular number as the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By the word *iti*, he states the definition of that which is worthy of being seen.

To the question "How is there mutual dependence?", he says: "That which is devoid of that [conceptualization] and is non-erroneous is to be treated as perception"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. And with the words beginning with *iti*, he concludes.
Since it is so,
therefore the state of being an object of direct perception is shown at the end by the force of the inclusion of the term "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
Timira is a disorder of the eyes;
this is a cause of error residing in the sense faculty,
such as the rapid whirling of a firebrand and the like.
For when a firebrand or similar object is rotated slowly, the illusion of a wheel does not arise;
therefore, the rotation is qualified by the term "swift.
And this is a cause of error residing in the object.
Traveling by boat is "boat-riding.
The mention of "vehicle" is because an illusion of moving trees and so forth arises for one standing on a moving boat;
this is a cause of error residing in an external support.
The disturbance of wind, bile, and phlegm:
for when the wind and the other humors are disturbed, an illusion such as that of blazing pillars arises; this is a cause of delusion pertaining to the internal.
And by all causes of delusion—whether they pertain to the external objects of the senses or to the internal basis—the sense faculty itself must be affected.
Because an error of the sense organ is impossible when the sense organ is unaltered;
those things beginning with these, ending with agitation, are described as such.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), ocular disorders such as cataracts and jaundice, which reside in the sense organs, are included.
The rapid movement of leading and bringing [objects] and so forth reside in the objects themselves;
for when the rapid leading and bringing of a firebrand is performed, there arises the delusion of a staff appearing with the color of fire.
Riding an elephant and so forth reside in external supports.

Blows to vital organs and the like, which reside in the internal basis, are understood here as causes of error. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that cognition in which no error has been induced by such [causes].
Because it is a cause of impairment for the eyes, "timira" (an eye disease) is classified as an impairment (*viplava*).
"Dependent on the sense faculties" means relying upon the sense faculties.
It is the cause of "error," that is, of delusion, by way of being its direct cause.
"Alāta" refers to a burning piece of wood.
He states the purpose of including the term "swift" (*āśu*) as follows: "slowly" (*manda*).

Although "swift whirling" is understood because a slowly whirled firebrand is not observed to be a cause of delusion, nevertheless, it should be understood that the author of the treatise included the term "swift" in order to avoid any lack of skill in his own expression.
He asks how this is stated as distinct from the previous [definition] and replies with the word "this" (*etad*). The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "because.
By the mention of "swift," travel by boat (*nauyāna*) is also to be understood as included.
For it is established by experience that when a boat moves slowly, there is no perception of trees and other objects as moving;
the word "iti" here indicates a reason.
To the question "Why is this stated separately?", he says: "And this... [etac ca].
Because it is that from which there is agitation, accumulation— that is to say, provocation.
When the question arises as to whose [it is], he says: "of wind," etc.
Dispelling the doubt that this [wind] is not the cause of the delusion, he says: "in wind and so forth.
The word *hi* means "because."
"When they have reached agitation" means when they are disturbed; that is to say, "in a state of commotion.

This might be argued: let it be that darkness (*timira*) is a cause of erroneous cognition because it is caused by an impairment of the sense faculty; but how can this be the case for those traveling in a boat and so forth, since the sense faculty remains in its normal state even while those [disturbances] exist? To this he says: "by all indeed."
The inclusion of cataracts (*timira*) and the like, which reside in the sense organs and are generally accepted as modifications of the sense organs, is for the sake of providing an illustration.

By this, the following meaning is established: just as a cataract residing in the sense organ causes delusion by modifying that very organ, so too other causes of delusion must likewise exist only by modifying it.
But why must these [faculties] necessarily undergo modification? To this he says: "unmodified," and so forth.
This is what is meant:
because they are modified by the modifications of that [consciousness], the eyes and other [senses] are its supports (āśraya).
The formal argument (prayoga) should be stated as follows: If those who,
having described that very same definition, have imagined the sense-faculty itself to be the seer and have pointed out a fault in the definition of mental perception, [then...]

Since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and the cognition of yogins have not been accepted [by others], he says— showing the different types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— in order to refute their misconceptions:
That is fourfold;
"that is fourfold" refers to sensory cognition (indriyajñāna). I-8.
Cognition arising from a sense faculty is sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*).
That which is dependent upon the sense faculties is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
A cause of sensory error, such as ophthalmia (*timira*) and the like, indeed vitiates that very sense faculty.
And the fact that traveling by boat and so forth is the cause of a sensory illusion is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

The illusory nature of such cognition is established through sublation (*bādhaka*), and its status as being born of the senses is established because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the senses.
Furthermore, the status of traveling by boat and so forth as the cause of such an illusion is established because it conforms to its own positive and negative concomitance.
Alternatively, this word "all" (*sarva*) should be understood as referring to the totality of what is relevant;
the portion from "these" (*ete*) up to "are grasped as the causes of error" (*vibhrama-hetavaḥ gṛhyante*) is easy to understand.
Only the term "limit" (*anta*) or "end" (*paryanta*) needs to be explained.
Kāca is a specific disease that causes a distortion of the eyes;
likewise, kāmalā (here) should be understood as a specific ailment that is the cause of distortions in the eyes, face, and so forth.
By analyzing the compound as "that in which no error has been introduced by them," he demonstrates that it is a three-word *bahuvrīhi*.
Having established that "that in which no error has been introduced" is so [described], one should then form the genitive *tatpuruṣa* "of those whose error has not been introduced.
However, this should be understood as a mere explanation of the meaning.
For that which has not been affected by error through those [causes] becomes [the nature] of them.
Since the definition is formulated within the context of cognition, "cognition" is understood;
therefore, it is called "cognition."
Now, showing the reason for establishing the sub-classifications of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the Teacher, he says: "Thus, in this way" (*tad evam*).
This collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) functions in the sense of "in the manner already stated.
The word "by which" (*yaiḥ*) is to be construed with each [member of the following list].
According to those Vaibhāṣikas who belong to our own school:
if cognition were the seer, it would perceive even what is obstructed because of its lack of resistance.
Therefore, proponents such as those who state, "The eye sees forms" (Abhidharma-kośa 1.42), have imagined that the sense-faculty itself is the seer.

By those Mīmāṃsakas, in response to the definition of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) given by Master Dignāga, a fault characterized by the apprehension of what has already been apprehended—which is a cause for invalidity—was raised.
Since the mention of that definition is illustrative, even when mental perception is accepted, there is a further fault characterized by the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth.

That too should be examined: by those Mīmāṃsakas who follow the opinion of Kumārila, as well as by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is not accepted because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself;
and by those Cārvākas and Mīmāṃsakas for whom even yogins do not exist.
"How could they possess knowledge?"—thus it follows that the proponents [of those views] do not accept the knowledge of yogins.
All three "ca" (and) particles serve to connect other points to be stated.

For the purpose of dispelling the various doubts held by these individuals here and there, [the author discusses] the variety—that is, the diversity or manifoldness—of the specific types of perception as defined by the aforementioned characteristics.
This means "the distinction between intermediate sub-types.
"That" refers to perception, which is fourfold, meaning it has four modes.
In that regard, explaining first one type of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), he says: "of the sense-organ" (*indriyasya*).
It is called "cognition" (*jñāna*) because it is by means of this that something is known.
In order to refute the objections raised by others regarding mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), he states its definition:

"That mental cognition which is produced by sensory cognition acting as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), with the assistance of the object immediately following its own object, is mental perception" (I-9).

One might object: "Since it can be said that 'sensory cognition' (*indriyajñāna*) consists of both the sense faculty (*indriya*) and its cognition (*jñāna*), how is disagreement [regarding the nature of sensory cognition] refuted? To dispel this doubt, the author demonstrates that in the term *indriyajñāna*, the Master intends a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound—meaning "the cognition of the sense faculty" (*indriyasya jñānam*). Thus he says: "the cognition of the sense faculty."
The meaning is that whatever is produced by a sense faculty belongs to that sense faculty.

Now, one might object: "But isn't the cognition of a sense faculty also produced from an effect, namely the inference of the sense faculty? Therefore, that too would incur the status of being perception. To this he says: "Dependent upon the sense faculty" (*indriyāśritam*).
The dependent [cognition] exists only when that [sense faculty] exists, by virtue of being produced by it;
however, the conformity to the sense faculty is not directly produced by the sense faculty itself, such that it could possess the status of perception— this is the intended meaning.

Even though cognition has multiple causes, it is designated by means of the sense faculty because that [faculty] is its unique cause; this is how it should be understood. By stating that "perception is the cognition of the sense faculty," it is shown that the sense faculty is not the seer.
Thus, the misconception is refuted.
Now, an objection has been raised by them: "If sensory cognition were the seer, then because it is non-obstructive (*apratigha*), it would follow that it could perceive even what is obstructed;
how is this fault avoided so that the misconception is refuted?
The intention [of our response] is this: cognition does not grasp an object by traveling to it.
Because there is no obstruction to its movement, it would grasp even what is spatially remote;
what then? It is said that it grasps that which arises in its own form.
Furthermore, an object situated in an unsuitable location is not known through positive and negative concomitance to possess that [consciousness's] own nature.
How then is it well-known that "its apprehension is by means of that"? What is the need for stating an argument in this regard?

Sense-cognition is perception; cognition produced by the causal complex of the sense-faculties and so forth is perception, because it is contradictory for a single entity to be both the producer and the produced.
The meaning is that it is not ignorance.

By demonstrating this, the author of the Vārttika— through such statements as "If the sense organ were the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), then its connection with the object [would be the cause]" (ŚV 4.60)— should be understood to have refuted even that status as a means of valid perception (pratyakṣapramāṇatā) which has been accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
For it is thus: that which leads one to the attainment [of an object] is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else.
And this quality of leading to attainment consists in being an instigator [of action] without mediation; otherwise, it would not be so.
And its status as an instigator [of activity] exists by virtue of having the nature of realization (*adhigama*), not otherwise;
yet it does not possess that nature [in the case of the scripture]. Furthermore, if it were an instigator through the mediation of realization, there would be no interruption at all.

And since that alone from which activity proceeds without mediation is rightly considered the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its being the instigator, and that is indeed cognition itself;
as it has been said: "Cognition is the means of valid cognition."
"Because activity regarding objects to be abandoned or accepted is primarily dependent upon it" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.5).

Alternatively, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is so called because it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of valid cognition (*pramā*). And since valid cognition is perceived as being delimited by a specific locus—such that "this is the cognition of blue, not of yellow"—it must be the instrument for that [cognition].
Since this [cognition] attains its established status as being of that very nature without any intervention,
and since the contact between sense-faculty and object and so forth are the basis for the determination of the distinction of blue, yellow, and so on,

and since the instrument (karaṇa) is the cause for the distinction of actions through its own distinctions, it is therefore logical that similarity (sārūpya), which consists of cognition itself, is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that serves as the basis for determining the distinction of the action of apprehension.
This twofold classification has been elaborated elsewhere by the Teacher, and thus it is not stated here, since this treatise was commenced for the sake of those who possess wisdom;
only a mere indication has been given.

[33] Aspaṣṭam—saṃsva means "one's own," referring to the object (*viṣaya*) of sensory cognition; *anantara* means that for which no interval (*antara*) exists. Thus, it is that which is immediately contiguous.
"Interval" (*antara*) is said to mean both "obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*) and "distinction" (*viśeṣa*).

Consequently, when an interval is excluded, what is grasped as the object of the sensory consciousness is a moment of the same kind that arises in the second moment as the "appropriated" (*upādeya*) moment;
that sensory cognition for which such [a moment] is the auxiliary cause is described in that way.
And that auxiliary cause (*sahakārī*) is of two kinds: that which assists mutually and that which assists in producing a single effect.
In this case, since it is impossible to impart an excellence (*atiśaya*) to a momentary entity, the auxiliary is understood as that which performs a single effect.

[Objection: But has the reason for the mention of the fourfold direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) already been stated by Dharmottara; so why does he state it again with the words "mental" (*mānasa*) and so forth?
Now, that which was the reason for the Teacher’s fourfold designation, which existed in his mind, has already been stated;
however, that very same reason must be stated as appropriate when designating specific individual instances of direct perception.

If so, why was that particular reason not stated by him here—just as it was elsewhere regarding self-awareness and so forth—for the purpose of refuting those who imagine the sense organ to be the seer, namely, [the statement] "sense-cognition"?
Therefore, it is appropriate to say that he has stated this even here in order to explain mental [perception].
This is true;

however, since mental perception cannot be ascertained with certainty and thus does not serve as a basis for practical activity (*avyavahārāṅga*), [the author] merely refutes the aforementioned objections.
In order to demonstrate that this alone is the cause for the explanation of its definition and nothing else, the very cause already stated has been reiterated;
thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Now, why is the definition of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) not stated, as it is for others? It is not stated.
Because there is no contradiction with the definition of a tall [person],
and because it has already been explained by the very word "sensory cognition" (*indriyajñāna*),
one might think: "The fourfold perception that is intended must be shown."
And since that [sequence] cannot be stated all at once, it must be expressed in a sequence.
As for whether the sequence should be of this particular kind or another—what need is there for such insistence? This sequence beginning with sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) has been established;
however, might there be some other reason for it as well?
It is said that there is yet another [type of cognition].
For indeed, sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*) is the basis for all worldly conventions; therefore, it was explained first.
By means of that very sensory perception, which has arisen in such a manner, mental perception (*mānasa*) is produced; thus, mental perception was explained immediately following it.
Following that, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is introduced as being personally realized (*pratyātmavedyatayā*), existent, and capable of being ascertained.

Subsequently, at the conclusion, the knowledge of the yogi is presented both as a demonstration of the mere causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the knowledge of the Omniscient One and as the ultimate human goal.
With the words beginning with "self" (*sva*), he explains the definition beginning with "its own object" (*svaviṣaya*).
And that which was stated as "that and so forth" is easy to understand up to this point.

Now, one might object: "If that which does not produce [an effect] were to be a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, it must be a cooperative cause that is beneficial (*upakārin*).

Furthermore, since the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) cannot exist between two things that are simultaneous, how can that momentary object (*viṣayakṣaṇa*) be its cooperative cause? Anticipating this objection, he says: "And it is of two kinds."
"Mutually," and so forth.
"For" (*ca*) means "because.
An entity (*bhāva*) that has the nature of acting together is of two kinds, that is, of two types.
To explain how there is a twofold nature, he says: "By way of mutual assistance," and so forth.
Being co-operative due to mutual assistance is secondary, pertaining to a continuum and dependent upon the determination of identity.
The primary [co-operation], however, consists in performing a single purposeful action.
If, even though there are two types [of action], the former one is what is grasped, then the fault remains as before; thus he says: "here" (iha).
Here, in the case of mental activity (*mānasakriyā*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The phrase "by virtue of performing a single purposeful action" (ekārthakriyākāritvena) is to be understood as following this [word].
For it should be concluded from the context that the "momentary object" (viṣayakṣaṇa) is what is grasped as the cooperative cause (sahakārī).
Why is it not grasped earlier?
For mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is produced by both the object and the sensory consciousness; therefore, these two possess mutual cooperation.

Since yogic cognition is also produced by such a sensory consciousness serving as its objective support (*ālambana*), the term "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) is employed to exclude that case. Furthermore, it is "equal" (*sama*) by virtue of being a cognition.

And it is "immediate" (anantara) because of its state of being uninterrupted; and since that [condition] is a condition (pratyaya) by virtue of being a cause, it is the "immediately preceding condition" (samanantarapratyaya); [the consciousness] is produced by that.
Thus he says: "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*). This is a qualification by way of being the cause.

Now, if—because it is impossible for an excellence to be imparted to a thing through its momentariness—a cooperative factor is not accepted on the basis of mutual assistance, then this [objection] refers to what was just stated, namely that there are two kinds of cooperative factors.
[Otherwise] it would be contradicted, and the *Hetubindu* would be rendered inconsistent; thus everything would be incoherent. [This is] not so, because the intended meaning has not been understood.

For it is intended that [the object] is "momentary" in the sense that it is a thing which, being non-streaming— that is, not possessing the nature of producing a subsequent homogeneous [moment]— is the very last one, designated as "sensory cognition," and is on the verge of cessation; it is not, however,
[meant] that it is a "mere thing" by way of the exclusion of non-momentary things, nor is it a "mere thing" by way of the exclusion of mere non-things.
This is what is meant:

if this sensory cognition, which is about to give rise to a mental cognition, were to carry on a stream of the same kind [as its predecessor], then one might imagine that the object is its auxiliary cause (sahakārī) by way of imparting an excellence through the assistance of the continuum.

However, since this [sensory cognition] exists within the continuum as something whose power to produce its own kind has already departed, how could the object be imagined to be its auxiliary cause in such a manner?
Now, one might ask: "What is that single thing which, when these two perform it, is said to have such non-cooperation? To this he says: "The object," etc.
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.
Because that single thing is produced by these two alone, therefore [it is so called].
The word "tat" (that) has the sense of "tasmāt" (therefore) in this context.
"Mutual cooperation" means acting as a cause for a single purposeful effect, according to the subject matter of the discussion.
By the phrase "by such [a cause]" and so forth, he demonstrates the exclusion of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

The meaning is that by such [a cognition], which acts as a cooperative cause for the apprehension of an object immediately following its own object, that which is apprehended— namely, the form (rūpa) serving as the objective support— is produced by that which exists as the nature of the apprehended.
This is stated for the purpose of refuting that [cognition], that is, for the purpose of refuting the mental nature of that yogic knowledge.

And by explaining it in this way, the interpretation offered by another—who claimed that "the mention of the 'immediately preceding condition' (samanantarapratyaya) is for the purpose of refuting the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth"—is cast aside;
for that very consequence has already been refuted by the inclusion of the term "sensory cognition" (indriyajñāna).
With the words beginning "samaś ca," [the author] states the etymological analysis and the meaning of the term *samanantarapratyaya*.
The meaning of "hetu" (cause) is the meaning of "pratyaya" (condition);
and due to its inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group, there is no lengthening of the vowel.

Even if such an etymology were the case, nevertheless, it is only the preceding consciousness that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*), being so established in the scriptures, and not anything else.
Thus it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: “Mind and mental factors that have arisen, excluding the final ones, are the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara*).
By employing this technical designation well-established in the system, the Master has demonstrated its status as being established within the system.

Thus, by this [statement], it is said that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is perception only when there is a relationship of producer and produced between sensory cognition and mental consciousness that belong to one and the same continuum.

Consequently, the cognition of a yogi existing within the continuum of another is excluded. [Objection: But what is the purpose of mentioning the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*), such that the cognition of a yogi is excluded by virtue of its being otherwise? To this he says: "That... (*tad*).
Because that which is produced by sensory cognition in the form of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is mental, for that reason,

by means of this mention of the "immediately preceding condition," it is established that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exists only when there is a relationship of producer and produced between two [cognitions] belonging to the same continuum and falling within a single stream.
Because it is not produced directly by the sense organs and because it relies solely upon the mind (*manas*), it is described as purely mental (*mānasa*).
Furthermore, this designation should be understood as intended to demonstrate that even in the scriptures (*āgama*), this very [knowledge] is expressed by the word "mind.
Nevertheless, one might ask: how is the knowledge of yogins excluded from being of such a nature? To this he says: "That... (*tat*).

Since there is a perception of that which stands in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), whereas there is an absence of such a causal relationship between things existing in separate continua,
therefore the cognition of a yogi is refuted and rejected on the grounds of being mental (*mānasatvena*).

The point is that if it were merely stated that [the yogic cognition] is produced by sensory cognition, then it would not be refuted, as it could be argued that it is first produced by that [sensory cognition] acting as its objective support (*ālambana*).
It might be argued as follows: if this [term] were for the sake of that purpose, then it should certainly not have been included at all;
for by the very phrase "having as its auxiliary the immediately subsequent moment of its own object," the cognition of a yogin has already been excluded.
Indeed, when producing a yogic cognition, sensory perception does not have as its auxiliary the immediately subsequent moment of its own object.
Now, it is argued: when sensory cognition produces yogic cognition, it necessarily produces its own effect, namely [the next moment of] cognition as well.

Therefore, with respect to the moment of cognition produced within its own continuum, that [sensory cognition] becomes an auxiliary cause for the immediately succeeding moment of the object of its own domain; thus, the definition of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) applies to that which is produced by it.
Oh, what skill in establishing the meaning of words!
For the status of being a "cooperative cause" (sahakārin) must be considered only in relation to that very thing which is under discussion as the produced effect;
it cannot be considered in relation to just anything whatsoever.
Furthermore, that sensory cognition is not a cooperative cause with respect to that very same yogic cognition, such that its being described as such would be appropriate.
Now, if it is argued that since that [object] is a cooperative cause for that sensory cognition by virtue of its actual nature, why consider it in relation to that [cognition]?
Even if this were so, the inclusion of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) would still be unable to exclude the cognition of a yogin. Thus it remains.

Just as that sensory cognition depends upon its own immediately preceding cognition and has as its cooperative cause the object immediately following its own object, so too does the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) likewise exist in dependence upon that very same [sensory cognition].
Therefore, how can the yogic cognition produced by such a [condition] be excluded from being of that same nature?

Is it not the case that its status as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) does not depend upon that [object]? Ah, then does its status as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) also depend upon that?
Or should "being an immediately preceding condition" be understood as being relative to the specific effect under discussion?
"But its actual form cannot be accepted as the object of apprehension, because in the absence of a result, it is impossible for that [actual form] to be a mere restatement (anuvādya).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all actual forms must be restated. If this is argued, [we reply:
this same point applies equally to the grasping of the momentary object immediately following one's own object, which acts as a cooperative cause.

Nor do we perceive anything equal to a royal decree by which one might conceive that, in this context, it is only the state of being produced by an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—in relation to the object under discussion—that is to be accepted as the defining characteristic, and not the cooperation with the momentary object immediately following its own object.
To this, it is replied: when a yogi, through some cause, [perceives] sensory cognition and the object-moment co-arising with it...

Desiring to see both of those [the object and the preceding moment of consciousness] by means of yogic cognition, he sees them; at that time, that yogic cognition is produced by that sensory cognition acting in conjunction with the immediately subsequent moment of its own object.
Therefore, if the term "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) were not included, mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) would be erroneously attributed [to that yogic cognition].
Consequently, this very inclusion of the "immediately preceding condition" must be made for the purpose of excluding that [mental perception].
And it is with reference to such a cognition of the yogi that Dharmottara stated, "by means of such [a cognition]," and thus everything is clarified.

Furthermore, when the object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is distinct from sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*), then the charge of invalidity based on apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhaṇa*) is refuted.

And when the moment that constitutes the object of apprehension for the sense faculty is grasped, then the undesirable consequence—that there would be no such thing as the blind or the deaf because other objects not grasped by sensory cognition would [otherwise] be grasped—is refuted. Now, demonstrating how the opponent’s objection based on the principle of "grasping what has already been grasped" (*gṛhītagrāhitva*) is avoided, he says: "And when... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "this is clearly evident," it means:
when this is so, [the objection] is refuted.
Anticipating the question—"From what [evidence] does this follow, that its object is other than the object of sensory cognition, such that it is thereby refuted?"—he says: "And when..."
The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

It should be understood as following the phrase "that which has become the appropriated object (*upādeyabhūta*) of the sense-faculty and its consciousness. That momentary state (*kṣaṇa*) which is the appropriated [effect] of that which is the object of sensory cognition is "grasped" (gṛhīta); that is, it is accepted as the cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) for the production of mental [cognition] from sensory cognition. Therefore, the punctuation (*cheda*) should be made right here.

It must be so established. This is the underlying intention of what they say: since it has a specific producer as its object, mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa) must necessarily have as its object a producer that is co-existent with the sensory cognition; and that [producer] belongs to it.
Thus, its object is different from the preceding momentary object of sensory cognition.
By this, the utility of grasping the cooperative cause—the momentary object immediately following its own object—is demonstrated.
Now, let the consequence of invalidity resulting from the fact that it would be grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*) be refuted in this manner.
Anticipating the objection, "How then can the fault of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth be avoided?", he says: "by means of sensory cognition.
Because it apprehends an object not already apprehended by this [sensory cognition], it is "by means of the mental [cognition]," as is clear from the context.
By demonstrating through this that what is not apprehended by sensory cognition is apprehended by the mental [cognition], he shows that for whomever there is a sense-organ...
There exists for that very person mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), because it is produced by that same sensory cognition acting as a cooperative cause with the simultaneous momentary object.
Therefore, it apprehends the simultaneous momentary object which was not apprehended by that [sensory cognition].
But for that person who possesses only sensory cognition having the object as its domain, how could mental perception arise?
It has been shown that one should grasp that momentary object (viṣyakṣaṇa).
Therefore, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth, is refuted.
By this, the utility of the apprehension of sensory cognition (indriyajñāna)—which is assisted by the cooperation of the immediately succeeding momentary object of its own domain—is demonstrated.

Even though the phrase "by cognition alone" (*jñānenaiva*) could be understood through the force of the qualification "having as its cooperative cause the momentary object immediately following its own object," nevertheless, it should be understood that the explicit mention of "sensory cognition" (*indriyajñāna*) was made for the sake of avoiding complexity in comprehension.

In the phrase "the blind, the deaf, and so forth," the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi) refers to those suffering from leprosy (*kuṣṭa*) and similar diseases; for even they possess tactile cognition through the mental faculty (*mānasa*).
Here, Śāntabhadra, presenting the view of the Sautrāntikas, states: "First, the visual consciousness [arises] with respect to the eye and visible form..."
Then, by that sensory consciousness acting as the simultaneous cause, direct perception of the object is produced in the third moment; thus it has been explained.
And this mental consciousness is held to be a direct perception when the visual faculty’s activity has ceased.
However, when the eye is active, whatever cognition of form arises, all of that is indeed dependent upon the eye;
otherwise, the dependence of any consciousness whatsoever upon the eye would be untenable. Disregarding this, he says: "And this... [etac ca].
The word "eva" (only) is used for emphasis;
it should be understood immediately after the phrase "whose activity has ceased.
The state of the eye while actively engaged [in seeing] is precisely what constitutes "application" (*praṇidhāna*).

The collective meaning should be understood as follows: this mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is accepted as a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), and it is maintained that it arises only when the operation of the eye has ceased.
If mental cognition is not produced when the eyes are directed [toward an object], then what indeed is produced? To this he says: "the operation" (vyāpāra).
The particle *tu* distinguishes the state possessing operation from the state devoid of operation.
The phrase "knowledge of form" (*rūpajñāna*) is a factual restatement (*vāstavānuvāda*), and not intended for the purpose of excluding other types of knowledge by means of their possible existence.
Alternatively, the word "form" (*rūpa*) denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus, the meaning is "knowledge of that which has intrinsic nature.
By using the term "all" (*sarva*), he expresses pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"Cakṣurvijñāna" means that which is based on the eye and produced by the eye; this is what is meant. He states the logical justification with the words "otherwise.

[Objection: Even when the eye possesses activity, there is no impossibility of its being based on the eye during the arising of mental consciousness (mānasa), because it is precisely this initial cognition that is established as being based on the eye.
True;
however, this is the intended meaning: even that initial visual consciousness must be established as being dependent upon the eye precisely because it conforms to the presence and absence of the eye.

Even if there were a conformity to the presence and absence of that [mind], if some [cognition] were considered mental, then in the case of the eye, the conformity to presence and absence would not be a factor in establishing its dependence on the eye; thus, the initial establishment of that [dependence] would not occur—this is a sound reductio ad absurdum.

It might be argued: "Is this mental [cognition] produced by the visual consciousness alone regarding the object of form, or is it also produced by the cognitions of taste and so forth regarding the objects of taste and so forth?"
What follows from this? If it were only form (*rūpa*), then the scriptural authority stating that “the five external objects are cognizable by two kinds of cognition” would be contradicted.
On the other hand, if it is held to have all [five] objects such as form and so forth as its domain, then it is impossible for it to have sound as its object.

For sound is not like taste and so forth, produced by the palate and other organs, and flowing in a stream, such that auditory sensory cognition—acting as a cooperative cause for the momentary instant immediately following its own object—might produce a mental [perception] therein.
It is said in reply: this [mental perception] has the five objects, beginning with form, as its domain.
But it does not have mere form as its object.
Thus the Master said: "by sensory cognition," and not "by visual consciousness."
Furthermore, as for what the Blessed One said—"O monks, form is apprehended by two means:
by visual consciousness and by the mind drawn along with it"—this was stated in the context of the apprehension of form;
it was not intended to mean that form itself is apprehended in two ways.
[34] The Abhidharmakośa should be consulted: "The five external [objects] are cognizable by two [kinds of consciousness]. (1.48).
But was it not stated that [the unmanifest] cannot exist as an object of sound? How, then, can such an admission be made?
This is true.

When a bell or the like, being struck, resounds, then the sound produced by it continues to flow in a stream for some time; at that point, a mental cognition (mānasa-jñāna) having that [sound] as its object is generated by the auditory cognition (*śrotra-jñāna*), which acts as a cooperative cause with the immediately succeeding moment of the object.
Even by this much, the statement that [the sound] is cognizable by two types of cognition has fulfilled its purpose.
This has been stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "Because it is spoken with reference to the genus (*jāti*) of form and so forth.

The meaning of this is: that was said by the Blessed One with the intention (*abhisandhi*) of referring to the genus of form and so forth, and not with the aim of referring to every individual instance (*vyakti*) of form and so forth.
In this regard, the predecessors [raise] the objection: "How is it to be known that such a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exists which has external objects as its support?

Having raised this doubt, they state: "If it were absent, there would follow the consequence of an absence of linguistic convention regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*), because of the absence of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) produced by its power.

Furthermore, having raised the objection that "there is no absence of conceptual construction because [the object] has been experienced by visual and other sensory consciousnesses," they reply: "Even by Devadatta..."
And this mental perception is established by way of the tenet system;
however, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that proves it.
If it were of such a nature, there would be no fault; thus, its definition has been stated so that one might say this.
However, [if that were the case], the undesirable consequence of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) would apply even to Yajñadatta when he is perceived.

Furthermore, having raised the objection that "it will not occur because of the difference in mental continua (*santāna*"), [the author replies]: "In this case as well, conceptual differentiation does not arise precisely because of the difference in mental continua."
For here too, the distinction between mental continua is due solely to the distinction between the bases of the sense faculties and to their simultaneous activity;
for in cases such as eating a long roll of cake, the simultaneous arising of cognitions is observed.
And when there is unity of the continuum, simultaneous activity is not logical.
Therefore, lest there be an absence of conceptualization regarding form and so forth, one must necessarily admit the existence of non-conceptual mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
By this same reasoning, the undesirable consequence of the absence of certainty and recollection should also be brought forward.
If non-conceptual mental consciousness did not exist at all, then it would follow that the knowledge of yogins (*yogijñāna*) could not exist.
If it is argued that non-conceptual mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) certainly exists, but does not exist as occurring subsequent to sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*),
then what contradiction is there in its existence when such a possibility exists?
For no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is observed here.
By which [reason] it might be that "it does not exist," yet a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence has been stated.
Therefore, it has been asserted in such passages as: "Consequently, there exists a non-conceptual mental consciousness (*manojñāna*) arising subsequent to sensory perception."
Considering this very thing to be as insubstantial as the core of a plantain tree, he says: "And this...
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis;
it should be understood as following the phrase "established in our own system."
He confirms this very point by way of its negative counterpart with the words "but not this.
The particle *tu* either emphasizes or distinguishes.
For although this [cognition] which does not initiate a stream is of the nature of self-awareness due to its being of the essence of knowledge, it is nonetheless as if unperceived.

Because this [non-conceptuality] cannot be demonstrated by saying "it is accessible through experience, like visual and other sensory cognitions," there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes or ascertains it.

Now, one might object: "Has not a proof been shown by way of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), such as 'otherwise, there would follow the absence of conceptual construction'? If so, why is it said that "there is no proof for it"?
"There is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This is his intention: "What has been said is true, but it is not the work of a logician.
For instance, as for what was stated—that there is a difference in mental continua because of the difference in the bases of the sense organs and because of their simultaneous activity—"
And it is not tenable that there could be a conceptual construction in one [mind] regarding what was experienced by another when there is a difference in the mental continuum (*santāna*);
therefore, that is inexpressible.

If the difference in the mental continuum arises from a difference in the basis of the sense faculties and from simultaneous activity, and if, due to that difference, there is no relationship of cause and effect, [then the objection stands].
In that case, the visual consciousness of a person who has just awakened from sleep would not arise;
for when it does indeed arise, it must originate either from a preceding mental consciousness or from a sensory consciousness.
It cannot arise from sensory cognition because that [sensory cognition] does not exist prior to it;
nor can it arise from sensory cognition occurring in the waking state,
because that has long since ceased.
Furthermore, a cause that has long since passed away is not observed [to produce an effect].
If it is argued that conceptualization arises only from other conceptualizations within distinct mental continua— and that conceptualization does not arise from a non-conceptual state—
then even when there is a difference in continuum, what is there to prevent the arising of conceptualization from a non-conceptual state, provided the relationship of producer and produced exists?
Nor is it logical that there should be a difference in the mental continuum due to a difference in the bases of the sense faculties or due to simultaneous activity,
because this would entail the consequence that they would be mutually imperceptible and so forth.
Therefore, whether abundant or slight, [an effect] arises only from a similar cause.
However, one should not accept a division of the continuum merely because of the arising of something abundant;
just as the flame of a lamp, which arises from a tiny spark and possesses an expanding radiance, does not bring about a division of its own continuum within itself.
Furthermore, although it is of such a nature, the fact that mental cognition (*manojñāna*) is not currently accepted as being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)—

Since that [object] arises from a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and possesses a specific form, and since there is no experience of a non-conceptual mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possessing that form in the absence of that causal complex, what is the point of taking this [mental consciousness] seriously?

One might object: "If there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish this, for what purpose is it introduced in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this way" (*evam*).
[The phrase] "of such a kind" means "possessing such characteristics.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of stating the definition of such a type?

[the answer is: It is for the purpose of refuting the objection that might arise if one were to accept the mental perception established in the system of the author of the Sūtras—namely, that if mental perception exists, its definition is as follows.
To explain self-awareness, he says:
"There is self-awareness of all minds and mental factors" (I-10).
Regarding the passage beginning with "sarvacitta" and so forth:
mind (*citta*) grasps the mere object;
mental factors (*caitta*), such as pleasure and the like, grasp specific states.
And "all those mental states and mental factors" refers to all mental states and mental factors;
pleasure and so forth alone are self-cognized because they are clearly experienced,
and not other states of mind— this inclusion of the word "all" was made in order to dispel such a doubt.
There is no state of mind in which the self's own cognition would not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For in whatever form the self is cognized, that form constitutes the direct perception of the self’s own cognition.

Regarding the distinction between mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) as stated by the Master according to the Vaibhāṣika system, he explains their meaning: the mind grasps the mere object (*artha*), that is, the mere thing (*vastu*).

Because of the statement, "In that regard, consciousness is the perception of the object," the mental factors (caitta) are those which grasp specific states, accept specific states, and— so to speak— take on the forms of specific states; for it is stated that "the mental concomitants (caitasāḥ) pertain to their specific distinctions."

To the question "What are those of such a nature?", he says: "pleasure and so forth. By stating "all," he demonstrates that one first forms a compound of the preceding terms—*citta* and *caitta*—and subsequently forms a compound with the word *sarva*.

With the words beginning with "sukha," he states the result of the inclusion of "all": "from its light" means from the manifestation of that which has a clear and distinct experience as its luminosity. He asks: when there is the inclusion of all, what kind of object arises by which the doubt is removed? To this he says: "it does not exist."
"Someone" means either one who is mistaken or one who is not mistaken.
