Now, raising the objection: "What other form of cognition, distinct from its object of awareness, could there be such that its self-awareness would be a direct perception (pratyakṣa)?"—anticipating this, he says: "For by which...
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because."
If it is argued that whatever is experienced must be experienced by something other than itself, as in the case of a jar or similar objects,
and therefore how can there be self-cognition of the self?
We say no, because such conventional usage occurs due to the capacity [of the cognition].
Knowledge possesses that capacity— namely, its exclusion from insentient matter and its nature as light— by virtue of which it does not require another illumination for its own manifestation.
Just as a lamp, by its very nature of being luminous, illuminates itself by itself and does not require another lamp.

Now, one might ask: by the force of the example of a jar and so forth, should cognition be considered cognizable by another light, or rather, by the power of the example of a lamp, should it be considered self-luminous (svaprakāśa) due to its independence from any other light? To this it is replied:
since the manifestation of the nature of a jar and such objects would be impossible if cognition lacked the quality of being self-luminous, its self-luminosity must indeed be accepted.

And here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): that which has an unmanifest manifestation is not manifest, just as something [is not manifest] when it is at some time and in some way unmanifestly manifested; and this jar and so forth have an unmanifest manifestation because they are beyond the reach of cognition (*jñāna-parokṣatva*). Thus, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
If it is argued that this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) because one cognition is manifested by another cognition, we say no.
Because at the time of the arising of the cognition of blue, the reason [of "simultaneous apprehension"] is unestablished, it would follow that blue is imperceptible;
moreover, even in your own view, not every cognition is known by another cognition inherent in the same object,
since such [secondary] cognition is absent when there is no desire to know it.
Just as consciousness has an object that is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*),
so too that very object to be disregarded would result in being unmanifest (*avyakta*) because it lacks manifest clarity; yet this is not the case.
Furthermore, when an object such as a form (*rūpa*) is being perceived here, an internal aspect consisting of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is experienced simultaneously.
Yet, it cannot be said that the perceived aspect—such as blue—is experienced as having the nature of pleasure;
for it is not determined that the blue and so forth are experienced as having the nature of pleasure.
For if it were certain that this blue and so forth is experienced as having a pleasant nature, then it would possess that nature of being pleasant and so on.
That form in which the direct-perceiving activity of perception is followed by conceptualization is what constitutes perception.

Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) should be declared to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. For instance, if even that which has an unmanifest manifestation were the object of the conventional usage of "manifest," then an entity possessing a manifestation consisting of the cognition residing in another person would likewise be conventionally designated as "manifest" at the very time its own cognition arises.

Because there is no distinction between two cognitions—one residing in one's own continuum and the other residing in another's continuum—due to their both having the nature of being non-self-cognizing (*asvasaṃvedana*).
If it is asked: "Since cognition does not exist within that [other person's] continuum, how can there be such a conventional designation (*vyavahāra*) for the object?", [we reply:
even if it were present, how could there be such a conventional designation if it were not manifest?
For nothing at all is produced by that [manifestation] for this [object]. In that case, why would that [manifestation] not likewise be within the scope of linguistic usage for another person?
Thus, this linguistic usage regarding manifestation is pervaded by the state of being manifest or unmanifest.
And once the relationship of pervader and pervaded is established, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
[35] That which was written outside the line is not read correctly—[the editor asks]: "But what is that other form (*rūpāntara*)?"
Anticipating the objection— "By what [definition] is it said that 'that by which the self is cognized is self-cognition, which is perception'?"—
and considering that this statement is merely empty of meaning, he says "here," and so forth.
"Internal" (*āntara*) means existing within; it refers to that which vibrates internally.
To the question "What is such a thing?", he says: "Bliss" (*sukha*).
But surely, when form and so forth are being perceived, they are experienced as being of the nature of bliss?
But there is nothing other than that which exists in the form of pleasure and so forth, by means of which its nature as feeling could be established; thus he says: "And not" (*na ca*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), or in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
The meaning is that its apprehended aspect is its nature as an object of perception (*grāhya-svabhāva*).
"Having a pleasant form" means having the nature of pleasure (*sukha-svabhāva*).
Since the mention of "pleasant" is illustrative, it should also be understood as "having the form of suffering" (*duḥkha-rūpa*).
By the word *iti*, he shows the form of the statement.
To the question "Why is it not possible to speak thus?", he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*).
The particle *iti* expresses the essential nature of certainty (*niścaya*).

It is asked: even if there is an ascertainment of that nature, how is the experience of that nature established, such that because of its absence at that time, it cannot be said [otherwise]? To this he says: "If... (yadīti).
"Hir" means "because. By the use of the particle *iti*, the nature of certainty (*niścaya*) is expressed.

The intention is this: whatever is ascertained as being such-and-such through a corresponding conceptualization (*anurūpa-vikalpa*) is precisely that which becomes the object of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) as being thus, just like blue and so forth.
But surely, experience is a means of valid cognition because of the appearance of that [object]; yet,
the nature of blue as being pleasurable is not apprehended.
Therefore, at the time of experiencing blue, something other than the pleasant object—blue—is experienced as pleasant;
and that is indeed cognition itself.
Consequently, there is an experience of cognition.
And that cognition, which is of the nature of awareness, is a direct realization of the self, non-conceptual, and non-erroneous; therefore,
it is perception (*pratyakṣa*),
whether certainty arises from it or not.
Anticipating the objection, "Why is it said thus?", he recalls what was stated previously with the words "yasmin" (in which).
"Rūpe" means in its own nature;
the rest has already been explained.
He says "and not" (*na ca*) because the perceived state of blue as being pleasurable is indeed followed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is as before;
the phrase "is followed by conceptual construction" (*anugamyate vikalpena*) carries over from the previous context.
He concludes what was stated by the words "therefore" and so forth:
because the form of the blue and so on that is being perceived is not determined as such, yet there is the experience of forms such as joy and so on; therefore [it is so].
Granted that pleasure is experienced,
it will nonetheless be of the nature of ignorance;
and if that is so, how can there be self-awareness of something whose nature is knowledge by means of ignorance?
And how is self-cognition direct perception? To this he says: "And that... The word "and" (ca) distinguishes [cognition] from the non-cognitive self.

For one who determines that it is cognition alone, the nature of being cognition belongs to that which has the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*), because otherwise luminosity would be impossible; such is the intended meaning.
Since this is so, there is therefore an experience of cognition;
the meaning is that for one who is inward-turned, there is the aspect of the apprehender, which takes the form of pleasure and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that what is experienced as pleasant should be other than the aspect of the apprehended, nor that it should be other than the aspect of the apprehender.
It would appear either as the object of apprehension or as the apprehender; yet since it is not the object of apprehension, it is therefore nothing but the apprehender.
Now, let it be granted that cognition is experienced in such a manner;

however, why is that [experience] a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consisting of self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*)? To this he says: "And that" (*tac ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) means "because" (*yasmāt*).
"Feeling" (vedana) is that by which something is felt;
the analysis of the compound is "feeling whose nature is cognition" (jñāna-rūpa).
Alternatively, it is so called because it is both of the nature of cognition and a feeling.
It is "directly manifesting" (sākṣātkāri), meaning it acts as that which makes [the object] non-remote, that is to say, it has a vivid appearance;
this is because it qualifies [the cognition] by way of being its cause.
And for this very reason, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*);
for that which is bound up with conceptual construction cannot possibly have a clear manifestation of the object.
To the objection that it might be non-conceptual yet [erroneous], like the cognition of two moons and so forth, he says: "and non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*).
The word "ca" (and) indicates that they possess an equal means [of cognition].
For that [cognition] does not function with respect to itself as being "that" when it is "not-that," such that there would be an error regarding it; this is the intended meaning.
He asks: "What is established from that [fact] regarding your [view] that [perception] is non-conceptual and non-erroneous? and answers with the word "tataḥ" (from that).
The sense is: because this [perception] possesses these two characteristics, therefore—from that—since perception is characterized by nothing more than this.
In this regard, the established rule is as follows:
it should be understood that the self’s fitness [for cognition] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the self-awareness is the result (phala).
It might be thought: "If that [object] sensation were thus perceptible, then the sensation whose nature is conceptualization would also be such;
yet it is not logical for that which is conceptual in nature to be perception.
It is indeed logical, because it does not involve conceptualization with respect to its own self and because it is non-erroneous.

For conceptual construction (vikalpa) constructs an external object, but not itself; it errs regarding the external, but not regarding itself. Therefore, why is it not a form of direct perception (pratyakṣa)?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is non-erroneous and free from conceptual construction is perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as the sensory cognition’s awareness of external objects known as "conformity" (*sārūpya*). And the awareness of the nature of conceptualization within the self is likewise non-erroneous and free from conceptual construction; this is the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

How the impossibility of conjunction arises within the nature of cognition, or how that which is conjoined with a word is not grasped as such, has been explained elsewhere in detail and is therefore not stated here.
In order to explain yogic perception, he says:
"And yogic cognition arises from the culmination of the intensification of the cultivation of a real object" (I-11).
"Real" (bhūta) means an existing object;
it is "real" because it has been perceived by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
such as the four noble truths.
The cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of what has become [an object] is its repeated placement within the mind.
The excellence (*prakarṣa*) of that cultivation is the commencement of the clarity of the cognition in which the object being cultivated appears.
The limit (*paryanta*) of that excellence is when the clarity of appearance becomes only slightly incomplete.
For as long as the state of vivid appearance is incomplete, so long does its intensification continue.
He states the intended meaning of the word *bhūta* by saying "real" (*sadbhūta*).
By using the word "object" (*artha*), he shows that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "that which is both real (*bhūta*) and an object (*artha*)."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the nature of objects as consisting of pleasure and so forth, as postulated by the Sāṃkhyas, is also real? [Reply: He says, "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*). It is "seen," meaning ascertained.
The word "and" (*ca*) illuminates the sense that this is clearly evident.
He asks, "What kind of object is intended here by such [a term]? and replies with the word "yathā" (just as).
By this term *bhūtārtha* (the real object), it is shown that the four noble truths are intended here.
And just as the knowledge born from the power of cultivating the four noble truths is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogin, [so too is the knowledge of the Buddha].

Likewise, it should be understood that there is also an object which is another real entity (*sadbhūtārtha*), just as the meaning of the word [is established]; for the *Viniścaya* states: “Like the vision of the four noble truths” (Pvin I 74,4). They are called *ārya* because they have gone far away (*ārāt*) from evil states (*pāpakadharmebhyaḥ*).
For this very reason, they consider those [objects] to be real; thus, they are called "truths" (*satya*).
And because there are four of them, it is said that there are "four.
[35*] CePvin I 74,4
The five aggregates that have become results, together with their afflictions, constitute the first truth, called suffering (*duḥkha*).
Those same aggregates, when they have become causes and are accompanied by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), constitute the second truth, called origin (*samudaya*).
The state of the mind free from afflictions constitutes the third truth, called cessation (*nirodha*).
The fourth truth, called the path, is a specific state of mind characterized by aspects such as selflessness, which serves as the cause for attaining that state.
He explains its etymological analysis and meaning through the word "bhāvanā" (cultivation) with the phrase "of the real" (*bhūtasya*);
it should be understood as "of the real object" (*bhūtārthasya*).
Furthermore, it is observed that due to the proximity of the word *bhūta*, the word *bhū* was inserted by the scribe in the first manuscript.

However, the reading "of that" (*tasya*) belongs to Dharmottara, who intends to show the analysis (*vigraha*) in an abbreviated form; otherwise, for one wishing to show the analysis exactly as it is, what point would there be in employing the word *artha*, such that the inclusion of the mere word *bhūta* would manifest both a redundancy of syllables and a lack of skill in composition?
Thus, by employing the word *artha*, the burden of comprehension is avoided and the clumsiness of the writing is revealed.
He says "again" for the purpose of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"Again" means not for the first time.
By the double mention, he shows the abundance of what is not the initial practice.
Furthermore, "establishment in such a manner" should be understood as being uninterrupted by heterogeneous factors;
that is to say, cultivation is a stream of similar mental states regarding the four truths that is not interspersed with heterogeneous ones.
[DhPr p. 68]
When it is complete, however, there is no further progression toward excellence.
Therefore, the state preceding the state of completion is called the limit of the excellence of clarity.
From that limit arises the yogin’s perception—a cognition that grasps the form of the object being cultivated even more clearly, as if the object were present before one.
Thus, in this context, the stage at which the onset of clear appearance begins is the culmination of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*).

When the object being cultivated appears as if veiled by a thin cloud, such is the sequence of cultivation for yogins as stated in the *Viniścaya* [section] beginning with "consisting of what has been heard" (*śrutamaya*). Furthermore, regarding the causal relationship between the culmination of cultivation and the clarity of appearance, it is explained in that very same work beginning with "desire, grief," and so forth.
It should be understood here as well in the same manner as it was shown [before]:
what kind of aspect of those truths— beginning with impermanence— is to be cultivated, the duration for which the cultivation lasts, extending through a succession of many births,
and the basis for the cultivation of Bodhisattvas, which is compassion.
The other [texts] discuss the agitation regarding *saṃsāra*; all of that should be understood here as it has been determined in the *Pramāṇavārttika*.
However, here the undertaking is merely to demonstrate the nature of the yogi’s cognition.
He states the analysis of the compound with the word "excellence" (*prakarṣa*) and its intended meaning: "of cultivation" (*bhāvanāyāḥ*).
The "commencement" (*upakrama*) of the state of being clearly manifest (*sphuṭābhatva*) is its beginning;
and that is precisely the arising of that cognition in the form of clarity, greater clarity, and so forth.
By means of the word "limit" (*paryanta*), he explains the analysis of that [compound] and its meaning through the phrase "of the excellence" (*prakarṣasya*).
"Limit" means the end.
And when is its end? He says:
"When..."—that is, at the time when the object of meditation becomes clearly manifest to the cognition; this is understood from the context.

This [definition] is slightly incomplete; for that which must subsequently become the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a yogin, at that time the limit and conclusion of the excellence (*prakarpa*) must be understood.
The meaning is that the "limit" is the knowledge that has reached such a state, characterized by that specific time.
Now, one might object: that which is the limit of excellence is that at which, when it exists, excellence ceases.
And since that very state of clarity is indeed complete [from the beginning], how can it be said that the yogic cognition arises only at the final stage? How so?
But fearing the objection that "that alone is not the limit," he says: "as far as" (*yāvat*). The word "for" (*hi*) means "because.
He shows that when [the state] is complete, there is no further progression toward excellence by saying: "complete" (*sampūrṇam*).
The particle "but" (*tu*) indicates that this state is characterized by differentiation.

The "going" (*gati*) of excellence (*prakarṣa*) means its movement. This is the intended meaning of one who speaks thus: excellence is the state of being brought to a peak; it is called a form that possesses a superior degree.
Furthermore, from the root *gam* (to go) with the prefix *pari-* and the suffix *-anta*, the compound *paryanta*—
formed as a *prādi*-compound meaning "the end all around"— denotes precisely "going without remainder. Therefore, that which follows immediately thereafter is called the culmination (*prakarsa*).
One should not be conceited;
for it is not for the sake of [personal glory] that these eminent ones have arisen.
He concludes this very point with the word "tataḥ" (therefore).
The preceding state is devoid of any interval, immediately after which there arises a more distinct cognition.
This refers to the state of fullness— the state of complete clarity, that is to say, the state of grasping a more distinct form—
of that which is proximate.

Just as for another person who has not cultivated [meditation], there is a perception that apprehends the clearer aspect of a jar, cloth, or other object situated nearby, so too, that cognition which apprehends the clearer aspect of the object being cultivated is the yogin’s perception.

He shows once again, under the guise of a conclusion, that very [knowledge] for the sake of easy comprehension—namely, that knowledge which has cultivation as its excellence, which has that culmination as its object, and which is the knowledge thereof—by means of the word "tat" (that).
"Tat" means "therefore.
"Iha" (here) refers to the state at the time of realizing the definition of yogic perception; it is the state of the knowledge of cultivation.
That state which is the culmination of excellence sees the actual object;
that perception of an object being cultivated, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogin.
For that [perception] has a clear appearance;
and precisely because it has a clear appearance, it is non-conceptual.
For a conceptual consciousness, in grasping an object as having been seen at the time of the linguistic convention, would grasp it as being fit for association with words.
And "being perceived at the time of the convention" means being the object of a cognition produced at the time of the convention.

Just as a previously arisen cognition that has now perished does not exist at present, so too the state of being the object of that previously perished cognition no longer exists for the entity at present.
Thus, grasping an entity in its non-existent form, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpaka*) with an unclear appearance, because it grasps an object that is not present.
Then, because it appears clearly, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*);
this follows from the context of the passage.
By means of the *abhraka* stone, due to its extreme transparency, [it is placed] at the side.
"By that which cannot be divided into two"—this is a remote reference, as it were, to what was previously stated in the context of the introduction;

namely, that the nature of the hand, the palm of the hand, is like that of something situated nearby. This is the conclusion of what was said before [at 30a]. Let such a cognition of the yogin be granted.

Furthermore, in order to dispel the doubt as to how that [cognition] can be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says "that indeed" (*tad dhi*), demonstrating its connection with the definition of direct perception. The word "for" (*hi*) means "because.
It appears clearly;
but how is it non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), such that it would be direct perception? To this he says: "precisely because it appears clearly."

Regarding the question of what constitutes "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*), the author subsequently combines [the definitions] by means of the phrase "having a single object with respect to clarity" (*sphuṭābhatvāpekṣaikaviṣayatva*).

This is his intention: since the association with the form of a word (*śabdākāra*) is incompatible with clarity (*sphuṭābhatva*), if such [association] were present, then it would not be clear at all.

Anticipating the objection—"How is there a contradiction between these two, given that even a manifestation capable of being associated with verbal expression will be clear?"—he begins to demonstrate the very contradiction with the words "conceptual" (*vikalpa*) and so forth.
For this reason:

since the object (*vastu*)—that which is being perceived—is already known as it truly is, one ought to grasp it; that is, one is capable of apprehending it. Furthermore, if it were to apprehend the object by virtue of having been seen at the time of the linguistic convention, it would have a non-present object as its domain.
Regarding the reason: "Let it be that [the object] was perceived at the time of the convention; what follows from this? To this he says: "And just as... and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of the phrase "what is to be said here":
let it be so; nevertheless, he asks how it is that [the object] does not appear clearly even when it is associated with the form of the speaker—and thus says: "that" (*tat*).
Because it is so, therefore (*tasmāt*).
It is called "conceptualizing" (*vikalpaka*) because it conceptualizes;
but from what [reason] does it have an indistinct appearance? He says: "Because it grasps an object that is not present. For an object appearing as if present would be clear.
Furthermore, when an entity that previously existed is apprehended as the object of a prior perception, it does not appear with a present form;
therefore, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indistinct.
Consequently, his intention is that the association with the form of a word is incompatible with the distinctness of the conceptual construction.
"How is it determined that its object is indeed non-present? To this he says: "having the nature of the non-existent" (*asadrūpam*).

That which was previously seen is now non-existent; thus, because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause, the meaning is "grasping the object being grasped as having the nature of the non-existent," i.e., because it grasps what has the nature of the non-existent.
Regarding what was stated, "precisely because of its clarity," he concludes that very point with the word "tataḥ" (therefore):
since it is not tenable for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to possess clarity.

By the sequence just mentioned, therefore, from that state of being "clearly manifest" (*sphuṭābh*), it follows from the context that the cognition of the yogin is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition touches upon a real object by virtue of having perceived it at the time of the convention (*saṅketa*) is not clearly manifest; for example, like [the cognition of] a long...
[DhPr p. 70]
And because it apprehends an object purified by valid means of cognition, it is non-discrepant; therefore, it is perception,
just like other perceptions.
Yoga is meditative absorption (samādhi). One who possesses that is a yogin.
His knowledge is direct perception (pratyakṣa).

The word "iti" (thus) signifies completion: "perception is only this much. Having thus established the different varieties of perception as being characterized by freedom from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneousness (*abhrānta*), he says the following in order to refute misconceptions regarding its object:
"Its object is the particular characteristic" (I-12). Regarding the phrase "of its," etc.:
the object of that fourfold direct perception is to be understood as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Its own unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is its reality; this is the "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For an entity possesses both a unique reality and a universal one.
In this context, that which is unique is the object of apprehension for perception:
it is the conceptualization of an object seen and then lost,
and the conceptualization that touches upon the visible object by virtue of its having been perceived at the time of the linguistic convention.
What is called "clarity of appearance" (sphuṭābhāsatva) is the manifestation of a form as if it were present.
And this is pervaded by the apprehension of a thing as having been previously seen, [which occurs] through the manifestation of a form that is not actually present.
For once the previous [moment of] cognition has ceased, the state of being an object of that previous cognition no longer exists for the thing.
Therefore, by means of the subsequent cognition of the knower, the fact that the object was the referent of a previous cognition—which is itself non-existent at that later time—is touched upon;
and the apprehension of being the referent of a previous cognition is precisely the apprehension of being qualified by the word perceived at the time of the convention.
This, then, is contradictory.
"Let it be non-conceptual because of the perception of pervasion;

but if it lacks non-erroneousness, how can it be direct perception? To this he says: "By means of valid cognition. An object apprehended by a means of valid cognition is said to be "purified by valid cognition" (*pramāṇaśuddha*).
And the four truths are of this very nature;
they are intended here precisely as purity.
The word "and" (*ca*)—meaning "in agreement"—therefore excludes, along with non-conceptuality, the state of being in agreement [with reality].
Or rather, while remaining in that very state, [the word "yoga"] has the sense of a collection of other causes in consideration of previous causes.
Therefore, because of this non-conceptuality and non-erroneousness,
he states the etymological derivation of the word "yogin" as "yaga."
Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Here, Dharmottara relies on worldly convention;
however, in the *Viniścayaṭīkā*, he follows the established position of the treatise (*śāstra*), and thus there is no contradiction.
Alternatively, since the mention of "concentration" (samādhi) is illustrative, wisdom (prajñā)—which has the power to effect discernment—should also be understood [as included].
The yogi who possesses this is one who is constantly concentrated and intent upon effecting discernment;
it is precisely this much that is delimited by the number four.

The passage beginning with "tad evam" and ending with "āha" is easy to understand. The object (*viṣaya*) is that which is to be known. When the question arises as to what it is, he says: "the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Explaining the meaning of the word *sva* (own) and the word *lakṣaṇa* (definition), he indicates the analysis [of the compound] with the words beginning "one's own" (*svam*).
"One's own" (*svam*) means belonging to oneself (*ātmīya*).
Whatever is one's own belongs to that very person and not to another; thus, by way of this definition, the word *sva* expresses what is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).

By the word *lakṣaṇa*, the intended meaning is "reality" (*tattva*) or "essential nature" (*svarūpa*). Having stated the meanings of the two individual words, he provides their combined form as the compound *svalakṣaṇa*.
By this, it is shown that the term is a *karmadhāraya* compound, meaning that which is both "its own" (*sva*)—that is, unique—and its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), or essential nature.

For the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold: that which is apprehended (*grāhya*), according to whose form the cognition arises, and that which is reached (*prāpaṇīya*), which it determines (*adhyavasyati*).
For the object of apprehension is one thing, and the object of determination is another.
For perception, the object of apprehension is a single moment;
however, the object of determination is the continuum itself, by means of the ascertainment produced through the power of perception.
Furthermore, it is the continuum (*santāna*) alone that is to be reached by perception,

because a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) cannot be reached. Likewise, inference (*anumāna*) also grasps what is not the object, since it functions by determining its own internal appearance— which is not the actual object— to be the object.
Is it not the case that a qualifier is meaningful only when there is both possibility and deviation?
And here, since every essential nature (svarūpa) is unique, there is only possibility and no deviation; so what is the purpose of the word "own" (sva)?

But it should be stated as follows: anticipating the objection that "the nature of the object is its [the cognition's] domain," he says "of the object" (*vastunaḥ*). The particle *hi* means "because. The particle *ca* is used for conjunction, referring to what is about to be stated.
The universal is the common form constituted by conventional cognition;
the particle *ca* is used for conjunction with reference to what precedes.
And if this twofold nature exists, which is the prior form?

Now, regarding the doubt that [the object] is the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): the remainder [of the sense] is that "that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*) is said to be the apprehended (*grāhya*) by direct perception.
By using the word "apprehended," he shows that the teacher intends the "apprehended object" (*grāhyo viṣayaḥ*) by the term "object" (*viṣaya*).

This might be argued: "The object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely the object toward which activity (*pravṛtti*) is directed; therefore, it must be stated that its object is the object of activity."

To the question, "What then is to be apprehended?", he says: "It is twofold. By this, a distinction is asserted; for [the word] "hi" (because) indicates that the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is of two kinds.
The singular number is used with the intention of expressing the genus (*jāti*).
One [aspect] is to be grasped; the other is to be reached.
He establishes the distinction: "Whatever form, whatever appearance a cognition has when it arises..."
That [object] is also twofold: the ultimate and the superimposed.
It should be understood that both indeed possess manifestation within one's own cognition.
That which is to be reached is what one determines.
"From that knowledge, wherever it proceeds"—this is the meaning.
The two *ca* particles serve to conjoin [the terms] with respect to what precedes and what follows.
Now, one might object: "Is there not a difference only between the words 'the apprehended' (*grāhya*) and 'the determined' (*adhyavaseya*), but not in the object itself?"
Since whatever is manifested is precisely what is determined, why is this said? He says: "For [it is] another," where "for" (hi) has the sense of "because" (yasmāt).
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
To [answer] the question of what kind of object is to be apprehended by which [means], he says: "of perception.
The particle "hi" (for/indeed) is used for emphasis and is to be understood as following the word "eka" (one).

What, then, is the "object to be determined" (*adhyavaseya*)? The particle *tu* distinguishes the object to be determined from the object of apprehension (*grāhya*). Now, is perception itself of the nature of determination (*avasāyātmaka*), such that this [object] would be its object to be determined? To this he says: "Perception... (*pratyakṣeti*).

The point is this: since the determination (*niścaya*) that arises subsequent to perception operates precisely upon what has been grasped by perception and does not add anything further, that which is determined by it is already determined by perception itself.

[Objection: But was it not stated that the object to be attained (*prāpaṇīya*) by perception is different from the object to be grasped (*grāhya*); now, however, you speak of the "object to be determined" (*avaseya*)?
Thus, he says that this third point has been reached: "The continuum alone" (*santāna eva*). The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because.
A continuum (*santāna*) is a series of moments established through the relationship of material cause and its effect, which is then conceived as a unity.

"Why is it that the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) itself is not reached by that [cognition]? To this he says: "of the moment" (*kṣaṇasya*). This refers to the moment of the form according to which the perception arises, as is evident from the context.

And thus, for one explaining this, the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) in the phrase "of this means of valid cognition" should be understood with the intention of referring to perception, specifically in the sense of perception produced by the senses (*indriyajā-pratyakṣa*).
Because for self-cognition and the others, a twofold nature of the object is impossible.
Now, let it be that one type of perception possesses a twofold object;
but how can inference be of such a kind?
Regarding the phrase "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasya*):
furthermore, that superimposed object, when being apprehended, is determined as having the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because...
Therefore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is established as the objective domain of engagement for inference,
whereas the non-entity (*anartha*) is its apprehended object (*grāhya*).
Thus, in this context, by demonstrating the apprehended object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is stated that the particular characteristic is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Anticipating the objection that even what has been stated is merely an admission—just like the twofold nature of objects—the author says "tathā" (so).

The meaning of the word "tathā" is: "in that same manner," by which mode characterized by appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), perception grasps one thing while determining another.
It is not only perception that grasps one thing [and determines another].
It determines one thing, but by the word "also" (api), he indicates that inference too apprehends one thing while determining another.
The break (punctuation) must be made right here; otherwise, the explanation would be inconsistent.
To the question "What does it grasp?", he says: "it grasps what is not the object" (*anarthagrāhī*).
Since "inference" (*anumāna*) is the subject under discussion, one might ask how this is possible; anticipating this doubt, he states the justification: "it is its own appearance" (*svapratibhāsa*).
The appearance is like its own manifestation;
due to the conjunction of two powers, it has a form that appears as such [an external object]. In that non-object, which lacks an external form...

Because [cognition] proceeds—that is, functions—by means of the determination of an object (*arthādhyavasāya*), which is characterized by the determination of non-difference consisting in the non-appearance of the distinction between that [internal representation] and the external [object].
Now, what is meant by saying that inferential conceptualization or another [type of cognition] causes one to act by determining its own appearance as an object when it is not an object?
What is being stated is that one does not perceive the distinction between one's own appearance and the object that is being superimposed and determined.
For there is no realization of discernment by means of that very [cognition], because it does not conceptually construct its own appearance as being such [i.e.,
as distinct]. And in this matter, experience is the authority.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-engagement with external fire and so forth;

nor can it be by means of another conceptual construction, because that too would function in the same way and thus fail to touch upon the appearance of the preceding conceptual construction. Enough of this elaboration here.
If this is so, one might ask: "What is the object being determined and to be attained? To this he says: "That" (*sa*).
The word "again" (*punar*) distinguishes it from everything else.
"Superimposed" (*āropita*) is a restatement of its essential nature.
"Object" (*artha*) means that which is grasped as an object, that which is being cognized, insofar as it is manifesting within that cognition;

by this, it is revealed that one determines the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as "this. Having thus explained the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*) through inference for the sake of establishing the probandum, [the author] now states those two explicitly for the sake of easy understanding with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

Since that [particular] is determined as a particular (svalakṣaṇa), therefore the particular, so determined, is the object of engagement for inference. Even the statement "the particular is determined" is expressed on account of a conceit (abhimāna);
however, the particular is not actually the objective domain of the determination.

If that [perception] were its object, then because it is partless, there would follow the undesirable consequence that inference could not occur, since even properties such as momentariness would already be determined [by perception].
We shall clarify this point somewhat further on in this very work;
however, we shall determine it in detail in the context of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) when the occasion arises.
Since it is precisely the object of activity that is to be attained, it is the object of attainment itself that is expressed by the term "object of activity.
The particle *tu* indicates that the graspable (*grāhya*) is distinct from the object of attainment.
When that cognition is manifesting, the graspable is said to be an "unreal object" (*anartha*) because it is manifested [merely as such].

It might be argued: if the determined particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were the object of engagement for inference, then how could Dharmottara have stated in his *Viniścayaṭīkā* that "the determined form is the apprehended object of conceptual cognitions"? For in that case, it would be established that the particular characteristic alone is the apprehended object, and not a non-entity (*anartha*).
Consequently, there is an apparent contradiction. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no fault, because it is expressed in that way for that purpose.

For, in ultimate reality, the form superimposed by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is what is determined as the object of apprehension; nevertheless, for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), [it is so described].

They imagine that they determine an external tree because the superimposed form itself— which is excluded from non-trees— is determined as such, since the external object is likewise so; for they do not perceive the distinction between the two.
It is said that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is determined in accordance with that [conceptual construction].
However, the status of being the apprehended object (*grāhyatva*) is attributed to that very superimposed object of inference (*anumeya*) by relying solely on the form as it appears.
Therefore, since that designation is made with the intention of referring to the form as it is determined as real, what contradiction is there?
He concludes with the words "Therefore, in this case," and so forth.
Since the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold— distinguished as the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavasāya*)— therefore,
by stating "showing the apprehended object here" at the time of refuting misconceptions regarding the object, it becomes clear that the Teacher intended the apprehended object by the word "object."
It might be argued as follows: the validity of perception cannot be established as dependent upon an apprehended object,
because its apprehended object is a single moment,
and the reaching of that [moment] is impossible.
Nor is the validity of inference dependent upon its object;
for its object is of one nature,
yet there is no attainment of that [object].
Furthermore, it is not accepted that a cognition has validity regarding an object which it does not reach,
for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, if it is argued that the very arising of perception in the form of a single blue characteristic is its reaching that object, [we reply:]...
Since inference (*anumāna*) also has the nature of determining fire and so forth, its very arising in that manner is said to be its "attaining" (*prāpaṇa*) of the object.
If that were the case, nothing would remain as a distinction;
for what cognition—whether conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)—does not arise with the form of this or that [object], such that it would not possess validity?

Therefore, the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not to be designated as twofold; rather, only one object, called the "object of purposeful activity" (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*), is to be made known. To this, it is replied: first, regarding cognitions, [there is] the apprehension of the object... (grāhyādhyavasāye).
The object, which is necessarily to be sought after, is of two kinds according to its distinction [as real or unreal], because it is established by experience.
Among these, validity (*prāmāṇya*) is determined with respect to the object of purposeful action (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*),
whereas the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) depends on both.
Since non-cognition cannot possibly possess validity, valid cognition—which is included within [the category of] cognition—is exactly like the two-fold nature of objects;
it is merely demonstrated that validity does not depend upon the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), but rather depends upon the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*).
The statement "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasya*) with respect to the object to be grasped, however, is merely a restatement of its essential nature.

Alternatively, by the word "pramāṇa," it is knowledge itself that is intended here; as he clearly stated in the *Viniścayaṭīkā* during the explanation of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*): "The object of cognitions is twofold: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*)," and so forth.
Therefore, there is nothing faulty [in this].
Furthermore, it might be argued:
if the apprehended object is never actually to be attained by perception, then what is the purpose of its being shown, such that it is said, "By showing the apprehended object here,
perception has its particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) stated to be its object"?
This is not a fault, because it is precisely by thus indicating the object of activity that perception functions.

For if perception grasps a single moment, it indicates the object of activity by generating a determination of the exclusion of non-blue and thereby determining the continuum; and [it likewise indicates] those things occurring within that continuum.
One might render cognitions invalid,

but not by failing to apprehend anything at all. For instance, even in the absence of a definitive ascertainment that explicitly delineates a temporal continuum, the exclusion of non-blue (*anīlavyāvṛtti*)— which is common to all future moments— is indeed apprehended and ascertained by perception.

The very ascertainment of that [initial cognition] is the ascertainment of the characteristic of blue as it exists in the relationship of material cause and effect (upādānopādeyabhāva) as excluded from all non-blue; for the subsequent continuum possesses an identity of acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) with it.
Furthermore, such ascertainment within the continuum is what is called "ascertainment.
For this very reason, that initial cognition, its corresponding practice, and the subsequent cognitions occurring in that continuum [perceive] that which is excluded from non-blue.

They grasp the form already grasped and produce the determination of its exclusion from non-blue which has already been produced; thus, even though numerous [factors] fail to impart any excellence, it is logical that the presentation of the object of apprehension—which deprives invalidity of its authority and appropriates validity for itself—is what constitutes the means of valid cognition.
Thus, everything is clear.

Here, the Master’s intention is as follows: that which is one's own, unique, and not shared with other continua—that reality which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*) and is excluded from everything else—is precisely the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic);
and it is intended that what is contrary to this is not even the object of inference.
What, then, is this unique object of cognition that is to be understood as the particular (svalakṣaṇa)? To this he says: [DhPr p. 74] "One's own... and so forth.
That object, through whose presence or absence there is a difference in the manifestation of cognition, is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "of that object" and so forth:
the word *artha* is a synonym for *viṣaya* (object).
The proximity of that object of knowledge is its abiding in a nearby location;
its non-proximity is its abiding in a distant location.
Therefore, due to proximity and non-proximity, there is a distinction between the appearance in cognition and the form of the apprehended object, characterized by clarity and lack of clarity.
For that which is the object of cognition, when present, produces a clear appearance in the cognition;
however, when not present—provided it remains in a suitable location—it produces an unclear appearance.
That is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For indeed, all things are seen indistinctly from a distance, but clearly when near.

These very [objects] are the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). By explaining that "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), "reality" (*tattva*), and "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) are synonymous, Dharmottara has indeed shown this; however, he did not make it explicit. Consequently, for one who merely hears the words "its object is the particular characteristic" (*tasya viṣayaḥ svalakṣaṇam*), but who does not know the Master’s intention and has not clarified the meaning of Dharmottara’s commentary—[for such a person, the point remains obscure].

If the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) is that form which is unmixed with the form of another, then it would follow—by way of a logical pervasion—that even "fire-ness" (agnitva), being unmixed with universals such as "cow-ness" (gotva), must be a particular; it is with this in mind that the question "What, moreover... and so forth is asked.
By the word "what," he asks about the object in its general form.
The word "again" (*punar*) indicates a specific mode [of inquiry].

Since the term *svalakṣaṇa* does not drop its gender when it is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is [neuter] as *svalakṣaṇam*. Anticipating the objection—"Why does the Teacher provide an answer concerning the meaning when he has been asked about the object (*viṣaya*) by the questioner?"—he says: "Regarding the meaning" (*artheti*).
Intending to show that the object of knowledge is apprehended because of its proximity to cognition, he explains [the verse] with the words "of which object of knowledge.

By explaining that the terms "proximity" (*sannidhāna*) and "non-proximity" (*asannidhāna*) mean being situated nearby or at a distance, he refutes what has been stated by others— that "non-proximity is the absolute non-existence of the thing in a suitable location."
And this is his intention: where an object does not exist, there cognition itself does not arise;
it is not that there exists a difference or plurality in its appearance.
Therefore, by the words "tasmāt" and so forth, he shows that "sannidhānāsannidhānābhyām" is a fifth-case dual ending.

"By way of being manifest and [being capable of causal efficiency]" (sphuṭatvābhyām) should be understood as "by way of being accompanied by the capacity for purposeful action" (arthakriyāsāmarthyānugatābhyām).
This instrumental case (tṛtīyā) is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūtalakṣaṇā),
according to Pāṇini 2.3.21.
Having explained the meaning of the individual words, he explains the meaning of the whole compound. This is the twofold style of commentators:
sometimes they explain the meaning of the whole compound first and subsequently expound the meaning of the individual words.

In some cases, having explained the meaning of individual words, they subsequently explain the meaning of the whole; here, *hi* is used for emphasis. By the phrase "situated precisely in a suitable place," he excludes one who is situated in a distant location.
The intention is that even that which is situated at a distance does not produce cognition at all, so how much less could it split [it]?
Dispelling the doubt that the definition of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) might be either non-pervasive (*avyāpin*) or impossible (*asambhavin*), he says: "all" (*sarvāṇi*).
The word "all" is for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*).
By this, the lack of pervasiveness is refuted;
for "hi" has the sense of "because," and "are seen" means they are perceived.
By this, the impossibility [of the definition] has been refuted. Dispelling the charge of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), he says: "those very ones" (*tāny eva*).
That is to say, those very things which are the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Nor is it the object of inference," according to the context.

And the intention of one who says that things are seen indistinctly from a distance is this: for an object being apprehended at a distance is apprehended as mixed with abundant dust, mist, and so forth;
therefore, it is apprehended indistinctly, but not [as a non-existent thing].

But why is it that only the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? For even fire, which is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is determined as having a perceptible nature; to this, he says:
"That alone is ultimately real" (I-14),
"that alone is ultimately real," and so forth.
The ultimate object (*paramārtha*) is the uncontrived, non-superimposed nature.
Therefore, that which "exists" is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
That very object which, through its presence or absence, produces a clear or unclear appearance is alone ultimately real;
and it is precisely this that is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because of that.
Therefore, that very particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not apprehended at all;
for even when a tree is apprehended in such a manner, it still performs causal functions such as providing shade and so forth.
Nor is the apprehension of something additional an error.
However, this point is further examined here:

if that very object which, through its presence or absence, differentiates the appearance in cognition by means of clarity or lack of clarity, is indeed the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then [in that case] touch and taste would both be particular characteristics.
They would not exist; for if those two were absent, cognition itself would not be produced—
how much less could they differentiate the appearance of cognition by means of clarity and lack of clarity?
Furthermore, in this case, consciousness would lack its own specific characteristic (asvalakṣaṇa).
Let alone its inability to produce indistinct cognition when not present, it lacks even the ability to produce distinct cognition when present.
Moreover, it cannot exist at a distance or nearby, because it is non-spatial (adeśatvāt).
How is it that the Master [Dharmakīrti], by proposing such a definition of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) without considering such a great lack of pervasiveness,
and Dharmottara, likewise explaining it so forcefully, do not fall into error? It is not so,
because their intended meaning has not been fully understood.
If this definition were established exactly according to the literal statement,
then this [objection] would indeed hold; however,

what is indicated here is that exclusivity— which consists in being inherent in a single object and not following after other instances— serves as a differentiator of the manifestation of cognition through its presence or absence.
For this reason, the *Hetubindu* states: "In that regard, that first [type of perception] has an uncommon object" (*pṛ.* 53).
For this very reason, Bhaṭṭārcaṭa explains: "[An uncommon object means] an object that is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" (*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
25). Therefore, by contrast with this, the common form of inference will be shown to have a common object.
Therefore, there is neither under-extension nor any other defect of definition.

Even when it is stated that "its object is the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), since the word *svalakṣaṇa* could be etymologically derived in other ways as well, the intended meaning might not be understood by the listeners. Thus, it should be seen that the intended meaning is indicated in this manner.

Regarding the statement "its object is the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), if it is restricted such that "only its object is the particular characteristic," then, according to the principle that "restriction applies to what is other than that from which the causal operation proceeds," perception would be restricted to the particular characteristic alone; consequently, perception would also have other things as its objects.

Now, if it is restricted to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, then since perception is restricted to the particular characteristic, an unrestricted particular characteristic would also become the object of inference. Therefore, a double restriction must be applied: "its object is that alone" and "the object is the particular characteristic alone."
Unable to tolerate this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) asks: "Why?
With "Why? he asks for the cause in general; with "Furthermore," he asks for it specifically.

Regarding the statement "that which belongs to whatever object," [the opponent] says this while disagreeing with the intended meaning that "only that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not the object of inference (*anumāna*"). His intention is: "Why do you say that it is only the object of perception? Is the object of inference not also a particular characteristic?"
Anticipating the objection, "Why is that very thing not so?", the proponent of the prima facie view himself provides the reasoning, saying:
"But why is that alone ultimately real?"—[DhPr p. 76]—he says:
Because a real entity (vastu) is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya), it is called an "object" (artha); that is, it is something to be sought,
namely, either that which is to be abandoned or that which is to be adopted.
For that which is to be abandoned is desired to be abandoned, and that which is to be adopted is desired to be adopted.
The "activity" (kriyā) of an object—that is, of a purpose—is its accomplishment;
the "capacity" (sāmarthya) is the power (śakti) for that [accomplishment].
He states that very characteristic form of the entity with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

The term "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) should be understood here as inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*), because it involves reflecting upon the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It consists precisely of the perceptible, that is, it consists precisely of the particular (svalakṣaṇa).

Now, since it has been stated that "the particular is that object for which there is a difference in the appearance of cognition based on its presence or absence," how is there any room for this question?

For there is no difference in the appearance of cognition based on the presence or absence of an object that is the domain of conceptual construction (vikalpa), from which [this question] might arise.
True;

however, this is his intention: that which you have understood to be the definition of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is not its definition at all, but rather, that alone is the particular which is determined as being perceptible.
Such is its definition.

And this being the case, the fact that even the object of a conceptual construction based on inference possesses that same nature [of being ultimately unreal] is indeed unavoidable; thus the question is well-posed.
Showing the Master’s response to this question, he says: "That very [same thing]."

Now, it might be argued: "If [the following] were stated, it would be appropriate; however, since this very point is not established, how can this manner of answering the question be justified? It is said in reply:
By "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), one's own unique, ultimate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is meant.
And that alone is called the ultimate intrinsic nature.
"That which alone is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyākṣama) is alone ultimately real (paramārthasat)"— this response, "that very thing," is logical.
By showing that it is the "ultimate object" (paramo 'rthaḥ), he demonstrates that this is a karmadhāraya compound.
"Uncontrived," and so forth, is the explanation of the word *parama*.

By that [word], the meaning of "existent" (*sat*)—namely, "it exists"—is stated. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "existent" (*sat*) in the sense of being present (*vidyamāna*) by way of that nature (*rūpa*).
This word *asi* ends in a *śatṛ* suffix; furthermore, there is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.32, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
Having explained the meaning of the term *paramārthasat*, he elucidates the phrase *tad eva* with the words *ya eva*.
"Appearance of cognition" is [the meaning] according to the context.

An "object" (artha) is that which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyāsamartha), and since the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is of such a nature, with this intention he says: "that very object is indeed that [appearance]."
"Let such a thing exist as an ultimate reality;
however, that will not be its object, nor will anything else be its object.
Thus, the intended meaning is not established," he says with the words "And if... (sa cet).

The particle *eva* (only) is to be understood as following the word "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*). Thus, the phrase "that very thing" (*tad etat*) means that the object established as the domain of perception is exclusively a real entity (*vastu*), and not also the domain of inference.
By this, one should understand that the conclusion has been made for the answer to the question: "Why, then, is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) the domain of perception alone?"
[37] That which is written outside the line is not recited—*saṃ*.
Now, unable to tolerate that only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), he asks: "Why?
His intention is this: indeed, that object alone is ultimately real which is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) as being an object.
Furthermore, since fire is also determined in that same way as the object of inference, why is it not also ultimately real?
To this, the reply beginning with "the object" (*artha*) is explained by the passage beginning with "it is sought after" (*arthyate*);
the word "and" (*ca*) conjoins [this point] with the equality of their respective strengths.
He asks, "How is that which is to be abandoned sought? and says: "That which is to be abandoned" (*heya*).
For (*hi*) means "because. If an object being sought is for the purpose of abandonment, then it is not an object to be accepted; thus he says: "That which is to be accepted" (*upādeya*).
This [particle *ca*] conjoins the fact that the object to be adopted (*upādeya*) is sought in relation to that which is to be abandoned (*heya*).
"Object" (*artha*) refers to the purpose (*prayojana*), such as burning and so forth.
And explaining it in this way, burning and so forth—which are the very things to be accomplished—are primarily the objects to be adopted or abandoned.
That is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*);
its existence [is established] because of that.
The word *vastu* is a synonym for the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
This is the meaning: because that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is called ultimately real;
and since an object that differentiates the manifestation of cognition through its presence or absence is what is capable of causal efficiency.
Therefore, that alone is ultimately real;
for it is precisely from the object of direct perception that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is obtained, and not from the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Consequently, although the object of conceptual construction is determined as if it were the perceived object, it is nevertheless not the perceived object itself, because causal efficiency is absent therein.
And because it is a perceptible entity, that very thing is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), not the object of conceptual construction;
anything else is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). I-16

"Other than this," and so forth: that which is other than this particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)—that is, that which is not a particular characteristic and is not an object of [direct] cognition—is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
For an object determined by conceptual cognition (vikalpajñāna) does not differentiate the appearance in cognition based on its presence or absence.
For instance, the fire being superimposed exists by virtue of that superimposition; and due to that superimposition, it is both distant and near.
Yet, despite the proximity or distance of that superimposed object, there is no difference in the appearance within cognition, whether in terms of clarity or lack of clarity.
Therefore, that which is other than the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is called the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
A characteristic by way of generality is a "general characteristic";
the meaning is that it is a common form (*sādhāraṇa-rūpa*).
For the form being superimposed is common to all fire;
therefore, it possesses the characteristic of a universal (*sāmānya*).

He shows that because it is possible to either adopt or abandon that [universal], one can likewise adopt, abandon, or otherwise act toward the means of its realization—such as fire—and thus it is logical for fire and so forth, which constitute those means, to be objects of adoption and the like.
The passage beginning with "In that" (*tasyām*) and ending with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is easy to understand.

Anticipating the objection—"If the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) is what is to be established, why has the Master demonstrated the nature of the thing (*vastu*) in such a way?"—he says: "The word 'thing' (*vastuśabda*)," etc.

The section of the text beginning with "This, then, is the meaning" (*tad ayam artha*) and ending with "not an object of conceptual construction" (*na vikalpaviṣaya*) is a summary of the points already stated.
And he is one of excellent wisdom.
In this context, the Master intends "otherness" (anyatva) to be relative to the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) under discussion.
Intending that the word *svalakṣaṇa* should take the ablative case when joined with the word "other," he says "from this" (*etasmāt*).
He clarifies this otherness by stating: "that which does not possess its own specific characteristic."
To exclude [the existence of] things such as a rabbit's horn, he says: "an object of cognition" (*jñānaviṣaya*).
Since the investigation of the objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the subject at hand, it follows that this means "an object of consciousness" (*vijñānaviṣaya*).
From that, its difference from what is unestablished (*asiddhi*) is established.
He says "vikalpa... and so forth, because this [conceptual cognition] also functions as an effect of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because.

From what is its state of not being differentiated from the appearance determined? Is it because it always possesses a form that is present, or rather because it possesses a form that is absent? To this he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*).
Being superimposed and thus perceived,
it exists in the form of fire due to that superimposition— which is characterized by such an arising— and due to the resulting determination;
let it be so through superimposition, yet even so, [the question remains] regarding its presence or absence.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of superimposition" (*āropāt*).
The [first] *ca* has the sense of "this is clearly evident.
The second *ca* conjoins the state of being near with the state of having a single object, in view of the state of being distant.
The passage beginning with "tasya" and ending with "ucyate" is clear in meaning.
And in order to show that which is to be apprehended by the one who infers, he says:
That is the object of inference (I-17).
That is the object of inference in its form as the apprehended.
The gender of the pronoun "that" (saḥ) is adopted according to the gender of its referent.

One who wishes to explain that the object of inference is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) would have to repeat this entire section explaining the nature of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, for the sake of brevity, the object of inference is stated right here in the chapter on perception itself.
He provides the etymological analysis (vigraha) of the word *lakṣaṇa* with the word *sāmānya*, saying: "by way of generality" (*sāmānyena*).
The compound means "the proof of the nature that is common [to all], not particular, and shared with other continuums. He clarifies the meaning of that term.

Regarding the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*): since even that which is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not uncommon [to other instances], it is unestablished; and since being common to other individuals is unestablished, he says: "And this fire is 'entire' (*sakala*), meaning it is distinguished by the various differences such as grass-fed (*tārṇa*) or wood-fed (*pārṇa*) fires. Thus it is.
The point is that it is common to those [two] because, by the force of such a mark (*liṅga*), there is the appearance of a mere entity excluded from non-fire.
But surely, such a universal is a non-entity (*avastu*) within the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
If inference has that as its object, how can it be a motivator toward the external world and how can it bring about the attainment of it?
If it is asked, "From what [source] would this [cognition] possess validity?
it is said:

These conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), indeed, due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), determine their own internal appearance—which is excluded from non-fire—to be "excluded from non-fire" even with respect to the external object; thus, it is precisely that superimposition (*adhyāsana*) whereby the external fire is determined.
Thus they think:

the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external fire that is similar [to the perceived object] by way of its exclusion from non-fire (*anagnivyāvṛttatayā*) is precisely the determination of an external fire. Because there is no realization of the distinction [between the two], for this very reason those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), having unified the perceptible (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*) objects, cause the world to proceed toward the external.
The unification of the visible object and the conceptual construction should also be understood as arising precisely from that [conceptualization] acting as the cause for its engagement.

Furthermore, because it is connected to what is externally related, inferential conceptualization is reliable; and with respect to the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus the proponent of logic says: "Even an error is valid cognition by virtue of its connection [to the object].
And this meaning is also to be understood here in the context of the statement: "Because it proceeds by determining an object in what is not an object within its own appearance.
In brief, however, we have already said something on that point.
"Since it is thus, therefore"—this is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
"That" (*tad*) refers to that which is being superimposed.
With the words "And that... and so forth, he shows the introduction to the phrase "it is inference.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has the form of the apprehended object as its intrinsic nature" (*grāhya-rūpa-svabhāva*).

Explaining it in this way, he shows that by the word "object" (*viṣaya*), what is intended here as the object is the objective domain of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely the determined particular (*adhyavaseya-svalakṣaṇa*); for it is precisely the particular that is established as such by virtue of being the object of determination.
However, because that [particular] does not appear there [in the conceptual cognition] in its own form, it lacks the status of being the apprehended object (*agrāhyatva*).
It has already been stated that "being an object of apprehension" is predicated by relying upon a form that is manifest.

This same intention applies to inference as well when its objective domain is observed: if this inference were to apprehend a non-entity—a mere exclusion of non-fire in the form of a universal—then that universal form would have to appear [as something distinct].
In that case, determining it as its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would take that specific characteristic as its object of engagement;
and by doing so, it would attain the status of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a real entity, and not otherwise. Thus he says:
[DhPr p.79]
Having refuted the misconception regarding the object, he states the following to refute the misconception regarding the result:
"And that very perceptual cognition is the fruit of the means of valid cognition" (I-18).
Regarding the phrase "that very": that which was just mentioned as perceptual cognition is itself the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
How is it the fruit of the means of valid cognition? He says:
because its nature is the apprehension of the object (I-19).
The apprehension of the object is its comprehension.
That which has that very [cognition] as its form—namely, the cognition of an object—is "that which has the nature of the cognition of the object.
Its state is "therefore";
this is what is meant: a cognition that leads to attainment is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the power of attainment does not arise merely from the fact that [the cognition] is invariably concomitant with the object;
for even though sprouts and the like are invariably concomitant with seeds and so forth, they do not possess the capacity to bring about attainment.

Therefore, although this cognition arises from the object to be attained, there must necessarily be some "activity of attainment" (*prāpakavyāpāra*) which, when performed, constitutes the attainment of the object.
And that very [cognition] is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), because through its application,
the knowledge becomes a bringer [of the object].
And it was stated previously that the so-called "function of the bringer" consists precisely in the bringing forth of the object of engagement.
And that very perception, which consists in the cognition of the object and the manifestation of the object, is therefore itself the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
To justify this reference in the masculine gender, he says: "all," etc.
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of *iva*.
The analysis of the compound is "the grasping of the mark (*liṅga*) in that same manner," [with the word ending in the genitive case].

Here too, it should be understood as a restriction that the object of inference is exclusively the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and not that it is the object of inference alone; for even a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in the wake of perception has that [general characteristic] as its object.
"Otherwise, the ascertainment of the logical mark (liṅga) would be impossible.

Now, since the current topic is the removal of disagreements regarding the object of perception (pratyakṣa), one might raise the objection: "Why have you undertaken the removal of disagreements regarding the object of inference (anumāna), which is irrelevant to the present context? To dispel this doubt, he begins with the words "sāmānya... and so forth.
And this, ending with the words "and thus it has been said," is easy to understand.
The portion beginning with "viṣaye" and ending with "phalam" is easy to understand.

Furthermore, this is the intention of the author of the Vārttika in demonstrating the result (*phala*): indeed, in common worldly usage, that which is the instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇa*) is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the resulting valid cognition (*pramiti*), which is the fruit to be accomplished by that instrument, must necessarily be shown.

Now, one might ask: "In what respect does the means of action operate? How so? Is there some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this, he explains the response beginning with "of the object" (*arthasya*), stating that this [question] should here be disregarded.
And this portion, ending with "tasmāt," is easy to understand.
Here, some writing has been omitted from the line;
because of its subtlety, it is not recited—saṃ-

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a cognition which is corroborative is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and that corroboration arises merely from the production [of the cognition] by that [object]?
Why, then, is the result sought as the comprehension of the object? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The following is what is meant."
Now, its status as a "means of attainment" (prāpaka) is due to its possession of the power of causing attainment;
and that power exists precisely because it arises from that [object].
And so, he says "prāpaṇaśaktiś ca" (and the power of attainment) to explain how the prima facie position is transcended;
the word "ca" (and) means "because.
It is not [attained] from the solitary one alone, which is devoid of the manifestation of the object.

The term *vinābhāvī* means "that which exists without" what is intended to be expressed; the suffix *ṇini* is applied here because the root belongs to the *grahādi* class, and thus it means "deviant" (*vyabhicārī*).
The compound is formed as "existing without an object" (*arthena vinā bhāvī*), by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of Pāṇini 2.1.30, *tṛtīyā*.
The state of that [is] "therefore. But how is it not from the seed alone? He says: "from the seed.
Since this is so, therefore [it is as stated].

Although it is the continuum itself that is to be attained, and not from that [continuum] does the [cognition] arise, nevertheless, having determined its unity with respect to the object, it is said that [the cognition] arises from the object to be attained.
This refers to the activity of cognition as the act of apprehension, which must necessarily be performed by the cognizer;
it is said, as before, that "it is attained" by way of its functional capacity (*yogyatā*).
"Let there be something else to be done by him;
nevertheless, that is not its fruit," he says with "sa eva" (he himself),
meaning that this is clearly evident in this matter.
Let it be granted that the operation which brings about [the result] must necessarily exist;
however, that [operation] will be of the nature of non-cognition.
