To the question, "In that case, how can cognition be the result?", he says: "It has been stated."
The word *yām* is used in the sense of *yat* (which).
*Purastāt* means "in the preceding [part].

If it is asked, "By whom was this said? [the answer is: by the passage beginning with, "Even the state of being an instigator (*pravarttakatva*) is nothing other than the indication of the object of activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya-upadarśakatva*)," and so forth.

Let it be granted that the cognition of the object is necessarily the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); nevertheless, one might raise the objection: "How can that very perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*) itself be the fruit, since it does not possess the nature of that [cognition]? Anticipating this, the author says "That very [is the fruit]" (*tad eva*), while demonstrating how its nature as the cognition of the object is established.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
[Objection: But has not the demonstration of the object been shown as that which is to be performed?
How then is that single [act] demonstrated within the cognition of the object? To this he says: "having the form of the demonstration of the object.
The intention is that there is no difference between these two [acts].
Since this is so, therefore, by implication, that very thing is perceptual cognition itself and not something other than the object.

If the result were a cognition distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what would be the consequence? For what reason is its non-difference from the means of valid cognition established with such great effort? If one asks this:
It is said:

"The validity of cognition [is established], because activity is primarily based upon it" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.4). In this regard, the validity of that which is not of the nature of knowledge has first been set aside.

Furthermore, although the fruit of this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which is of the nature of knowledge, is not distinct [from the cognition itself], it must necessarily be admitted that its essence consists in the determination of the object;
otherwise, it would not even possess the nature of knowledge.
Furthermore, if being a cognition were defined by the capacity to produce valid knowledge (*pramā*), then the eyes and other sense organs would also have to be considered cognitions.
Moreover, the nature of being consciousness (*bodharūpatva*) cannot be the determining factor if it is not self-cognizing (*asvasaṃvedanatayā*).
Or, if it is of the nature of self-cognition, then the very cognition of the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*) is itself the cognition of the object; so how can there be a distinct result?
Furthermore, because the systematic arrangement of individual cognitions would be untenable, one must not accept that consciousness is formless.
It is a principle established in all schools of thought that cognition itself is the manifestation of the object;
therefore, no one should dispute that cognition possesses the nature of apprehension.
And if that identity [of the cognition] with the object were real, then that alone would be the appropriate result,
since the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is completed by that much.
Furthermore, if cognition did not possess the capacity to determine the object by virtue of its own nature as the determination of the form of the object, [it could not be a means of knowledge].
However, [it is] by virtue of its producing a distinct determination (*paricchitti*); otherwise, the immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) of the object's determination could not be established.
For what would it mean to say that the first cognition determines the object and makes the object immediate? It means that it produces a determination whose object is the thing itself.

If that [cognition] also makes the object manifest, then it would produce another cognition; and if the same were the case for each subsequent one, there would be an infinite regress of determinations, but never the manifestation of the object itself. Thus, total blindness of the entire world would result.

Now, if it is accepted that among those [cognitions], one is itself of the nature of the determination of the object and consists in the immediacy of the object, then being a determiner does not consist in producing a distinct determination.
What then? It consists in its own being the very self-nature of the determination of the object. Thus, the same status applies to the first [cognition] as well.
And if that were so, how could the result be distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
In this world, the action itself is not the instrument, because the two exist as distinct entities.
Furthermore, if this action characterized by cognition were the result, [it would be indistinguishable from the means].
If, then, cognition is the fruit of the means of valid cognition because it consists of the result of valid knowledge, what then is the means of valid cognition? To this he says:
Its validity consists in its similarity to the object (I-20). That which is the similarity or resemblance of this cognition with the object is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For in this context, whatever object from which a cognition arises, that cognition becomes similar to that very object.
Just as that which arises from blue is similar to blue,
and that similarity— termed resemblance (*sārūpya*), likeness (*sādṛśya*), aspect (*ākāra*), and also appearance (*ābhāsa*)—
is indeed non-different from cognition.
This being the case, that very cognition would be both the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
And it is not logically possible for a single entity to be both the object to be established (*sādhya*) and the means of establishment (*sādhana*).
Therefore, he asks: "In what way is similarity (*sārūpya*) the means of valid cognition? and replies:
"Because the comprehension of the object is established by virtue of that [word]," I-21.
This concludes the section on direct perception (pratyakṣapariccheda).
Having asserted, "What other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) could there be?", the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) says "yadi" (if).
"Yadi" expresses a possibility;
the word "tarhi" expresses intolerance.
The meaning is that this very [claim]— that direct perception is knowledge *thus* (or *in this way*)— is not acceptable;
for the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is to be established.
In that case, one should apply the question: "What is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) at that time?
Here, he explains the answer, "conformity with the object" (arthasārūpya), by saying "by the object" (arthena);
that is, by the object which is the referent (viṣaya).
The conformity with the object (*viṣayasārūpya*) of cognition called "perception" is its arising in a form identical to that of the object.
With the words beginning "here," [the author] establishes this very conformity;
and everything up to the end of the passage, "and this is similar to blue," is easy to understand.

The intention of one who speaks thus is simply this: although consciousness arises with a manifold prior manifestation, it bears the form of the object alone and not that of anything else; this is established by experience and is beyond questioning, because the ascertainment of similarity always arises in accordance with that very form.
For if that object were to possess a form other than its own, then at some time a cognition bearing the form of something else might be produced;

just as, for example, mother-of-pearl, despite the occasional arising of a continuous stream of cognitions with the form of silver, produces a cognition that conforms to its own form for one who has approached its location.
Yet, a non-erroneous cognition of blue never possesses the nature of having another form.

Therefore, it is determined that the object also possesses such a form; for when the conformity of the cognition to the external object is understood, this alone is the means of apprehension. But is it not stated elsewhere that the appearance of the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as is its objective form?
But here there is a conformity with the object;
anticipating the objection as to how this is not a contradiction, he says: "And that," where "and" (ca) means "because" or serves as an emphasis, and by this word "also" (api).
The intention is that since the conformity with the object itself is what is expressed by each respective word, there is no contradiction.
Rather, by asking "What then is the means of valid cognition? he now explicitly states what was previously held in his mind with the words "But surely... and so forth.
This section, ending with the words "and this is the means of valid cognition," is easy to understand.
"By virtue of that" means:
"that" refers to similarity;
"by virtue of that" means by the power of similarity.
The comprehension of the meaning is its understanding; its accomplishment is the establishment of that [understanding].
It is because of that accomplishment as the cause.
The meaning is that perception, which consists of the cognition of an object, is established— and thus becomes cognized— by virtue of its similarity [to that object].
For since the cognition has the appearance of blue,
therefore the cognition of blue is determined.
For from those [faculties] such as the eye by which consciousness arises, that cognition cannot be established as the perception of blue merely by their power;
rather, it is established as the perception of blue when it is experienced as resembling blue.
This is because the eye and other faculties are common [to all cognitions].—Ṭ—
And here, the relationship between the probandum and the probans is not based on the relation of producer and produced, such that there would be a contradiction within a single entity.
Rather, it is by way of the relationship between the object to be established and the means of establishment.

Therefore, it is not contradictory for one aspect of a single entity to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and another aspect to be the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
In response to this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he explains the Master’s [Dignāga’s] reply beginning with "by virtue of that" (*tadvaśāt*) as follows: "That" (*tat*).
He clarifies the meaning of the word *tat* (that) and the meaning of the word *vaśa* (under the influence of) with the phrase "by way of similarity" (*sārūpyeṇa*).
By the term "of the object" (*arthasya*), it should be understood as "of that which is qualified by its nature as blue, yellow,
and so forth," because this cognition is perceived as being delimited precisely by such a qualified object.
He clarifies this very point with the words "of the object" (*arthasya*) and so forth.
He reveals the meaning of the word *siddhi* by saying "it is cognized" (*pratītam*).
The meaning is that it becomes ascertained in such a form as: "This is the cognition of blue, not of yellow," and so on.
He concludes the stated point with the words "blue," etc.
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
Since this is so, therefore, the cognition of blue is determined to be "this is the knowledge of blue alone."
One might object: "Surely this determination of knowledge will arise from its causes alone;

for since they are capable of producing knowledge, why should they not be capable of determining it? Therefore, this restriction of cognition does not depend upon similarity (*sārūpya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From those... (*yebhyaḥ*).
"Hir" means "because.
The intention of one who speaks thus is this: the sense organs and light are not the restrictive factors [for perception], because those two are common to all cognitions.
Even a distinction residing in the object is not a determiner;
for that distinction must be understood from cognition alone.
Since there is no such distinction [in the cognition], how could it be a factor for establishing a distinction?
If this same principle applies even to the similarity with blue, then how can that [similarity] itself be the regulator? To this he says: "Blue...
The particle *tu* indicates that the similarity is distinct from the sense organ and so forth.
The cognition or consciousness being experienced as similar to blue is established as belonging to blue alone, and not to anything else.

This is the meaning of the present context: if cognition were not similar in form to its object, but rather formless and consisting solely of pure awareness, then—being indistinguishable due to its uniform nature as experience alone—it would not attain the status of an object of determination (*paricchedya*) with respect to blue, yellow, and so forth. Consequently, the distinction between individual objects, which is established by experience in the form "this is the cognition of blue" and "this is the cognition of yellow," would be lost.
Furthermore, the form as it pertains to the object is doubtful because its apprehension depends upon cognition; thus, it is doubted due to uncertainty regarding the specific nature of that cognition.
And it is not possible to determine that very same doubtful form by means of that very same doubtful form.
Moreover, no distinction residing in the cognition other than one produced by the object through similarity (sārūpya) is logically tenable.
Even if it exists, this [object] cannot yet be pointed out by her;

nor can there be a determination of the restriction of action (*karmaniyamaniścaya*) through that which is not ascertained. And when that specific form and that determination of the restriction of action belonging to the cognition have been ascertained, what kind of establishment of its having that form remains? Just as...
For similarity is the cause for establishing that cognition,
and what is to be established is the form of the experience of blue.
If it is asked, "How can there be a relationship of the determined and the determiner within a single cognition?
it is said:
because that cognition, having experienced something resembling blue, is established as the apprehender of blue by means of a determining cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*).
Therefore, similarity is the cause for establishing that which has been experienced.
And that cognition, being established by a determinative cognition as the "experience of blue," is the object to be established (*vyavasthāpya*).
Consequently, similarity—by way of the exclusion of non-similarity—is the cause for establishing the cognition.
And the nature of the cognition of blue is established through the exclusion of the cognition of non-blue.
Since the blue object and so forth cannot be defined when momentariness is not yet determined, its [the cognition's] form is likewise not defined.

Therefore, that very thing from which this comprehension attains reality without mediation—that whose operation is unimpeded by anything else—is the differentiator through its own distinction, the instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor, however, is it the case that its operation is obstructed by this very [object].
And such [cognition] is indeed similarity itself.
Furthermore, this argument has been stated by us at length in the *Viśeṣākhyāna*; therefore, it should also be consulted there.
But even so, how can a single cognition be both the object to be established (*sādhya*) and the means of establishment (*sādhana*)?
For an axe itself does not become the act of cutting.
Therefore, one might suspect that the non-difference between the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) cannot be accepted; anticipating this, he says "na ca" and so forth.
The word *ca* is used in the sense of "because.
Here, in this investigation of the means and result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*), there would be a contradiction or an impossibility.
If it were not so, how indeed could it be? To this he says: *api tu*—but rather, however.
"Vyavasthāpyam" means that which is to be regulated in a specific form.
"Vyavasthāpananimittam" refers to the cause of regulation, intended as that by which something is regulated—that is, established—in its particular nature.
The reading "vyavasthāpanabhāvena" is inconsistent with what is to be said later.

But when the reading "vyavasthāpakabhāvena" (by way of being the establisher) is seen, then it should be understood in that way by intending the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) for the instrumental case (*karaṇe*), just as in the expression "the sword cuts well. By that [means], namely, by the state (*bhāva*) of those two— the established (*vyavasthāpya*) and the establisher (*vyavasthāpaka*)— which serves as the cause for cognition and verbal designation (*jñānābhidhāna-nimitta*), [the form is established].
This is an instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Because it is so, therefore, from that [fact], a certain form of a single entity—namely, of cognition characterized by direct perception—is conceptually constructed as an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), like "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth.
In this regard, there is this establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so on with respect to the external object.

The aspect of the apprehended (grāhyākāra), known as the conformity with the object, reveals the self's cognition as the cognition of the object; therefore, it is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the object.
For this very reason, the external object is the object of cognition (prameya).
In reality, although this is self-cognition, when it is determined as being connected with the object, it is the result (phala), namely the cognition of the object.

Now, one might ask: "What here is the cause for establishing [the distinction], and what is that which is to be established, by virtue of which this would be so? To this he says: "vyavasthāpana" (establishing).
Establishing is the cause of the establishment.
In other words, it refers to the operation of the causal agent (*prayojaka*) within the established arrangement.
Its cause is its motive (*nimitta*).
The word "hi" means "because."
Of that direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
What, then, is to be established?
The word "but" (*tu*) distinguishes the object to be established from the cause of its establishment.
The cognition of blue in the form "this is of the blue, not of anything else" is *rūpa* (form).
Not accepting this, [the author] says "having established," and so forth;
by the word "also" (*api*), he shows that it is not only the relation of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) for a single entity that is untenable.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "It is said," and so forth.

For, since one says "I have experienced something resembling blue," what is restated is the actual form [of the experience]; however, there is no certain cognition that "I am experiencing something resembling blue."
Rather, it is established as the apprehension of blue by means of the thought "I am experiencing blue itself";
and this establishing conceptual cognition should be understood as arising through the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), perception alone cannot establish itself as having the nature of the cognition of blue.
Even if a consciousness has the nature of the cognition of blue, if it is not established by a determinative cognition (*niścayapratyaya*), it is as good as non-existent.
Therefore, a consciousness that is established by a determinative cognition as having the nature of the cognition of blue becomes existent by virtue of its identity as the cognition of blue.

Therefore, perception becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when it performs a determinative act (*adhyavasāya*). However, if the determinative act is not performed, consciousness remains undetermined as being of the nature of the cognition of blue;
and thus the fruit of the means of knowledge, which consists in the apprehension of the object, remains unestablished.
Therefore, because it lacks the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), cognition itself would not even be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, it might be argued that cognition does not establish itself by itself in such a manner,
because its nature is one of non-determination (*aniścaya*).
Furthermore, even a definitive cognition (niścaya) is not capable of establishing itself in such a state, because it is non-conceptual (avikalpaka) with respect to its own nature.
To the question "By what, then, is it established as such?", he says: "by the cognition of certainty" (niścayapratyayena).
It should be understood that this refers to a subsequent determinative cognition (*niścayātmaka-jñāna*) which is concordant with it.
Therefore, the similarity (*sārūpya*) experienced and realized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the basis for the determination: "This is the awareness of blue."
"Of that which has been perceived" (*na pītasya*) refers to the reason or cause for establishing a restriction.
Furthermore, this is a support for the statement: "For similarity (*sārūpya*) is the cause for the determination of that cognition.
If similarity alone is the cause for determining that cognition, then he asks: what is it that is determined, and of what nature? To this, he says: "ascertainment" (*niścaya*).

The word *eva* (only) is used for emphasis; it should be understood as following the word *tat* (that). The meaning is that only that very cognition which possesses the aforementioned similarity (*sārūpya*) is to be established—that is, it is to be restricted by the form "of blue alone."
[40] “By the phrase ‘with the word *iti*’ up to ‘and the nature of the admission,’ he shows the admission.

This reading is seen in the manuscript written outside the lines in connection with the eighth line; however, it is not known where it should be inserted—i.e., what its proper placement is. To this he says: “blue,” etc.
By the exclusion of the cognition of yellow and so forth, this cognition of blue—that is, the knowledge—is established and determined.
When there is the expectation of "by what is it being established?", it should be connected [to the answer] that it is by the determining cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*).
Now, is similarity (*sārūpya*) distinct from knowledge, such that similarity is mentioned in that way?
Anticipating the objection that "knowledge is indeed described in this way," he says "therefore" (tasmāt) by way of a concluding summary:
because a cause for the determination of something else through similarity is not possible,
and since similarity cannot be established as something other than knowledge, for that reason.
And this— namely, the conclusion established through the reasoning beginning with "a certain form of a single entity"—
is the meaning of the treatise.
Relying on the distinction created by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) within a single cognition itself, he speaks of the relationship between the object to be established and the means of establishment.
And based on their actual non-difference, the non-difference of the means of valid cognition and its result is stated;
nor is there any deficiency whatsoever.

Now, by saying "by means of the determinative cognition," [the author] clarifies the nature of the determination intended by him under the guise of a conclusion, starting with the words "the establisher."
It is called "the establisher" because it establishes;
and that [establisher], although produced by the power of that [object], should be understood as being concordant with it.
For it is impossible for there to be an establishing and an established even when they are established by a discordant conceptualization.
Just as when one sees a mirage, there is no such reality in the two cognitions of similarity to water that are established by a conceptual construction arising from its power;

however, when a cognition in the form of the awareness of blue is established by the resulting determination (*adhyavasāya*) through the force of similarity, then similarity— being the cause of that establishment— is established as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that, in this case, perception would be a valid means of knowledge only when accompanied by conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) and not by itself, we say:
this is not so;
because an object is determined as "seen" through a conceptual determination produced by the power of perception.
Not by way of conceptual construction (*utprekṣitatva*).

Furthermore, perception (*pratyakṣa*) has the function of directly realizing an object, which is called "seeing" (*darśana*); however, conceptual construction (*utprekṣaṇa*) is the function of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*).
For instance, [it functions] toward an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).

He clarifies the intention with which it was stated that determinate cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*) is the establisher [of the object], using the words "but not" (*na tu*). The particle *tu* indicates that perception is distinct from determinate cognition. He states the reason for its inability to establish [the object] with the words "because it is non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpakatvāt*).

One might object: "If, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), that cognition is indeed blue and thus possesses a form similar to [the object], then let there be such a determination (*niścaya*) or not; even though it is itself non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), it will nevertheless become the object of the conventional usage of existence by virtue of that form. Anticipating this, he says: "by a corresponding determinative cognition," and so forth. That is, by a determinative cognition that conforms [to the object].
Because even a momentary cognition, though established by a non-conformable conceptualization of non-momentariness, is fit for the conventional usage of "existent";
whereas that which is not so established is like a mere false construction (asatkalpa) and is equivalent to the non-existent, because it is incapable of functioning with respect to its own object,
like the cognition of grass seen while walking.
He concludes this point with the words "Therefore" and so forth:
because that which has been definitively established in such a manner becomes like the existent despite being non-existent;
therefore, by way of its nature as the cognition of blue—in the form "this is the cognition of blue"—it becomes existent, that is, fit for the conventional usage of existence.

Because that which is established by a corresponding determinative cognition (niścayapratyaya) produced through its own capacity exists as such and not otherwise, for that reason, while performing a corresponding determination (adhyavasāya), it excludes the conventional usage of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇavyavahāra) regarding the state of non-performance by means of the word "eva.
Strengthening this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), he says: "But if [it] is not performed," and so forth.

The word "tu" (but) expresses that the state of the instrument possesses differentiation. [The opponent asks: "Let it be so established; what follows from this? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
And when that mode of non-establishment by means of that nature exists.
He asks: "Even if that [result] is not produced, why is it not a means of valid cognition? and replies: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
"Therefore" means because the action of comprehension, which is the result, is not produced.
Alternatively, there is a syntactical split: [the reason is] "because of the absence of being the most effective instrument" (*sādhakatamatvābhāva*).

Therefore, because it lacks the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), [the sense organ cannot be the instrument]. For it is that which is the most effective means toward the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—characterized by the apprehension of an object—that is called the "instrument" (*pramāṇa*).
If that [apprehension] has not yet been accomplished, then with respect to what could it appropriate for itself the status of being the most effective means?

The collective meaning is: "by means of which that cognition may attain validity. Now, one might object: "If this [process] occurs in the absence of a determinative judgment (*avasāya*), well; but even if it occurs when such a judgment is present, if the process remains exactly the same, then there is no such thing as perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Anticipating this doubt, he now speaks by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "By what has been produced" (*janitena*).
Here, the particle *tu* shows that the state of non-production is distinct from the state of production.
He states the reason for establishing it in that manner and for its being the establisher: "by virtue of similarity" (*sārūpyavaśāt*).
[The opponent replies: "It is established through cognition.

[The author] intends to say: "If perception, being alone and unable to function without assistance, necessarily depends upon a determinative judgment (*niścaya*), then it would follow that only that [judgment], accompanied by perception, constitutes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
He says: "If it is so. If what was just stated is accepted, then it would be thus.
The word "ced" (if) indicates the opponent's acceptance.
"No," he negates;
this being so, this does not exist. He states the reason:
[DhPr p.86]
"Conceptualizing, we imagine, but we do not see"—thus they determine through experience that conceptualization has the nature of imaginative construction (*utprekṣā*).

Therefore, setting aside its own operation, it displays the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); in whatever object there is a determination preceded by direct perception, there direct perception alone is the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The first chapter, on direct perception, in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* composed by Ācārya Dharmottara.
[41] Thus ends the first chapter of the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā*, titled "The Means of Valid Cognition."
May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* composed by the teacher Dharmottara, titled "The Means of Valid Cognition."
May there be auspiciousness!
Regarding the phrase "because" (yasmāt): it means by way of being visible (*dṛśyatva*), that is, by way of being distinguished by perception. He excludes any other alternative by saying "no" (*na*).
"Being [merely] imagined" means being a state of knowing devoid of the conceit of direct perception.
One might object: "But isn't seeing the activity of conceptual construction?
Therefore, what harm is there in that [conceptualization] determining an object qualified by its own activity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And seeing... and so forth.
The word "co" has the sense of "because. If this is so, then what is the function of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? He says: "it is imaginative projection (*utprekṣaṇa*).
This very point is established by the passage beginning with "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and ending with "they necessarily [perceive]" (*avaśyam*).
He supports this with the text:

"Let it be so; nevertheless, how is it that direct perception alone possesses authority and not conceptual construction as well? Anticipating this objection, he says "Therefore" by way of a concluding summary. This is easily understood.
When this is stated, the following intention must be understood:
indeed, conceptualization might possess vitality if it were to assist perception while being engaged solely in its own specific function;
however, it does not operate in such a manner.
Since activity is observed only in one who has already accepted the operation of perception,
and since that operation characterized as "seeing" has been accomplished by perception itself, how could this [subsequent cognition] also attain validity while performing what is already ground?
Or, if it is argued that perception first depends upon it for the sake of its own practical application of validity;

If, therefore, the cognition "he too is indeed a means of valid knowledge" arises, then since a father necessarily requires a son for the sake of the conventional usage of "father," it would follow that the son is also a father; thus, enough with this investigation into the words of those who are not logicians—everything is now clear.
The first chapter of the *Dharmottarapradīpa*, titled as such, being a commentary on the *Dharmottara* composed by the scholar Durveka.
Chapter Two: The Determination of Inference for One’s Own Purpose. Having thus explained direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says the following in order to explain inference (*anumāna*):
Inference is of two kinds.
(II-1) Inference is of two types, meaning it has two modes.
Now, while the definition of inference ought to be stated, why is this distinction of modes mentioned so abruptly?
It is said:
inference for the sake of others consists of speech,
whereas inference for one's own sake consists of cognition.
Because these two are absolutely distinct, there is no single definition for them; therefore, in order to declare their respective specific definitions, the difference in their modes is stated.
For the difference in modes is indeed the difference between individual instances.
And when the distinction between individual instances has been stated, it is possible to state a definition that is restricted to each individual instance;
not otherwise.
Therefore, the statement of the different types is merely an ancillary part of the instruction on the definition.
Having understood that it is impossible to provide a definition of [the means of valid cognition] without first explaining its various types, the classification of types is stated at the outset.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was indicated as being twofold, through the distinction of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Among these, perception has already been explained.
Now, intending to explain inference (*anumāna*) as its turn has arrived according to the original enumeration, he says: "In this way" (*evam*).
"In this way" means by the method of refuting the fourfold misconception just mentioned.
Showing that the suffix *-dhā* here denotes a manner, he says: "of two kinds" (*dviprakāram*).
"Now, one who wishes to state the definition of inference must indeed state its definition;
why then is this irrelevant statement being employed?"—with these words, he raises the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, the word *atha* signifies a question.
The indeclinable *akasmāt* expresses the absence of a cause.
He provides the rebuttal with the words "it is said," and so forth;
[the rebuttal concerns] those two, which consist of cognition and its designation.
"Single" means common.

The sense is that if it were possible, the definition alone would have been stated first— just as for all four types of perception, a single common definition is possible because they all share the nature of cognition and the quality of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
"Pratiniyata" means individual or specific.
"Prakārabheda" means diversity or manifoldness.

Now, one might object: since a characteristic restricted to each individual cannot be shown without pointing out the distinction between individuals, it is precisely the difference between individuals that must be stated.
If it is asked, "In that case, why is the distinction between types being stated? he says: "prakāra" (type). The word "hi" means "because.

If it is argued, "Even if that [general type] is shown, if it is impossible to state the specific definitions [of individual instances], then what is the use of stating it? he replies: "vyakti" (individual instance).
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Here, the prefix *prati* functions with a restricted meaning;
therefore, it means that a specific individual (*viśiṣṭā vyakti*) is restricted (*niyata*) therein.
What, then, is this twofold nature? He says:
"For oneself and for others" (II-2).

This is for oneself (*svārtha*); that by which one realizes it for oneself is "for one's own sake. This is for another (*parārtha*); [that by which one realizes it] for another is "for the sake of others."
That by which one causes another to understand is for the sake of another (*parārtha*).
The compound is formed by the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40) through a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*).
Alternatively, it is impossible to state a fixed or specific definition.
Anticipating the objection as to where [this] is established as certain, it is said: "in each individual" (*prativyakti*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "in every single individual.
Because otherwise it would be impossible to describe their specifically determined characteristics, therefore—for that reason—[it is so stated].
The phrase "only as a component of the description of characteristics" means precisely for the purpose of describing characteristics.
By this, the objection is answered: "When only the general characteristic has been stated, let the specific characteristic—whether it be one or many—be as it may;
what is the use of stating its various subdivisions? Thus, that [objection] is refuted.
For if this were stated with reference to a common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), then why would it be said that "it does not exist"?

On the other hand, if it refers to a specific characteristic (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*), then if it were possible to state it even without mentioning the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti-bheda*), why would it not be stated?
It is simply that [the specific characteristic] does not exist at all.
Therefore, it is shown that its mention is logically proper at the very beginning and not later; thus he says:
"the impossibility," meaning having recognized the impossibility of defining [the object] by either one of those two.
The word "co" is used for emphasis.
"Prāk" means before the statement of the definition.
One might object: "If inference for oneself has such a definition and inference for others has such a definition, why is it not possible to state a specific definition?"
Even so, why has the duality of inference not been made known, such that number, together with its objects of counting, is said to be twofold—inference being of two kinds: for oneself and for others?
This is true;
however, we say that this statement of division is for the sake of restriction.
Inference is of two kinds— how indeed might one understand that it is exclusively of this nature?
Otherwise, while only this much has been introduced here as the subject to be explained,
the suspicion that elsewhere there is yet another kind of inference to be explained would not have been directly dispelled.
Since a twofold classification is possible in other ways as well—such as by means of *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and so forth—one who is uncertain asks: "But what [is it]?
He asks with the word "what" (*kim*) in a general sense, and with the word "but" (*punar*) in a specific sense.
He shows the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *svārtha*—namely, "for oneself" (*svasmāi*).
He provides the word-analysis (*padavigraha*) for this by means of the word *artha*, because it is a mandatory compound (*nityasamāsa*).
The word "this" (*idam*) refers to inference (*anumāna*).
"svārtham" (for one's own purpose) is a designation of a compound word;
its meaning is that the purpose [of this work] is the realization of the self.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "by which."
By means of that inference which serves as the instrument, the inferrer himself understands an object that is beyond the senses;
this is the ellipsis, or it is obtained from the context.
That is "knowledge for one's own sake" (svārthajñāna), meaning its purpose is the personal realization by oneself.

This is the intended meaning: the cognition of the three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga) arises in whose mental continuum for that very purpose; because by means of it another [person] does not achieve comprehension, it is therefore called "for one's own sake" (svārtha).
However, there is no knowledge whatsoever that is restricted to any particular person such that it could be called "for one's own sake" (svārtha) in relation to him;
for this is the intention of one who says, "by which [knowledge] he himself understands."

Although comprehension consists in the nature of inferential cognition, nevertheless, by way of the relationship between the established and the establisher, a distinction between the action and the instrument is shown; thus, the factor of similarity (*sārūpya*) is the instrument, while comprehension, which is of the nature of apprehension, is the state of the result.
In that context, inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is the knowledge regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*) derived from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing three characteristics.

Among those two—namely, inference for oneself and inference for others—he asks what kind of knowledge constitutes inference for oneself and says: "from that which possesses three characteristics" (*trirūpāt*).
That which has three characteristics (*trirūpa*), whose definitions will be stated hereafter, is "that which possesses three characteristics."
He provides the etymological analysis (vigraha) of *parārtha*— meaning "that by which an object is indicated or understood"— as *parasmai*.
The analysis of this word is as before.
The term *parārtham* is stated as a compound;
its meaning is that the purpose (*prayojana*) is the comprehension by others. This meaning is indicated by the word *yena*.

That statement by which one conveys to another what is to be expressed—that is, which makes known an object that is not present to the senses—is the statement consisting of the exposition of the three-fold mark; this is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
Here too, this is the intended meaning: although inference, even in its form as verbal expression, is not restricted to the person [who utters it], nevertheless, it is indeed for the sake of another.
For whatever proceeds with reference to something is said to be for the sake of that thing.
Furthermore, a word functions with reference to another object and not to itself;
therefore, a word does not have an infinite regress of being for the sake of another.
This is because the "other" alone is the prompter of the meaning intended by the speaker's desire to communicate.

It should be understood that although this [inference for others] is not distinct from inference for oneself in its indirect object, it is stated separately because its fruit is the comprehension of an imperceptible object, and because there is a direct difference in the operation of these two.
Now, one might object: just like the statement that produces an inference for others, is there not some statement that is useful for the direct perception of another?
For example, the sentence "This young elephant runs.
Therefore, why is perception for the sake of others (*parārtha-pratyakṣa*) not explained here, just as inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is?

To this it is replied: that collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*) which brings about the comprehension of an imperceptible object—namely, the presence of the logical mark in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and its pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*)—is metaphorically called "inference for the sake of others" because it consists of a statement (*vākya*) that explains those [conditions].
It is said:
but not there [in that case] by way of being a mere constituent factor (*aṅgabhāva*) in any respect, because it would follow that even health and so forth would be such.

Furthermore, this sentence, "This is a young elephant," and so forth, does not receive its designation as being the cause of the arising of perception—by denoting that causal complex such as the sense organs, light, and so on—such that it would even undergo the process of being learned [from experience].
What then? It does so merely by generating a desire to see in someone.

If, by any means whatsoever, the mere fact of being an auxiliary factor in the arising of another's perception constitutes identity with that perception, then even when an object is present before one's eyes like a festival for the sight,

the act of turning someone who is somehow averse toward it by another person— consisting as it does of speech directed toward the head— that too would result in "perception for the sake of others" (parārthapratyakṣa) for the instructor, falling under the category of what is to be explained.
And what person of sound mind would take this to heart? Moreover, let such speech be directly for the sake of others;
what is lost to us?
If it is argued that since the meaning of that [treatise] has not been explained, negligence itself is a great flaw, we say no;
for there is no such explanation because there is no disagreement [regarding it].
For elucidation consists in the demonstration of the true nature [of a thing] by means of refuting misconceptions;
yet, no one harbors such misconceptions regarding a statement of that kind which is useful for perception for the sake of others,
such that even that would need to be elucidated.

In inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), even when one understands the object of proof, it is observed that [the proponent] speaks by means of the positive pervasion (*vyāpti*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*) of its property (*dharma*), because the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is not explicitly stated, and because of the employment of the application (*upanaya*), the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*), and the statement of its recurrence (*tadāvṛtti*); therefore, this is now explained.
If, however, others were not to disagree even with that, then even that would not have been explained; so, enough of this excessive detail.

[42] Aspaṣṭam — saṃ: Here, just as an object beyond the senses has been apprehended by oneself, it is communicated to another exactly in that same way; since inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is preceded by inference for one's own sake (svārthānumāna), inference for one's own sake is stated first.
And since the definition must be formulated exactly according to the enumeration, such is the characteristic of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*):
namely,
"the cognition that arises from the threefold characteristic (*trirūpa-liṅga*)."
This is a qualification by way of the cause (*hetu*).

Furthermore, since [inferential cognition] also arises from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa-liṅga*)—which has as its objective support a mark possessing the three characteristics—he qualifies it by saying "the inferable" (*anumeya*).
And this is a qualification by way of the object (*viṣaya*).
"Inference for oneself" is that cognition which arises from a mark possessing the three characteristics and has the object of inference as its objective support.

Having refuted misconceptions regarding its definition, he says— in order to refute misconceptions regarding its result— "The determination of the means of valid cognition and its result here is also like that of perception" (II-4).
The determination of the result of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) should be understood here in inference just as it was in perception, exactly as in the case of perception.
Regarding the definition, which was taught by the Teacher from the very beginning with the words "In that regard... and so forth, he explains it with the word "therein" (tatra).
From the collection of inference for oneself and inference for others, inference for oneself is distinguished by its specific nature as being for one's own sake.

Therefore, by explaining that "that which is born from the mark possessing three characteristics," he demonstrates that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the phrase "from the mark possessing three characteristics" in the root text is indeed an ablative (*apādāna*), having acquired the technical designation of *apādāna* by the rule "the source of the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*, Pāṇini 1.4.30), with respect to the implied action of being born.
By means of the "door of the cause" (*hetudvāreṇa*), that is, by way of the producer (*janakamukhena*),

the Teacher, in stating "from the mark possessing the three characteristics" (*trirūpāl liṅgāt*), has revealed his intended definition of the mark (*liṅga*) by rejecting the six positions through the exclusion of one or two terms and by adopting the seventh position.
And how this is so, we shall clarify in detail while composing the treatise by the venerable Arcata, known as the *Arcatāloka*.
He shows what is to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "from" (*auṃeya*): "and from the three-fold [reason]" (*trirūpāc ca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason.

"Having the three-featured mark as its objective support" (trirūpaliṅgālambana) should be explained as the cognition that, having seen smoke, [realizes] "this [smoke] is invariably concomitant with fire in all cases.
For that [cognition] is produced, through a causal chain, from the three-featured mark.
By the word "iti," the nature of the qualifier has been stated;
it is knowledge itself that is qualified.
To the question "What, then, is qualified? he says: "And this..."
Since it is so:
by way of the object—that is, by way of the object being determined—the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which performs exclusion (*vyavacchedaka*).
Having explained the meaning of the individual components, he explains the meaning of the whole compound with the words "possessing the three forms" (*trirūpa*), and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is that which has as its object the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), which is the inferable (*anumeya*).

The particle *iti* marks the completion of the sentence's meaning; thus, having this sense, it is not connected with anything further—namely, having refuted the misconception regarding the definition in the manner just stated.

Now, if it is intended by the Teacher that the result belongs to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and Dharmottara explains it in this way, then what was said by the Teacher in the *Pramāṇabhāga-vyavasthā*, and why will Dharmottara later [on p. 91] show that "the conformity with the blue (*nīlasārūpya*) is the cause for establishing [the object], and thus the means of valid cognition"?
This is not a fault.
For, as stated in the passage beginning with "na hi pramāṇasya" [DhPr p.
just as direct perception (pratyakṣa), while being experienced as having the same form as blue, establishes itself as having the nature of the cognition of blue;
Therefore, the conformity with the blue object (*nīlasārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the cause for establishing [the result],

while the nature of the cognition of the blue (*nīlabodharūpa*), which is being established, is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*); likewise, inference, arising in the form of the blue, establishes itself as having the nature of the cognition of the blue.

Therefore, its similarity to the blue object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while its nature as a conceptualization of the blue is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*);
for it is by virtue of that similarity that it is established as having the form of the cognition of the blue.
"Not otherwise.
For in this way there are disagreements regarding number, definition, and result;
however, in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the disagreement concerning the object-sphere (*gocara*) has already been refuted.
In the course of explaining the definition [of inference], the three-fold mark (trirūpa-liṅga) has been introduced.
To explain that very point, he says:
"The three-fold nature of the mark, moreover, consists in its presence in the object of inference (anumeya) alone, and its presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) alone."
"And its absolute absence in what is not the similar class" (II-5) refers to the "three-fold nature" and so forth;
the ellipsis is that this which is the three-fold nature of the logical mark— that is, the three characteristics— is what is being stated here.
What, then, is this threefold nature? He says: [it is] the inferable object, whose definition will be stated;

in that [object], the existence of the mark (liṅga) alone is ascertained—this is one form. Although the term "ascertained" (niścita) is not used here, nevertheless, because it is used at the end, it must be understood as applying to both of the two forms under discussion.

Since a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not the cause of indirect cognition by virtue of its fitness— just as the analysis of the primary word *pramāṇa* with the word *phala* was shown to be merely for the purpose of illustrating the meaning— it is,
however, an exposition of the meaning that has been provided.
And this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, whatever is the means of accomplishing the result, its systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is also included.

However, in the root [text], the author of the Vārttika intended only a *dvandva* compound. Because the rule regarding the priority of placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is not mandatory, the word "result" (*phala*) does not appear as the first member.
Therefore, the certainty is this: "There is no difference in the object between the atom and the result.
[43] ... [The compound] *lakṣaṇagocaraphalaviṣaya* means:
the similarity to blue, which is an indistinct similarity to blue.
Because there is no direct perception (*aparokṣīkaraṇa*) through inference,
and because inference cognizes only that which is excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*),
the form of the cognition of blue— that is, the form of the conceptualization of blue— is established and ascertained.
[43] That which is written outside the sequence is not seen—namely, "saṃ".

Now, one might object: "Surely only the disagreements regarding the number, definition, and result of inference have been refuted, but not the disagreement regarding its object. To this he says: "In this way" (evam).

Thus, by the manner just described, [these views] are "refuted" (nirākṛtāḥ)—this is the ellipsis—here in this section on inference; or else, the word "refuted" (nirākṛtā) in the passage to be cited later should be connected here by changing its grammatical number.
This is the origin of the text beginning with the words "the threefold nature" (traiprūyam).
He demonstrates this with the words "that [is] the definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
By way of a relevant introduction (*prasaṅga*), he makes known that those very three forms are indeed "thus" (*tathā*).
Since "this threefold nature" (*trairūpya*) is the subject under discussion, the remainder is to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
Since multiple forms such as "having an uncontradicted object" are possible, he asks, "But what?
He asks "what" in a general sense,
and "but" in a specific sense.

But why must that be relied upon? He says: "Because... [The word] *yataḥ* [indicates the reason]. Of that cognition which pertains to an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), the "seed" is the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
He asks why it is not so, and replies: "Because of the unperceived.
This refers, by the context, to the non-comprehension of an object beyond the senses.
That is to say, if it were unknown.

If the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not the cause of the cognition of an imperceptible object, then let it be that which is already known through its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); for this alone is the seed for the manifestation of the imperceptible, just as the seed is for the sprout.
For fire is not apprehended from smoke that has not been seen;
nor does [the sense organ] illuminate an imperceptible object by depending on a cognition of its own object,
as a lamp [illuminates] a jar and so forth.
For even if [the mark] is seen, there is no comprehension [of the object] if its connection is not ascertained.

Therefore, the very function of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in communicating an imperceptible object consists solely in the ascertainment [of that object] through its being invariably concomitant with it;
there is no other [function].

Therefore, since the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) constitutes the very operation of the logical mark (*liṅga*), it must necessarily be performed; thus, the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) must be required for all the characteristics [of a valid reason].
Among these, by the word "existence" (*sattva*), the unestablished [reason], such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), is excluded.
By the particle "only" (*eva*), the partially unestablished (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is excluded.
Regarding the argument "trees possess consciousness because they sleep":
among the trees that constitute the subject of the thesis, sleep characterized by the closing of leaves is not established as a property of every part;
for not all trees close their leaves at night, but only some do.
Raising the objection, "What is the use of the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance for that statement of the proponent? he says: "Nor even... (nāpi).
The word "liṅga" (logical mark) is to be connected [with both].
The word "api" (also) indicates that the lamp is [a sign] even when seen from an uncertain [perspective],
not only when it is unseen.
Since it is thus, for that reason:
*antara* means an interval or separation; *nāntara* means not so, i.e., without interval.
In the sūtra beginning with *nabhrāṭ* (Pāṇini 6.3.71), the absence of the elision of the *n* is due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by the word "na.
[The term *nāntara* is derived as follows: because it means "not existing within," the suffix *cha* is applied according to the *gahādi* group;
from that, the suffix *kan* is added as an affix denoting the same meaning (*svārthika*).

The state of being "inseparable" (nāntarīyaka) refers to the non-occurrence without [the probandum] of a hidden object such as fire; its "being that" (tattā) is the ascertainment thereof, which is the conceptual construction: "In every case, this is inseparable from that.
This is the active form, or operation, of the mark (liṅga), which is the indicator.
For it is only a form that has been mounted upon such ascertainment that possesses the status of a mark.

By the word *eva*, that which is excluded— the fact that for anything else this [invariable concomitance] does not constitute its essential operation— is restated by the phrase "not another," for the sake of clarity.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the cognition here that "this [effect] is inseparable from this [cause]" is inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*),
whereas the preceding [cognition] is the cognition of the mark (*liṅga-jñāna*).

Therefore, because there is no comprehension [of the object] from a mark (liṅga) that is not ascertained as existing or from a relationship that is not ascertained, the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth must necessarily be performed.

Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how it should be performed, [the author], while showing the same reason already stated by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), also demonstrates it by way of positive concomitance (anvaya), saying: "liṅge" etc.

The suffix *kan* should be applied in the reflexive sense (*svārthika*) to form "ātmaiva tathā," meaning that the very nature of the operation of the mark—the operation of the indicator in establishing what is beyond the senses—is such [as described].
Taking the phrase "tasmāt" (from that) as the expression of the reason— namely, "the state of being that"— this is the conclusion.
Regarding all the forms and characteristics, such as the existence of the object of inference (*anumeya*),
he says "therein" (*tatra*) in order to demonstrate, in sequence, that which is to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) by each individual form at present.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is a collection of the non-locus-unestablished (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*), the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), and the unestablished qualified (*viśeṣyāsiddha*).
These too are included within the single category of the unestablished in its essential nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).
As to how they are divided and how they are subsumed, we shall explain that further below.
Only certain [plants], such as the *tintiṅka* and others.
Furthermore, it might be argued that this smoke is also "unestablished in one part" (*ekadeśāsiddha*), just like sleep;
for instance, here the mountain and so forth constitute the subject (*pakṣa*), and smoke is established only in a certain location therein, not everywhere.
Furthermore, a mountain or the like is not accepted as a single composite whole (*avayavin*).
If, on the other hand, such a thing is nonetheless said to pervade the subject (*pakṣavyāpaka*), then what wrong has sleep committed that it alone is not considered suitable as a single entity?
By the word "only" (eva) placed at the end, the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason is excluded.
For if one were to say "existence only in the inferable object," then audibility itself would become a [valid] reason.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), all doubtful-unestablished (sandigdhāsiddha) reasons are excluded.

The similar class (*sapakṣa*) has its definition to be stated [later]. The second characteristic is that [the reason] is ascertained to exist only in that [similar class]. Here too, some offer the following rebuttal:
For the subject (*pakṣa*) is stated by way of its possessing the specific property that one wishes to know;
and as for that mountain or other locus, it is not fire that is wished to be known there,
but rather [fire] in whatever particular location it may be.

In that case, even when smoke is seen in only one part, the fire in that same part is what is sought to be known and is thereby known; so what is the use of smoke that pervades the entire mountain? However, if it were the case that the presence of fire in every single part were what was sought to be known, then this [reason] would indeed be "unestablished in a portion of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
But this is not the case;
therefore, how could it be so for him?
Furthermore, since consciousness is what is sought to be known here in all trees, the purpose must be served by a sleep that pervades the entire tree.

Just as when it is sought to prove that the entire Veda is of human origin, the property of being a sentence (*vākyatva*)—which pervades the whole of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)—is required [as the reason];
yet this [property] does not pervade all [sentences]. Therefore, it is said to be "unestablished in part of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
However, some [hold] that this conventional usage proceeds by relying on the unity of mountains and so forth as established by worldly determination;
yet the world does not determine such unity for all trees,
whereby the same [unity] would be established even for sleep.
Consequently, they concluded, "What indeed could be faulty here?

Then it is said: if someone were to take only certain trees, such as the *tintiṅka* and others, as the subject (*pakṣa*) and then employ "sleep" as the logical reason (*hetu*), then why would this not establish consciousness (*caitanya*), since it would not be the fallacy of being unestablished in a part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*)?
This is untenable because the conceptual alternative is impossible.

If you intend "sleep"—also known by the name "nidrā"—to be the cause, defined as a specific state of affairs well-known to all people that is contrary to the operation of the sense organs, then [the reason] is unestablished even in those trees;
how, then, could it lead to the inference of consciousness?

Now, if the reason is some object denotable by the mere word "sleep" through whatever limiting condition (*upādhi*), then such sleep lacks a proven pervasion (*vyāpti*) with consciousness; thus, because its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

The genitive case [in *svāpasya*] is used because the word *sattva* is employed in connection with the word *paścāt*, according to Pāṇini 2.3.30: "The sixth [case-ending] is used when there is a word meaning 'after' (*atasartha*) as a suffix."
"Uncommon" means that which is not common to both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*);
that is to say, it is a property belonging to the subject (*pakṣa*) alone.
"Set aside" means rejected as a valid reason (*hetu*).
He shows that [the definition] would not be refuted if the restriction were placed on the former [term] by means of the word "yadi" (if). For "hi" means "because.

His intention is this: if the definition were "that which has existence only in the inferable," then the statement "existence only in the similar instance (sapakṣa)" would become a superfluous, separate definition.
Or else, there will be a contradiction.

He shows what is to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), which is required here, with the word "ascertained" (niścita). The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both doubtful and unascertained"—meaning it is unascertained because it is not established [as a reason] either as a logical mark (*hetu*) or as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus is the analysis of the word "aniścita."

The "unestablished due to a doubtful qualifier" (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the "unestablished due to a doubtful subject" (*sandigdhaviśeṣyāsiddha*) are both included within the category of the "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*);
thus, they too are refuted by this very [definition].
We shall demonstrate later how these two differ and how they are subsumed.

Here, because it is based on the principle that [the reason] must reside [in the subject], the particle *eva*— which is uttered together with this [term "reason"]— should be understood as excluding the non-connection of the property (*dharma*) [with the subject], since the existence of the reason functions as a qualifier.
By the inclusion of the term "existent" (sattva), the contradictory [reason] is excluded;
for it is not the case that [the reason] does not exist in the similar instances (sapakṣa).
By means of the particle *eva*, the inconclusive reason that is common to both sides (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is excluded;
for that [reason] does not reside in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) alone, but rather in both.

By the inclusion of the term "existence" (*sattva*), the status of being a logical reason (*hetutva*) is stated even for that which follows immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*), provided its existence is not pervasive across all similar instances, by virtue of the restrictive statement made previously.

If, however, the restrictive particle *eva* were placed at the end [of the definition], the meaning would be: "That which exists only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is the logical reason" (*hetu*). In that case, "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) would not be a valid reason.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason whose positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful is excluded;
for example, [the argument] "someone is omniscient because he is a speaker."
For the property of being a speaker is doubtful in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). The dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) is that which will be defined [later];
in that, its absolute non-existence is certain—this is the third characteristic.
In this context, by the inclusion of the term "non-existent" (*asat*), the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is excluded,
for the contradictory reason exists in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). By the particle "only" (*eva*), the common reason (*sādhāraṇa*) that occurs in a portion of the dissimilar class is excluded.
For when "being produced immediately after an effort" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "impermanence" exists in some parts of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as lightning,
but does not exist in others, such as space; therefore, it is necessarily excluded from [the latter].

For if the restriction were placed before the word "asattva" (non-existence), the meaning would be this: "That which exists only in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is the reason. And in that case, the property of "being produced immediately after an effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) would exist even in the similar instance (sapakṣa); furthermore, because it occurs in both the similar and dissimilar instances, it would be "inconclusive" (anaikāntika), being undetermined with respect to either the probandum or its opposite. Thus, it follows that [the reason] is likewise rejected.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that whose existence (*sattā*) does not pervade the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), meaning it does not occur in all similar instances.

It should be understood that "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) has been cited as an example because it is a reason capable of establishing impermanence (*anityatva*), even though it does not pervade all similar instances.
In reality, however, every reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*), such as smoke and the like, should be understood to subsist in only a portion of the similar instances.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of "thus.
This being the case, because this [property] is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), even smoke and the like would not be a reason (*hetu*) due to their being immediately preceded by effort.
"That of which there is doubt" is what is meant by that [term].

Here, because it functions as the locus (*āśraya*) according to the principle of the actual meaning (*ārthanyāya*), and because the subject (*dharmin*) defined as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the particle [“eva”] uttered together with this [word “sapakṣa”]— having obtained its application to the subject (*pakṣa*) or the tree (*vṛkṣa*)— should be understood as an exclusion (*vyavacchedaka*) of the connection with another subject defined as the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*), since it possesses the nature of a conjunction-restrictive (*samuccīyamāna-avadhāraṇa*) [particle].
He says "asapakṣe" in order to explain the third form [of the reason].
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has this [following] definition, which is about to be stated.
He asks, "How is this excluded? and replies, "For it is contradictory," and so forth.
"Here" means because;
regarding the "common" [reason], that is, the one common to both the similar and dissimilar instances (sapakṣa and asapakṣa), he asks:
"In what probandum is such a thing [found]? and answers: "By effort," and so forth.
Effort (*prayatna*) is human activity;
it is by way of restriction (*niyamena*), that is, by way of determination (*avadhāraṇena*).
It does not exist; therefore, it would not be a reason (*hetu*).
Consequently, it was not established previously.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful is excluded.
But surely, when it is stated that "existence only in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*) is required, it is already understood that there must be "non-existence in the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*).
Why, then, has both been mentioned again? It is said in reply:

Both have been mentioned in order to demonstrate that whether one employs positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it must be employed as something restricted (*niyamavat*), and not otherwise.

For if both [the presence in the similar instance and the absence in the dissimilar instance] were unrestricted in their application, this would be the meaning: "That which exists in the similar instance (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is the logical reason (hetu).
And that being so, [one could argue]: "He is dark-complexioned because he is his son, just like the son who is seen"—this is the sense of the word "only" (eva).

"Why is it not restricted to 'only the non-homologue' (asapakṣa)? To this he says, "And thus" (tathā ca). The mention of "following immediately after effort" (prayatnānantarīyaka) is an illustration, as before. He says "ascertained" (niścita) for the purpose of excluding [the case of] the mention of "ascertainment" (niścita).
"Exclusion from the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*) means exclusion from that which is not the similar class.

That [reason] whose exclusion from the dissimilar class is doubtful is "one with doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class. Now, is it not the case that this so-called "doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class" is not a fault of the reason?
How, then, is this objection refuted?
For instance: that very reason which is observed in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) would not establish the intended [probandum], just like "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth.
But how could that reason—which, even when sought with great effort, is not perceived in the dissimilar class—not establish the probandum? Indeed, it must establish it.
This is flawed;
for even a reason that is observed in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is considered defective.
How so? If it is argued that this is because [the reason] is perceived even in the absence of the probandum (sādhya), [we reply: no.

Now, one might object: even if this [reason] is indeed observed elsewhere without the probandum (*sādhya*), why does it not nevertheless establish the probandum in the subject (*dharmin*) under dispute?
For there is no proving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that it occurs here too without the probandum.
Nor is it established that whatever is observed in one place without something else must necessarily occur everywhere without that same thing.
Because it is frequently observed otherwise as well.

Now, since there is no rule that what occurs in the absence of the probandum must necessarily occur only when the probandum is present, it cannot serve as a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) for the doubt regarding the subject of dispute.

Alas! In that case, by conceiving of its occurrence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—that is, in the subject of the probandum devoid of the probandum—it follows that the reason becomes a cause of uncertainty (*aniścaya-hetu*).

And this being the case, even the non-observation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the presence of the reason in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*)— namely, the possibility that "this property may exist, yet the probandum does not follow from it"— if one entertains such a mode of its occurrence, then how could this [reason] be fit to be a cause for certainty? Therefore, whether there be observation in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), or such a seed of doubt, or the non-observation of a subverting proof in the opposite case, what difference is there?
And thus the author of the Vārttika said: "But existence or non-existence in the similar and dissimilar instances is not dependent upon certainty;
for even when there is certainty, the fault arises precisely through the door of doubt.
Since that [fault] is equal even in the absence of certainty, pointing out such a thing here is indeed a refutation."

"Likewise, how could one internalize the status of being a prover (*gamakatva*), which is to be obtained by the exclusion of any suspicion regarding the presence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)?
With the words "But surely... and so forth, he raises an objection against the definition.
The intention of one who says, "It is understood that it exists only in the counter-example," is as follows:

Once the presence [of the reason] in the subject (*pakṣa*) has been established, the certainty that it exists *only* in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is indeed a conclusion involving a restrictive conjunction (*samuccīyamānāvadhāraṇa*).

And this [conclusion] is not possible if its non-existence in dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*) is either uncertain or doubtful; therefore, there must necessarily be non-existence in the dissimilar instance alone.
Thus, being his son would be the logical reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, one must employ positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) only when they possess a necessary restriction (*niyamavat*), so that the invariable connection (*pratibandha*) of the probans with the probandum may be understood.

Since the employment of those possessing such restriction is mandatory, only one of the two should be employed and not both; thus, for the sake of instruction, it is said that either the positive concomitance or the negative concomitance alone, provided it possesses the necessary restriction, should be employed.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of two":

in the course of explaining the three characteristics [of a logical reason], the inferable object (*anumeya*), the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) have been mentioned; their definitions must now be stated.
Regarding this, he asks: "What is the object of inference?
He replies: "The object of inference here is the locus (dharmin) whose specific property is sought to be known; it implies what is already certain. (II-6)

Thus, because this [reason] serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is indeed certain; by this, the mere presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is already obtained. Since that alone fulfills the purpose, it should be understood that there is no need for the phrase "existence only in the similar instance. To this, the following response is given: The response is stated as follows: [text continues]

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the probans is its own internal property consisting in being accompanied by the probandum, or in being present where the probandum exists. The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason is its own internal property consisting in being excluded when the probandum is absent, or in not being present [where the probandum is absent].

Whether it be positive or negative, when it is employed and communicated by means of words, it must be used as something characterized by necessity—that is, as something non-deviant; otherwise, it would not be stated as a constituent factor for the cognition of that which is beyond the senses.
And how is he so engaged?

When, in the positive statement (*anvaya-vākya*), the means of proof is necessarily concomitant with the probandum, and in the negative statement (*vyatireka-vākya*), the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the means of proof;
