[that is,] by enjoining the probandum preceded by a restatement of the means of proof, or by enjoining the absence of the means of proof preceded by a restatement of the absence of the probandum; [and when it is] joined with words of universal application (*vīpsā-pada*), connected with the word "all" (*sarva*), and endowed with the particle "only" (*eva*).
Otherwise, it is not explained.
The reading "prayujyamānaḥ" is not found in the root text;
it has been placed in that bracketed box in accordance with the *Pradīpa* commentary.

If such a cognition of positive and negative concomitance exists even through non-restricted usage, then what is the purpose of usage that possesses restriction? To this he says: "For in the case of the non-restricted...

(*aniyate hi*). The word "for" (*hi*) means because; in the case of the non-restricted, which does not express the intended restriction—let alone in the usage of one [term], the meaning would apply to both as well, which is why the word "even" (*api*) is used.
The word "iti" shows the form of the meaning.
[The opponent] says, "Let this be the meaning; what is the harm?"—to which [the author] replies, "If that were so... (tathā ca).
And this should be understood as applying to those sons of his who are dark-complexioned and nearby, according to the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya-nyāya*).
Otherwise, there would be room for the objection that even an indefinite negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has not been stated here.
Since this is so, therefore, by means of that necessary application, there is a connection (*pratibandha*), which is to say a state of being bound (*pratibaddhatva*) or dependence (*āyattatva*).
To the question "Of what? he says: "Of the means" (*sādhanasya*). To the expectation "Where? he says: "In the probandum" (*sādhya*).

If this is so, one might suggest that both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), each possessing the necessary restriction, should be employed within a single statement of the means; to this he replies: "And of the two [concomitances] possessing the restriction."
This is intended as a conjunction of other things that ought to be said—

the underlying intention being this: since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is revealed by force of implication through a properly formulated statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and the negative concomitance is likewise revealed by force of implication through a statement of positive concomitance, what purpose is served by a second sentence that merely communicates what has already been understood?
Since it is so,
[the author] shows the nature of "instruction" by saying "the second. Instruction is the making known of something to one who is ignorant.
"For that purpose" means for that cause.
By this, it is shown that there is only a synthesis of application (*prayoga*), not a synthesis of form (*rūpa*).

Through the repeated practice of observing such applications, someone may, by the very manner of the application itself, understand even an imperceptible object on their own; thus, this was established in the context of explaining the definition [of inference] as a case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
Therefore, it should be understood that there is no fault;
and this will be explained further below.
“*Anumeya* here,” and so forth.
Here, when the definition of the reason (*hetu*) is to be ascertained, the subject (*dharmin*) is the object of inference (*anumeya*).
In other cases, however, at the time of the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) that is the object of inference;

whereas at the time of ascertaining the pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is the property (*dharma*) that is the object of inference. To demonstrate this, the word "here" (*atra*) is employed. That subject (*dharmin*) whose specific property (*viśeṣa*) is desired—that is, wished to be known—is described in that manner.

What is the similar instance (sapakṣa)? A similar instance is an object that is similar by virtue of possessing the general property of the probandum (sādhyadharma). It is a similar instance because it is a similar object. II-7 It is a similar instance because it is a similar object.
That object which is similar—that is, identical—to the subject (pakṣa) is called "similar" (samāna) by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra), and is thereby distinguished by the word "samāna.
A similar subject is a "similar instance" (sapakṣa); furthermore, the substitute "sa-" is applied to the word "samāna."

Now, if the collection of the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is taken here as the primary object of inference (*anumeya*), then it would be impossible for any means of proof (*sādhana*) to be apprehended as having that [collection] as its property (*taddharmatva*). Or, if it were so apprehended, its uselessness would be manifest. With this intention, he asks: "Among those, which one? He explains the intended meaning of the word "here" (*atra*) with the passage beginning "here," and so forth.
Furthermore, both the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*) are objects of inference.
This should be understood as being figurative (*upacāra*), because at that particular time, each constitutes a single part of the object of inference. As it has been said:
"Because the whole (*samudāya*) is what is to be proven, [the term 'probandum'] applies to the mere property when the locus is present."
"Even though it is not primary, because it is a part [of the whole], it is metaphorically designated as the probandum. Thus [it is said].

Now, if "sapakṣa" is intended to mean that which exists together with the *pakṣa*, then there is a lack of semantic coherence. Alternatively, if it is thought to mean "equal to the *pakṣa*," then the form would have to be *pakṣasamāna*; having this in mind, he asks, "What [is it]? The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) replies, "It is an equal object."
He states the meaning of the word *samāna*: "The object (*artha*) is similar (*sadṛśa*).
Here, the word *artha* is used in the sense of that which is perceived, because it is "sought" (*arthyate*) or understood;
it does not mean an object in the sense of something capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), nor does it mean a denotable referent (*vācya*).

Since the absence of causal capacity in a non-momentary entity—due to its incompatibility with both successive and simultaneous action—is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), even things like sky-lotuses are intended to be included as part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Now, one might ask: why is it not intended that [the term] means "that which is both similar and a subject" (*samānaś cāsau pakṣaś ca*)?

In that case, since this subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmī) is itself the subject of the thesis (pakṣa), how can it be distinguished by the word "similar" (samāna)? To this he says: "the subject" (pakṣa).
How can it be so called by that word which has a different meaning? To this he says: "by metaphorical usage" (upacārāt).
In some places, the reading is "stated as the similar class" (sapakṣa).

In this context, it should be understood that "that object" refers to what is called the *pakṣa* (the subject). Furthermore, the basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is its connection with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
That which is called the *pakṣa* by way of such metaphorical designation is [the locus] qualified by...
It is excluded—that is, distinguished—from what is not its own class.

If the word *samāna* (identical) is its qualifier, then how is there the hearing of the word *sa* (with)? To this he says: "of *samāna*. The substitution of the word *sa* in place of the word *samāna* occurs by means of the formal division (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *samānasya* [Pāṇini 6.3.84].

If it is asked: "Why did Dharmottara not adopt the *bahuvrīhi* compound 'one whose side (*pakṣa*) is equal'—by which [analysis] this self [of the term] would have been spared such effort?"—it is true;
however, he proceeded in this way solely out of deference to the *Viniścaya*.

It might be asked: what is that commonality between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by which the similar instance is similar to the subject? To this he says: "by way of the commonality of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmasāmānyena*).
And that [property] is "to be proven" (*sādhya*) because it is not yet established.
And since the property (*dharma*) depends on something else, it is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*);
moreover, it is not the particular that is to be proven, but rather the universal.
Therefore, what is intended here is the universal as the probandum (*sādhya*).

The meaning is that the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is that which is similar to the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of the universal of the property to be proven—that is, because it possesses the universal of the property to be proven.
He asks: "What is the dissimilar instance" (*asapakṣa*)? And he says:
Non-sapakṣa is that which is not sapakṣa. That which does not exist as a sapakṣa is the non-sapakṣa.

And what is it that does not constitute a similar instance (sapakṣa)? It is the conduct [of others]. For in the *Viniścaya*, in the section explaining the presentation of the nine properties of the subject (pakṣadharma), it is stated: "A similar instance (sapakṣa) is a subject that is similar by virtue of possessing the general property to be proven (sādhyadharma); the absence of that is the non-similar instance (asapakṣa)."

Therefore, just as for the author of the *Vārttika*, the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) is intended as the "subject" (*pakṣa*) by way of metaphorical designation; thus, there is no fault here either, as he explains it in this manner.
This should be construed with the statement from the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*: "The similar case (*sapakṣa*) is that which is similar to the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of a commonality."

By the word "sādhya" (the probandum), fire and so forth are intended through metaphorical usage. He states the reason for its being the probandum: "because of its unestablished nature," that is, because it is not certain therein.
Now, it is intended that this is a karmadhāraya compound containing within it another karmadhāraya, namely: "that which is both the property to be proved (sādhya-dharma) and a universal (sāmānya)."

Anticipating the objection—"Since it is a particular (viśeṣa) that is being proved, how can there be a compound of the word 'sādhya' with the word 'dharma', which is a general term (sāmānya)?"—he says "na ca" and so forth. The word "ca" is used in the sense of "because" or for emphasis.
"Sāmānya" means the mere thing (vastumātra) as excluded from what is not of that nature.
The intention is that the reason is pervaded by exactly such [a property].
Since this is so, therefore, at the time of defining the similar instance (sapakṣa) based on this very reason,
having stated that the universal is the probandum (sādhya), he demonstrates the analysis of the word "universal" together with the word "probandum-property" by saying "sādhyeti."
He concludes with the words "sādhyadharme" and so forth;
the restriction is that it must be "exactly the same," and not merely "in general."

Furthermore, because of similarity through other properties such as "being a real entity" (*vastutva*), it would follow that the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) lacks the status of being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

If the non-similar instance (*asapakṣa*) were simply that which is other than the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by virtue of possessing a different property, then any reason (*hetu*) existing in that non-similar instance would result in being a non-reason (*ahetu*) due to its universal inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

Alternatively, if the term "non-similar instance" (*asapakṣa*) is applied to what is contradictory to the similar instance—meaning it is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) by way of the characteristic of "incompatibility" (*sahānavasthāna*)—then a reason characterized by fire would not lead to the cognition of heat (*auṣṇya*).

Now, if the negative particle (*nañ*) is intended to signify non-existence, then, since it is impossible for anything to exist within non-existence, there would be no such thing as a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason. Bearing this in mind, he asks: "What is the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*)? This question is either from one who does not hold such a view or from an ignorant person.

"Not a similar instance" (*na sapakṣa*) and so forth is the response. "That which is not a similar instance" means that which does not possess the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*). By speaking thus, [the author] shows that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
If this is so, one might ask: how is the compound formed? It is because it is expressive (gamaka), like the expression "not seeing the sun" (*asūryampaśyāni*) and others.
The *sāman* chants are such that they need not be known again.

"One who eats food without salt," "faces that do not see the sun"— [these are examples of] neuter nouns according to Pāṇini 1.1.43, *suḍanapuṃsakasya*. However, the restriction regarding the number of usages according to the author of the Bhāṣya is untenable, as has been demonstrated by the Teacher himself in the *Viniścaya*.

The statement beginning with “Alas, this ascetic is suffering,” which was preceded by derision, has already been established by the passage beginning with “just as through a dwelling place one attains [knowledge],” and thus is not discussed here.
[DhPr p. 99]
"Other than that, its opposite, and its absence" (II-9):
other than that [homologue],
and contrary to it.

And for that [reason], there is an absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). As long as the absence of the nature of a similar instance is not cognized, it is impossible to apprehend either its difference from the similar instance or its opposition to it. Therefore, by the force of the cognition of difference and opposition, the two—difference and opposition—are cognized as having the form of the absence of a similar instance. [Note: Regarding the reading *anyatvaviruddhatvapratītisāmarthyāt*, some manuscripts read *anyatvaviruddhatve pratīti-*; the former is adopted here.]

This being the case, since those that are other than [the similar instance] and those that are contradictory would not qualify as "dissimilar instances" (*asapakṣa*), he begins with the question "And what... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that the term *asapakṣa* includes all three: its absence, that which is other than it, and that which is contradictory to it. The particle *ca* has the sense of the word "again" (*punaḥ*).
"Other" (anya) refers to that which is not the substratum of the intended property;
for even when the negative particle (*nañ*) has another object as its domain, it functions through a distinct application [of meaning].
Indeed, that very person is not a Brāhmaṇa merely by virtue of connection with that caste.
And an "abrāhmaṇa" (non-Brahmin) is recognized in the world as such because of the inclusion of other properties [within that category].

It is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it is contradictory by way of contradiction characterized by coexistence and contradiction characterized by existence through the mutual exclusion of essences.
The word "and" (*ca*) conjoins it with the state of having contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*) in relation to another [subject], namely, the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
And its non-existence is of a void nature, consisting of a simple negation (prasajya), having as its sole essence that which is to be excluded.

This is the meaning of the present context: the "non-sapakṣa" (asapakṣa) is the absence of the sapakṣa; the meaning is that it is that which does not possess the property to be proven (sādhyadharmin).

Because the term *asapakṣa* has the meaning of the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), the *asapakṣa* is not merely a negation. What then? Every counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is both a negation (*niṣedha*) and an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Because the non-example (*asapakṣa*) does not possess the characteristic of reality,
this is equivalent when applied to the intended counter-positive (*pratiyogin*),
since the understanding of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is identical in all cases.
"Either directly or by implication"—
the word "and" (ca) refers back to the preceding [term] in a conjunctive sense;
for both other [factors] and contradictory [factors], whether they exist as real entities or are merely conceptualized, are not considered "similar instances" (asapakṣa).
In that regard, because it is a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) for that which exists [in the subject], there is no fault of its absence;

and by the description of the nature of the other two—the contradictory and the non-contradictory—the fault stated regarding the position that they are non-homologous (*asapakṣa*) is refuted; thus, everything is clear.

Now, one might object: by the statement "that which is not a homologous instance" (*sapakṣa*), it is established that only that which has the very nature of the absence of a homologous instance is what constitutes a non-homologous instance (*asapakṣa*).
Furthermore, it is not possible for two mutually contradictory things to have the nature of being that [same] thing, because they are positive entities (*vidhirūpa*).
Anticipating the objection, "How then can those two be so," he says: "from the similar class" (*sapakṣāt*).
"Otherness" (*anyatva*) means being differentiated from that, which is to say, being distinct (*pṛthaktva*). Furthermore,
it is not possible to know its contradictory nature as long as its essential character— the absence of any similar instance (*sapakṣa*)— is not recognized.
Thus, it is "other" and "contradictory" by implication.

This is the intended meaning: if that which is intended to be other than something else were to have the same nature as that from which its otherness is to be designated—if that [identity] were unestablished or doubtful—then there would be no otherness at all, just like the nature of that very thing itself.
Or, just as in the case of smoke that is being doubted as being vapor and so forth, there is no certainty that it is something other than vapor;
and when that which is contradictory [to a certain nature] is established— whether definitely or doubtfully— as having that very nature, then it exists together with that [nature].
How could there be a persistence [of the subject] by excluding that very nature,
and how could it be ascertained to possess that nature— like the previously mentioned smoke?
Since this is so, therefore...
The meaning is that in those two cases, there is an absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*).
Since this is so, for that reason, [the term] "directly" (*sākṣāt*) means without mediation.
By this, it is indicated that if only one non-concordant instance (*asapakṣa*) were to be mentioned, then it would simply be its absence.
Because of the absence of the former, its own absence is directly perceived as having the form of the absence from the similar instances (sapakṣa).
However, the other two [reasons], by their very capacity, are understood to be of the nature of non-existence;
therefore, all three are non-concordant (asapakṣa), and there are exactly three types of logical marks (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics. II-10
By the three-fold nature already mentioned, there are exactly three types of logical marks (*liṅga*) that possess these three characteristics.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include other things to be explained.
First, the three-fold nature was asked about, and then the logical marks possessing those three characteristics were asked about by the opponent.
In that regard, the three-fold character has been stated; and the "three-featured" [reasons] are now being explained— namely,
there are exactly three types of reasons characterized by these three features.
The meaning is that there are three types of the three-fold logical mark (*liṅga*).
To the question "What, then, are they?", he says: non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and effect (*kārya*)—II.11.
The non-perception of the probandum to be negated possesses the three characteristics;
and the nature of the probandum to be affirmed possesses the three characteristics, as does its effect.
He states the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) regarding the other two types: the contradictory and the incompatible.

Since another [reason] has been stated according to the aforementioned principle to consist in the absence of similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the absence of dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), therefore—let it be for one, two, or even three [reasons]; the word "even" (*api*) implies this.
"By the three-fold nature" (*trairūpyeṇa*) means by that which possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpeṇa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "those which have three forms as their characteristics.
The term *trīṇy eva* means "only three" or "precisely the number three.

By the phrase *tri-rūpāṇi*, he refutes the opponent's assertion that the reason (*hetu*) possesses four or six characteristics, on account of its connection with other forms such as having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).
By the phrase "only three," the plurality of numbers [of reasons] is excluded through distinctions such as those based on concomitance (*saṃyogin*).

In the reading "asked" (*pṛṣṭa*), the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) is to be supplied as the subject. Whether it be the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) that was asked about, or the three-fold nature that was asked about—that three-fold nature has been stated by means of the composed text.
Alternatively, since the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) was asked about by the Teacher, that three-fold nature was therefore stated;
and the particle *ca* conjoins this with the fact that he has stated the three-fold [reasons] in accordance with that three-fold nature.
If it is objected: "But surely this pair of questions has not yet been heard from the opponent; so how can a twofold inquiry on the part of the opponent be mentioned? It is said in reply:

The proponent who has heard [the rule] "from a mark possessing the three characteristics" must necessarily inquire: "What are those three characteristics? And how many are the three characteristics of the mark?
It is said that he has asked this. If it is asked, "How is this determined? [the answer follows].

Since the Teacher has stated that "the three-fold nature of the logical mark (liṅga) is of such a character," it is understood that the opponent, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin), asks a question regarding its nature. Furthermore, because he has stated that "there are exactly three [reasons] possessing the three characteristics," there is a question concerning their number.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "The three-fold nature at the outset," and so forth.
The varieties of the *liṅga* are the essential natures of the *liṅga*.
He asks—"Which ones?"—because a triad is impossible due to the distinctions such as conjunction and so forth;
the question is posed by way of both general and specific forms.
And "the effect" refers to that which is to be enjoined, as is the subject under discussion.
It should be understood that previously, by implication, it was the non-distinct (*anarthāntara*) thing to be enjoined that was meant;

now, however, it is the distinct (*arthāntara*) thing to be enjoined. Thus, the formulation should be connected as follows: "the three-fold characteristic is the function of the distinct thing to be enjoined."
The two occurrences of the word "ca" (and) serve to indicate a conjunction with what precedes.
[DhPr p.
101] To provide an illustration of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says:
"In that regard, non-apprehension is as follows: for example, there is no jar in a certain particular place."
"Because there is no perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility" (II-12),
"just as," and so forth.
The word "just as" (*yathā*) is used for the purpose of illustration.
The meaning is that just as this non-apprehension is [an indicator], so too are others; it is not this alone. "Place" (pradeśa) means a particular location (ekadeśa).
That which is distinguished is a "particular" (*viśeṣa*), which is perceptible to the cognizer;
and not every location is of such a nature.
Thus he says: "in some place."
In the case of perception by the cognizer, the locus (*dharmin*) is "in a certain place";
"not a jar" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*);
and "perception" is the cognition.
Its definition is the causal complex that produces it; for in this way, perception is defined,
since the object reached by it is included within that causal complex by virtue of being its producer.
The meaning is that "perceptible" refers to that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
"Because of its non-apprehension"—this is the reason.
Now, how can that which does not exist in a particular place be perceptible there?
The superimposition of visibility is such that even what is non-existent is called "visible.
And that which is thus conceived— namely, "if this were present here, it would be visible"—
is a superimposed visible object, even though it does not exist there.
And who indeed can be so expected?
One for whom all the causes for one's own support and vision are present. And when are those [causes] understood to be complete?
When there is the apprehension of another object associated with a single cognition—

where two objects, perceivable by the same sense faculty and directed toward the focus of the eye and so forth, are said to be "associated in a single cognition" because they are mutually dependent— it should be understood that for those two,
the absence of the jar is the fitness for the conventional usage of the term "absence of the jar."
Because the absence of a jar is established by perception,
and this will be explained later.
By saying "it is characterized by that," it is made explicit that a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is so called because "one is characterized by means of it" (*lakṣyate 'nena*).
"That" refers to the characteristic of being perceived.
To the question "How is it attained?", he says: "By way of being its producer.
To the question "Is it produced by that single [cause] alone, such that it is stated thus?", he says: "Because of being included within the causal complex (sāmagrī)."
He clarifies the meaning of the compound:
"visible" (dṛśya) means fit for seeing; "iti" is used in the sense of "thus."

Thus, regarding that word which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), if its referent (*abhidheya*) is non-existent yet is called "visible" through superimposition (*samāropa*), then there is also a multiplicity therein consisting of things graspable by different sense faculties. Anticipating the objection that in that case the same [fallacy] would apply to that [multiplicity] as well, he says: "And that which is thus... (*yaś caivam*).
The word "eva" (only) serves as a restriction; the meaning is that such a thing alone is to be superimposed as an object of perception, and not everything.
He then asks: "Who is it that can be conceived in this way?"
The word "again" (punaḥ) has the sense of "and" (ca).
"Of whom" (yasya) refers to the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin).
"Of whom" (yasya) refers to the negation.
It is called an "object" (ālambana) because it takes itself as its support;
these are the causes of that vision.

The intention is that if that [external object] does not exist, how can there be an understanding of the causal totality for the perception of it? Thus he asks, "When? as before. Furthermore, "conjunction" (saṃsarga) refers to the appearance within a single cognition; that which possesses this is [the object].
And it has been stated that "when there is the apprehension of that [object] as being 'that' and 'a distinct entity'," the cognition of two existing things is not restricted to one.
Because the capacity [for perception] is equal in both cases, therefore,

when one object associated with the same cognition is being perceived, if the other were present with its entire causal complex for perception complete, it would necessarily be perceived; thus, its potential perceptibility is superimposed upon it, and its non-apprehension is "non-apprehension of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalambha*).

Therefore, that very spot devoid of the jar and the cognition having that as its object are called "non-perception of the perceptible" because they are the cause for determining the non-perception of the perceptible.
For as long as the object associated with the same cognition is not determined, and its cognition is not [determined], there is no determination of the non-perception of the perceptible;
hence, both the object and its cognition are termed "non-perception."
However, the mere cessation of perception is not itself a means of knowledge because it is not itself ascertained.
Therefore, by the force of the statement, the place devoid of the visible jar and the cognition thereof must be understood as being of the nature of the non-perception of the perceptible.
In that context, if the established position is that consciousness is formless (*nirākāra*), then the word "one" (*eka*) is for the purpose of excluding numbers such as two and so forth.

But when the position is that [cognition] possesses aspects (*sākāra*), then there are two alternatives: either cognition is a single, variegated (*citram*) entity consisting of multiple aspects that cannot be distinguished from one another;
or it is multiple with respect to each object, conforming to its respective aspect.
In the former case, the term "single" (*eka*) is used as before.
In the alternative view, however, the word "one" is used figuratively because [the two eyes] originate from a single sense-base (*āyatana*) and have a single form as their object.

Now, one might object: "If that which is being negated were to appear together with this [perceived surface], such as the ground, within a single cognition, then it could be described as 'associated with a single cognition' in relation to that; but since this very [negation] does not exist [in that way], how can it be so? Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates their actual state of being so through the passage beginning with "by means of a single sense-organ."
The *praṇidhāna* (aspiration) of Locanā and the others consists in becoming fit for the production of their own cognition; "facing toward" that [cognition] means being conducive to it.
"Mutually dependent" means, for example, that the ground and so forth depend on the jar and so forth, and the jar and so forth depend on that [ground]. This is the meaning.
Even if two things were present there, nevertheless only one would appear there; thus he says, "of those two.
The word "hi" means "because.
He states the logical justification: "of the capacity."
Precisely because the co-occurrence (*saṃsarga*) of those two— the jar and so forth, and the ground and so forth— is possible within a single cognition, therefore, when one [of them],
such as the ground, is being perceived, the other, such as the jar, should be understood as possessing the complete causal complex for perception.
Thus he shows that even that which is non-existent (*asad*), being absent, is said to be "seen" due to superimposition (*samāropa*).
The particle *iti* expresses the form of a possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
Of that very object which is fit for such possibility, there is non-perception, which consists in the perception of something else that is not distinct from it.
This is because the non-perception of that [object]—such as the ground—is determined from the sight of that which is associated with it in a single cognition; therefore [it is so].

[Objection: "Surely non-apprehension must be the very ascertainment of the cognition of the ground and so forth, since that [ascertainment] is the cause for the ascertainment of its non-apprehension; but how then is the ground and so forth [established]? To this he says: "As far as... (*yāvat*).
The word "for" (*hi*) means "because.
By this [statement], the ground and so forth are qualified by the cognition.

It has been demonstrated that cognition delimited by the ground and so forth determines the non-perception of the perceptible—that is, the absence of perception—as having the single nature of being that which is to be conventionally designated.
"Entity" refers to the ground and so forth;
"cognition" refers to that which apprehends it.
This [text] combines [the two] because their means are equal.
But what is this "attainment of the conditions for perception"? He says:

The fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) consists in the completeness of the other conditions for apprehension and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). (II-13) "Attainment of the conditions for apprehension" means that a jar possesses the state of having attained the conditions for apprehension, which is the completeness of the other conditions for apprehension. For the cognition [of a jar], the jar is a producer, as are others such as the eye and so forth. Other causes than the visible jar are the "other conditions. Their completeness is what is meant.
Proximity (*sannidhi*). Its very nature is distinguished from others; thus, "distinguished" means "distinguished by its particularity.

Therefore, this twofold [condition]—this distinguished nature and the completeness of other causal conditions (*pratyaya*)—should be understood as the fulfillment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) in the case of a jar or similar objects.

If non-apprehension consists in the fact that when there is a connection between two things within a single cognition, the apprehension of one is the cause for the certain determination of the non-apprehension of the other, and from that [non-apprehension] follows the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of its absence— then, upon the experience of the cognition of blue, there would be no linguistic usage of the absence of the cognition of yellow,
because there is no connection between those two within a single cognition.
If it is argued that, according to your view, cognition is not known by another cognition because that would entail the consequence of the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
this is true.
By the expression "associated with a single cognition," what is intended here is the state of being perceived as mutually non-deviating;
and this [state] exists even in the case of cognition itself.
For if that cognition were present, it would necessarily be cognized just like the cognition of blue.
And since it is not perceived, it is conventionally designated as "non-existent"—what is the fault in this?

It might be asked: by means of the negative particle (*nañ*) functioning through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), which negates the perception of the attributes of the knower and the known, is a twofold perception characterized by the attributes of the knower and the known thereby established?

Fearing that [the opponent] might think that mere non-apprehension (*upalambhābhāva*) is being stated by way of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), as Īśvarasena believes, he says "darśana... and so forth.

"Darśana" means apprehension; its cessation is its absence, which is of the nature of a void (*tuccharūpa*). That itself is "mere that" (*tanmātra*), namely the exclusion of connection with any other entity.
The particle *tu* highlights the difference of this [non-apprehension] from the previous [kind of] non-apprehension.

By stating "because it is not ascertained by itself," the proponent indicates that there is an absence of a means of proof for that [non-perception], since the consequence of an infinite regress would arise if one were to apprehend it through non-perception.
Because it is not ascertained, it is not a prover.

By explaining it in this way, he indicates the following: such a non-perception is inconclusive (*anaikāntikī*) when proving the conventional usage of non-existence, because even when a means of valid cognition has ceased, the absence of the object is not necessarily established.
The phrase "by the force of the statement" means by the force of the statement "of that which has reached the conditions for perception";
the intention is that otherwise, this [statement] would be redundant.
Now, it is said that one who possesses the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is [so called];
just as one who possesses "attainment" (*āpti*)—in the form of seeing things as they truly are and so forth—is called an "authoritative person" (*āpta*).
And if this condition for perception consists in the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-sannikarṣa*),...
The conjunction of the sense organ and the mind, the contact between the sense organ and its object,
and the conjunction with the illumination of the object.

Considering that, according to your own view, the possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*) and manifest color (*rūpa*) have been declared [as conditions for perception], yet these are impossible in the case of these [atoms], and thus their fulfillment of the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) is untenable, he asks: "What, then..."?
This question is posed in terms of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*).
The Teacher also does not intend these [conditions] by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti*).

Rather, with the intention of asking "What then is this?", he begins to explain the response beginning with "that which is characterized by the conditions for perception" (*yad upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, using the phrase "perception" (*upalabdhi*) and so on.

He restates the very thing to be explained by means of the term "the state of having attained the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptatva*), which has the same meaning as the term "attainment of the conditions for perception."

And this is his intention: for whatever possesses the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), there necessarily exists the state of possessing the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*).
For this very reason, it is said that "the conditions for apprehension" means "the state of possessing the conditions for apprehension.
When the expectation arises as to whose [these conditions are], he says: "of the jar."
Now, is it not the case that "completeness" (sākalya) is a manifold property, and that there are not many causes for a single cognition?

Furthermore, if even the object of negation were a cause of cognition, then other conditions than that condition would be called "other conditions" (pratyayāntara); anticipating this objection, he says "of cognition" (jñānasya).
What kind of specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is it? He says:
that nature which, while other conditions for perception are present, becomes directly perceived—that is the specific nature. II-14
"In the presence of," and so forth.

That specific nature which, while those other conditions for perception—such as [the visibility] of a pot—are present and existing, becomes directly perceived, is the "specific nature" (svabhāvaviśeṣa).
This is the meaning here: this definition of direct perception is relative to a single cognizer.
And this being so, for a single observer who has set out to see, the object currently being perceived possesses both [qualities].
However, those objects remote in space, time, or nature—which are not being seen—are devoid of specific qualities of nature, yet they possess the completeness of other causal conditions.
For those very conditions by which that observer sees are present.

And for this reason, he says "svabhāva... [to show that] when one has set out to see what is present, it is not only the completeness of other conditions (*pratyaya*) and the fulfillment of the criteria for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), but something else as well.
The word "ca" (and) conjoins these as being of equal force.

It is distinguished from others, such as *piśācas* and the like, by its capacity to produce cognition. Although it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) by virtue of this capacity, because the word *viśeṣa* is listed in the *rājadantādi* group, it does not undergo the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*).
The word *viśiṣṭa* refers to the meaning of the word *viśeṣa* when derived as a passive noun (*karmasādhana*).
By means of the summary beginning with "that" (*tat*), he shows that these two combined are what is expressed by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*).

Since the attainment of the conditions for perception is intended to mean both the completeness of other causal factors and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), therefore, the state of having attained the conditions for perception— which is denoted by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception"—
belongs to the jar and so forth, which are the objects to be negated.

Now, intending to ask whether the nature (*svabhāva*) is something more substantial, or a particularity of nature, or rather consists of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) unmixed with the forms of others, he asks: "Of what kind?
He provides the answer beginning with "When [the conditions] exist," and explains it with the words beginning with "of perception.
[An objection: But how can this be possible—that even when all other causal conditions are complete, the nature itself becomes directly perceived?

For indeed, even though a jar possesses such a nature, it does not become perceptible to a person standing at a distance even when his eyes and other faculties are directed toward it; anticipating this objection, he says "Therefore, this...

Since the Teacher has stated that these two [conditions] constitute the fulfillment of the criteria for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), therefore, in this context, this is the intended meaning that must be expressed. He asks, "What is it? and replies, "The single... and so forth.
And since it is both "one" and the "intended perceiver," this definition of perception is dependent upon that [perceiver].
Its nature is such that, while other conditions for apprehension are present, that which exists becomes directly perceived;
and the "one perceiver" to be spoken of is precisely he who, being in a location free from obstructions and so forth, has set out to see.
And when there is such a perceiver, such [an object] necessarily becomes directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).
Nevertheless, [the author] asks, "How is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) overcome? and says, "In that case" (*tathā ca*), meaning: when that mode [of perception] exists;
"being seen" (*dṛśyamāna*) is a qualification used as a reason (*hetu*).
It possesses both [the general nature and the specific nature], it possesses its own specific nature, and it possesses the completeness of other conditions. However,
for one who has not set out to see, even those things situated in a perceptible location cannot be seen because they lack other conditions.
But those things endowed with specific intrinsic natures,
even if they are distant in space and time, lack both [the other conditions].
Thus, for one who sees in this way, there is nothing whatsoever that lacks another condition.
But it would be deficient in its intrinsic nature and specific qualities;
however, that which is situated in a suitable location and lacks other conditions can be seen by one who is unable to see [it],
whereas others are deficient in both respects.

If [it is argued that] even though they are not being seen, they possess specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), then what is the use of grasping those specific intrinsic natures? To this he says: "though not being seen. The particle *tu* distinguishes the unperceived from the perceived. Being remote in terms of place and so forth is the cause for their being unperceived.
Because they are qualified by being causes,
those [factors] possess the completeness of other conditions; however,
due to the absence of a specific intrinsic nature, he distinguishes them by means of their possession of the completeness of other conditions.
This should be understood as following from the phrase "of one who has begun to perceive.

This is the meaning of the context here: with respect to a single perceiver, even if such a nature [of the object] is not taken as fulfilling the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), then for those things remote in space and so forth, there exists the fulfillment of the conditions for perception in the form of the completeness of other causal factors (*pratyayāntarasākalya*). Thus, because there is no perception of those things that have fulfilled the conditions for perception, there is the conventional usage of their non-existence.
It would have to be so presented;
however, this is not tenable.

Therefore, this definition of the specific nature [of an object] is in relation to a qualified cognizer; thus, the definition of "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) is well-stated.
Establishing that they indeed possess the completeness of other conditions, he says "by which" (*yair*).
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because.
To the question "How is this established? he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
The particle *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason that will be stated later. The word *ca* is used in the sense of "this must be said. The meaning is:
those conditions are present, because he has set out to see [them], that is to say, he has set out to see them as distinct from that [other object]. Thus is the sense.
Or rather, when one proceeds to examine that very thing from which [the effect arises], then one should be regarded as acting with prior reflection (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*). This is because,
in relation to the person engaged in observation, the object itself possesses such a nature.
To explain what that [object] is like for one who has not set out to see it, he says: "for one who has not set out to see.
By the particle *tu*, he indicates the distinction between one who has not set out to see and one who has set out to see.
In whatever location the object exists such that other cognitions perceive it, that very location is the suitable place; those situated there [perceive it].

Therefore, those other causes such as the eye and so forth, which are distinct from that visible object, are the "other conditions" (*pratyayāntara*). Their deficiency is their absence; they possess this [absence] because they are qualified by their status as causes.
For this very reason, they cannot be seen. Showing that they nevertheless possess a specific intrinsic nature (svabhāva), he says "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
By the particle *tu*, he distinguishes them as being endowed with a specific intrinsic nature, because they lack other conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*).
Regarding such persons, he asks what can be said of those who are remote in terms of place and time, and thus says "dūre" (remote).
Those for whom place and time are remote are so described.
The sense is that those who are separated by space are "remote in place," while those who are separated by duration are "remote in time."
The word "tu" distinguishes these from the preceding [arguments].
Here too, the phrase "of one who has not proceeded to see" is understood to carry over.
He thus concludes what was already stated by the words beginning with "tad evam."

Alternatively, this [definition] is explained differently with reference to a single cognizer: by the phrase "of that which has reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), those things which have not reached the conditions for perception due to being remote in terms of place, time, or nature (*deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*) are indeed to be excluded. Yet, even they cannot be said to have reached the conditions for perception such that they could be excluded [from the scope of the definition]; for even a *piśāca*, though remote in place, is certainly perceived by members of its own kind. Thus, even that which is remote in place [is perceivable].

Likewise, since there is no object to be excluded by those of the same time even for that which is remote in time, [the author], having cited non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), says the following in order to cite intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): [DhPr p.106]...upā-... 〔omitted〕...he says.
The essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the reason (*hetu*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists solely by virtue of its own existence.
[This begins with] "essential nature," etc.;
the connection is that "essential nature" is the reason.
To the question, "What kind of cause is the nature (*svabhāva*) of the probandum (*sādhya*)," he says: it is its own existence (*sattā*).
That alone is "mere self-existence" (*svasattāmātra*).
[The term refers to] that which has the character of coming into being when that [self-existence] is present.
That which exists in dependence upon the existence of the reason itself,

and does not depend upon any reason distinct from the existence of that reason, is the probandum that occurs by the mere presence of its own existence (*svasattāmātrabhāvī*). The reason for such a probandum is its very nature (*svabhāva*), and nothing other than that.
The example is as follows: "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*. Regarding this, "as follows" (*yathā*) introduces the instance; "this" (*ayam*) refers to the subject (*dharmin*).
"Tree" is the thesis (*sādhya*);
"because it is a *śiṃśapā*" is the reason (*hetu*). Thus, the meaning is this: "This is fit for the conventional designation (*vyavahāra*) of 'tree'."

"Because it is fit for the conventional usage of *śiṃśapā*. In a region where *śiṃśapā* trees are abundant, when a dull-witted person who is unacquainted with the conventional usage of the term *śiṃśapā* is shown a tall *śiṃśapā* by someone and told, "This is a tree," then, due to his dullness, he [mistakenly] attributes the height of the *śiṃśapā* to the conventional usage of the term "tree."
When one determines the sign, then whatever non-tall *śiṃśapā* one perceives, one determines that very thing to be a non-tree.

Suspecting that for such a fool—who has apprehended the mere sign of a *śiṃśapā*—the qualification "that which has reached the state of being perceived" (*labdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) is redundant, he says: "Therefore, this is the meaning here."

In that case, however, by the term "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), what is meant to be expressed is the state of having reached the conditions for apprehension; this previously mentioned definition should be applied to it.
This definition of perception, namely "the conditions for apprehension," is with respect to a single cognizer—this is the meaning.
Even so, he says "And thus... to explain how the objection is overcome.
The remainder has already been explained previously.
Now, in order to explain the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he begins with the words "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) and so forth.

Although this word "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) applies in a general sense, because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has been mentioned, he says "the essential nature of the probandum" (*sādhyasya svabhāvaḥ*) with the intention that it refers specifically to the essential nature of that [property].
Since the intrinsic form of the reason is being considered, its own self (*ātman*) is intended by the word "own" (*sva*).
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "that which is the reason for this," etc.;
[it refers to] that reason which makes known the probandum.
One is engaged in the conventional usage of "tree";
here, height and so forth are not a separate cause for this conventional usage of "tree."

Rather, the mere state of being a *śiṃśapā* is the cause—the meaning is that the possession of branches and so forth belonging to a *śiṃśapā* is the cause. To provide an example of an effect, he says:
"An effect is, for example: 'There is fire here because of smoke. (II-17)
"Fire" is the probandum (*sādhya*);
"here" is the locus (*dharmin*);
"because of smoke" is the reason (*hetu*).

Since the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is well-known in the world as being based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), the definition of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) was not stated [separately] as it was for the essential nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*). "Example" (*udāharaṇa*) refers to this point according to the context;
that by which the essential nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is illustrated or demonstrated is the "example," namely, the statement that establishes the essential nature-reason.
This is an explanation of the meaning of the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), but not a demonstration of its formal application (*prayoga*).
The formal application, however, is as follows: "Whatever is fit for the conventional designation of being a *śiṃśapā* is fit for the conventional designation of being a tree;
for example, a previously perceived *śiṃśapā* to which the conventional designation of 'tree' has been applied."
"And this [object] is fit for the conventional usage of 'śiṃśapā'.
Now, one who sees a *śiṃśapā* necessarily knows it to be a tree;
so how can there be a relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) here? To this he says: "Therefore, this... [and so forth].

Since the *śiṃśapā* is presented as the probans (*sādhana*) and "tree" as the probandum (*sādhya*), this does not accord with the literal meaning [of the words]. Therefore, [the intended inference is]: "This is a tree, or this is fit for the conventional designation 'tree', because it is a *śiṃśapā*."

The meaning that must be expressed by this sentence, "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*," is "because of its fitness for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of *śiṃśapā*"; this is understood from the context.

The particle *iti* shows the very nature of the meaning of the sentence. Now, one might object: "Surely, a person who already knows the conventional usage of 'tree' will apply that usage to the object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself; so how does this inference find its application? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*), introducing the statement.
The phrase "the sign" (*nimitta*) and so forth is easy to understand.
By this continuous exposition, it has been shown that for the deluded person, this inference is the means of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
Only this much remains to be examined here.
And when the conventional usage of "treeness" is being taught, it is based on superimposed causes such as height; at that time, by what example could he be made to understand?
For from the very beginning, he has not grasped that the mere possession of branches and so forth is the cause.
This is true;
however, effort must be made toward awakening.
Then, due to his dullness, he will inevitably perceive even height as a cause [of fear]; this point should be applied to such a deluded perceiver.

Suppose someone, having first determined that the mere possession of branches and so forth belonging to a *śiṃśapā* tree is the cause [for the application of the term], initiates the linguistic usage "tree";

later, however, due to dullness, he forgets that mere cause and, becoming confused at the time of using the term "tree," thinks that height was also a cause, and thus conceives of height as well as being a cause for the linguistic usage "tree."

And such a dull-witted person can indeed be made to understand that the object is fit for the conventional designation "tree" by means of the reason— its fitness for the conventional designation "śiṃśapā"— using as an example a śiṃśapā tree that was previously engaged with under the causal condition of that very [tree-]designation and is thus recalled at that time.
However, in the case of one who from the very beginning has superimposed other causes such as height and so forth, the presentation of a logical reason is simply not appropriate.
What then? It must be understood that this person is merely to be made to grasp the conventional usage regarding the term "tree"; thus, everything is clear.
[DhPr p.
108] But surely, because it possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*), it is logical that there is only one type of logical mark (*liṅga*).

Now, if it is argued that there is a distinction based on the difference in modes, then since a single essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) possesses infinite modes, it would be incorrect for it to have only three forms. To this he says:
"In this context, two are proofs of an existent thing (*vastusādhana*), and one is a reason for negation (*pratiṣedhahetu*). (II-18)
Regarding the phrase "here two":
among these three [types of reasons] mentioned here, two reasons are *vastusādhana*—that is, they are the means of establishing or making known a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
One is the reason that makes known a negation (*pratiṣedha*).

The term "negation" (pratiṣedha) should be understood as referring to non-existence and the conventional usage of non-existence. Now, in order to explain the effect-reason (kāryahetu), he says: "the effect. Since the reason is the subject under discussion, it should be understood that "the effect" means the effect-reason, for the sake of easy comprehension.
He states the nature of the probandum and so forth with the words "fire" (*vahnir iti*).
This too is an explanation of the meaning of the reason (*hetu*),
but it is not a demonstration of its formal application (*prayoga*).
Because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that ought to be demonstrated is not demonstrated,
and because a thesis (*pratijñā*) that ought not to be stated is stated;

furthermore, even for a person who already knows the pervasion, when the reason is stated in its form as the subject of a description, it must be stated in the nominative case alone, as in "here is smoke" (*atra dhūmaḥ*).

But it is not [the case] that [it is established] "from smoke. Nor, even with respect to such a person, is there a thesis; otherwise, who would call this a non-member of the proof? And if it were a member of the proof, a hundredfold contradiction of the rules of debate would ensue.
However, the formal argument (prayoga) should be formulated as follows: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire everywhere, as in a kitchen;
and there is smoke here.

Anticipating the objection—"Why has the Teacher not formulated a definition for the 'effect-reason' (kāryahetu), just as he did for 'essential nature' (svabhāva) and 'non-perception' (anupalabdhi)?"—he says: "The effect... and so forth.
"In the world" means among people who engage in worldly discourse; "well-known" means established; "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason.
"It was not stated by the Teacher"—this is the ellipsis.
This is the intended meaning: indeed, many are mistaken regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Īśvarasena considers non-apprehension to be merely the absence of apprehension (*upalabdhyabhāvamātra*).

Kumārila, however, describes non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a means of valid cognition for absence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) by defining it as the mere cognition of another thing, without depending on its connection with a single act of cognition.
Likewise, he describes the non-modification (*apariṇāma*) of the self—characterized by not being the locus of the intended cognition—as such, even though it is common to states such as deep sleep.
As he says: "It is either the non-modification of the self, or the cognition of another object. [46]
[46] ŚV Abhāvapariccheda 11cd: Regarding the self, there is either a transformation (*pariṇāma*) or consciousness (*vijñāna*) with respect to the object;
likewise, many have disagreed even concerning the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Some have determined that a property (*dharma*), even though it depends on something else, is an essential nature as a reason.
Some, however, maintain that the nature [of a thing] is based on a specific property (*dharmin*) of the entity.
To refute such misconceptions, the definitions of those two were stated.
But since no one disputes the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in this context, its definition was not mentioned here.

Even regarding the disagreement that if the relationship of signifier and signified were based on the relation of cause and effect, it would follow that everything could be signified by everything else, there is no disagreement concerning the definition of the effect itself; rather, the disagreement concerns its status as a signifier.
And that [disagreement] has been refuted elsewhere; here too, the wise should infer it for themselves, since this work is undertaken for the benefit of intelligent people.

Now, unable to accept that there are exactly three [reasons] possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*), he says: "But surely" (*nanu*). Here, *nanu* is a particle of inquiry; the word *atha* has the sense of the word *yadi*.
Due to the difference— that is, the distinction— of the mode, which is its own nature, there is diversity, meaning manifoldness;
this being the case when such an admission is made,
"of one" means of that which is non-different.
And non-difference exists everywhere because of the presence of the exclusion of the reasons "lack of intrinsic nature" (*asvabhāva*) and "non-existence of the reason" (*ahetutva*).
This is the meaning: the reason is a member of the probandum (*sādhyāṅga*) because it is for the sake of establishing the probandum, while the probandum is the primary element.
Therefore, the distinction among reasons that serve as instruments for a probandum arises from the difference between the primary probandum and its accessories,
not from a difference in their own intrinsic nature; and the probandum is sometimes a positive affirmation (*vidhi*).
There is a certain negation;
and since affirmation and negation exist through mutual exclusion, the reasons for the two are distinct.
Furthermore, even a certain affirmation is distinct from the reason.
Some [logicians] hold that there is no difference [between the two].
However, since identity and difference exist by each maintaining its own nature through the exclusion of the other, the reasons (hetu) are distinct.
Consequently, because the properties to be proven (sādhya) are mutually contradictory, the reasons are distinct.
But not by itself alone.

Having raised the doubt as to why these three alone possess the status of a reason (*hetu*) and why others do not, [the author] says— in order to demonstrate both why these three alone are reasons and why others are not—
"For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one thing makes another thing known" (II-19).

The intention of one who says "because of having infinite modes" is as follows: it is because [the object] possesses an infinite nature due to distinctions such as being qualified by attributes, being devoid of attributes, being distinct from its attributes, or being non-distinct from its attributes.
By explaining the term *gamakau* (the two indicators), he shows that in the word *sādhanau* (the two means of proof), the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
And in this context, it must be understood as a restriction that they are "only the means of proof of the object," and not that they are "only the object."

Since the exclusion of others (*itaravyavaccheda*) is also established by those two [reasons], their status as means for establishing a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) is stated only in accordance with the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer. It must be understood that the reason is indeed a negation (*pratiṣedha*), but not that it is exclusively so; for even by the two preceding [types of reasons], a negation is established through their inherent capacity.
But is it not the case that non-existence is not established by the non-perception of the perceptible, since that [non-existence] is already established by direct perception?
Rather, it is the linguistic convention [that is established].
Therefore, how can negation be established by non-perception?

Now, if the conventional usage of "non-existence" is said to be a negation (*pratiṣedha*), then when the non-existence of the pervaded and so forth is established by means of the non-perception of the pervader and so forth, by what is that non-existence established?
Fearing the objection, "What, then, is to be understood here by the word 'negation'?", he says: "Negation."

The word *iti* refers back to the word *pratiṣedha* (negation). Therefore, the meaning is that by this term "negation," both non-existence (*abhāva*) and the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) are to be understood as expressed.

The intention is that the inclusion of one [non-existence] is by way of its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), while the inclusion of the other [the conventional usage] is by way of its secondary function (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), namely, as the basis for negation.

The cognition that "it does not exist," the verbal expression that "it does not exist," and the activity characterized by coming and going free from hesitation constitute conventional practice (*vyavahāra*).
Since that [activity] cannot be set in motion by force, it should be understood that what is to be proven is precisely its fitness for such activity.

Thus, although non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), it is treated separately from that due to the determination of the cognizer; this is how it should be understood.

One might object: "Even if these [reasons] serve as means for establishing injunctions and prohibitions, their possession of the three characteristics (trirūpatva) remains unchanged; and since this very point was already raised in the objection, how can this response apply to that prima facie argument? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.

Since this has been set forth by the Teacher in accordance with the scripture and does not overstep the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), therefore this is the meaning of the sentence; that is to say, this is its intended purport (*tātparyārtha*).
He establishes this very point in the section of the text beginning with "the reason" (*hetu*) and ending with "but not by itself" (*na tu svata eva*).
Now, how is it that one thing does not deviate from another thing, such that these three are considered reasons (*hetu*)?

Thinking that if these [three] possess the capacity to make [the object] known by establishing their own probandum (*sādhya*), why should others—consisting of non-observation (*anupalambha*), non-causal effect (*akārya*), and non-essential nature (*asvabhāva*)—not also possess it, he begins with a question:
"Why? (*kasmāt*).

"Why" asks for the cause in general; "again" [asks] for it specifically. Of the three, beginning with non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the particle *ca* has the sense of adding another cause in relation to the previously mentioned sign.
"For others"— that is, for those such as the "conjoined" (saṃyogin) and so forth, whose nature is not like this—
there is no essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha).
The connection is by way of essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The compound is formed according to the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.33).
"Being connected by way of essential nature" means having an essential nature that is necessarily connected.

When either the cause (*kāraṇa*) or the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the connection (*pratibandha*) by way of essential nature is indistinguishable for both the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature; thus, both are included by a single compound.
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).

Because, when there is a connection by way of essential nature, the meaning of the probans (*sādhana*) causes the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) to be understood, therefore these three possess the capacity to indicate, while others do not.

But why is it that the relationship between the signifier and the signified exists only when there is a necessary connection of essential nature (*svabhāvapratibandha*), and not otherwise? To this he says: "Because for that which is not connected to it, there is no rule of non-deviation from it" (II-20). Regarding the phrase "for that which is not connected to it": [The commentary continues: For example, smoke is not connected by way of essential nature to the property of being produced by wet fuel; rather, its connection is through dependence on a cause. Since it is not connected by way of essential nature, it lacks the necessity of non-deviation from that [property]. Therefore, even if one perceives smoke, one cannot infer the presence of fire produced by wet fuel, because the inference would be subject to deviation. Furthermore, the property of being produced by wet fuel is not connected to smoke by way of essential nature; rather, its connection is through dependence on a cause. Since it is not connected by way of essential nature, it lacks the necessity of non-deviation from that [smoke]. Therefore, the relationship between the signifier and the signified exists only when there is a necessary connection of essential nature, and not otherwise. The word "that" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That which is not connected with that intrinsic nature is "unconnected with it" (*tadapratibaddha*).
For that which is not connected with something by way of its intrinsic nature, there is no rule of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra-niyama*) regarding that [unconnected thing].

The non-deviation of that [reason] whose object is not connected by way of essential nature (*svabhāva*) is "its non-deviation" (*tad-avyabhicāra*). The necessity of that is "the necessity of its non-deviation" (*tad-avyabhicāra-niyama*). Because of the absence of that [necessity], this is the meaning: for indeed, that which is not connected by way of essential nature to a certain object does not necessarily not deviate from that object which is not its point of connection; thus, there is no necessity of non-deviation between those two—the necessity of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-niyama*).
"Non-deviation" means by way of its own nature or essential form (*svarūpa*).
This is a sūtra belonging to the author of the Pāṇinian Bhāṣya: "The instrument is expressed by the past passive participle" (*sādhanaṃ kṛtā*, Pāṇini 2.1.33).

Therefore, having set aside the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* [Pāṇini 2.1.32], the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā* was formulated for the sake of establishing forms such as *galecopaka*. For those who follow the Vārttika-sūtras, however, the compound is to be understood through the analytical division (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *tṛtīyā* [Pāṇini 2.1.30]. And since both the nature of the effect (*kārya*) and its inherent essence (*svabhāva*) are subsumed by this instrumental compound alone, the earlier commentators have explained that the inclusion of both the effect and the essence is achieved through repetition (*āvṛtti*) by means of both genitive and locative compounds.
That was declared to be a false explanation.
He states the meaning of the word *samas* as "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature);
by this term *pratibandha*, he shows that what is meant is "being bound" (*pratibaddhatva*), that is, dependence (*āyattatva*).
He clarifies the meaning of this very point:

"Dependent" (*pratibaddha*) means that whatever is dependent upon something else by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), its own-being (*svabhāva*) is dependent upon that [other thing]; thus, because there is no difference in meaning, the sense is that it possesses a dependent nature (*pratibaddhasvabhāvatva*).
This is what has been made clear.

One might object: "By rejecting the compounds favored by previous authorities and demonstrating instead a compound with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), what exactly has been gained? You have merely displayed a desire for self-aggrandizement (*āhopuruṣikā*). Anticipating this doubt, he says "kāraṇe" (in the cause) in order to clarify what was already present in the mind; of what, then, is this [the cause]?
[DhPr p. 111]

And the relationship of indicator and indicated exists by necessity; for a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not accepted as the cause for the cognition of an imperceptible object merely through its capacity, like a lamp, but rather as something determined by its non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*).
Therefore, when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), there is the determination of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*).
From that follows the relationship between the signifier and the signified.

Therefore, it is established that when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one thing makes another thing known, and not otherwise. But surely, a connection belongs to that which is dependent on another, not to that which is independent?
Regarding this, he states which of the two—the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*)—is related to which, and where that relation lies:
"And that relation [belongs] to the mark (*liṅga*) with respect to the object to be proven" (II-21).
When the question arises as to what kind of relation this is, he says: "It is [the relation of] effect and essential nature," because those two alone are under discussion here.

"Unqualified" means common. "Inclusion" (*saṅgraha*)— that is, acceptance— of the excellence (*atiśaya*) in both the effect and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the sense that this alone constitutes excellence.
An object characterized as a means of proof (*sādhana*) is able to cause one to understand— that is, to make known— an object characterized as that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Since this is so, it follows that for others— namely, those distinct from them—
there is an absence of an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*).
And the absence of that [relation] is due to the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from it (*tadutpatti*),

as well as the absence of any other relation. The point is that if identity and origination from it were present, they would be included within the categories of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Having demonstrated the compound with "tad" and so forth, Dharmottara, by connecting it with "tadapratibaddhasya," has shown the reading "tadapratibaddhasya" in the root text.
Furthermore, the reading "tadapratibaddhasvabhāvasya" is frequently seen.

Even in that reading, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be made as follows: "that which has a nature (*svabhāva*), i.e., an essential form (*svarūpa*), not connected to that [probandum], meaning not connected to the probandum (*sādhya*)."

Invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is the state of being connected (*pratibaddhatva*), that is, dependence; its object is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), which is the impossibility of [the probans] existing without [the probandum]. Its necessity (*niyama*) is its inevitability (*avaśyantā*).

One might object: "Even if that [future event] is not invariably concomitant, does not the sunrise of today fail to deviate from its non-obstructed object, namely the sunset? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, this is the meaning. Since it has been stated thus, for that reason, this is the intended sense:
for even the sunrise will indeed occur.
And there was no sunset on that day, because it is possible for the sunset to be obstructed by the Great Sage or by some other person possessing great supernatural power (*mahardhi*).
Therefore, what must be proven is the very capacity of the sun for that sunset: "This rising of the sun is capable of being followed by a sunset, because it is a rising."
"Like the rising of tomorrow.
The sense is that, this being so, it follows that this [reason] is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
Now, is it not the case that the purpose is fulfilled by mere non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) alone?
To the question "Is that [the case] by necessity?", he says:
"Infallible" (*avyabhicāri*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis or to indicate a reason.
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies, "For not...
[45b]. The word "for" (hi) means "because.
A lamp serves as an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Rather, however, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is the subject under discussion, [the reason] must be ascertained as being invariably concomitant with that probandum.
For if there is no necessity (*niyama*), how can there be an ascertainment of non-deviation? This is the intended meaning [of the objection].
[The opponent replies: "Let that non-deviation be ascertained; let it be so for others as well."
But why is the invariable concomitance (pratibandha) sought? To this he says: "Therefore" (tataḥ).

Since the absence of deviation (avyabhicāra) must necessarily be ascertained, therefore—from that reason—it is shown by implication that otherwise the absence of deviation itself could not be ascertained.

To the question, "How does [the reason] possess the quality of being a prover even by this much? he says: "From that. Since the prover-status (*gamakatva*) of the mark (*liṅga*) is established through its ascertained non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), the status of the probandum (*sādhya*) as the proven (*gamya*) is also established; thus, both are presented.
Summarizing the stated point, he says: "Therefore."
The object is characterized by its mark; the object has its mark as its defining characteristic.
Therefore, in this investigation of the means of inference and the object of inference, or rather, in the investigation of the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*),
"that" refers to that essential connection of the logical mark (*liṅga*) with the object to be proven (*sādhya*).
The *liṅga* (logical mark) is "constrained" (*pratibaddha*) because it is dependent on another;
however, the object to be proven (*sādhya*)—being independent—is the object of the constraint (*pratibandhaviṣaya*), but it is not itself "constrained. This is the meaning.
In this regard, the point is as follows: even though there is no difference in their identity (*tādātmya*), that which is constrained is the indicator (*gamaka*).
That which is the object of a necessary connection (pratibandha) is what is to be understood (gamya).
And whatever is the fixed intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a given property is necessarily connected to that [property];
for example, the property called "being immediately subsequent to an effort" is connected to impermanence.
But for that [reason] which is both itself and another, and whose nature is the object of the connection (*pratibandha*), yet is not itself connected—
such as the property called "impermanence" with respect to the property called "arising immediately after effort."
