For the relationship between the signifier and the signified depends upon certainty;
and it is precisely the state of being produced immediately after an effort that is ascertained to be the very nature of impermanence.
Therefore, that [state] alone is necessarily connected to impermanence.
Therefore, the relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) exists only when the object is restricted, and not otherwise.

Now, if the relationship between the signifier and the signified pertains to two distinct things, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is connected [to the probandum] through "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), because it is dependent on another;
whereas the probandum (*sādhya*), being independent, is the object of the connection itself.
And the restriction of the relationship between the probandum and the probans would have that [inherence] as its basis.
However, in the case of two essential natures (svabhāva), the reason's dependence on identity (tādātmya) exists when that [probandum] is present;
and this identity is indistinguishable for both.

Consequently, it follows that being related, or being the object of a relation, applies equally to both; and thus, the specific relationship of probandum and probans (sādhyasādhanabhāva) based upon that [relation] would result. To this he says: "In this case, the meaning is as follows.
The word "api" implies that this is not only the case when there is a difference in meaning (arthāntaratva).
"That which is dependent" (pratibaddha) should be understood as that which is determined to be contingent upon [the probandum] by virtue of its being dependent on it.
Furthermore, the object of dependence must also be understood as determined in its true nature.

Now, since there is no difference in their identity (tādātmya), one might ask: "Why is this distinction made—that in that case, one is the object of dependence, while the other is not the dependent? To this he says: "Of which... (yasya).

Alternatively, for one who does not understand what is bound to which in a pair that experiences identity (*tādātmya*), such that one is the indicator (*gamaka*) and the other is the object indicated (*gamya*)—the subject being the scope of that bond—he says: "of which" (*yasya*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason; in the second sense, it serves as an emphasis.
Of whichever property (*dharma*)—which is conceptually constructed through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—there is a fixed, specific nature (*svabhāva*), that alone is its essence and nothing else.

The word "sa" (he) refers back to that which was expressed by the genitive case ending in "yasya" (of whom); the word "tat" (that) refers back to that which was expressed by the nominative case ending in "yaḥ" (who). The analysis of the compound is: "bound to that.
The word "is determined" (niścīyate) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Or [it is] obtainable from the context.
To the question "What, then, is such a thing?", he says: "Just as" (*yathā*).
Effort (*prayatna*) is the activity of a person; immediately after that is "without interval" (*avyavadhāna*).
In that context, [the word] *bhava* [is formed] with the suffix *yat* according to the rule for words beginning with *diś*;
then the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*).
The state of that is *tattva*.
That which has that as its designation is so called;
for indeed, the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that which follows immediately upon effort is impermanence itself, and not permanence.
Therefore, it is determined to be necessarily connected with impermanence.
He says "of whom" (yasya) to show what the fate of another would be compared to such a person as this:
"Of whom [there is] dharma," because the word "dharma" is understood from the previous context; the particle "tu" indicates a distinguished dharma.
And that [other thing]— namely, that which is called "immediately following effort" as well as that which does not follow immediately after effort, such as forest flowers and the like—
is the object, the domain, of the "obstructed," meaning that which is obstructed by the means of proof.
He confirms this very point by way of its contrapositive with the words "but not" (*na tu*).
The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "furthermore.
To the question "What is such [a person] like?", he says: "Just as... (*yathā*).
It should be understood that what is called "impermanence" is connected with what is called "immediacy following effort.

And thus, by implication, it remains established that [the connection exists] within the domain of the connection. Furthermore, this statement—that impermanence has an indefinite nature because its essence is non-existent—was spoken with reference to the generality of impermanence.
Otherwise, how could the impermanence residing in things such as a jar persist in the absence of its being immediately preceded by effort?
For it is by virtue of having that other nature (i.e., being produced by effort) that its non-occurrence elsewhere would be possible.
But why is there an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*)? He says:
"Because of identity and origination in reality" (II-22), beginning with the words "in reality" (*vastutas*).
That which has as its nature (ātman) the object to be proven (sādhya-artha) is "that-natured" (tadātman);
the state of being that is "identity" (tādātmya).
From that reason [it follows].
Since the means of proof (*sādhana*) has the nature of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), the meaning is that there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) between them.

If the means of proof were of the same nature as that which is to be proven, then—because of the non-difference between the probandum and the probans—the reason (*hetu*) would be merely a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*); therefore, he says "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*).
This means that their non-difference exists in terms of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattā*).
However, that superimposed form which is the object of conceptual construction—
relative to that, there is the distinction between the probandum and the probans;
for the relationship between the signified and the signifier depends precisely upon ascertainment.
Therefore, from the perspective of those whose forms are obstructed by conceptual determination (*niścaya*), a distinction between the two is logical; however, in reality, there is no difference.

It is not merely due to identity (*tādātmya*), but rather because the mark (*liṅga*) arises from that object which is the probandum (*sādhya*); and because of that origination, the mark has an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) with the object to be proven.
This might be so: identity certainly exists between the two.

Is the establishment of the relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) based on the ascertainment of being connected and being the object of that connection? To this he says: "by ascertainment" (*niścaya*).
The word "for" (*hi*) means "because.
Even when that [ascertainment] is required, why is it that only "being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is the signifier? To this he says: "effort," etc. (*prayatna...*).
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).

Since that [nature] is determined to be of such a nature, therefore it is said—this is the ellipsis—that it alone is connected to impermanence. Because, even though there is no difference in their identity (*tādātmya*), that which is ascertained by way of being connected is the indicator (*gamaka*), while the other is the indicated (*gamya*); therefore, the indicator is restricted to that which is necessarily concomitant with effort (*prayatnāntarīyaka*).
And impermanence is indeed to be understood; that relation of the signifier and the signified (gamya-gamaka-bhāva) which has such a nature as its object is "of that form.
He confirms this very point by way of exclusion, stating "not otherwise."
Now, surely that which is the dependence of one thing upon another—its being contingent upon that—is not without a cause.
With the intention of asking what that cause is, he poses the question: "Why?
And this is a question regarding the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
To explain the fundamental response "because of identity" (*tādātmyāt*), he says: "since" (*yataḥ*).

In that regard, the connection by way of essential nature (*svabhāvena pratibandhaḥ*) refers to the sign's (*liṅgasya*) state of being connected; this is the ellipsis. A proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Its meaning is the aggregate of the property and the property-bearer (*dharmidharmin*).
And since, in this case, the identity of the probandum and the probans is asserted, it follows that the reason would be identical to the object of the thesis, which is characterized as the probandum.
Consequently, just like the property to be proven, the property serving as the proof would also remain unestablished.
The sense is that if [the identity] were established, the reason would be redundant.

If, on the other hand, there is non-difference in the ultimate sense, how then can there be the relationship of the signifier and the signified based on difference? To this he says: "by conceptual construction" (vikalpa).
The word "tu" (but) expresses a difference [from the previous position] because of its non-difference from the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).
What is that object of conceptual construction (*vikalpaviṣaya*)?
If it were external, then the same fault would remain; thus he says: "That which... (*yad*).
Why does one depend on that? He says: "The essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) of the mark (*liṅga*) arises from two causes, and not from any other."
Because that which does not have that nature and that which does not arise from it lack an essential nature (svabhāva) that is necessarily connected to it.

Regarding the phrase "of that which does not have that nature" (*atatsvabhāvasya*): that which is its nature is "that-nature" (*tatsvabhāva*). [That which lacks this is "that-which-does-not-have-that-nature."]
That which does not have that nature is "not of that nature.
Therefore, because this [effect] arises from that [cause], it is "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*).
For that which does not have that nature and does not arise from that, [the relationship of cause and effect] does not hold.
In this context, "having an unobstructed nature" means that its own nature is unobstructed with respect to that which does not possess that nature and that which does not produce it;
the state of being such is "unobstructed-naturedness.
Therefore, it is because of this unobstructed-naturedness.

If something were to have a nature that is dependent [on another], even though it does not possess that other's nature and does not arise from it, then the dependence of nature (*svabhāvapratibandha*) could occur through some other cause;
for the dependence of nature is indeed the state of having a dependent nature.
Nor is there anything else whose nature is dependent [on another].
Therefore, the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) occurs only through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*); thus, it is dependent on those two.

The meaning is that "diversity" (*nānātva*) refers to the distinction between the means of proof and the object to be proven, in the form of "this is the means of proof" and "this is the object to be proven.

[An objection: Even if this distinction is indeed constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*), how can there still be the relationship of the indicator (*gamaka*) and the indicated (*gamya*)? To this, he says: "Because of certainty" (*niścaya*).
For (*hi*) means "because."
"Dependent upon certainty" means dependent upon that form which has been made the object of certainty;

since this is so, therefore, the distinction—the diversity—between those two, the probandum and the probans, is logical, that is, consistent with reasoning. It is "real" (vāstava) because it arises from the uncontrived nature of the thing itself.

It might be thought: "There is no identity between two things conceived as distinct that could serve as the basis for the relationship of the signified and the signifier; and since they are one in their real nature, there can be no relationship of signified and signifier. Thus, how can a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) possess the capacity to signify?
Yet, it is not the case that it lacks causality."

Since these two properties, having come within the range of perception, are perceived in such a way [as being identical], they are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), of that very nature; thus, there is no deviation of one property from the other.
What contradiction is there in saying that the indicator (*gamaka*) is that which possesses a real identity (*tadātmya*)?

This is the meaning of the context: the indicator and the indicated do not exist in a superimposed form established by conceptual determination (*niścaya*), because they are determined as being superimposed; rather, they exist as being determined as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

In that case, there is identity (tādātmya). This is what is meant: the form being superimposed, the particularity (svalakṣaṇa) which possesses the difference superimposed upon it, and the particularity which resembles that which has been superimposed.
That which is followed by a superimposed form is determined as distinct;
the relationship of signifier and signified (gamya-gamakabhāva) is based on that determined distinction, yet it has identity with it (tādātmya) in its own right.
Thus, he says "not from the mere [form]," in order to explain the second cause of the necessary connection (pratibandha).
And the word "ca" (and) conjoins the common cause.
But surely, an obstruction is not impossible even due to causes such as inherence (*samavāya*);

so why is it said that it occurs only through identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*)? With this intention, he asks: "Why? Since no other cause has been mentioned, he replies: "Because of these two causes."

The intention of the Master in stating "not having that as its intrinsic nature" (*atatsvabhāva*) and so forth is this: the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) would indeed arise from another relation only if another relation, such as inherence (*samavāya*), were not sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And yet, it is not the case that this [object] does not obstruct [the cognition];
for how could that which is non-existent serve as its cause?
He explains the meaning of the collective whole: "whatever has such-and-such an intrinsic nature..."
Regarding the phrase "because of having an unobstructed nature," he provides the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) by omitting the abstract suffix from the root: "unobstructed" (*apratibaddha*).
Its state (*bhāva*) is its essence (*tattva*);
the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "yadi" (if).
Why, then, does it not arise from any other cause? He says: "because it is dependent.
For ("hi") means "since."
He says "not" [in the verse] to show that the state of having a dependent nature will belong to one thing in relation to another.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis or as a reason.

Having understood from the context that this is because there is no other relationship—namely, the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—it has been stated that "there is no other [relationship] whatsoever whose nature is dependent."

But surely, even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causal origination (*tadutpatti*), one thing may be connected to another that is neither its own nature nor its product—just as, for example, sunlight is connected to the shadow of a tree;
or the bending down and rising up of the near side of a scale to the rising up and bending down of the far side;
or the near side [is connected] to the far side.
Taste [dissolved] into form;
the hand into the feet;
the water fell into the vessel.
The crane [indicates] water;
the swelling of a river [indicates] rain that has fallen above;
and the rising of the moon [indicates] both the increase of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lily.
The rising of the Kṛttikās [predicts rain] at the rising of Rohiṇī;
the swarming of ants and the agitation of fish [predict rain] during the rainy season;
and the clarity of water [predicts rain] at the rising of Agastya in autumn.
An excellent cloud and so forth [are required] for the act of raining; today’s rising of the sun [is required] for its setting and for its rising on the morrow;
and a *kuṣmāṇḍa* seed-pellet with a seed situated within it [is required].
The wandering mendicant [is afraid] of the staff;
the mongoose is terrified of the snake.
How much more could be illustrated?

This much, however, is said: that which is seen to be inseparably connected (avinābhūta) with something else is bound to it, and that [bound thing] is the mark (liṅga). For this very reason, the restriction of the number [of marks] to exactly three is also untenable.
One need only state the forms of the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself,
from the observation of which its status as a reason is established;
this is not a fault.
Among these, for those things that possess a causal connection (*pratibandha*), one of the two—identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from it (*tadutpatti*)—is possible;
whereas for those in which that [connection] is absent, there is no connection, and thus they lack the capacity to indicate [the object].
For instance, the connection between a tree and its shadow exists solely by virtue of their dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*).
Therefore, the cognition of that [shadow] arises solely from the effect as its logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*).
For shadow is indeed a real entity (*vastu*), possessing a manifested form and configuration and performing causal functions such as cooling;
it is not merely the absence of light.
And that [motion], following from the prior taking up of the swinging [rope], arises together with the moment of the tree immediately preceding it;

likewise, the bending down and upward movement of one side of the scale arise simultaneously with the rising up and downward movement of the opposite side, due solely to such human effort acting as a cooperative condition for that material cause.
Likewise, even though the near-side portion and the far-side portion are dissimilar, they are nonetheless dependent upon the same causal complex;
the hand, however, is not so restricted, since it can exist even when the object is unmanifested.
And in the case of non-deviation, the very basis is dependence upon a single connection;
and such [dependence] is precisely the effect of the container with respect to the water, and such is the crane with respect to the presence of water.
A river flood of that same kind [serves as an example] due to rain falling above;
and in every case, the subject (*dharmin*) should be understood as an aggregate of both visible and invisible factors, as appropriate.
Furthermore, another type of river flood can also be mentioned.

The river is the subject (*dharmin*). Its connection with a region that has received rain above is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). The mere fact of having such a flood is the logical reason (*hetu*).

In this way, even the rising of the moon, the swelling of the ocean, and the blooming of the night-lotuses are dependent upon a single causal complex; for these arise from that very same specific great element which is the object of the conventional designation "time," in dependence upon the arising of those [other phenomena].

Likewise, that very specific great element (mahābhūta) designated as "time" which is the cause of the rising of the Kṛttikās is itself the cause of the rising of Rohiṇī after an interval of some time; therefore, by observing that [effect], the property of being capable of producing it is indeed inferred from the cause.

Similarly, that which is the cause of the swarming of ants and the agitation of fish is itself capable of bringing about rain after an interval of some time; hence, as before, there is an inference of the causal property.
Alternatively, the inference of simultaneous rainfall may proceed through dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), just as in the case of color and taste;
in that case, however, the inferrer must be understood as being situated within an inner chamber or similar space where the external sound is inaudible.
Likewise, the clarity of the waters in autumn and so forth is indeed the effect of the rising of the star Agastya.
If, upon seeing the clarity of water, one infers that it will rise,
then that clarity of water arises from that very same great element designated as "time.
[DhPr p.116]

Granted that the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) exists only through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), how is it that only the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*) possess the capacity to prove [the probandum]? To this, he says:

"And those two—identity and origination from that—exist only in the case of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*); therefore, the establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) occurs through these two alone. (II-24) The word "those" (*te*) refers back to the preceding context. The particle *iti* here signifies "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since identity and origination from that are established only in the case of essential nature and effect, and since the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is based upon them, it follows that the affirmation of a real entity occurs only through these two: the effect and the essential nature.
[The word] "accomplishment" [is used].
Now, why is it that the accomplishment of a negation is not accepted even from the non-perception of the perceptible? To this he says:
"The accomplishment of a negation, as previously described, is indeed [derived] from non-apprehension alone. (II-25)
The establishment of the conventional usage of negation occurs precisely from that aforementioned non-perception of the perceptible; for this reason, it is not stated to come from anything else.
To the question, "Why then does it arise from that? he says:
because that [non-perception] is impossible when an object exists. II-26
Since the non-perception of the perceptible is not possible when that object to be negated exists, the negation is established from that impossibility.
And because that [rain] arises after an interval of some time, there is an inference of the property of the cause as before.
In the case of a cloud of such a kind, its incapacity for producing rain is to be inferred through the exclusion of absolute unfitness;
however, this is not so because of the possibility of deviation from future rain.
And since that [invariable concomitance] is inferred as being of the very nature [of the probans], identity (*tādātmya*) alone is the basis [for the inference].

However, in the case of the rising of the sun, because there is the possibility of an obstruction by something possessing superior power, such as clouds and the like, there is no invariable concomitance at all.
Otherwise, the seeing of a donkey today would likewise have the same relationship with its setting today and its rising tomorrow.

This, however, is logical: that "this [seed] will arise tomorrow, being fit for arising at dawn. And thus, the very basis for the identity between the arising and such fitness is simply their dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), as is the case even with a *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourd.
The wandering mendicant and the mongoose are indeed unimpeded by the staff and the snake,
because they can exist otherwise;
for how far can one possibly refute this?

This much is said: [the opponent argues that] if there were no identity (*tādātmya*) or causal origination (*tadutpatti*), and if something were to indicate another through a relation of restriction (*pratibandha*) based on its having that nature (*tādrūpyeṇa*), it would follow that everything would be restricted to everything and thus indicate everything.

Therefore, for the proponent of the prima facie view who asks how the capacity to indicate belongs only to effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*), the underlying intention is this: identity and causal origination will simply belong to other things, and from that, the capacity to indicate will follow.
And when both "effect" and "essential nature" are uttered, this is its meaning: that non-perception itself is included within these two.
When it is stated that [the object] is unperceived, from where does this prima facie objection arise?
This is true;
however, it is precisely because of that very non-perception [of the object]... [that this objection arises].
[DHPr p.
117] Now, he asks why it is for that very reason:

"Otherwise, because there is no certainty regarding non-existence due to the cessation of one's own perception with respect to objects remote in place, time, or nature, even though they meet the conditions for non-perception" (II-27).
"Otherwise" means that since this non-perception of the invisible is possible when the object actually exists;
for this reason, the establishment of negation does not result from any other kind of non-perception.
From what [source] is this known—that its occurrence is possible even when an object exists? To this he says: "among those things that have reached the conditions for non-perception," and so forth.
Here, an object is said to have reached the conditions for perception because of the completeness of other causal factors and because of a specific nature.
When either one of these two is absent, the object is said to have reached the conditions for non-perception.
In this context, the phrase "among those that have reached the conditions for non-perception" refers to those characterized by the deficiency of other causal factors;
the phrase "those remote in terms of place, time, and intrinsic nature" refers to those lacking specific characteristics of intrinsic nature.
The analysis of the compound is: "remote (viprakṛṣṭāḥ) by way of place, time, and intrinsic nature."
Because there is an absence of certainty regarding their non-existence;
for even when an object exists, its [certainty] is admitted to be present.

To the question "Why is there an absence of certainty?", he says: it is because of the cessation of that perception which belongs to the perceiver himself with respect to those [objects]; for that reason, there is an absence of certainty.
Since there is no certainty regarding non-existence when things have reached the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) due to the cessation of one's own perception,

therefore, even when an entity is present, it is possible for there to be a "non-apprehension of the invisible" (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*), characterized by the cessation of one's own perception. Consequently, the establishment of a negation occurs only through the aforementioned [type of] non-apprehension.
There is no fault in the engagement of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the intention that a negation is possible;

for by the word "negation" (pratiṣedha), conventional usage (vyavahāra) is intended, thus it is explained as "the conventional usage of negation. In the root text, however, the word "api" serves to include another thing to be proven (sādhya).
To the question "What is this as it has been stated?", he says "yeti" (which).

It clarifies that [the object] is established by the power of its own root; therefore, the connection with the subject at hand is: "Because there is no perception of that which is invisible from anything else, the establishment of negation has not been stated.

If [negation] does not arise from the non-perception of the invisible, then, intending to show that it should not occur even in the case of the intended [non-perception] since there is no difference in their being non-perceptions, he says "tatas tāvad" (firstly, from that).

Therefore, because of that impossibility, the phrase "from that" (tataḥ) is intended to mean "precisely from that non-perception of the perceptible"; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to state the proof of the negation of other things as well.
"Is it not the case that [the cognition] arises from that as well as from something else?
How, then, is the restriction 'from that alone' obtained?"—with this intention in mind, he says "atha" (now).
The word *atha* is used here in the sense of a question.
Explaining the subsequent phrase "and otherwise," he indicates the point of division right here;

and since the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because," the Master's intended meaning is that the non-perception of the imperceptible is of a different kind—that is, it possesses a different nature—from the manner of non-perception of the perceptible already described.
[DhPr p.118]
Now, at what time is this non-perception of the perceptible a means of valid cognition,
what is its nature, and what is its function? To this he says:

The cessation of the cognizer’s direct perception—whether past or present—of that which possesses unimpaired memory-impressions is the means for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence. (II-28) In this context, "cessation" refers to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). It is the instrument for accomplishing the conventional designation of non-existence.
The object, such as a jar, is perceptible to the cognizer;
its non-perception is its cessation, which is to say, it is of the nature of that [object's] absence.
For this very reason, absence is not something to be proven, because it is established through the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Furthermore, although a jar or the like is non-existent, when the ground—which is conjoined with that same cognition—is appearing and is known as possessing its complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is described as "perceptible" because its perceptibility is possible.
Therefore, the object being perceived and the cognition thereof are called the "cessation of perception.

For, from that perceived object and that cognition, the absence of the jar (or similar object) is determined, since its perceptibility was possible by virtue of its having a complete causal complex for observation.
Therefore, it is only when there is cognition of the object that the absence of the jar is said to be perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Here, "absence" does not consist in mere cessation, because from mere cessation alone there is no certainty regarding the cessation of the perceptible.
[49] *amūḍha* etc.; [omitted in H and N].

[50] And just as non-perception is said to be the location and the cognition thereof when the perception of the perceiver has ceased, so too he shows by means of the words "even though it is non-existent," etc.—
[51] *ca* is omitted in C; [52] *bhūtale* is omitted in AEP.
[53] Because it is being perceived, BDHN;
[54] because of its association with a single cognition—
showing this, [the author] says "satī" (being existent).
Because that [non-perception] is possible when the object exists;
however, regarding the root [text], the meaning is consistent only through the single syntactical unit "but otherwise, among those things that have reached the condition of being unperceivable.
This is not an explanation of the meaning of the word *na*.
Nor is there any effort made to present the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the explanation of the latter member [of the compound];
yet, since Dharmottara did not proceed in that manner, what can we do about it?
Having stated this in general terms with the words "Whence [is this]?", he establishes the specific point with the words "Even though... and so on.
This portion, ending with the word "vigrahe," is easy to understand:
because there is no certainty regarding non-existence with respect to those things that have reached the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*).

"Even though the object exists, its non-perception is accepted [as possible]. By this he means: we have no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here to prove that it occurs only when the object exists;
rather, it is said thus because, even when that [object] is present, the cognition wavers."
Now, seeking the limit of the absence of certainty, he asks: "From what [source]?

If it were impossible to ascertain [the absence of perception] from the mere cessation of another's perception, then the term "one's own perception" (*ātmapratyakṣa*) is included for the purpose of excluding that [other's perception].

If it is objected: "If this is a question regarding the ablative case (*apādāna*) and not a question regarding the cause (*hetu*), then how can he say that 'the absence of certainty is due to the cause of its cessation'? [The response is: No.
Because the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) has a different meaning [from "source"].
This "source" (*prakṛti*) is the cause from which the absence of certainty arises by means of a word or through reasoning;
for by the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.30], the intended meaning is that [the source] receives the technical designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*).
Otherwise, however, there would be an inconsistency.
He summarizes the meaning stated by the words "because" and so forth;
and this portion, ending with "the establishment of the negation," is easy to understand.

Since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is now established as a cause for inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*), its validity (*prāmāṇya*), specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), and function (*vyāpāra*)— though already mentioned— are set forth by means of the question beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, through the inclusion of specific times and persons.
The word "now" (*atha*) signifies a commencement, as before.
[DHPr p.
119] But is it not the case that the absence of the perceptible is determined through the non-perception of the perceptible?
This is indeed true.
When only that which is associated with a single cognition is being perceived, if a jar were present, it would necessarily be perceived; thus, its perceptibility is postulated.
Consequently, the non-perception of the perceptible is ascertained, and in this way, the absence of the perceptible is determined.
For if the object were present there, its non-perception would not occur;

therefore, by the ascertainment of the non-perception of the perceptible, the absence of the perceptible is determined through implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Since it has not yet been conventionally expressed, it must be expressed by means of the non-perception of the perceptible. Consequently, the object co-occurring with that single cognition and the cognition itself—both being perceived—are to be understood as "the cessation of perception," because they are the cause for the ascertainment of the cessation of perception.
[55] -anupalambha- CD; [56] *ca* omitted in E;
[57] *na tu vyava-* APHEN.
A jar or similar object is "perceptible" because it is to be delimited by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By the word "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), the Teacher intends non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); he shows this by stating, "its cessation is non-perception.

Furthermore, by the word "non-perception," what is intended is another object that is associated with the same cognition, as well as that cognition itself—defined through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the perception of the agent's, the object's, or the property's characteristics that were intended [to be perceived].

This very point is clarified by the phrase "having that non-existence as its intrinsic nature" (*tadabhāvasvabhāva*) up to the word "as far as" (*yāvat*). The meaning of the word "as far as" is this: whatever meaning has been expressed by the term "having that non-existence as its intrinsic nature"—namely, that the non-existence of the object to be negated, such as a jar, is a specific kind of existence whose very nature is that [non-existence]—that same meaning is also expressed by the term "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*). This is the sense of the word "as far as."

Since the non-apprehension of that [object] is simply the apprehension of something else, and that alone constitutes its absence—and nothing other than that—for this very reason, the absence of a jar or the like is not something to be proven.
Why is it not to be proven? Because it is established through the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-apprehension of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
To the question "Why is it not the probandum? he says: "Because it is established," that is, because the absence of the jar is ascertained, according to the context.
He thinks as follows: the object associated with that single cognition and that cognition itself constitute the non-perception of the jar and its absence;
and since that is established by sensory perception and self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the absence is not proved by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Now, one might ask: how can a pot or the like, which is non-existent, be perceived?
And if it is perceived, how can its non-apprehension be asserted? To this, he says: "Even though it is non-existent," and so forth.
The word "api" (also/even) indicates that not only that which exists is called "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a complete (*samagrā*) or total (*samastā*) causal complex (*sāmagrī*, i.e., a collection of causes).
The suffix *kap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.154: *śeṣād vibhāṣā*.
By the rule *na kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14), there is a prohibition against shortening [the vowel].

A thing being known—that is, being ascertained [such as a jar, etc.]—is [related] to that which is associated with a single cognition... it must be determined that this is due solely to the non-apprehension of that [object].
The cessation of perception is the non-apprehension of the jar and so forth.
But why is this pair described in such a way? He says: "For from that" (*tato hi*).
The word "for" (*hi*) means "because.
Because these two alone are the causes for determining the exclusion of the insubstantial forms of visible objects such as jars, for that reason [the pair is so described].
The object (*artha*) is another entity associated with the same cognition,
and the cognition belongs to that very [entity] itself.
He confirms this very point by way of negation (*vyatireka*) with the words "but not" (*na tu*).
"Merely ceasing" means merely the absence of perception.

To the question, "What fault is there if that is so? he says: "From mere cessation," because there is no certainty regarding the cessation of the visible object, and thus no certainty regarding the non-existence of the visible object.

Dharmottara’s intention is that mere cessation (*nivṛtti*), being of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), cannot be ascertained and therefore its status as a logical reason (*hetu*) is not tenable; this is because, as he says, "from mere cessation, there is no ascertainment of the absence of the perceptible.
However, the proponent of the prima facie view understands it thus: "This [opponent] denies [the reason's validity] on the basis of mere cessation, which is devoid of any qualification."
Thinking, "I shall thus demonstrate that [the absence] is merely the cessation of the object, qualified by its specific attributes," he says, "But surely...
(*nanu ca*). The cessation of the perceptible is the non-existence of the perceptible.

In the phrase "due to the non-perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalambhāt*), the word "non-perception" (*anupalambha*) is intended to mean the mere absence of perception; otherwise, the position of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) would be undermined.
By this, there is established merely the absence of apprehension, which is a non-affirming negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) characterized by qualifications;
and just as the perceptibility of a jar is superimposed upon a perception that is in contact with a single cognition even though the jar is non-existent, so it is here.

In that case, it should be understood that the various forms superimposed upon a jar— which is past, yet possesses unerring memory-impressions associated with a single cognition, and which is present— are non-existent. By this, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is stated to have the nature of the cessation of the perceived jar.
And that [non-perception] is established;
therefore, it has been stated that it is not the absence of the jar that is to be proven, but rather the conventional usage of "absence.
This applies to a jar in the past or the present, provided its memory-impression is not obscured.
[59] Its form— ABPHEN [60] and om.— by this, it is visible— ABPHE [61] not— om.— therefore, a jar— B.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) demonstrates that while there may be an indicative mark (liṅga), it is not a thing associated with the same cognition as the negation through the function of exclusion (paryudāsa), nor is it the cognition of that thing.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is true," and so forth.

However, when a surface or the like—which is in contact with a single cognition—is being perceived, that which is to be negated is that which is perceptible, possible, and [mentally] superimposed; this is understood from the context.

Therefore, due to the superimposition of perceptibility, the non-perception of the perceptible—that is, the absence of the cognition of the perceptible—becomes ascertained as a mere void-like form, which is simply a conventional designation.

"Let it be determined that the absence of perception [is established]; however, since the absence of the object of knowledge has not yet been determined, he says 'dṛśya' (perceptible) because the mere cessation [of cognition] will function for the sake of determining that [absence], due to the impossibility of anything else [being the cause] and by the power of determining the absence of the cognition of the perceptible;
the word 'ca' (and) is used in the sense of a reason."
The non-existence of the visible object of knowledge has as its sole nature that which is to be conventionally designated;
he demonstrates this with the words "if it is indeed capacity," and so forth.
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because."
"Non-perception of the perceptible" means the absence of the perception of the perceptible.
Therefore, from this ascertainment of the non-perception of the perceptible,
the absence of the perceptible object of knowledge is determined by implication.

It should be understood, however, that the ascertainment of the absence of the perception of the visible object occurs through the perception of another object that is conjoined within the same cognition.

Now, one might ask: "If the absence of the object of knowledge has already been ascertained, how then can it be established by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*)? To this he says: "it has not been [conventionally] treated.
The point is that because there remains a suspicion of the existence even of those things not seen, perception alone is unable to bring about conventional usage.
He asks, "By what, then, is it conventionally designated? and replies: "By the non-perception of the perceptible, which serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
... [This results in] the very conventional usage of existence ... and [the term] 'cognition'.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that these two stand on an equal footing.
And both [the absence of the object and the absence of the cognition] serve as the cause for determining cessation:

because it is impossible to ascertain that "there is no jar or the like" in this bare location without [the prior presence of] cognition; and likewise, because it is impossible to determine that "that cognition does not exist" without the object, since there is the direct perception of the bare location. This is how it should be understood.
Since the perception of a jar or the like is the cause for determining its absence, the "cessation of perception" [should be understood as stated].
Now, one might object: even though the object of negation, such as a jar, is non-existent, let it be so that it possesses perceptibility;
however, how can that which was not there at all possess the status of being "past"?

Anticipating the objection— "How can that which does not exist at all have presentness, and how can there be an operation of non-perception with respect to it?"— he says "yathā" (just as): "In whatever manner [one considers] a jar, if it were [present], it would necessarily be perceptible"— it is in this form [that the pervasion is established].
The word "ca" (and) refers to the cause;
that is, when [the object] has passed away while still associated with a single cognition, and its impressions for non-deluded recollection remain intact.
The second "ca" is used as a conjunction to include another point to be stated.
And [the word] "varttamāne" (in the present); the particle "ca" (and) serves to indicate a conjunction. Likewise, in that manner, if a jar had previously been situated there, if it were so—
It would have to be perceived;

yet it is not perceived. Thus, through the superimposition of the self onto the jar, the pastness and presentness of that [jar]—which are non-existent at that time—are superimposed upon it. This form of perception, established by such superimposition, demonstrates the aspect of the object as it is seen.
This is to be construed as: "it is to be seen" and "it is to be known.
That jar or other object in which there exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—which is unconfused, undiminished, produced by seeing, and whose nature is to generate memory—is described in that way.
The connection is that [this applies] to that past direct perception of the cognizer;
and the connection is that it also applies to the present direct perception of the cognizer.
However, the inclusion of the phrase "whose mental traces for memory are unimpaired" is not a qualification of the present [perception].

Because, when one perceives a location devoid of a jar in the past, there occurs a confusion regarding the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of memory, as well as a confusion regarding the non-perception of the visible jar and the visible jar itself.
However, when one perceives a location lacking a jar in the present, there is no confusion regarding the latent impression of memory;
for this very reason, there is neither confusion regarding the absence of the jar nor confusion regarding the non-perception of the jar.

Therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "having unimpaired memory-impressions" (*amūḍhasmṛtisaṃskāra*) is not a qualifier for the present object that is to be negated, because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the memory-impressions of a present thing.

For this very reason, the word "and" (*ca*) has been employed after "of the present" (*varttamānasya*), so that it may be understood as a conjunction of the present— though lacking a qualifier— with the past, which possesses a qualifier, as in the case of "the present jar" (*varttamāne ca ghaṭa*).

[63] For this very reason, there is no delusion (*moha*) regarding the non-perception of the jar, nor is there delusion regarding the jar itself. — ACDPHEN. For this very reason, there is no delusion regarding the non-perception of the jar, nor is there delusion regarding the jar itself. — B [64] The inclusion [of the word "non-perception"] is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity (*vyabhicāra*). — C. [65] Thus [the word] is omitted. — *vijñāyeta* (it should be understood). — *tad* (that). — B.
Thus, the meaning is this: the past non-perception, when clearly remembered, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as is the present [non-perception].
Therefore, it is possible to know: "There was no jar here, because it was not perceived" and "It does not exist, because it is not being perceived.
However, it is not possible to know: "A jar will not exist here, because it will not be perceived."
"Because there is no apprehension of what has not yet come into being, and because of doubt regarding its existence"—thus has the specific time of non-apprehension been explained.
[66] Clearly—BPHEN.
[67] Because it is not being apprehended—A.
[68] It can be known—C:

"Now, at what time is non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is its nature, and what is its function? To this threefold question, the Teacher has been asked; anticipating the doubt as to what has been explained by the Teacher in that regard, he says: "By this... (*anena*).
By this statement, "the cessation of the perceiver's direct perception," the word "ca" (and) functions as a restrictive particle [meaning] "only" with respect to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, it should be understood immediately following that [non-apprehension].

Since it is the cause for determining the cessation characterized by a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) of a directly perceived jar, the cessation of the directly perceived jar is the non-apprehension of the directly perceived jar.
By way of the exclusionary function (*paryudāsa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*):

that object which is associated with the same cognition as it, and that cognition itself—these two constitute the nature or form of the non-perception of the perceptible; she (non-perception) is thus described, the word "explained" being understood as the ellipsis.
Now, one might object: let the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the non-perception of the perceptible be of the nature of an exclusion.
He asks: "Why does the probandum (*sādhya*) not take the form of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*? He replies with the word "that" (*sā*).
The conjunction "ca" means "because.
The sense is that it is by this term—namely, "that such non-apprehension is the instigator of the conventional usage of absence"—that it was stated by the Teacher (*ācārya*).
And for this very reason, Dharmottara stated that "non-existence is not the probandum"; rather,

what is produced by the perception of a place devoid of a jar is an *āropita* (superimposed) *saṃskāra*, which is a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of a cognition endowed with a specific capacity, and not the so-called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) as asserted by the opponent.
One who is incapable of producing a corresponding recollection is designated as "deluded.
This occurs when there is non-perception of a visible jar— that is, in the absence of the perception of a visible jar, which is of the nature of a mere void—
and for that very reason, with respect to that visible jar.

To the question, "Why is the inclusion of 'unconfused memory-impression' (*amūḍhasmṛtisaṃskāra*) not a qualification of the present [object]? he says: "But in the case of the present" (*vartamāne tu*).
The particle *tu* expresses the difference of the present from the past.

Therefore, because there is an absence of confusion (*moha*), [the cognition does not arise] with respect to the non-existence of a jar, which is of a single nature as that which is to be designated in linguistic usage (*vyavahartavya*).
Nor [is it] in the non-perception of a jar— that is, in the absence of the perception of a jar, which is of the nature of a mere void—
[can there be such a cognition], because, like direct perception, it would involve a superimposition of a presently existing object such as a jar;
for this very reason, because the apprehension of the present is itself without qualification.

He demonstrates the operation [of non-existence]: the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding non-existence consists of a cognition of the form "it does not exist" and a verbal expression of that same form; furthermore, physical activity characterized by moving about and coming and going without hesitation constitutes the bodily convention regarding non-existence.
For when the absence of a jar is known, one proceeds to go or come without hesitation;
this is characterized by going and coming without hesitation.

Thus, for these three kinds of conventional discourse regarding non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*), the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the means of establishment, the proof, and the instigator.
Thus, for this—CD; thus, for this, etasya.
That very thing belongs to that—[B. 71] even to the linguistic convention of non-existence—[C.
72] [it is that which causes it to proceed; om. ABCDPHEN].

And although the cognition "the jar does not exist" arises from non-apprehension alone, and this itself is the ascertainment of absence, nevertheless, because the bare location has been apprehended by perception, the ascertainment of absence follows the operation of perception in the form "there is no jar here. Therefore, the ascertainment of absence— which follows the operation of perception consisting in the grasping of the bare location— is produced by perception.
[73] And "om" is omitted in C.

Now, one might object: "Just as non-apprehension of the past, when made an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is said to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is it that future non-apprehension, being likewise conceptualized, is not similarly a means of valid cognition, given that the range of conceptual construction is unimpeded? To this, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.

Because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the perception of the bare location is grasped without confusion regarding the past jar and so forth, and because confusion cannot possibly arise regarding that same [jar] when it is present while the impression for recollection exists—this is the intended meaning.

Since the bare location and so forth are the cause for the certainty of non-perception, the non-perception is evident; thus, being made an object by way of recollecting it exactly as it was experienced as bare, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And it should be understood that such a present non-perception is clearly apprehended by non-erroneous cognition;
"from this" means from the fact that such a non-perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "Why can it not be known? he says: "of the future [non-perception]."

The intention is that a reason (*hetu*) which is ascertained as being such-and-such is indeed a prover; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) known as "doubtful unestablishedness" (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*).

By the term "cessation of perception," the nature of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) has been shown. But what is shown by the words beginning with "not deluded" (*amūḍha*)? He says: "time. Thus, a specific time is explained as the [condition] for non-perception. [The other meaning is: "in this way, a specific time is not explained as [the condition] for non-perception."
The specific division of time— past and present— has been explained and stated by him;

the remainder [of the sentence] is that this is an illustration of the designation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) in the past and present times,
since those two [other types of reasons], namely the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), are also valid means of cognition in those two times.
For instance: "There was fire here, because smoke was perceived";
"Fire exists here, because smoke is being perceived"; and "There was a tree here, because a *śiṃśapā* was perceived."
The inference "there is a tree here because a *śiṃśapā* is perceived" is indeed possible as well.

[Objection: Granted that there may be a conventional usage characterized by cognition and verbal expression regarding the non-perception of what is perceptible; but how can there be a physical [action]? To this he says: "a jar," etc.
For this reason—
"it proceeds"— is stated by way of fitness;
that is to say, it first becomes fit for activity.
For this very reason, the fitness for non-existence is stated as the probandum (*sādhya*).
This is a common worldly expression meaning "this belongs to that.
The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound should be understood as "this and that" (*tac ca etac ca*).
Alternatively, "yad vā" means "since," [referring to] that from which the ascertainment of non-existence is caused by non-perception; "tasmāt" means "therefore.
The word "api" is used in the sense of emphasis.
Let it be [understood] as applying to either one or both.
The meaning is: "as far as the operation of the threefold [nature].

Regarding this term *pravartanī* (the operative), there are these two explanations for the sake of clarity: it is called *sādhanī* (the accomplisher) and *pravartikā* (the activator). It is called *pravartanī* (the operative) because it acts [to bring about] by way of its fitness (*yogyatā*).
It is fit to operate the conventional usage of non-existence regarding the three natures, because that [usage] has only that much as its cause.
Whether or not a person engages in those linguistic conventions when there is a need for them, the ultimate point is this:
it is precisely for this reason that the suitability of a location and so forth for the convention of non-existence is established by the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
[DhPr p.123]

Furthermore, by the very capacity to establish the certainty of the non-perception of what is perceptible, non-existence is indeed determined through perception itself according to the principle previously stated.
However, because it is possible for even unperceived things to exist, one cannot employ the conventional expression "it does not exist" due to the suspicion that it might still exist.
Therefore, non-perception brings about the conventional usage of non-existence; since there is no perception of what is perceptible, it follows that "it does not exist."

Therefore, the non-perception of the perceptible causes the cognition of absence to proceed, but does not produce what has not already been produced. Thus, although the ascertainment of absence proceeds from non-perception, it is said to be "produced by perception" and "set in motion by non-perception. Consequently, non-perception is that which sets in motion the conventional usage regarding absence.
But why is it that non-apprehension in the past and the present is a means of cognition? He says:
[74] It is able to establish non-existence—C [75] ['existence' om. — A]
[76] Thus, *om*. — C.
[77] Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is that which operates in the conventional discourse regarding non-existence (*abhāva*). — C; apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is that which operates — A.
"Non-apprehension that operates"—PH; "non-apprehension that operates"—B.
Because there is a certainty of its very absence (II-29).
That is, because there is a certainty of the absence of that very non-apprehension as described with respect to time.
For non-apprehension in the future is itself of a doubtful nature;
since it is unestablished, there can be no certainty regarding non-existence, but rather [certainty] pertains to that which is past or present.

Now, one might object: "If the cognition in the form 'it does not exist' arises from non-apprehension as its logical mark (*liṅga*), then how is it said that absence is determined by perception? To this he replies: the phrase *yady api* is a collection of particles that, like the word *yady api*, functions to express an acceptance of a specific qualification;
because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "ascertainment of absence," it is designated as being precisely this [perception].
The word "ca" (and) here functions in the sense of "this must be stated.
It should be understood that this is said because the certainty of non-existence at that time attains stability precisely through non-perception (*anupalambha*).
Furthermore, the phrase "even so" (*tathāpi*) is a common worldly expression used at the commencement of a formal statement.
Therefore, since the word "because" (yasmāt) implies the word "therefore" (tasmāt), the meaning is as follows:

because the determination of non-existence—that "the jar does not exist"—follows from the operation characterized by the apprehension of the bare location alone, it is therefore said to be produced by perception; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
When the question arises as to whose operation this follows, it is stated: "of perception, which is a specific means of valid cognition.
Now, one might object: "If this [non-apprehension] is produced by perception, then it too must be set in motion by perception.
Why, then, is it performed by the non-apprehension of the perceptible? Anticipating this doubt, he says "moreover" (*kiñca*), in order to add another point to be stated.
The absence—the negation consisting of a non-presumptive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—is ascertained by that very perception which apprehends the isolated location and so forth.

How so? Because the non-perception of the perceptible is the absence of perception, which is of the nature of a void; this is due to its capacity to bring about that ascertainment, for it could not otherwise be accounted for.
According to the principle and reasoning stated previously, if indeed the perceptible were present there, [it would be perceived].

If perception, having the nature of the thought "the non-perception of the perceptible would not occur," determines in this way the absence of the object to be negated, it is certainly able to cause [one] to engage in conventional usage as well; thus he says: "only, however, it is not able to cause [one] to engage in usage. Because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is inherent in the expression, the sense is "to cause [one] to engage in usage."

To the question "Why is it not possible? he says: "By the suspicion of existence" (*sattva-śaṅkayā*), meaning by the cause which is the doubt regarding the existence of the very nature of that which is to be negated. [Objection: But even in the absence of perception, how can there be doubt? To this he says: "Unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). Because there is the possibility—that is, the conceivability—of the existence (*sadbhāva*) of even things like *piśācas* which are not perceived by that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed characterized by a constant deviation from non-perception due to such suspicion.
Such is the meaning.
Therefore, since perception is incapable in that regard, he asks how even that [conceptual cognition] brings about worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and says: "the visible" (*dṛśye*).
For this reason—by virtue of the context—it is established by means of perception.

He confirms this very point by way of negation with the words "but not" (*na tu*). Since the determination of non-existence follows the operation of perception, therefore [it is] the determination of non-existence.
[DhPr p.124] Now, in order to show the different varieties of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says:
"And that [non-apprehension] is of eleven types due to the difference in its formal application" (II-30).
And this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is of eleven types—that is, it has eleven modes—hence it is called "of eleven types. From what source does the distinction between these modes arise?
From the distinction in their formal application (*prayoga*).
Application (*prayoga*) or employment (*prayukti*) is said to be the denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) of a word.
For a word directly denotes either a certain positive entity in some cases, or it denotes a negation of another entity in others.

However, in all cases, the non-perception of the perceptible is understood even when not explicitly stated; thus, the distinction between types of non-perception arises from the difference in the function of the expressive word, but not from a difference in its essential nature—this is the meaning.
[78] This [cognition] is of eleven types— APE.
[79] He states the distinctions among the types of denotation— ABCDPHEN.

Non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is as follows: "There is no smoke here, because of the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension" (II-31).

Although [the absence] proceeds from non-perception and is even strengthened by perception—which, by its very capacity, cognizes the bare location and so forth—it is produced, brought about, established, and set in motion by the non-apprehension of the perceptible; this is what was stated by the Master regarding the procedure for the linguistic usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).
"By this word" refers to what is present in the mind.
The conclusion is made with the words "thus," and so forth.
"Thus" means by the sequence already stated; "non-perception" refers to the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), because that alone is the subject under discussion.
The passage beginning with "Why? and ending with "of the present" is easy to understand.
To the question, "Why does the determination of non-existence not also occur for the future because of its non-perception?", he says: "Because of the future," etc.
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because."
The word *tasyāḥ* here ends in the ablative case.

This very meaning, established by the force of the context, is the primary sense [of the term], which Dharmottara has stated earlier in his *Dharmottara-ṭīkā* with the words "for the future... and so forth, for the purpose of quelling doubt.
It might be argued: [the passage] beginning with "the establishment of negation" (*pratiṣedhasiddhiḥ*) and ending with "due to the absence of certainty" (*niścayābhāvāt*).

"Since this meaning has already been established by the [previous] text, and because there is certainty regarding its very non-existence, this passage by the Teacher (ācāryīya) is redundant. [Response:
It is not redundant.

Since, just as in the past time the determination of the non-existence of a jar or the like occurred through the recollection of a past non-perception of that which was perceptible at that time, why should the determination of the non-existence of a jar or the like not likewise occur in future time? By whom has this been refuted, such that it would be redundant to state it again?
Now, the distinction—that is, the manifoldness—of the types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and their essential natures (*svarūpa*)... the various types of non-apprehension... should be observed.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate other points to be stated.
"That" (*sā*) is a restatement of the root term.
The word "this" (*eṣā*) is its explanation.

The mention of "eleven" by the Teacher is for the sake of illustration, just as the mention [of a specific number] occurs in the *Pramāṇavārttika*...; however, it should be understood as "sixteen spokes.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate this later in another explanation of the perception of an effect that is incompatible with the cause.

Intending to ask how this distinction can be established—given that non-perception of the perceptible has the single nature of being the perception of something else intended to be expressed—he asks: "From what?
[DhPr p. 125]
"Of its own nature," and so forth.
"The non-perception of that which is the nature of the object to be negated, as follows.
Here, "here" refers to the locus (*dharmin*).
"Smoke does not exist" is the thesis;
"because of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility" is the reason;
and this reason is to be explained as before.

The non-perception of the effect of that which is to be negated is illustrated as the "non-perception of the effect" (*kāryānupalabdhi*), as follows: "There are no causes of smoke here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of the absence of smoke. (II-32)
[80] Thus, *om*. — *BPHEN*.
Regarding the word "yathā" (as): here, "iha" (here) refers to the subject (*dharmin*).

The probandum is that those things which possess an unimpeded and unimpaired capacity for producing smoke do not exist; that is, they are "those whose capacity is unimpeded" (*apratibaddhasāmarthyāni*), and it is their non-existence that is to be proven.
"Because of the absence of smoke" is the reason (*hetu*).
Having cited the Teacher’s reply, "Because of the difference in formulation" (*prayogabheda*), he explains the word "formulation" (*prayoga*) by saying "formulation" (*prayoga*).
He states "word" (*śabda*) for the sake of explaining its application (*prayukti*).
By the word "sound" (*śabda*), the expressive sound is understood due to the context.
"Denotation" (*abhidhā*) is the manifestation of the meaning.

In this regard, "activity" (*vyāpāra*) means engagement or operation; alternatively, denotation is the manifestation of the meaning, and the activity is that which has that as its characteristic. This is because it is distinguished by the difference in the application of that [denotation], which is easy to understand.

Dharmottara did not provide an explanation [for this]. Now, one might object: "Since the non-perception itself is the denotatum of the word 'non-perception' which expresses it, how can there be a difference in formulation such that a distinction between types of non-perception is stated? To this he says: "For the word... (*śabdo hi*).
The particle *hi* means "because."
"Directly" means without mediation.
In some cases, such as the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalambha*), it expresses a different object—such as fire—in place of the object to be negated, such as a cold touch.

In other cases, such as the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), it expresses another negation—such as the negation of "tree"—in place of the intended negation, such as the negation of "śiṃśapā."

If both the affirmation of another object and the negation of another object are being performed, then [the objection] is raised: "In all cases... The word *tu* (but) serves to indicate a distinction.
"Not conveyed by words" (*aśabdopāttā*) means not conveyed by the words that express its own [meaning].
And how that [meaning], although not directly expressed by the words, is nevertheless understood, will be explained further on.
The particle *api* is used here either for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or to indicate excellence (*atiśaya*).

The word *iti* signifies "therefore" (*tasmāt*) or "thus" (*evam*). Therefore, it should be understood that the author has spoken by resorting to an implied understanding (*gati*), and not to a literal verbal expression (*śābdī*).
Since non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is the subject under discussion, it should be understood that [the term] refers to its various types.
Its non-apprehension is to be determined—according to the principle previously stated—as the location devoid of that object and the cognition thereof.
Thus, in cases such as the non-apprehension of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), non-apprehension possesses two forms, as indicated by the illustration.
Now, what is this "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*)?
And how can that which is non-existent... and this [be perceived]?
This is like the previous explanation regarding the definition of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
The word *ca* (and) should be understood as having the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*) or "in order to restrict" (*avadhāraṇārtha*), and it is to be seen immediately after the word *pūrvavat*.

Furthermore, this has been provided by the Master as an exposition of the meaning of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), but he did not demonstrate the formal logical argument (*prayoga*).

This is because he employed a thesis (*pratijñā*) which is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), failed to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which is a member of the proof, and did not state the reason (*hetu*) in its form as something to be restated (*anuvādya*), ending in the nominative case.

In this same way, it should be understood regarding all other non-apprehensions (*anupalabdhi*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever, being present and meeting the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is not apprehended there, all that is fit for the conventional designation of "non-existent" (*asadvyavahārayogya*) in that place—just as, for example, smoke which meets the conditions for apprehension is not apprehended on the head of a horse.

By this, it should be understood that the Master has shown that the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is to be employed in the refutation of universals and the like, because the same logic applies. Furthermore, since causes do not necessarily possess their effects, it is only the absence of those whose capacities are unimpeded that is to be proven by the non-observation of the effect, and not that of others.
And those whose power is unimpeded are only those occurring at the final moment,
because for others, the possibility of obstruction exists.
This is what is being established.
And the non-perception of the effect is employed where the cause is invisible;

however, when the cause is visible, it is only the non-perception of the visible that serves as the means of cognition. In this regard, one standing atop a white house may not see the courtyard itself, yet sees the four sides of the courtyard up to the walls.
And one perceives the space designated as "light" to be level with the edge of the wall and devoid of smoke;
this is because there is a certainty regarding the absence of smoke there.
For smoke, being produced by fire located in a particular place, would necessarily occupy that same place.
And the absence of that fire, whose capacity is unimpeded, must be understood.
Furthermore, the smoke produced by the fire located in the courtyard of that house would occupy that same location;
therefore, the absence of fire at that location must be understood.

He takes as the subject (*dharmin*) that portion of the courtyard of the house enclosed by walls, together with the space of the sky—which consists of light and is devoid of smoke—and which is itself enclosed by the perimeter of the walls. Here, the non-perception of the white [object] and the mere location, etc., constitute the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*); and the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahārayogyatā*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). For the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), the basis for the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamakabhāva*) is precisely the bond characterized by identity (*tādātmyalakṣaṇa*).
Such is the opinion of some.

However, others have maintained that when non-perception (*anupalambha*) and the fitness for the conventional usage of absence (*abhāvavyavahārayogyatā*) stand in the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*), the basis (*nimitta*) is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by either contrariety (*viparyaya*) or identity (*tādātmya*).
For this very reason, non-perception is specified as distinct from the [other two types of evidence], namely effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
This is because [the first reason] does not depend on a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum, whereas the other two are the opposite of that;
and thus they explain it in this manner.
For it is thus: because perception is non-deviant, the existence of such [an object] consists in nothing other than its non-perception.

Therefore, since there is an identity (*tādātmya*) between the existence of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility and its perception, there exists the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between non-perception and the conventional designation of non-existence.

However, if one were to claim that the cause is the identity between the non-perception—which is of the nature of perceiving a location devoid of that object—and the fitness for the conventional designation of its non-existence, [then...]

At that time, since the very nature of the ground and so forth consists in their fitness for the conventional treatment of non-existence as characterized by non-apprehension, non-apprehension would also establish the conventional treatment of the absence of ghosts and the like, due to the necessary connection between them.
[Objection: "Surely, let the absence of the cause be established from the absence of the effect;

what is the purpose of the qualification of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) as 'having unimpeded capacity'? To this he says, "The causes," where the word "ca" (and/because) means "for the following reason."
Therefore,
the meaning is that what is to be proven (sādhya) is fit to be proven.
He confirms this very point by way of its contrapositive with the words "but not" (na tu).
The particle "eva" (only) has the sense of exclusion (*vaidharmya*) or restriction;
it does not apply to other things which, by virtue of being the cause of a cause, possess a metaphorical "active form" (*kurvad-rūpa*).
Now, even if the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is complete, an obstruction might be suspected because of the possibility of a counteracting force (*vidhāraka*).
This is impossible;

therefore, the locus (*dharmin*)— consisting of parts of the spatial location that are both visible and invisible, and thus a collection of both perceptible and imperceptible elements— is established by the force of the cognition of the absence of fire.
It is not only that which is currently being perceived;
rather, the demonstrative "here" (*iha*) as a direct perceptual reference depends upon the state of being perceived.
It is not only in this case that the subject (*dharmin*) consists of a collection of both the perceived and the unperceived.
Moreover, this applies elsewhere as well:
when the momentariness of sound is to be proven, one particular sound may be perceptible while another is imperceptible; likewise here too.

And just as in this case the subject (*dharmin*)—which serves as the locus for the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*)—is shown to have both visible and invisible parts, so it should be understood for oneself in all subsequent applications as well.
[83] Like the visible space—CA. [84] He states that it is a qualifier; and the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "tu" (but), or it signifies a reason.

To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Of others. Furthermore, even by a yogi, causes that have reached their final moment cannot be obstructed; otherwise, their very nature as such would be lost.
Therefore, such causes, which do not deviate from their effects, are pervaded by the effect;
consequently, it should be understood that when the effect is absent, those kinds of causes are also excluded.

In this context, although it is not cognized by means of this final moment that "this effect has been produced," nevertheless, a certain state of the entity while producing the effect is indeed perceived, immediately after which the effect is apprehended.
