And that very state is what is being negated here;
for this reason, this is a negation of an excellence of state that is common to both momentary and non-momentary things.
[Objection: But surely, in this case, the reason to be employed must be the non-perception of the effect, provided that it is perceptible.

Raising the objection, "How could this be possible—that only the effect is visible and not the cause, such that the non-perception of the effect is employed? [the author] speaks in order to demonstrate its scope, saying "The effect...
He asks, "What kind of scope is this? and answers, "In that case," introducing the statement.

Furthermore, with the intention that if one were to see the courtyard of the house, only the non-perception of the perceptible would have been employed, he says, "even without seeing the courtyard of the house."
The word *api* is used here as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). "The edge of the courtyard wall" (*aṅgaṇabhitteḥ paryantam*) means the limit or end;
it is "equal to," that is, identical with, the edge of the wall.
For the Sautrāntikas, space has the very nature of light and darkness;
it is described as being "designated by the term 'light'" because they consider it to consist of that.
Regarding what is to be understood here in the case of space, he says: "yaddeśa" (in whatever place).
When the reading is "yadā yaddeśe ca," then the analysis of the compound is "yo deśo 'sya" (that which is its place).
But when it is "yaddeśasthena," then the analysis is "yaś cāsau deśaś ca tatra tiṣṭhati" (that which is both this place and where it stands), thus [forming] "taddeśastha."
The analysis of the compound is "that place belongs to him.
Even with this much, it is not known which locus (*dharmin*) has been made [the subject] by that cognizer; therefore, he says "tadgṛhe" (in that house).
This is a compound meaning "that which is both it and the place of the courtyard of the house."
Since the courtyard is the subject under discussion, the connection is that the wall makes that very [courtyard] its delimited substrate (*dharmī*) by surrounding it.
To the question "Is it only this much?", he says: "the wall.
[This means] the wall belongs to the courtyard itself.
The edge of the wall must be stated; its limit, end, or conclusion—by that [edge] it is encompassed or delimited.
The particle *ca* serves to conjoin [the term] with equal force.
With the words "Therefore," etc., he shows the subject (*dharmin*) established by worldly consensus under the guise of a conclusion.
The aggregate of the visible and the invisible is perceived by the world as a single unity.
Of what nature is that much of a space which is being seen,
and of which it is a part— a constituent portion?
The non-perception of that property which is the pervader of the negated (pratiṣedha) pervaded is cited as an example:
"it is thus. To the question "How is the subject (dharmin) of this kind? he says: "due to the absence of fire," and so forth.
"Fire" refers to a specific fire whose power to produce smoke is unimpeded.
Since this too is merely an illustration, one must understand that the non-existence of any other [fire] that is not obstructed in producing smoke is what is being cognized.
The meaning is this: when people do not perceive smoke in such a place, they cognize the absence of such a fire in that location.

And since this [reason] does not occur without such a subject (*dharmin*), its capacity—namely, the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*)—necessarily follows and is present. For this very reason, when the Teacher [Dignāga] stated: "Even in the case of a contradictory effect, there is dependence on place, time, and so forth" (PV I 6 = 8), his intention was that the subject must indeed be intended.

Now, one might object: "If even that which is not perceptible can be the locus (*dharmin*), how is it that the word 'here' (*iha*) is used here? Anticipating this objection—that there must be a reference to another cognition of "here"—he says: "here" (*iha*). The particle *tu* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
The word *iti* here refers back to the form of the term *nirdiṣṭa* (indicated) that has been mentioned. A "demonstration" (*nirdeśa*) is said to be that which establishes a perceptible object.

Now, one might ask: if a subject (*dharmin*) consisting of a collection of both visible and invisible [factors] is tenable, then why would this not also be possible for the effects-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*)? To this he says: "Not only... (*na kevalam*).

It is precisely here that the non-perception of the effect [is established]; however, it is not only in this case, but also elsewhere—in regard to specific effects and specific intrinsic natures—where the probans consisting of an effect (*kāryahetu*) is unestablished, such as in the case of smoke, speech, fire, or human authorship, a subject (*dharmin*) of that kind is quite evident.
Therefore, it was not demonstrated there, because of its similarity [to the present case].
Or rather, it should be viewed as follows:
how is such a subject (dharmin) possible even in the case of a reason? To this he says: "of sound.
One [sound] is being heard and is thus perceptible, while another is not being heard and is thus imperceptible.
By this, it is necessarily shown that here the subject (*dharmin*) is the collection of words consisting of both the perceptible and the imperceptible;
and that the subject must consist of the word in its nature as both perceptible and imperceptible follows from the doubt and the [erroneous] attribution of the person to be instructed.
For the person to be instructed, being in doubt regarding the impermanence of the word, does not fall into error.
That is to say, it is the word "jar" itself,
while being heard,
that one doubts or misapprehends.
However, when words such as "pot" or "cloth" are being heard— whether already heard or yet to be heard—

it follows from that very fact that, in order to conform to them, the collection of both perceptible and imperceptible sounds necessarily falls as the subject (*dharmin*) when impermanence is to be proven.

Likewise here, too, when the effect is not perceived, he says "And just as... in order to extend this very same principle to other cases as well. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis; by means of the qualification "that which serves as the locus for the apprehension of the probandum," the definition of the subject (*dharmin*) has been stated under the guise of that very attribute.

The formal application (*prayoga*) of the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) should be formulated as follows: Wherever the effect of something is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception, that [cause] does not exist with its capacity unimpeded in producing it; just as, for example, when a visible sprout is present, there is no such seed.
"And here, smoke meeting the conditions for perception is not perceived.

By this demonstration of the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalambha*), that which was prattled by Jalpamahodadhi is refuted: namely, when the absence of sound in general is to be proven in a silent place, what is that "perception of another object associated with the same cognition" (*tadekajñānasaṃsargivastvantaropalambha*) by means of which the linguistic convention of the absence of sound is established?
That which might be the case for the Buddhists should be regarded as already refuted;
for in this case, there are no causes for auditory cognition whose capacity is unimpeded. Thus, because of the absence of auditory cognition, the non-perception of the effect is indeed clear.
Furthermore, the non-apprehension of auditory cognition exists as a matter of fact in the form of the apprehension of other cognitions;
and it has been stated previously that "co-occurrence in a single cognition" means the state of being invariably concomitant with one another's apprehension.
The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is to be understood as in the immediately preceding case, namely, by virtue of being a cognition.
[The non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is as follows: "There is no *śiṃśapā* here, because of the absence of trees.
Regarding the word "as follows" (*yathā*): "here" (*atra*) refers to the subject (*dharmin*).
The non-existence of a *śiṃśapā* tree is not what is to be proven;
rather, the reason is "because of the absence of the pervader, which is 'tree'.
This non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is also employed when there is an absence of the pervaded—namely, the state of being a *śiṃśapā*—which is itself unobservable.
However, when the conditions for perception are met, the non-perception of what is visible serves as the means of cognition by pervading [the area].
In that case, suppose there are two adjacent regions:
one is filled with a dense thicket of trees, while the other consists of a single stone slab and is devoid of trees.
Even for one who sees those trees but does not discern the distinction between them, such as *śiṃśapā* and so forth,
"treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is perceptible, whereas "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapatva*) is imperceptible.
For he determines the absence of a tree on a single rock where no trees grow by means of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), since it would have been visible [if present].
The absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness, however, [is established] because of the absence of its pervader, *vṛkṣa*-ness (*tree-ness*).
Such is the application of this [type of inference] for proving non-existence in a given object.
An example of the perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) is: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire. (II-34)
An example of the perception of that which is contradictory by its very nature to the negation is given as "for instance.
Here, "here" refers to the subject (*dharmin*).
"There is no cold touch" is the negation of cold touch, which is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Of fire" is the reason (*hetu*).
And this non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is to be employed where cold touch is perceptible,
because the application of the non-perception of the perceptible is restricted to what is perceptible.
In order to explain the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), he says: "of the object to be negated" (*pratiṣedhyasya*).

Although there is no difference in their being identical in nature (*tādātmya*), it has already been determined by Dharmottara that only a certain subject (*dharmin*) is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) while the other is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
And the term "property" (*dharma*)—such as "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and so forth—is used in relation to the subject (*dharmin*).

"It is not a *śiṃśapā*" means "it does not possess the nature of being a *śiṃśapā*. Furthermore, by the phrase "of the tree," there is a reference to the property (*dharma*), namely "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*), by means of the substratum (*dharmin*).
Now, one might object: first of all, the non-perception of "tree-ness"—which has reached the conditions for perceptibility—must be employed [as the reason].

And likewise, since even the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is to be negated as something perceptible, it is only the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) that is fit for formal application; thus he says, "this too.
The word "too" (*api*) implies that it is not only the former [type of non-perception] in a specific object, but this one as well.

Regarding the phrase "of the state of being a *śiṃśapā* which is imperceptible": the meaning is that it refers to that which has transcended the possibility [of perception], such that if it were present, it would necessarily be perceptible.

In the same way, even further on, "invisibility" (adṛśyatva) should be understood as being of this very same nature. The word "in its absence" (tasyābhāve) is to be supplied as the probandum (sādhya).

Therefore, this [inference] is employed in a case where fire is visible due to a particular color, while cold touch—though present—is invisible because of distance.

the perception of a contradictory effect, as in "there is no cold touch here because of smoke" (II-35).
This means that the perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the object to be negated is the indicator, as in the example provided.

"There is no cold touch" means the absence of cold touch is the probandum (*sādhya*).

Thus he says, "For that" (*sa hi*). "For" (*hi*) means "because.
To the question, "How does he determine [the absence] from the non-perception of the perceptible? he replies, "Because of its being perceptible, like 'treeness,'" according to the context.

To the question, "From what, then, does one understand the absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness?", he says: "The word 'śiṃśapā'. The particle *tu* indicates a contrast (*vaidharmya*). The particle *iti* has the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
By the word "non-existence" (abhāva), both non-existence itself and the conventional usage regarding non-existence are to be understood.

This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be formulated as follows: where that which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of something is absent, that thing does not exist there.
Just as there is no validity [of a cognition] in the absence of an object of cognition (*prameyatva*),
and tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*) is not the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of *śiṃśapā*-ness (*śiṃśapātva*);

by this demonstration that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) establishes the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*), [it is shown that] eternal things lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), because their two pervaders— succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*yaugapadya*)— are absent, and so forth.
That which is to be seen has been shown.

With the words "the object to be negated," etc., he explains the perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*); showing that the word "is exemplified" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied [from the root text], he says "it is exemplified. In order to facilitate easy understanding, he says "here," demonstrating the fundamental division of the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth. By this, it is shown—by way of the consequence of perceiving the incompatible—that in the case of God (*īśvara*) as well, when there is an alternative such as a single material cause (*upādāna*), the absence of alternatives such as a recipient (*sampradāna*) follows.
This is because the contradiction characterized by the non-coexistence of one conceptualization with another is established within its own continuum;
consequently, it follows that [the mind] acts as an agent that does not determine [its object].
Otherwise, the non-arising of those things seen to arise simultaneously would result as an undesirable consequence.

Furthermore, if agency were to consist merely in being a sovereign without performing any specific action, then the proofs for God, such as the fact that He is the cause of effects, would result in proving what is already established by [the agency of] karma; this and other points have been demonstrated.
Explaining the perception of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*), he says "by that which is to be negated" (*pratiṣedhyena*).
He uses the term "gamika" to show that what is intended is that which leads to the root [inference] and establishes the intended absence.
As before, there is the mention of the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth.
In that case, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) would be the means of cognition;
whereas where fire, which is contradictory [to cold], is perceived, there the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is the means of cognition.
When both [the object and its absence] are imperceptible, however, the perception of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is employed.

In that case, when one perceives a specific mass of smoke emerging from a room— serving as the inferential mark (*anumāpaka*) for fire capable of dispelling the cold present throughout the entire room— then, based on that inferred specific fire, [the cold is negated].
One infers the cessation of cold touch [as follows]:

"The entire interior space of the room, together with the visible portion of the doorway, is the subject (*dharmin*); this is to be understood as being 'like the previous case' (*pūrvavat*), because it follows from the realization of the property to be proven (*sādhya*)."

"Destruction" (*vināśa*) is the subject (*dharmin*).

Of two contradictory cold sensations;

He states the justification: "sādhyeti.

"As before" (pūrvavat) means that, just as previously in the case of the non-perception of an effect, the cognition of the absence of fire and so forth was derived through the force [of inference], so too is the subject (dharmin) of that same kind.
The meaning of this is as follows: when this very cognition of the absence of cold touch is reflected upon, it necessarily entails a subject (*dharmin*) of such a kind.

Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) for this must be formulated as follows: "Wherever there is a particular kind of smoke, there is an absence of cold touch, as in the case of a kitchen and so forth."

And regarding the statement "the smoke here is of such a kind," it should be understood that this refers to the state prior to mastery: when, through intense habituation, the perception of smoke instantly gives rise to the cognition of the absence of cold touch, the Master has described this as a single inference arising from the observation of an effect incompatible [with the presence of cold].
The phrase "even of an existent entity" (*bhūtasyāpi bhāvasya*) is a qualification of the subject (*dharmin*).

The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is: if even for that which has come into being—that is, that which has been born—the perishable nature is not necessarily present, how much less so for that which has not yet been born?
A cause other than the cause [of production], such as a hammer, is "another cause" (*hetvantara*). That which is perishable depends upon it;
the reason for this is "because of its dependence."

Dependence upon another cause is pervaded by non-necessity of occurrence, just as the dependence of a dye on another cause such as the act of coloring in the case of a cloth is pervaded by non-necessity of occurrence.
Furthermore, non-necessity of occurrence is the opposite of necessity of occurrence.
And destruction, being of the nature of that which is perishable, is held to depend upon another cause.
Therefore, because one observes the requirement for another reason that is pervaded by the opposite, there is a negation of "necessity of occurrence" (*dhruvabhāvitva*).
[95] From production—APHE. [96] The hammer and so forth—C.

In this context, permanence (*nityatva*) consists in being invariably present, while impermanence (*anityatva*) consists in not being invariably present.
Since permanence and impermanence exist by way of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), there is a contradiction within a single locus.
This being the case, when one of two mutually exclusive properties is observed, the identity of the second with that locus must be negated.
And the negation of identity is possible only for that which is accepted as being perceptible;

for it is precisely because of this that the negation of identity is formulated: "If this perceived thing were eternal, it would be seen without form [i.e., without change]," yet it is not seen as having an eternal form.
Therefore, it is not eternal.
And thus, the negation is performed by having accepted that the eternity which is to be negated possesses a perceptible nature.
Even in the case of a real entity that is imperceptible, such as a *piśāca* demon, if there is a negation of its being of the nature of a perceptible jar, [the same principle applies].

Alternatively, let it be granted that such a negation applies only to the non-entity of permanence.

Following that, where there is no fire, there is no sensation of cold, as in the area of a kitchen; and since there is fire here, this is the second [type], arising from the perception of the incompatible.
With the words "of that which is to be negated" and so forth, he explains the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
As before, there is the demonstration of the probandum (*sādhya*) and other factors.
The collection of particles *kim uta* functions in the sense of *kim punar* ("how much more so").
Now, do some maintain that even for an entity that has not yet arisen, destruction—which is necessarily bound to occur—is accepted, such that the word "api" (even) is explained as a conjunction?
This is not a fault; for since an unarisen entity is simply not admitted [as existing], its destruction cannot be necessarily bound to occur.
The word "even" (*api*) in the root text [of Dharmakīrti] indicates that even for that which has been born, destruction is not necessary;
however, this meaning was not made explicit by Dharmottara, who explained it merely as "how much more so for that which is unborn.
In that context, his intention was: "How much more so for the unborn, whose very destruction is not even admitted?"
One must accept that it possesses a perceptible nature;
for if this visible jar were of the nature of a *piśāca*, then the *piśāca* would be seen.
And it is not seen;
therefore, it is not a piśāca.

This is preceded by the admission that [the object] has the nature of being visible, and constitutes the negation of the identity—whether as a real or unreal entity—of a visible thing such as a jar with that which is currently being perceived, whether visible or invisible.

And this being the case, just as the negation of a jar— having accepted its perceptibility— is based solely on the non-perception of the perceptible, so too the negation of everything that exists in mutual exclusion, when something else is perceived,
is based solely on the non-perception of the perceptible. Thus, this type of formal argument is included within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

The ellipsis is: "that which is perishable depends upon a hammer or the like in order to perish."

Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) regarding that other cause (*hetvantara*) should be stated as follows: whatever depends upon another cause for the attainment of a particular state does not necessarily become of that very nature;
just as cloth, which depends upon contact with a dyeing substance for the attainment of a red color, does not necessarily become red.
Furthermore, it follows that an entity would require another cause in order to perish; this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) based on the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory.
For this very reason, even the word "also" (*api*) in the root text is understood to indicate the purpose of establishing a *prasaṅga*.

An independent proof (*svatantrasādhana*), however, which is termed the "perception of a pervasion by the contradictory," should be seen as follows: that which possesses a conjunction with contradictory properties is not a single [entity], just like the liquid and the solid.

"And the universal (sāmānya) and so forth possess the association with contradictory properties. Now, one might raise the objection: "What is the contradiction between two objects, and what is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes this contradiction? Furthermore, that which was previously explained by this author while glossing the term "inevitable occurrence" (dhruvabhāvitva)—namely, that it "occurs certainly and necessarily" (dhruvam avaśyam bhavati)—would be contradicted.

"In this way" means by the manner that is about to be stated;
he states that very point with the words "if this [is so].
And it is not the case that such a nature—which would necessarily be eternal—is seen or perceived.

Thus, by the sequence just mentioned, when there is an establishment of contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between the perceived and the unperceived non-entity, the non-perception of the perceptible is precisely the means [of proof].

"Of that which is of such a kind" means of that which possesses such a nature.
If one were to say "of that which is of such a type," there would be a deficiency in the expression (or: it would be obtainable from the wording).
The point is that its inclusion therein has already been demonstrated.

Now, if one asks: "If the negation of the identity of one thing with another—whether that other is perceptible or imperceptible—is based on the non-perception of the perceptible, how then does the apprehension of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) come into play?"
There is no fault;

for at the time of apprehending the contradiction, the operation belongs to the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*). However, when something is perceived as pervaded by that which has been understood to be contradictory, the cognition of the absence of the intended object arises precisely from the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory. Thus, what is there to be censured?

With the words "of that which is to be negated," etc., he explains the perception of what is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*). As in the previous case, the subject (*dharmin*) and other factors are to be demonstrated.
By the term "of fire," it should be understood as referring to a specific fire capable of removing cold.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), because the very nature of the lamp being illustrated would itself exclude coldness.
The perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) is as follows: "There is no sensation of frost here, because of fire" (II-38).
Regarding "because of fire": one should provide an example of the perception of that which is incompatible with whatever pervades the object to be negated. Thus it is said.
In this context, "the subject" (dharmin) is "here";
"there is no touch of frost" is the "probandum" (sādhya);
and "because of fire" is the "reason" (hetu).
In a case where the pervaded, namely the sensation of frost, and the pervader, namely the sensation of cold, are not perceptible, this reason [of non-perception] is applicable;
for it is when both of those are perceptible that the non-perception of the essence and the pervader must be employed.
And such being the case, it establishes non-existence.
Furthermore, for an observer situated at a distance, the touch of frost—which is a specific instance of cold touch—and mere coldness are imperceptible;
however, fire, due to its specific color-form (*rūpa*), is perceptible even when far away.
Consequently, the absence of mere coldness is established in relation to that fire.
Consequently, there is the ascertainment of the absence of the touch of a particular cold, such as that of frost;
since a particular cold is pervaded by coldness in general, this [inference] is employed with respect to a qualified object.

"In the case of the general direction (*uddeśa*) and the specific location (*pradeśa*), the reason for the non-perception of both the cold touch and its cause is the distance from the perceiver. 'Because of having a brilliant color' (*bhāsvaravarṇatvāt*) is the basis for the perception of fire;
that is, because it possesses a color which is brilliant, meaning habitually luminous."

The word "api" (also) implies that it is not merely "nearby. In that case, in that place, the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be formulated as follows: Where there is a specific fire, there are no causes of cold whose power to produce cold is unobstructed.
Just as in a certain previously experienced location,
so too here there is fire;

and this should be understood as one type of inference based on the perception of what is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalambha*), which the Teacher has described as arising from the immediate perception of fire through habituation, which in turn produces the cognition of the absence of such a cause of cold.
Otherwise, however, these two are inferences arising from the perception of the contradictory and the non-perception of the effect.

For instance, the inference "wherever there is no fire, there is no sensation of cold" is one, arising from the perception of what is contradictory to its own nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalambha*). And the second is that which arises from the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalambha*), namely: "where the effect of something is absent, the cause of that thing—possessing the unimpeded capacity to produce it—is not present."
Thus, "the absence of fire" is the probandum; "because of the absence of fire" is the reason.
Where the effect, though existent, is invisible, this [non-apprehension of the cause] is the formal argument (*prayoga*).
But when the effect is visible, it is the non-apprehension of the visible that establishes it;
therefore, this too is a means of proving non-existence.

In a lake filled with steady, unmoving water, where a sparse mist rises as is appropriate for winter, and while the twilight darkness is present, smoke—even if it exists there—is not seen; thus, it is negated by the non-perception of its cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
Fire, however, if it were impossible for it to exist there, would be perceived simply by its specific form if it were blazing while floating above;
but if it were not blazing, it would be situated within the fuel.
In that case as well, since the fuel—the locus of the fire—is perceptible, the fire must be visible either in its own nature or in its form as a support; thus, it is employed there.

Anticipating and dispelling these three doubts—namely, how those two [the sun and the moon] can be invisible, how fire can be visible, and why the touch of frost is not simply the touch of cold—he says "dūra-" (at a distance).

and blue and other such objects are invariably perceived together with the cognition [of them], and so forth.

A "lake" (*hrada*) is a particular reservoir of water.

It must be established that "they do not exist.

The inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding such [a case].
That which has a particular fire proximate to it is described as such; the state of being that is the reason (*hetu*).

That in which a particular fire exists such that its cold touch, though present, is invisible—this is what is meant by that [term]. Its state (the abstract quality of being so) is the reason (*hetu*).
Where the cold touch, though present, is invisible, and particularities such as horripilation are also invisible.

In this regard, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: when a specific effect such as horripilation is perceptible, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is to be employed;
when the sensation of cold is perceptible, the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) is to be employed.
Therefore, this is a proof by means of non-existence;
for it is from a specific form that things are distinguished from a distance.

Thus: "floating" (*plavamāna*) and "standing still" (*avatiṣṭhamāna*).

[He goes] by way of his own nature, by way of the form of the flame, and by way of the form of the support established in the fuel.

In that specific location,

Furthermore, we do not understand why one who abandons such an object and brings about another object would exert oneself for the sake of the self. Rather, the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be stated as follows: where the cause of something does not exist, that thing does not exist there;
just as, in the absence of a seed, there is no sprout.
And here there is no fire as the cause of smoke. By this it is shown that wherever consciousness is not preceded by a preceding consciousness as its cause, there consciousness does not arise,
just as in a fragment of stone.

And since there is no consciousness belonging to a previous existence at the stage of the *kalala*, the consequence of the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) has been indicated, the meaning of which is based on an identical logical principle.
In order to explain the perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*), he says "of that which is to be negated" (*pratiṣedhyasya*).
As before, this indicates the locus (*dharmī*) and so forth.
"Udbheda" means the bristling of the hair (*pulaka*).
The two rows of teeth situated above and below the ivory lute are being struck rapidly, producing a *kaṭakaṭa* sound.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the trembling of the body is included. By the inclusion of the word "from pleasure" (*sukhāt*) and so forth, joy and the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) are included.
One perceives the vehicle;
however, the sensation of cold touch is invisible, as are the specific effects such as the bristling of the hair.
Since one realizes their non-existence through the non-apprehension of those causes, that constitutes its formal application (*prayoga*) in this context.

For this reason: *iti* means "thus," by the principle just mentioned;

This, however, is the formal argument (prayoga) that should be stated: Wherever there exists something that is incompatible with a particular cause, that [cause] does not exist there;
for example, where there is bile (pitta), which is incompatible with phlegm (śleṣman), there is no phlegmatic disease.
And here, there is fire, which is incompatible with the causes of horripilation and so forth.

This too, due to extreme familiarity, should be understood as follows: when the mere cognition of a specific nearby fire arises instantaneously, there occurs the realization of the absence of specific effects such as horripilation; thus, one [type of non-perception] was stated by the Teacher (Dharmakīrti), and it should be seen that Dharmottara has likewise explained it.
Otherwise, however, when the perception of a contradictory [object] and the non-perception of a cause are possible, these two are [distinct] forms of inference.
For instance: "Where there is fire, there is no sensation of cold"—this is one inference arising from the perception of a contradictory [property].
"Where there is an absence of the sensation of cold, there is no horripilation or other such effects thereof"—this is a second [inference] arising from the non-perception of a cause.
With the words "of the object to be negated" and so forth, he explains the perception of the effect of that which is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*).
The presentation of the subject (*dharmin*) and other factors is as before.

Śāntabhadra has explained this by forming a *karmadhāraya* compound—“this person is endowed with specific [symptoms] such as horripilation”—and then stating that “that [place] exists where he is, and thus it possesses that.”
And that is a fault;

for, according to the rule that "a *bahuvrīhi* is more concise than a *karmadhāraya* with a possessive suffix (*mattvarthīya*)," a great grammarian—considering that once the specific location is understood as "the place where a person possessing [qualities] such as bristling hair exists"—would ask: "What is the use of a possessive suffix?"
As Dharmottara said: "Yoga" and "yukta" are nouns formed with the suffix *niṣṭhā* in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
If this is so, then [the term] "kṛṣṇasarpa" [is likewise].
When the specific quality such as horripilation is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).

When the cause, namely the sensation of cold, is perceived through direct perception, there is the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). However, when fire is perceived through direct perception, the perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) should be employed.
Even though these [causes] are invisible, this is the formal argument (*prayoga*).
Therefore, this is a proof for non-existence (*abhāva-sādhana*).
In that regard, for an observer situated at a distance, the specific qualities of fire—such as heat, the sensation of cold, and horripilation—are imperceptible, even though they exist.
However, where smoke is perceived, this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But that kind of smoke which is capable of inferring a fire capable of removing the cold situated in that place is what must be apprehended here.

However, even when fire is inferred merely by means of smoke, the cessation of the sensation of cold is not established, nor can the cessation of specific effects such as horripilation be determined; therefore, it should be understood that mere smoke is not the [conclusive] logical reason (hetu).

If one were to argue that in cases such as *yasmin valmīke lohitaḥ śāliḥ*, *yasmin grāme gauraḥ kharaḥ*, and *yasminn araṇye*, these must be analyzed as *bahuvrīhi* compounds—
so that there would be no instances of "an anthill possessing a black snake," "a village possessing red rice," or "a forest possessing a white donkey"—
and yet these usages are correct, then how can it be explained by this [interpretation]?

This is not a fault, because this statement— that a *bahuvrīhi* is more concise than a *karmadhāraya* with a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*)— is to be understood as excluding technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*).
And since these words— *kṛṣṇasarpa*, *lohitaśāli*, *gaurakhara*— are technical terms, it was rightly said that "the application is appropriate."

Furthermore, the meaning of the particle *hi* (for/indeed) should be understood here from the context.

But where is it that the three are not perceived while smoke is perceived? He says: "There," which introduces the statement.

Even though they exist, if they were not perceived, they would certainly have been criticized; thus, they have transcended the bounds of possibility. The qualification "of one who is far away" functions as a reason.
Therefore, the meaning is this: because the perceiver is at a distance, those things, despite existing, are not perceived.

In that case, this proof (*sādhana*)— which consists of an effect that is incompatible with the cause— is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it generates the means of valid cognition known as inference (*anumāna*).
However, when the cognizer is not at a great distance, this application should be understood as occurring in a location separated by a wall or similar obstacle.
He shows that by the word "smoke" (dhūma), a specific kind of smoke is intended, with the words "But smoke... (*dhūmas tv*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to indicate a distinction.
Strengthening this very point by way of contrast, he says: "...by mere smoke" (*dhūmamātreṇa*).
The particle *tu* expresses a contrast with what preceded;
the first *iti* indicates a reason,
while the second *iti* has the sense of "thus."
If only one reason for negation has been stated, how can there be eleven reasons for non-existence? To this he says:

"All these," and so forth [146]:
these are the applications of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*);

It should be understood that this was stated by the Teacher (*ācārya*). Otherwise, these three would be inferences consisting of the observation of an effect (*kāryahetu*), the observation of the contradictory (*viruddhopalambha*), and the non-observation of a cause (*kāraṇānupalambha*). For instance, the sequence is as follows: "Where there is smoke, there is fire"—this is one inference arising from the observation of an effect.
The second [type] arises from the perception of a contradiction (*viruddhopalambha*), as in: "Where there is fire, there is no sensation of cold.

The third arises from the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalambha*), as in: "Where there is an absence of the sensation of cold, there is no presence of a person characterized by specific effects such as horripilation.

Pervading the permanence that is to be negated is the quality of being without increase, because [permanence] is devoid of gradation;
opposed to that is the quality of having increase,
which is pervaded by the property of performing an action only occasionally.
And the applications for these [types of non-perception] should be inferred by oneself according to their respective natures and as appropriate.
They are subsumed under the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) by way of identity (*tādātmyena*).
The meaning is that their intrinsic nature is the non-perception of intrinsic nature.

But surely, since the non-perception of effect and the other types differ from the application of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), how are they included within it? To this he says: [156] "They are included," he says. C.
"Indirectly, through the affirmation or negation of another object, they are included even when there is a difference in formulation.

whereas in the applications such as the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*),

"By the negation of another meaning, [there is] the affirmation," etc.— PHEH. "Meaningfully," om.— B.

Some, however, maintain that here there is the perception of something pervaded by what is incompatible with the effect— namely, "there are no causes of fire here whose capacities are unimpeded, because of the touch of frost"—
and they also maintain the perception of something pervaded by what is incompatible with the cause— namely, "there is no smoke here, because of the touch of frost."
Not accepting the statement that "it is of eleven types due to the difference in its application," the opponent objects with the words "If...
Here, the intention of the objector is that by the statement "two establish a positive entity and one is a reason for negation," only one reason for negation has been mentioned.
With the words beginning "kārya" (the effect), he explains the intended meaning of the mention of the number ten.
The word *api* is used in the sense of a doubt.
He states the intended meaning of the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*)— the word *tatra* being used to introduce the statement—
and the word *api* is as before.
"Only those [factors] have been cited that were merely mentioned.
By this, it is shown that the word "all" (*sarva*) is understood here as functioning with respect to the totality of substances.
To the objection, "In that case, let there simply be the mention of 'all'; what is the point of mentioning 'ten' (*daśa*)?", he says: "Ten."

It is stated [in the commentary] that "the entirety [of the examples] employed should be understood," because in common usage we observe the word *sarva* functioning to indicate the entirety of what has been presented, as in the example: "All those who are warriors here," and so forth.
To the objection, "If this is so, why would it not be the same even when ten are mentioned? he replies: "Because of the mention of ten."
He states the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from the position that lacks the apprehension of sound:

"That which is *atiricyamāna*—meaning becoming excessive or redundant, i.e., having its meaning already established—serves for the sake of demonstrating the equality [of the cases] to those who have not understood.
This might be the case: one could simply say, "All these are ten applications of non-apprehension," and by this much alone, the consequence of grasping [the full scope] would be avoided.

If it is argued: "Since [the point] has already been refuted, how is the Master’s mention of 'non-perception of the effect' and so forth not redundant? And how is this explanation by Dharmottara of the intended meaning—namely, that he says 'tat kiñcit' (that certain... when something is applicable—not an unconsidered interpretation?"
This is not a fault;

for, since the previous mention of eleven [reasons] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), other applications such as the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) are also intended.
Thus, by setting aside the first category of applications—such as the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*)—the number ten is completed.
To dispel that suspicion, the Teacher included the mention of "non-perception of the effect" and so forth;
Dharmottara has also explained it in this way.
If it is argued, "In that case, the mention of 'ten' should not be made," [the response follows].
No— since this is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtha*), there is no fault here;
nor do the applications differ.

If [it is asked], "How then are the affirmation and negation of other objects included within other formal arguments (prayoga)? he says: "Indirectly" (pāramparyeṇa), which means "by way of a sequence" (praṇālikayā).

This is what is meant: these arguments do not directly express the non-perception of the perceptible; rather, they express the affirmation or negation of another object that is non-deviant from the non-perception of the perceptible.
Therefore, their inclusion within the non-perception of essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi) is by way of this sequence, not directly.
If this distinction is due to a difference in formulation, then this must be stated regarding inference for others (*parārthānumāna*),
for a difference in formulation is indeed a difference in words,
and inference for others consists of words; anticipating this objection, he says:
[159] Then, *om*.
— C. [160] The distinction is due to the difference in application — APHEN.;
the distinction is due precisely to the difference in application — BC.

[161] However—BC. Through the repeated observation of formal applications (*prayoga*), one comes to have such a cognition of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) even by oneself; thus, this [threefold division] is specified as an application even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
[162] "Cognition of exclusion"—this is a specification of its subdivisions even in the context of inference for oneself. —C.
"Observation of applications," and so forth:
the observation of applications—that is, their perception—as they are recited in the treatises;
the practice thereof is their repeated rehearsal.
"From that cause";
"even by oneself" means even by the practitioner's own self;
"in this way" means by the sequence just mentioned.
The word "iti" signifies "therefore," meaning that there occurs the cognition of exclusion, which is to say, of negation.
[Regarding the phrase] "of those constructed by the treatise"—APHEN reads *śāstraghaṭitānām*;
B reads *śāstraparighaṭitānām*.
Regarding the variant readings mentioned in the treatises:
the phrase "by means of the sequence of practice through the observation of usage" (prayogadarśanābhyāsakrameṇa) is omitted in CB.

To explain how they are included within [the category of] "inclusion" (saṅgraha), he says: "by way of identity" (tādātmyena). Its essence is its own nature; that which has this as its essence is "that-essence" (tadātmā). By means of that state—namely, by way of being the non-perception of intrinsic nature (svabhāvānupalabdhitvena)—the meaning is that they have non-perception as their intrinsic nature.
This clarification should also be understood as indicating that they have that as their nature, insofar as it serves to remind one of the non-perception of intrinsic nature.

If it is asked, "Why is it not called 'sound' (śabda) itself?"—the answer is no; because that would entail the contradiction of [the doctrine of] successive apprehension (*paramparāgrahaṇa*), and because it would entail the contradiction with the commentary by Dharmottara which will be cited later, beginning with the words "these are not direct [expressions]," and so forth.
This is despite the fact that the function of sound, characterized as "denotation" (*abhidhāna*), undergoes differentiation when it is differentiated.
By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "contradictory by nature and so forth," the "contradictory cause" (*kāraṇaviruddha*) and others are included.
By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" in the phrase "non-perception of the effect and so forth," the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) and others are included.
Demonstrating that in the root text the word "by means of" (*iti*) following "arthāntara" is in the instrumental plural, he says: "arthāntareti."
In this case, [the author] combines those that possess equal force.

They "differ" means they become of various forms. Regarding the phrase "in other applications," the word *antara* signifies "other" in relation to the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
"Succession" (*paramparā*) means a sequence (*paripāṭi*). The suffix in *pāramparya* is used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*).
He clarifies this very point with the word "by way of a channel" (*praṇālikayā*).

Now, one might object: "If these are included within the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), then they should be designated directly as such; and if that is the case, how can it be said that they are [established] through a mediated sequence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The following is what is meant: if they were not so designated, then the qualification 'not directly' (*na sākṣāt*) would not need to be stated.
[DhPr p. 143]

Thus, the meaning is this: since one also understands for oneself by means of this very method through the practice of application (*prayoga*), therefore this distinction of application, which is employed even in one's own comprehension, is designated under "inference for oneself" (*svārthānumāna*). However, that which is employed solely for the comprehension of others must be stated as "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*) alone.
[166] By this measure— the reading is *pāṭhaḥ*—
[167] as for that which is the three-fold statement of the mark (*liṅga*), he asks how there is a summary (*saṅgraha*) and says: "By the visible" (*dṛśya*).
The particle *tu* is used either for the sake of specification (*viśeṣārtha*) or to express the sense of "because" (*yasmād-artha*).
[It indicates] an affirmation (*vidhi*) such as fire and so forth,
or a negation (*niṣedha*) such as the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and so forth.
The word "ca" has the sense of "vā";
therefore, because it expresses injunctions and prohibitions that are non-deviant [from the object],
it does not do so directly, nor without mediation.

Furthermore, regarding the non-deviation of the perception of other objects from their non-perception when there is an affirmation or negation of another object, one should consider that which recalls the non-perception of the perceptible as it occurred at the time of grasping the relation of cause and effect and so forth.
"This is the distinction" refers to the forms such as the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
To the question "Why is it to be stated in that context?", he says: "By means of words," and so forth.
"Here" means because.
"Difference in words" refers to the multiplicity of statements containing the three-fold logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).
Even though this is so, he says "And the word... to explain how one should speak in that regard.
Regarding the phrase "in the cause":

it should be understood as referring to those statements recited in the treatises—specifically, those statements that express the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, which have been fully understood by way of their recitation in the treatises.
Apprehension (*upalambha*) is twofold: consisting of the expressed form (*vācya-rūpa*) and consisting of the expressive form (*vācaka-rūpa*).
For this very reason, repetition (*āvartanam*) is also twofold: repetition of the verbal form and repetition of the meaning.
Among these, repetition of the meaning is the repeated internalizing [of the object] in the mind.
"Repetition of the word" (*śabdāvartanam*) means uttering it again and again.
With the intention that the word "self" (*svayam*) in the root [text] is understood as functioning in the sense of the genitive case (*ātmanaḥ*), he says: "of the cognizer's self.

Since this occurs in the context of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), by the word "cognizer" (*pratipattṛ*), one who cognizes an imperceptible object through a three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*) is understood.
The word "api" (also/even) should be connected with the phrase "the other person also understands from that.
However, in the root text, it should be construed as "not only for the other person.

This refers to the sequence of formal arguments, such as the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), which was indicated by the previously mentioned enumerated types of non-perception of intrinsic nature and so forth.
Since the word *iti* has the sense of "therefore," the meaning of what follows is "for that reason. Because of the connection with the word *yasmāt* (since), the word *tasmāt* implies "because.

Anticipating the objection that one might understand [the object] through this means characterized by the application of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) and so forth, he reminds us of what was stated previously: "through the practice of the formal arguments" (*prayogābhyāsāt*).
It might be thought: "A word uttered by oneself is not the cause for the cognition of that [object], because the word is employed only after [the object] has already been cognized."
Otherwise, a specific application [of words] would be impossible.
Therefore, how can it be said that a word which performs a "grinding of what is already ground" is an *upāya* (means)? This is not so;

for one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been awakened by the perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*) or some other cause, and who possesses a recollection of the object with slow movement due to extremely practiced application—[it is for such a person that this is meant].

Having uttered such an application and thus comprehending the reality, one understands its meaning— just as someone, having uttered the statement that "in the world, reflection upon properties proceeds with respect to a substratum" through practice, understands its meaning; likewise,
having uttered a sentence expressing the three marks of a valid reason, someone who has practiced the application understands an imperceptible object.
If it is argued that this [method] is indeed a means,
and that because it arises dependently for another as well, there would also be inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*);
Let it be so;

what is the harm? Inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) has as its purpose one's own comprehension, while inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), having as its purpose the comprehension of another, occurs when another person comprehends at that very same time through that [inference].
Therefore, we have stated that even though it is not verbal, there exists something determinate [in the case of inference for others].

But is it not the case that in the case of the non-perception of the effect and so forth, there is a negation of causes and the like precisely when they are unobservable? For if there were a negation of what is observable, it would follow that one must employ the formal argument of the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
This being so, their negation is not by means of the non-perception of the observable.
How, then, are these applications included within the non-perception of the perceptible? He says:
[168] Negation—APHEN.
[169] Non-perception of the essential nature—ABPHEN.

[170] When there is a negation of things that are imperceptible— in all cases where this non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) serves as the means for establishing the conventional usage of absence— those things such as the "contradictory to the nature" (svabhāvaviruddha) and so forth, whose negation was stated through apprehension, or those such as causes (kāraṇa) and so forth, whose negation was stated through non-apprehension, are apprehended only when they have reached the conditions for perceptibility (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta).

And non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) should be understood as that which establishes the conventional usage of the absence of an absence— namely, [the non-apprehension] of things that are contradictory. II-45 [171–172] E [172] C.
"Everywhere," and so forth [173].
"Non-existence and the conventional usage thereof" constitute the two non-existent usages [174].
In the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the conventional usage of non-existence is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
There is an absence [of the probans] in the remaining cases;
that is, when those two are not perceived as being established.
The word "ca" (and) in the phrase "sarvatra ca" has the sense of the word "hi" (for/indeed).

Since the negation stated for those things whose non-perception is universal applies only to those that have reached the conditions for perception— that is, to those which are visible— it follows that [all other types of non-perception] are included within the non-perception of the visible. [173] The phrase "and in all cases," etc., is omitted— HN.
[174] And its conventional usage consists of the two types of usage regarding non-existence— APHE [175] when there is— BHL [176] of those things being perceived— B.
[177] He asks, "Why is this so only for visible things? and replies with the words beginning "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature).
Here too, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of a logical reason (*hetu*).

Since the negation of those things which possess a nature contradictory [to the perceived object], etc., has been stated by means of their perception, and the negation of those things for which a cause, etc., is the basis has been stated by means of the non-perception [of that cause], therefore the negation applies only to perceptible things.

Even if the negation has been stated through the perception of what is contradictory to its nature, etc., and through the non-perception of the cause, etc., how is it that the negation applies only to perceptible things? To this he says: "Perception," etc.
Here too, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

For those things which are known to be contradictory, or to stand in the relation of pervader and pervaded, or in the relation of cause and effect, their perception must necessarily be understood as being preceded by perception; that is, non-perception is to be understood [only] as having perception as its antecedent.
Furthermore, those things for which both perception and non-perception exist are precisely those that are perceptible (*dṛśya*).

Therefore, when the negation of contradictory factors and so forth— whether by the perception of what is contrary to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) or by the non-perception of their causes (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*)— is performed by those who possess perception and non-perception, it should be understood that this negation applies only to those things that are perceptible (*dṛśya*).
[178] By the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhyā*) — [179] *jñātavyā* is omitted in ABPHEN.

Some, however, explain as follows: by the passage beginning with "by himself" (*svayam*), the author of the *Vārttika* has stated that through the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, and through the perception of contradictory factors (*viruddha*) and so forth, the cognizer understands— according to the circumstances— the absence [of an object] and the linguistic convention regarding it, quite independently of formal logical application (*prayoga*).

It is not only during the moment of practice that one utters the application through the habituation of practice, but rather one understands it prior to that; otherwise, there would be no utterance of specific words.
Regarding the phrase "by this means," they explain that the "means" here is the sequence of uttering the words in such a manner.
And by this same logic for establishing the formulation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*),
when many objections have been raised, the particle *ca* (and) serves the purpose of stating a reason (*hetvartha*) in order to aggregate the refutations.
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that because these various solutions exist, those respective objections are untenable.
But why should the perception and non-perception of the things to be negated—such as the contradictory and so forth—be understood? To this he says:
"Because for others, contradiction, the state of being effect and cause, and non-existence are not established" (II-46).
[Note: The variant reading *kāraṇabhāvāsiddheḥ* is noted in the manuscript E.]
—The non-establishment of the causal relationship (kāraṇabhāvāsiddhi) — [as stated by] BPH regarding "others":
those which are other than the perceivable and the unperceivable, and are themselves unperceived; for them, both contradiction and the causal relationship [are not established].

Furthermore, coexistence with anything is established through the absence of the pervader when the pervaded is absent; because of that, since contradiction, the relation of cause and effect, and non-existence cannot be established [otherwise], those things such as the contradictory and so forth that are to be negated must possess both perception and non-perception.
And those possessing both [perception and non-perception] are necessarily perceptible.
Therefore, there is a negation only of those things that are perceptible.
This is the meaning:
contradiction, the relation of cause and effect, and the absence of the pervaded when the pervader is absent—all these result only from the non-perception of the perceptible.
Contradiction (*virodha*) is known when one thing is perceived in the absence of another.
The causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is determined when the absence of what is considered the effect is perceived upon the absence of what is considered the cause.
Likewise, [the pervasion relation is determined] when the absence of what is considered the pervaded is perceived upon the absence of what is considered the pervader.
[181] In the absence of the pervader— C [182] the effect of the contradictory— ABPEHN [183] and omits— APHEN.
[184] When one is present, the non-existence of the other is perceived— [185] having ascertained the relationship of cause and effect—
APHE [186] *ca* is omitted— ABC PHEN.

Others, however, maintain a different position: they hold that the phrase "even by oneself" and so forth was not stated with reference to an [external] manifestation of the linguistic usage (*prayoga*), but rather to that which occurs at the time of one's own internal realization, proceeding in the form of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*).
In this matter, whether the explanation is correct or incorrect, it is for the learned alone to determine.

This might be the case: one might suspect that just as a distinction in formulation is stated in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), so too there would be nothing at all to be expressed in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). Anticipating this, he says: "But that which... The purpose of the restriction is to indicate that [the formulation] is only for the sake of another's understanding, and not even for one's own understanding.
Now, unable to accept that all non-perceptions are included within the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), he says: "But surely...

(*nanu ceti*). This being so, when there is a mode of negation for invisible causes and the like, it should be understood that "non-existence" (*abhāva*) also applies to the remaining or residual cases.
But it is not merely non-existence [that is established], because even conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is thereby accomplished.
Through the non-apprehension of causes and so forth, which functions as the instrument,

when the apprehension and non-apprehension that previously existed at the time of grasping the relation of cause and effect and so on are negated, that negation should be understood and known as applying only to those things that are perceptible.

Just as the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is necessarily present at the time of apprehending a contradiction with the object and so forth, this will be established immediately thereafter by Dharmottara.
Now, one might object that because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of the cause and so forth," there must necessarily be a sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how can it be explained as having the sense of a reason (*hetu*)?", he says—"in the case of many"—while clarifying what was previously present in the mind.
He thinks as follows: this [particle *ca*] exists in the sense of a reason precisely while existing in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
However, its meaning as conjunction is not thereby negated.
Because the mutual conjunction of the reasons is perceived,
it does not constitute the meaning of "reason" (hetu) in that way;
thus, the word "iti" has the sense and purpose of the particle "ca."
When the absence of the subject (the *mata*) has been ascertained, the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is ascertained.
In that case, non-existence (*abhāva*) must be understood as the cause for the cognition of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.
For here, when the absence of a tree is apprehended upon the apprehension of the absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness, the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is established;
and the cognition of absence occurs everywhere solely through the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).
Therefore, [the relationship of] contradiction and the relationship of cause and effect—

Furthermore, for one who remembers the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*)—which is based on the cognition of the absence of objects characterized by contradiction, cause-and-effect, and pervader-and-pervaded relationships—must be remembered.
If there were no remembrance of the non-perception of the perceptible, there would be no remembrance of those [relationships] such as contradiction.
And that being the case, the cognition of the absence of another [thing] would not arise through either the affirmation or the negation of [states such as] "ceased" (*niruddha*) and so forth.

And since non-perception at the time of grasping the contradictory and so forth must necessarily be remembered, the cognition of absence arises from that very [non-perception]. In the cognition of its absence, [the relation of] pervasion— B.
The connection is as follows: for those beings such as *piśācas* who are remote in terms of place, time, and nature, no contradiction with any fire is established;
likewise, a causal relationship between those *piśācas* and any smoke is not established. — Note:
Although the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) does not exist at the present moment, it did exist at the time when the contradiction and so forth were being apprehended.
The very non-apprehension of the perceptible that is currently being remembered is the basis for the cognition of absence.

Therefore, since the non-apprehension of the perceptible does not exist at present, the applications of the non-apprehension of the effect and so forth differ from the application of the non-apprehension of the perceptible as a means of proving absence. [191] It exists at present—A.B.P.H.E.N.
[191] Regarding "the perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyopalabdhi*): by the word "contradictory" (*viruddha*), that which is contradictory to the object of negation is to be understood.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakārya*) and other such reasons is intended.
Those which are perceived at one time are precisely not perceived as other than that [at another time];
they are simply unknown at some place or at some time.
Furthermore, because the absence of the pervader does not establish the absence of the pervaded.

This is the intended meaning: if, prior [to the inference], the absence of that which is considered the pervaded were ascertained upon the absence of that which is considered the pervader, then the relationship of pervader and pervaded would be established;
and only then would the non-perception of the pervader be a means of cognition, and not otherwise.

This is the point of the present discussion: according to your own position, when the absence of one thing occurs upon the presence of another, there is the apprehension of their opposition (*virodha*).

Furthermore, since the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and that by which it is perceived must be established through the five types of perception and non-perception, and the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is likewise to be determined through perception and non-perception, how can these be established for that which is invisible?
[Objection: But surely, let them be visible in other cases.
In that regard, for the time being, only those [non-perceptions] pertaining to the invisible (*adṛśya*) should be mentioned;
for if they were visible, they would be included under the application of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).

Therefore, having raised the objection as to how the other types of non-perception are included within the non-perception of the perceptible, he says "that" (*tat*) in order to demonstrate how they are so included.

Since the inclusion of contradictory reasons (*viruddha*) and the like within non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is not tenable even when they are elsewhere [classified as] perceptible,
and since that has been stated by the Teacher, therefore this is the meaning— the intended sense of the sentence beginning with "in all cases" (*sarvatra ca*).
He establishes this point, namely "how [it follows] from the non-perception of the perceptible," by means of the word "one" (*eka*).

To the question, "What is the status regarding the relation of cause and effect? he says: "The cause... [etc.]. If that is so, what is the fate of the relation between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)? To this he says: "The pervader... [etc.]. Now, one might object: "Since those two are identical once the relation of the pervaded and the pervader is ascertained, what is the use of ascertaining their non-existence? To this he says: "In that case," meaning when the ascertainment of the relation between the pervaded and the pervader is to be performed.

To the question, "How is the cognition of non-existence the cause for the cognition of the relation between the pervaded and the pervader? he says: "In this case," by means of the affirmation of the contradictory.

And since the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is implied by the negation of causes and so forth, the comprehension of absence [is achieved] through that very non-perception of the perceptible which occurred at another time and has become the object of memory. Furthermore, these applications are included within the non-perception of the perceptible.

Thus, it should be understood that by all of this, the inclusion of the ten applications of non-perception within the non-perception of the perceptible has been demonstrated both directly and indirectly.
[192] — Let alone the cognition of non-existence in all cases such as contradiction;
but where is the non-perception of the perceptible (dṛśyānupalabdhi) of use? To this he says: "abhāva... and so forth.
Regarding the reason: even if non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) did indeed exist at the time of apprehending the contradiction and so forth,

nevertheless, it does not currently persist in the scope of the application of [reasons] such as the apprehension of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) or the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
To the question, "How then are the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth included therein? he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since the establishment of contradiction and so on is not possible without the cognition of non-existence (*abhāva*), and since the establishment of non-existence results from the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), one should understand that the phrase "one should remember the contradiction and so on" refers to the time of employing the logical reasons such as the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalambha*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
For it must also be observed that if there were no recollection of that [logical reason], then since the contradictory and so forth exist here,
and since this pervader and so forth does not exist,
the cognition "therefore that is not there" would be impossible.

And it was stated [in the verse] that "one must remember," because at that time there is the apprehension of contradiction and so forth, and conceptualization occurs only of what has been apprehended.
But why must that [non-apprehension] necessarily be remembered? He says: "because it was seen. Now, it might be argued: let the previous non-apprehension of the perceptible be remembered always.

Nevertheless, how does this [non-perception] serve to establish the absence of the intended object, such that it includes other types of non-perception within itself? To this he says: "By way of contradiction" (*virodha*).
Since that [non-apprehension] exists when there is a certain recollection, one might ask:

"But surely that [non-apprehension] does not exist in the case of the application of non-apprehension of the cause of a contradictory perception (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth; how then can that which is non-existent be the basis for the cognition of absence? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*)—this introduces the statement—"now," at the present moment, "that very thing being recollected" is the basis for the cognition of absence, meaning it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the knowledge of the absence of the contradictory and so forth.

How, then, is there a distinction between the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) and the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth? To this he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). Because the non-perception of the perceptible—which was operative at the time of grasping the contradiction and so on—is now being remembered, it does not exist at present.

Therefore, in this case, non-existence is what is being proven; thus, by virtue of being a proof of non-existence, the applications of "perception of the contradictory" (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth are distinguished from it.

He summarizes the point stated in the passage beginning with "by the affirmation of the contradictory" (*viruddhavidhinā*); the phrase "by the affirmation of the contradictory" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
This is because even by means of the formulation of contradictory effects and so forth, the non-perception of the perceptible is implied;
otherwise, those [other types of non-apprehension] would not be included therein.

Now, you have previously demonstrated that the ascertainment of non-existence occurs through that very [non-perception] independently, and within that, the other types of non-apprehension are included.

Fearing that this might not be the intended meaning of the Teacher, he says "tadaneneti" (by this), showing that this is indeed the intended meaning of the Teacher himself—from the words "anena ime sarva...
(by this, all these... up to "...vyāpakabhāvasiddheḥ" (because of the establishment of the absence of the pervader).
The meaning of this section is as follows: since the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is itself inexpressible, all ten types of non-perception are included therein;
furthermore, there is no utility for them in the cognition of the absence of contradictory factors and so forth.
The non-apprehension of the perceptible has been stated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when proving both non-existence and the conventional usage of non-existence.
But what is the nature of the non-apprehension of the imperceptible?
And what is its function? He says:
