Furthermore, non-apprehension whose object is remote—characterized by the cessation of perception and inference—is a cause of doubt.

Regarding the phrase "remote," etc.: that whose object is remote by way of the three types of remoteness—namely, remoteness of place, time, and intrinsic nature—is "that which has a remote object," and it is thus a cause of doubt. II-47.

To the question "What is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva)?", he says: that which has as its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and intrinsic nature the cessation of perception and inference is "non-perception" (pratyakṣābhāva);
that is to say, it does not have the nature of cognition or an object of cognition.

Furthermore, some here argue as follows: "In this context, non-perception (*anupalambha*) is the perception of another object that is associated with the same cognition [as the object in question]. Now, when the negation of cold is to be proven, it is not logical that the perception of the luminous form of fire due to its distance constitutes the non-perception of the sensation of cold; for if that were so, non-perception would be established."
This is because color and touch lack co-occurrence within a single cognition.

Nor can it be said that [the non-perception] possesses the status of "non-perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalambhatva*) by virtue of its being a reminder of the non-perception of the perceptible that occurred at the time of grasping the contradiction;
for if that were so, it would follow that it must also be "perceptual" (*pratyakṣatva*) by virtue of reminding one of a prior perception.

For this very reason, it is not tenable that non-perceptions (*anupalabdhi*) are included therein as reminders of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) which was operative at the time of grasping the contradiction and so forth;
nor does the ascertainment of the absence of that [contradiction] itself follow from its being remembered,

because it would then follow that inference for others (*parārthānumāna*)— which functions as a reminder of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— would be included within that same [non-perception].
For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the intended cognition could arise from the very memory of the means of valid cognition itself.

Therefore, in every case, the present non-perception of the perceptible must be demonstrated; it is by its power alone that the ascertainment of non-existence is to be stated, and not an ascertainment of non-existence based on a previously occurring non-perception of the perceptible that has been made an object of memory.
Nor can it be said that non-apprehensions possess such a nature by virtue of being reminders of that [object].
If this is so, one might ask: "In what manner, then, is it demonstrated?
It is replied:

Having seen from afar a specific quality of form belonging to fire, one forms the inferential cognition of a specific warm touch, [thinking]: "Wherever there is such a specific quality of form, there exists a specific touch of frost pervading that location, as in the case of a kitchen and so forth; this very form is of that same kind.
And that [cognition] itself is the non-perception of a cold touch, because the warm and cold touches are associated within a single cognition.
Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is an apprehension other than the apprehension of that which is intended to be apprehended.

This [non-apprehension] consists sometimes of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and sometimes of inference (*anumāna*); thus, there is neither contradiction with the treatises nor contradiction with reasoning.
Precisely from that non-apprehension of what is visible, there arises the cognition of the absence of cold touch.

Because the non-perception of the perceptible does not arise [in this case] due to its being directly perceived (*āhatya*), it is specified as distinct from the non-perception of the perceptible; for this very reason, this is an inference based on an inference (*anumitānumāna*).
It is only because of extremely intensive practice that such a cognition arises instantaneously that a single inference was stated;
in reality, however, this consists of multiple inferences.
In the same way, all cases should be understood, including the perception of the effect of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-kārya-upalabdhi*) and so forth.
And likewise, in cases such as the perception of what is incompatible with a pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), another single inference is to be understood as floating [as the underlying basis].
Furthermore, where there is a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is quite evident.
Therefore, in cases such as the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), the non-perception of the perceptible exists at this very moment.
The distinction [between these types of non-perception], however, arises through a succession of steps.

Thus, in the case of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpaka*) or a cause (*kāraṇa*), since the very property of being a non-cause or a non-pervader is not perceived, its absence is established; and from that very fact, by implication, the absence of the effect (*kārya*) and so forth is established.
It is for this reason that the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is now of utility only in the present instance.
It does not refer to the non-perception of the perceptible as previously apprehended by memory and so forth; rather,

because the non-perception of the perceptible functions directly toward the realization [of absence], and indirectly toward the presence of the absence of contradictories and so on, there is the employment of the non-perception of causes and other types of non-perception as distinct from the non-perception of the perceptible.

Regarding "inference for the sake of others": it is the statement of a logical mark possessing three characteristics.

The three forms—those designated as positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—belong to that which possesses them; thus it is "three-formed" (*trirūpa*).
It is both three-formed and a mark (*liṅga*); the explanation of that is its "explanation" (*ākhyāna*).
It is called an "explanation" because by means of it something is explained or made manifest—namely, the "three-formed" [mark].
What, then, is that? It is the statement (*vacana*).

This is because the effect, which is knowledge, is metaphorically attributed to its cause, the statement, through superimposition.

Now, since some maintain that being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*) and so forth are also characteristics of the mark, and because such conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) are observed, it is appropriate to explain those [characteristics];

If it is argued that this is because there is no disagreement regarding that [point], we reply:

no; for even here, since those who disagree express themselves through both non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and exclusion (*vyatireka*), it is likewise proper to provide an exposition of this [point] as well.

Thus, "that which is eternal" is a restatement of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), while "it is unproduced" is a prescription of the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāvavidhi*).

The intention of one who says that the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is different is as follows: in the formulation characterized by similarity (*sādharmyavat*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are the subject matter;

however, what is to be revealed is non-different and common to both formulations. By the phrase "that which is aimed at" (*yad uddiśya*), he clarifies that the word *artha* refers to the purpose (*prayojana*) and its application, and does not denote the subject matter (*abhidheya*).

That by which one is impelled is the "purpose" (prayojana); he shows that the purpose of the argumentative statement (*sādhanavākya*) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as a real entity that prompts action, not the fruit (*phala*).
That indicative mark, which must be made manifest and is endowed with the three forms (*rūpa*), is non-different and common to both types of formal arguments (*prayoga*).
Because both [types of statements] establish that very same thing;
since they are causes for inference, when sentences possessing similarity (sādharmya) or dissimilarity (vaidharmya) have been stated in the context of inference,
the word "tataḥ" (from that) is in grammatical apposition with the "purpose" (prayojana), and is not a term denoting the "reason" (hetu).

Now, one might object: "Surely only the denotable object (*abhidheya*) is what is to be manifested; how then can there be non-difference from that which is manifested? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This is what is meant. The phrase "something else is to be manifested" implies that the manifested object is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*);
the intention is that the operation of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) does not apply there.
Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*), which introduces the statement:
if positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the intended meaning in a statement based on similarity (*sādharmya*), then how can negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) be manifested?
[This applies] to the statement based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

In that regard, the formal argument based on similarity (*sādharmyavat prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever, being capable of being perceived (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is not perceived, is established as an object of the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāraviṣaya*);
for example, a rabbit's horn or the like, which is observed to be otherwise.
And a jar, which has reached the conditions for perception, is not perceived anywhere in a particular location; this is the formulation of non-perception (anupalabdhi), as in [III-8]:
"That which is present in a given object..."

[220] Regarding the two types of inference—those based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and those based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) exemplified by the cases of "the jar" and "there"—[the author], first illustrating the one based on similarity, states non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) with the words beginning "that which... [221].
By the phrase "that which has reached the conditions for apprehension"—meaning that which is visible—and "is not apprehended," the non-apprehension of the visible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) is restated.

Thus, it is established that [the object] is the domain of the conventional usage of "non-existent"—that is to say, it is to be conventionally designated as "non-existent. By this, the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent" is positively established.
Consequently, non-perception of the perceptible is stated to be invariably concomitant with the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent."

The meaning is that the visible object, being unperceived, is indeed fit for the conventional designation of "non-existent. Furthermore, the statement of the prover's necessity with respect to the probandum is the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*). To illustrate this very point, he provides an example...
The object, in its fitness for that, is the cognition; the senses are fit for it.
And if exclusion (vyatireka) were the thing to be expressed, how could inclusion (anvaya) come to be manifested? To this he says: "Inclusion" (anvaya);
for (hi) because...
It is consistent with the principle that will be established by the argument to be stated later, beginning with "Even by way of similarity" (*sādharmyeṇāpi hi*).

One might think: "The referents of two [expressions] being different, their meanings understood through implication (*sāmarthyagamyam*) must necessarily also differ—just as in the cases 'a hamlet on the Ganges' (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and 'the Garga family at the well' (*kūpe gargakulam*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
The word *ca* is used in the sense of "because.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the purpose for which a sentence is employed. He states the justification with the words "from restraint" (*yāmād*).
One sentence has as its expressed meaning the absence of eating during the day, while another has eating at night; thus, there is a difference in the expressed meanings of these two sentences.

Even though that difference exists, just as the fatness of Devadatta qualified by eating does not differ in what is to be established, so too here, the expressed meaning—characterized by the property of the subject in the positive form (*anvaya-pakṣadharmatā*) and characterized by the property of the subject in the negative form (*vyatireka-pakṣadharmatā*)—does not differ.
Even though there is a difference, that which is understood as one is called "non-different.
Now, if it is argued that what is conveyed is said to be understood through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*),
then that [implication] indeed differs between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

For instance, the eating at night is implied by the sentence prohibiting eating during the day, while the prohibition of eating during the day is implied by the sentence enjoining eating at night; likewise, in the case of the example under consideration, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is implied by the statement possessing the property of the probans (sādharmya), and the positive concomitance (anvaya) is implied by the statement possessing the dissimilar property (vaidharmya).

In brief: that which is the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*) of one [sentence] is the implied meaning (*gamyamāna*) of the other; and that which is the implied meaning of one is the expressed meaning of the other.
Therefore, how can it be said that the implied meaning of the two sentences is the same?
Why is it not stated?
Because here the word *gamyamāna* (being traversed) has another intended meaning.
For, by the word *gamyamāna*, both the denoted object (*abhidheya*) and that which is revealed by implication (*sāmarthyaprakāśya*) are indicated here.

However, that which is intended by the qualifier "merely being perceived as a pair" is one and the same in both the illustrative sentences— characterized by fatness caused by eating— and in the two sentences concerning the subject of the illustration— characterized by the mark (liṅga) consisting of the three features [of a valid reason], namely, presence in the similar class, absence from the dissimilar class, and subsistence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā); this is what must be understood.
Showing by way of an example that which possesses a common property (sādharmya) as its denotable object, he states non-apprehension (anupalabdhi).
The word "tāvat" indicates sequence.
As it has been said: "Pervasion (vyāpti) is either the necessary presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) there, or the presence of the pervaded (vyāpya) only there.
[Hetubindu-pṛṣṭha 53] The example (dṛṣṭānta) is the object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes pervasion.
To demonstrate that very point, he says: "Just as another.
This means that the example is something other than the subject (dharmin) of the thesis.
"Seen" means ascertained by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For a rabbit’s horn has not been made an object of the eye; rather, it is known through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the non-perception of the perceptible—to be fit for the conventional usage of "non-existent.
That which is the object of such conventional usage of non-existence, such as a rabbit’s horn, is described in that way.
For in the case of a rabbit’s horn and the like, the conventional usage of non-existence is established by valid cognition, being based solely on the non-perception of the perceptible.
Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) expressed by this statement must be understood from that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and of that pervasion...

[227] It should not be stated that "it is ascertained by direct perception" (pratyakṣeṇa niścitaḥ). [228] [This is because it is established by the means of proving pervasion (vyāpti). Having now explained the pervasion, he says "and it is not perceived" (nopalabhyate ca) in order to demonstrate that non-perception of the perceptible possesses the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva).
And that [term "non-perception"] should be understood here as well by repeating [the word] twice.
Therefore, the meaning is this: first, while illustrating the case of similarity (*sādharmyavat*), he states non-perception;
afterwards, while illustrating the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat*), he will speak [of it].

Thus, he first states non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and will later speak of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*). Now, one might object: "Since the Teacher himself has already provided examples for both the similar (*sādharmya*) and dissimilar (*vaidharmya*) cases here, why did Dharmottara provide them again—using the passage beginning with ‘whatever is produced’ (*yat kṛtakam*) and so forth—for both the similar and dissimilar cases? If this is asked:
This is not a fault;
for the similarity (sādharmya) called resemblance between the example and the subject to be proven,
as well as the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) called disparity, exist solely by way of the logical reason (*hetu*) and not in a general sense.

Otherwise, since similarity and dissimilarity exist in some form even in relation to a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), that [point] would not have been refuted; thus, that example was cited to demonstrate this.
It was not cited by the Teacher (Ācārya), yet it is said to have been "cited.
Therefore, even in this example of the Teacher's, it should be understood as being established solely on the basis of the reason (*hetu*).

The conventional usage regarding the non-existent (*asad-vyavahāra*) consists of the cognition "it is non-existent," the designation "it is non-existent," and unhesitating activity such as coming and going.
Since the non-perception of the perceptible has occurred, the fitness for the conventional usage of the non-existent is thereby established;
therefore, from that [reason].
The word "co" (ca) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
The intention is this: that which is restated (*anūdyate*) is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and that which is prescribed (*vidhīyate*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
And that which is the pervaded (vyāpya) is necessarily present in the pervader (vyāpaka);
thus, the sequence of restatement and injunction should be understood in the same way for what follows.
Now, when a proof-statement consisting of two members is to be shown, both the pervasion (vyāpti) and the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā) must be demonstrated.
Nor has pervasion (vyāpti) been demonstrated here; rather,
only the sequence of restatement and injunction has been shown, and the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) will be demonstrated [later].

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how will this statement of proof (sādhana) be complete?", he says: "Of the proof" (*sādhanasya*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. Now, one might object: "If the understanding of an imperceptible object is achieved, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is entirely useless; so why is it mentioned? To this he replies: "Pervasion" (*vyāpti*). Pervasion is characterized by the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*); that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which it is established—that is, ascertained—has its domain (*viṣaya*) therein.
A "region" (pradeśa) is a single part of the earth;
that very thing is distinguished from others, and thus it is a "particular" (viśeṣa), being one.
"In a particular location" means in one location;
"somewhere" refers to even a single location that is perceptible to the cognizer.
That alone is the locus for the conventional usage of "non-existence" which is perceptible to the cognizer, and nothing else.
"Having reached the conditions for apprehension" means being visible;
and how even a non-existent jar can have the status of not having reached the conditions for apprehension superimposed upon it has already been explained.

[229] Regarding perception (*pratyakṣa*): in order to demonstrate an application (*prayoga*) based on similarity for the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "Likewise, the application of the reason of essential nature is as follows: whatever is existent, all that is impermanent."

"Just as a jar, etc."—this is the formulation of the pure essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*). [III-9] "The formulation of the pure essential nature" means: just as [the formulation] of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), so too is the formulation of the essential reason one that possesses similarity (*sādharmya*). This is the meaning. "That which exists," etc.
The functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) ascertains the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

And that object, being seen and certain, is called by the term "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) according to the etymological derivation: it is that in which there is, as appropriate, a limit (*anta*)—meaning a conclusion (*avasāna*) regarding the probandum and the probans—and which is skillful in its domain of necessity and restriction. In order to explain precisely this, the Teacher said: [the following verse].

By this, the following intention is expressed: the example, by serving as the locus for the means of valid cognition that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), is an auxiliary factor for the comprehension of the pervasion that constitutes a member of the proof;
however, it is not so directly for the proof itself, nor for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*).
That statement also serves as a member of the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*) by way of reminding [the opponent] of that [reason];
for this very reason, it is said that the statement of the proof is both a member [of the syllogism] and something to be employed.
To the question "Why not anything else?", he says: "[Because it concerns] the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*)."

He clarifies that the meaning is "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) because things such as a rabbit's horn serve as examples by being the locus of the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
[An objection is raised: "But why not explain *dṛṣṭa* as 'known by the eye'? Why, then, is it explained in this way? To this he replies with the words "rabbit... and so forth.
The word "hi" means "because.

By employing the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the words "made an object" (*viṣayīkṛta*) and "cognized" (*vijñāta*), he demonstrates that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇa*) occurred previously.
To the question, "How then can things such as a hare's horn serve as an example by which that [pervasion] is explained? he says: "A hare... and so forth.
"Here" (*hir*) means "because.
"That which has as its cause only that [perception] which is the non-perception of the perceptible" (*tanmātra-tannimitta*) refers to such [an instance].
By this, he states that it takes the form of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because it serves as the locus for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

If it is asked: "What is that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which, when applied therein, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the absence of perception and the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence is established?
It is said in reply:

By the logic stated in the *Vādanyāya*, since the absence of cognition, designation, and so forth, serve as the causes for the conventional usage of "non-existent," and since no other cause exists, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) alone is the cause, independent of anything else.
Whatever has a specific cause arises only when that cause is present;
for example, a sprout, which has the mere collection of causes such as a seed, arises only when those are present.

Since the conventional usage of "non-existent" has the mere non-perception of the perceptible as its cause, the inference operating therein determines the pervasion between the probandum and the probans.

By this statement, beginning with "that which has reached the conditions for apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), that which is expressed and illuminated—namely, the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—is to be understood from that very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of inference (*anumāna*) mentioned immediately prior.
What is meant is this: the pervasion, already established by that [inferential] means of valid cognition, is merely being recalled by this statement.

With the words beginning with "svabhāva," he begins to explain the formulation of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) by way of similarity (*sādharmyavat*). The meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) is "without remainder" (*aśeṣatā*).
By that very [meaning] being established, the restriction—known as the dependence of the probans upon the probandum—is established.

Having restated the subject (*sattva*), its permanence is enjoined by the statement "all that is eternal"; and the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
Everything is eternal;
nothing is eternal.
Whatever exists is indeed non-eternal.

Because existence does not occur elsewhere than in impermanence—that is, in what is permanent—existence is thus shown to be restricted to impermanence when it is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). This being the case, the statement "just as a jar, etc. is the presentation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*); this is the description of the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the pervasion.
"Of the pure" means of the nature that is without qualification; this is the application [of the reason].

"Because of the contradiction of causal efficiency with respect to both permanence and succession or simultaneity" is the subverting proof (*viparyayabādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the pervasion—[as noted in the *ṭīkā*].
[232] To show the qualification of the application (*prayoga*) by means of a qualification of the "visible" (*dṛśya*), he says:
"Whatever has an origin is impermanent"—this is an application of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) through the differentiation of a property that constitutes its very nature. III-10
Regarding the phrase "that which has origination":
origination (*utpatti*) is the acquisition of its own nature (*svarūpalābha*); that which possesses this is "possessing origination" (*utpattimat*).
Having restated the state of possessing origination, the prescription of impermanence is made by stating, "that is impermanent."
And this being so, it is declared that having an origin is necessarily concomitant with impermanence.
That which is an origin, and that which has an origin— thus, "having an origin" (utpattimattva) is restated (anūdya).
That gain exists because it is a phenomenon whose nature is that of the causal process (*vidhi*) and which consists of that very essence.
By means of its distinction— that is,
taking its distinction as the reason— the formal argument is as follows:
for a thing is said to be "arisen" by relying on its exclusion from those things that have not arisen.
When that very exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is intended to be expressed as independent of any other exclusion, it is then indicated as if it were distinct— namely, "the arising of an entity.
And just as a thing is said to possess arising when it is qualified by an arising that appears to be distinct,
so too [is it designated] by means of a property that is actually its own nature (svabhāva), though a distinction is conceptually constructed between them.

[236] Although at the beginning Durveka himself accepted the reading "svabhāvabhūtaḥ" alone— as in the passage beginning with "svabhāvabhūtaḥ svabhāvātmakaḥ"— as the one favored by Dharmottara, nevertheless, since he has also accepted it here in the form "svabhāvaṃ bhūtaḥ," [the term] is to be understood as a future passive participle (bhāvin) in accordance with the commentary.

Being of the nature of intrinsic being (*svabhāvabhūta*)—[237] consisting of intrinsic being (*svabhāvātmaka*). Now, one might ask: "How can there be a distinction for that which is of the nature of intrinsic being? To this he says: [238] *ṭi-* (the commentary).
[239] "Existence" (bhāva) is said [to be so called].
[240] The inclusion of the term "all" (sarva) is for the purpose of making known the rule that a specific entity (vastu) comes into being.

"Otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be no remainder"— this clarifies the meaning of "all" and so forth. And "that being the case" refers to the manner of demonstrating that [the object] is restricted and is the domain of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

This statement, which consists of "whatever exists is impermanent," refers to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes pervasion (vyāpti). It should be understood as follows: for whatever [entity] there is an impossibility of successive or simultaneous action, there is no capacity whatsoever anywhere, just like a lotus in the sky;

and since this [impossibility of successive or simultaneous action] exists in the case of a non-momentary entity, there is the possibility of an inference based on the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha).
This is a matter of much discussion that has been elaborated elsewhere; it is not expanded upon here as it is not relevant to the present context.

But how can "origination" (*utpatti*) be a qualifier of the "entity" (*bhāva*)? To this he says: "its own-being" (*svabhāvam*). The word *bhūta* means "having attained" (*prāpta*), and the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the active sense. The compound is formed by the division of the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.24], *dvitīyā*, through a separation of the yoga.
The clarification of this very point is given by the phrase "consisting of that" (*tadātmaka*).
[An objection is raised: "If it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can it be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)?
For it is perceived as distinct [from the qualified]. To this, he says:
A specific intrinsic nature (svabhāva) should be understood as being employed [as the reason].

Regarding the statement "whatever is produced is impermanent" (III-11), by means of a distinction in its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*): having restated "producedness" in the phrase "whatever is produced," "impermanence" is predicated; thus, producedness is stated as being invariably concomitant with impermanence. Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of producedness by impermanence is demonstrated.
The connection is that there is an application of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by means of a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). A limiting condition is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that the intrinsic nature, qualified by a distinction—that is, by a distinct limiting condition—is applied.
[241] Regarding the reality of impermanence:
[242] here, sometimes the mere object itself is expressed, sometimes it is qualified by a non-distinct qualifier, and sometimes by a distinct one.
"Devadatta" is [the name of] a pure individual;
"long-eared" is distinguished by the two unseparated ears;
and "owner of a brindled cow" is distinguished by a brindled cow that is distinct [from himself].
In the same way, existence (*sattva*) is pure;
"having an origin" (*utpattimattva*) is a non-distinct qualification,
while "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is a distinct qualification.
[242] Regarding inference for others (*parārthānumāna*):
the word "of that" (*tasya*) refers to the qualifier, characterized by being distinct yet non-separate from the qualificand, as presented through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, the statement "a property (*dharma*) that has become its own nature (*svabhāva*), whose essence is its own nature," is stated with the intention of referring to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Showing that this third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), he says "bhedam" (by way of difference).

Having made the difference established by conventional usage—the distinctness from the producer—the reason (*hetu*), and having made it the basis (*nibandhana*), there is the formal argument (*prayoga*) of a qualified essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), according to the context.

To the question, "Even through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), how is there a difference such that [the entity] is said to be 'possessing origination' as distinguished by origination? he says: "from those not yet originated."
"Since" (hir) means:

having relied upon—that is, having conceptually constructed—the exclusion or differentiation from unarisen things such as space; if an arisen entity is spoken of by relying on such exclusion, then how can the formulation "how is there its arising? be applied? To this he says: "That very [exclusion]."
When another exclusion, such as "largeness" (*mahattva*) and so forth, is intended to be expressed independently of that [prior exclusion], then the meaning is as follows:

the application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is for that which is qualified by a non-distinct qualifier—an exclusion consisting in being a different object (*arthāntaratva*) that is conceptually constructed or superimposed (*samāropita*) by means of a property called "origination" (*utpatti*), which is its own ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). This is the sense.
Previously, there was the employment of a nature (*svabhāva*) qualified by a non-distinct qualification;
now, however, it is [the employment] of one qualified by a distinct qualification—this is the difference, which he states with the words "by a distinct [qualification].
Alternatively, it means "by one distinct" from the previous, that is, of a different kind, being included [in the cognition] by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
But it is not [denoted] by its own existing designator;
for this very reason, this application is distinguished from others.
"Here" refers to the employment of words for the purpose of communicating to another.

"Pure" means without qualification. Now, is it the case that a single entity is sometimes seen by the learned to be used as qualified by an inseparable adjunct (*avyatiriktopādhi*), and sometimes as qualified by a separate qualification (*vyatiriktaviśeṣaṇa*), such that when it is spoken of in this way, it nourishes the opponent's position? To this he says: "Devadatta."
In this context, the word *yadvat* should be understood as being equivalent to the word *tadvat* which is about to be mentioned.
Since it is both variegated (*citrā*) and a cow (*gauḥ*), the suffix *ṭac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.92, *gor ataddhitaluki*;
because the suffix is marked with *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and [the compound] is qualified by that [word].
The application of the example and the illustrated point should be made exactly in that order.
Thinking that there is no similarity between the word "citrabhu" (the painting-master) and the word "kṛtaka" (produced), the opponent says: "But surely... [nanu ca].
This is because the operation of causes is their necessary prior existence, since there exists no operation distinct from that.
But is it not the case that what was said—that in the word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) there is no word expressing a qualifier—remains exactly as it was? To this he says: "Even though...
(*yady api*). "Included" (*antarbhāvita*) means manifested. How so? [DhPr p. 159]
Now, one might object: in the word *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), there exist the words *citra* and *go*, which express distinct qualifiers;

however, in the word *kṛtaka* ("produced"), there is the employment of a term that expresses nothing other than the thing itself without any qualifier. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For an entity whose operation depends on something else is called 'produced' (*kṛtaka*) with respect to the accomplishment of its own nature" (III-12).

"Dependent" (*apekṣita*) means that the operation of other causes is required for the accomplishment of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That which requires the operation of others for the sake of its accomplishment is described as such.
The particle "hi" is used in the sense of emphasis (*yasmāt*).
Because that which depends upon the operation of another is called "produced" (*kṛtaka*), therefore its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is said to be qualified by a distinct qualifier.
Even if a separate word for the qualifier is not employed, nevertheless, by the word "produced" itself, the distinct qualifier is already included.
For this very reason, this word "produced" is a type of technical designation (*saṃjñā*), since the suffix *-kan* is prescribed here in the sense of a name.
And where a qualification is included within [the meaning], the word expressing that qualification is not employed;
nor is it employed when the qualification is internalized.
In some cases, however, the qualifier is understood; for instance, when "done" is said, the phrase "by causes" is understood.
In that case, the word "cause" may sometimes be employed, or it may not be employed at all.
In some cases, the cause itself is thus; other factors such as being differentiated by a variety of conditions should also be understood in this way. III-13
[247] And when its own term is employed, it is like the term "difference of conditions" within the phrase "distinguished by the difference of conditions" [248].

In both of these two types of formal argument (prayoga), the statement of the thesis (pakṣanirdeśa) is not necessarily required. III-34 [354]:

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of a statement of the probandum (*sādhya*), how could there be an understanding of it, such that its non-statement would be possible?"—he says: "That which... (*yad iti*).
"Fixed to the probandum" means being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvin*).
This is understood through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Precisely from that proof (*sādhana*), when it is observed within the subject (*dharmin*) which is the locus of dispute and has been apprehended by valid cognition, there arises the realization of the probandum—the composite of the property (*dharma*) and the subject (*dharmin*).
This is what is meant: [the reason] must be stated by one who intends to convey a meaning already understood.

Śaṅkarācārya, in the passage beginning with "In the case of God as the cause... a distinction would be perceived," provides the answer that the statement of the probandum (*sādhyavacana*) is for the purpose of eliminating contradictory doubts;
for the meaning of that passage is as follows: if the statement of the probandum were absent, [one might think] that whatever is produced is entirely impermanent.
Just as... from some cause of error such a statement of pervasion might be possible;
or, if the speaker were of such an intention while employing the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), he might state its pervasion by permanence (*nityatā*).
That is incorrect.
For one who asserts the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between those two [the probans and the probandum] might say:

...he too must be regarded as a proponent of a contradictory position.

One might show the pervasion [of the reason] in a jar that is indeed similar to a pot due to its deficiency;

In that case, there is a deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) in the jar, and a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the pot; yet one might still be confused even regarding a pot similar to a jar,

"It is determined by that [means of knowledge].

For no proponent of a proof ceases after merely stating the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*).
What then? He also employs the conclusion (*nigamana*): "Therefore, sound is impermanent.
And when this has been stated, how could there be any suspicion of permanence?
For what reason would there be a contradiction regarding the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*)?
Furthermore, since the elimination of the suspicion of contradiction has already been accomplished by the conclusion (*nigamana*) itself, the statement of the example (*udāharaṇa*) is purposeless.
As Akṣapāda said: "The conclusion is for the purpose of eliminating the suspicion of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*)."
Likewise, it follows that the statement of the reason (hetu) would also fail to arise.
If it is argued that there is no confidence in the conclusion (nigamana),
then alas, the lack of confidence is equally present in the statement of the proposition (pratijñā).
Whatever resolution is provided there [in the *upanaya*] will also apply to the *nigamana*.

Therefore, even according to that view, since the intended probandum (*sādhya*) is understood from the *nigamana* alone, there is no need to employ a statement of dependence for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding contradiction.
Thus, it is as if someone were [to try to illuminate] with the flame of his own finger...
The account arose that one who desires to burn another may or may not burn him,
but first experiences the burning of his own finger.
What was cited here as the word of Akṣapāda does not exist in the *Nyāyasūtra*, but rather in the *Vārttika*.
“The restatement that is made for the purpose of negating the undesirable consequence that is the opposite of what is to be proven is the conclusion (*nigamana*); this is understood [from the sūtra].
If it is argued that, in this case, the conclusion would also result in being meaningless, let this be another fault.

How indeed do the Tathāgatas triumph? It is said that when the conclusion (*nigamana*) alone exists, there is no need to state the thesis (*pakṣa*), because the removal of doubts regarding contradiction is accomplished by the conclusion itself.

Trilocana, moreover, stated this in his *Nyāyabhāṣyaṭīkā*: "The statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not a statement that is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), because in debates, regarding the comprehension of another, no restriction on the formulation [of arguments] is possible;
for the comprehensions of others are unstable due to their being sharp, dull, and so forth."
For instance, some person understands from the statement of the reason alone;

however, another person, even without the statement of the reason, follows the speaker’s intended meaning simply by reflecting on the nature of the speaker—perceiving the activity of the lips and other articulatory organs prior even to the production of the sound.

Therefore, this knower, having no regard for the understanding of another, [communicates] the object residing in his own cognition while explaining it to that [other], [an object] which has been mounted upon his own cognition.
In this very way, he demonstrates the meaning in the application of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*):
"this."

Because even in an application based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*), when it is stated: "That which, being capable of being perceived (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is not perceived, is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāraviṣaya*);
and here, a jar that meets the conditions for perception is not perceived," it follows by the very force of this statement that "there is no jar here. Thus, the object is established.

"Thus, it is the object of the conventional designation of non-existence"—this is the affirmation of its fitness for the conventional designation of non-existence.
And this being the case, the non-perception of what is perceptible is established. Anu-...
One ought to employ a word that is expressive.

Therefore, since the opponent must be made to understand the object residing in [one's] own cognition, that [logical mark] alone is the means for the other person.
This clamor of the Kārpaṭikas and Karṇāṭas is not to be believed by the wise.
For instance— it is true that an object already established through one's own realization is indeed what is communicated to another.
Let this alone be considered: whether that object is established by the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) together with the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or not.

If it is established, what purpose is served by stating that which has already been understood? For one who denies the comprehension of that [object] from those very words—[such a person would be] denying [the fact].
But there is nothing at all that is called "unconcealed.
Otherwise, how could there be comprehension at the time of inference for oneself without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)?

And since at the time of one's own comprehension the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) arose from as many factors as were present, those very same words must be employed even at the time of inference for others.
And in that case, the cognition of the probandum did not arise from first perceiving the subject as qualified by the property to be made known, followed by the perception of the reason and so forth.

What then? It arose from the perception of the property in the subject (pakṣadharma), accompanied by the recollection of its invariable concomitance (avinābhāva); therefore, it is only this much that is logically consistent to state.
Now, it might be argued that because the cognitions of others vary according to whether they are sharp or dull, there can be no fixed rule for the formulation [of the syllogism].
What has been said is true; however, it is merely intended to incite an action that leads to one's own destruction.

For, since there are many types of cognizers—distinguished by being acute, dull, and so forth—it may well be that some person does not understand what is to be communicated unless the five-membered syllogism is employed preceded by statements of doubt, desire to know, and the like.
Thus, because that statement must necessarily be employed and constitutes a constituent part [of the argument], the five-membered nature of the proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*) is established;
and if this is accepted, it applies to the persons of Gauḍa, Kāśmīra, and others.
The narrative, a source of curiosity, unfolds:

according to the established position of the treatise, the five members—proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*)—constitute the parts [of a syllogism]; thus, even a deviation from tenets (*apasiddhānta*) restrains him like a king of fierce command.

Now, is there any possibility for this, wherein, when the probandum (*sādhya*) or the means of proof (*sādhana*) has been stated, and the example has been pointed out, and even after the application has been made and the conclusion reached—all the functions of the members having been performed?
Is it that one does not understand the probandum (*sādhya*)?
But surely, is there any possibility for this cognizer as well, such that— having been made to understand the means of proof (*sādhana*) regarding a given subject (*dharmin*),
and having even been reminded of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*) with the probandum— he would still not comprehend the probandum therein?
If it is argued that this is possible due to dullness of intellect, we reply:
all of this is the same, except for the difference in dogmatic attachment; so enough with further elaboration.

By the statement beginning with "It is shown to be pervaded by fitness for the conventional usage of 'existent' (sadvyavahāra-yogyatva), and yet it is not perceived," the presence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) has been demonstrated. Furthermore,
if the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) were not present there in that subject of the thesis, the property serving as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*) would likewise not be present.
This is because that property of the means of proof is necessarily restricted to the probandum; such is its logical capacity.

[362] And likewise, in the formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat-prayoga*) as well: whatever is the object of the conventional usage of "existent" and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived.
When it is stated, "In this case, such a jar is not perceived," it follows by implication alone that "it is not an object of the conventional usage of existence here.

Nor is it the case that, as in the formulation with similarity (*sādharmya*), so too in the formulation with dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), it is only by implication that "the jar is not an object of the conventional usage of existence here" comes to be understood. III-36 [363–364]
In order to demonstrate the capacity of the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), he says: "That which is the object of the conventional usage of existence" means that which is present;
"having reached the conditions for perception" means that which is visible. This is the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*).
"It is indeed perceived" means that the reason (*sādhana*) is absent;
by this, it is shown that the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is pervaded by the absence of the reason.
"Not so"—that is, just as another visible object is perceived elsewhere, such a visible jar is not perceived here in this location.
By this, it is shown that the absence of the pervader—the absence of the probandum—is non-existent in the locus of the probandum.
For if the property to be proven were not present in the locus of the probandum, the proving property would also not exist.
Sa—omitted.
[366] And—omitted;
by this, [367] it is not the case that the probans would not exist in the subject of the thesis (*sādhya-dharmin*).
[368] It would exist in the subject of the thesis.

Furthermore, Viśvarūpa and Uddyotakara, in their *Nyāyabhāṣya-ṭīkā* and *Vārttika*, state: "In the past, it was observed that the operation of an instrument is necessarily preceded by the determination of its object;
and an instrument is a means (*sādhana*)."
It must be set in motion;
therefore, the determination of the object is performed by means of the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*),
because otherwise it would be impossible to operate the instrument.
[369] That too is not tenable;
for if it is maintained that when one employs a reason (*hetu*), the object to be proven must be examined and introduced into the intellect,
then our very admission [of this requirement] constitutes the answer.
For no one indeed utters a statement of proof for the sake of another's understanding without first ascertaining the probandum themselves.
Now, if it is thought that the object of the logical reason— the instrument— must be shown by means of words,
then what is the purpose of showing it by that very [statement] alone?
"If the cognition of another were not otherwise, everything would be well"—this is the reply; so what is the point of this excessive grinding of what is already crushed?
[369] It is not found in the *Nyāyavārttika*.
However, Saṃadhyayana stated this in the *Ruciṭīkā*: "The subject qualified by its property (*dharmin* with *dharma*) is pointed out for the sake of providing reassurance to the listener."
However, it is not logical to indicate at the outset a subject qualified by its property; for that [qualified subject] is not observed when [the property] is being cognized.
Therein, one perceives a mere location and the property residing therein;
then one recollects their invariable concomitance (avinābhāva), and immediately thereafter, one reflects upon it as "this is that very same thing."
From that, one realizes the excellence of the location, but not from the very beginning;
and the consideration [of the object] is preceded by its own specific purpose.

Furthermore, there is no perception of a subject (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma) for its own sake; therefore, it serves no purpose even in the case of comprehension. Nevertheless, it is performed at the outset.
"Regarding the phrase 'for the purpose of producing this in that which is to be established':
the capacity [of the reason] consists in the fact that the property to be proven (sādhanadharma) indeed exists [in the subject]. [DhPr 176]

Therefore, by implication, because there is the cognition "there is no jar here," there is no explicit statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*). Likewise, for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), there is no statement of the thesis because it follows by implication; thus, from that implication, [the thesis is understood].
What kind of thing, moreover, is to be designated as the "thesis" (*pakṣa*)? The thesis is that which is to be designated. (III-37) The thesis is the object of designation.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "thesis" (*pakṣa*)—by which term it should be defined? To this he says:
"A thesis is that which is intended by oneself in its own form and is not refuted" (III.38). [373] "Intended" means...
Thus, "to be indicated by its own nature" means [to be indicated] precisely as that which is to be proven;
"by oneself" means by the proponent.
"Intended" (iṣṭa) means not only what has been explicitly stated, but also what is intended;
being thus, an object that is not refuted by perception and the other means of valid cognition is called the "thesis" (pakṣa).
If that which has been established as the meaning is not to be specified as a thesis, how can a definition of what is unspecifiable be stated?

The definition of this [pakṣa] was not stated because it is a member of the syllogistic argument (sādhanavākya); rather, some maintain that what is not to be proven (asādhya) is to be proven (sādhya), while others maintain that what is to be proven is not to be proven.
Therefore, the definition of the thesis (pakṣa) was stated for the purpose of removing such misconceptions regarding what is to be proven and what is not to be proven.
[376] Now, if there is no thesis, [377] nothing whatsoever— [378] nothing whatsoever. — om.
The explanation of the phrase "desired by its own nature" (svarūpeṇeṣṭa) is as follows:
"by its own nature" means "desired as that which is to be accomplished" (sādhyatvena iṣṭaḥ). This is stated in verse III-39.
Thus, [the term] "desired as that which is to be accomplished."
Since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), there is no other form [for it];
therefore, its own nature (*svarūpa*) is its state of being the probandum.
To explain the word "only" (*eva*), he says:
"By its very nature" means it is intended solely as that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), and not also as a means of proof (*sādhana*). Thus,
"intended by its very nature" refers to being intended precisely as the probandum.
But surely the word *eva* alone should be referred back; for what purpose, then, is the word *svarūpa* used?
How, then, has that poor fellow spoken so much in a coherent manner?
What is the purpose served merely by generating confidence in the cognizer?
And how is it correctly established that this [confidence] is produced from the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) which expresses a matter about which there is doubt?
For "confidence" (*āsthā*) is indeed the firm conviction that "I think this is the very object."
How could that [inference] arise from mere words? Or, if it were already born, how could the statement of the proof (*sādhana*) and so forth not be rendered useless? Enough of this prolixity.
Here, by virtue of the context, the word "himself" (*svayam*) is explained as meaning "by the proponent," but it does not mean that the word "himself" is [identical to] "the proponent.
This will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
Is it considered together with the reflective awareness (*pratyavamṛṣṭa*)? It is said:
the word *eva* is a particle (*nipāta*) that functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*).

It is not [mentioned] as a means (*sādhana*) either.
That which is mentioned as a means is intended as a means.
And because it is unestablished, it is also intended as something to be proven;
the word "only" (eva) is used precisely for the purpose of excluding that.
Because of this, he provides an illustration for the sake of the point to be proven: [382]—
Just as when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is a reason that is itself to be proven because it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in sound;
yet, in this case, it is not intended as something to be proven.
Because it is designated as the means of accomplishment (sādhana), and because it is also designated as that which is intended to be accomplished (sādhya).

Regarding "yathā" (as): when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, the property of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) is a reason that is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to sound; therefore, by this [statement], he says that it is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*). Regarding "yathā":
the word "tad" (that) refers to the property of being visible.
The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the term [in question].
By stating "only as that which is intended to be proven" (*sādhyatvenaiveṣṭam*), he expresses the absence of a restriction that it must be intended solely as something to be proven (*sādhya*).
[He says] "because it is expressed as a means of proof" (*sādhanatvena abhidhānāt*); that is, because it has been stated as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
Therefore, it is intended as a means of proof (sādhana) as well,
and not solely as that which is to be proven (sādhya).
Having introduced the word *svayam* as that which is to be explained by the term "itself," he states its meaning:
"by the proponent" (*vādinā*) in III-42. The particle *svayam* refers to both the genitive form *ātmanaḥ* (of oneself) and the instrumental form *ātmanā* (by oneself).
Thus, in this context, the word *svayam* is used in the sense of the word *ātman* ending in the third case;
and the word *ātman* is a relative term,
while the proponent (*vādī*) is its proximate correlate.
Therefore, that disputant whose self (*ātman*) is connected with the third meaning is the one indicated by the disputant as being "connected with the third meaning";
however, the word *svayam* ("himself") is not a synonym for the word "disputant" (*vādin*).

In the passage beginning with "desires his own destruction" (nāśaṃ svayam icchati), the meaning is that he desires the destruction of himself— [as stated in] Ṭīkā 387— being joined with the sense of that [verb], it is proximate to that which belongs to him.
[389] It is indeed endowed with the third sense;
[390] — omits [391] — surely not.
Of the subject, which is the object of inference.
The instrumental case in the word *svarūpaśabdena* is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).
The term "it is said" refers to the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*).
He says "because it is unestablished" (*asiddhatvāt*) to address the question: "How can that which is intended as a means of proof (*sādhana*) also be intended as the probandum (*sādhya*)?
The word "and" (*ca*) means "because.
The collective meaning is this: even when something intended as the probandum is stated as a means of proof, it is then not the subject (*apakṣa*); such is the function of the particle *eva*.
Who, then, is this proponent? He says: it is he who at that time states the proof (sādhana). III-43
"Whoever at that time"—that is, at the time of debate—states the proof (*sādhana*).
Even though there may be many debaters, this is a qualification of the debater who is denoted by the word "himself" (*svayam*). When there is such a possibility, [the word] "himself" [is used].
It has been stated: "If that is so, the probandum (sādhya) is what is intended by the proponent.
What is meant by this statement?
By this, it is said that at the time of the debate, whatever property (*dharma*) that proponent himself intends to prove is alone the probandum, and no other property.
The fruit of this statement is, in short, the exclusion of the probandum being a property not desired by the proponent.
[393] If indeed [394] by this [395] it has been stated that the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) is [the subject], and not the other.
[396] Dharma—om.

Now, it must be stated: given what being present is there the possibility of being established by another property (*anyadharma*), such that its cessation is required? To this he says: [397] —and this is for the sake of the goal (*artha*).

By this, even if one states a proof while remaining within a particular treatise, although the author of that treatise may accept many properties regarding that subject (*dharmin*), it is only that property which the proponent himself intends to prove at that time that is established by him as the probandum.
Therefore, because it functions with two meanings;
the word "himself" (*svayaṃ*) is understood as being included here in the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*).
The meaning to be conveyed by the instrumental case here is the state of being the agent of the seeking (*eṣaṇa*).
Because, in the expression "desired by oneself" (ātmanā iṣṭa), the third case ending is prescribed for the agent.
"Even though there may be many disputants"— that is, even though there may be a plurality of proponents such as those who maintain that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇa*)—
and "disputancy" (*bāditva*) is understood here by way of functional capacity (*yogyatā*),
rather than referring at that time to those who actually compose formal arguments (*vāda*) characterized by speech for the purpose of establishing or refuting one's own or another's position.
The qualifier is that which excludes; this refers to the statement of what is not a means of proof.
"If it were so," says the opponent.
And this collection of particles occurs at the beginning of an undesirable consequence.
The phrase "by this statement" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To the objection, "Let it be stated thus; what fault is there?", he replies with the words "by this.
The word *ca* has the sense of *api*.
If it is argued that what is desired by the author of the treatise is also desired by the proponent,
and therefore what excellence has been established by this [definition], the intention of the questioner is as follows:
"By this" refers to the established tenet (*siddhānta*) and so forth.
By this, [it is meant] by the word "himself" (*svayam*) as delimited by the qualification "who at that time states the proof" (*sādhanam āha*).
This is what is being said:
even when a proponent states a proof in some cases by virtue of his acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra-abhyupagama*), [it is still considered his own].

If the author of that treatise intended only as much as was desired therein, and if he intended that very thing to be the probandum (*sādhya*), then it would simply be "intended by him" (*iṣṭam*); it would not be "intended by himself" (*svayam iṣṭam*).

"Not otherwise" (*netarat*) means that what is intended by the author of that treatise—such as [the property] "being a quality of space" (*ambaraguṇatva*)—is what remains in the mind [of the opponent].
The term "vādinaḥ" (of the proponent) is a clarification of the very first [term].
It has been stated by the author of that treatise that only what is intended is the probandum (sādhya), and not anything else. III-44.

Regarding the treatise that has been accepted by that proponent: when the author of that treatise accepts many properties within that subject (*sādhyadharmin*), there arises the possibility of proving other properties as well.

For instance, there is a misconception that "whatever property is established by a treatise accepted by someone, all such properties must be proven by him. This [definition] excludes that [misconception].
Even though many properties may be present, that alone is what is to be proven which is intended by the proponent, and nothing else; thus,
it is established as such among those many properties.
But is it not the case that the logical mark (*liṅga*) functions by the power of the real entity (*vastubalapravṛtta*) independently of treatises?
Therefore, since it is not dependent [on them], one should not conduct a debate while remaining within a treatise.
True.

However, even if someone, out of self-importance (*āhopuruṣikā*), has adhered to some treatise and accepted a certain system of thought, and thus states a proof, it is nevertheless said here [in this context] in order to make it known that whatever is desired by that person is precisely what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
[401] Because of identity and origination from that— [402] that very thing is what is [403] being proven of it.
Introducing the word "iṣṭa" (intended), he explains:

"The intended" refers to that object regarding which a proof has been presented amidst dispute; by one who desires its establishment, even if not explicitly stated in words, that object is the *sādhya* (that which is to be proven). III-45 That object is...

Where a contradictory discourse has been introduced regarding a certain object— such as the discourse denying the self, "The self does not exist," which is contradictory to the discourse asserting the existence of the self because affirmation and negation are mutually exclusive—

the proponent who, by means of that dispute as the reason, presents a proof desiring the establishment and ascertainment of that object, has indicated by the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) that such an object is the "probandum" (*sādhya*).
The apprehension at the end, namely "that which was said to be 'thus spoken'," must be taken into account here to complete the sentence.
Even though in the case of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the probandum (*sādhya*) has already been stated, the sentence must be brought to completion.
Even though it is not explicitly stated by words, it is nonetheless to be proven,
because it is implied by the force of the argument.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "nevertheless.
There exists a misconception—namely, a view contrary to reason—held by some;
this is set aside by means of this qualification of the self.

He concludes with the phrase "by one who asserts many [properties]. Even when there is the acceptance of multiple properties by the author of the treatise—that is, even when there is the acceptance of multiple properties regarding that subject (*dharmin*)—he employs the word *svayam* ("himself") as a term standing for the meaning of the genitive case ending in *vādinaḥ* ("of the proponent"). Thus, he means "of himself."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* here denotes the agent (*kartari*), meaning "accepted out of self-conceit" (*āhopuruṣikayā*).

"Contradictory" (*viruddha*) refers to a statement that presents a meaning opposite to what is intended by the opponent; it is a speech for the sake of establishing one's own position and disproving that of the other. "Engaged" (*prakrānta*) means set in motion.
Regarding the phrase "it is said," since this is not heard here, one asks: "How is it explained in this way? To which he replies: "That which... (*yat tad*).
And this is a common proverbial saying:
"In this explanation of the desired term, one must bring it to completion and make the meaning coherent."
To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
"Because that is the locus of the dispute" (III-46).
“*Tat*”: that object (*artha*) is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the basis (*āśraya*) of which; that is “having that as its locus” (*tad-adhikaraṇa*), namely the dispute (*vivāda*).
The state of being that is its “nature” (*tattva*). “From that” means from that [nature].
[The phrase] beginning with “*tat*” refers to that.
This is what is meant: since a proof has been presented by a proponent who wishes to refute a dispute, therefore that very locus of the dispute is the probandum (*sādhya*).
For if that which was presented as a proof in order to remove a contradictory position were not the probandum, then what could possibly be the probandum fixed by its own nature? [408]
[408] In the world, that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*) in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is necessarily accepted, even if it is not explicitly stated.
[409] He illustrates this:
The desired is the "exalted" (*udāra*); the probandum is called the "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*).
For example: "The eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another, because they are composite, like the parts of a bed, a seat, and so on."
[410] Here, even though "for one's own sake" is not explicitly stated, being for one's own sake is what is to be proven.
[411] Thus, it is stated that it is not merely what has been said that constitutes the probandum (sādhya).
III-47 [410] Thus, "for one's own sake" is not mentioned.
By that [means], one's own welfare is accomplished;
by this [other means],
the welfare of others is accomplished.
Those things beginning with the ear which have the eye and so forth as their [components] are the "eye and so forth"—this is the subject (*dharmin*).
"These are for the sake of another" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), namely, being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
"Because they are composites" (*saṅghātatvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*).
And the demonstration of the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is "like the members of a bed, a seat, and so forth.
A bed, a seat, and those which are their "beginnings" constitute "bed-and-seats-and-the-rest"; these are aggregates that serve as the instruments for a person's enjoyment.

Similarly, in this proof, although the fact that the eyes and other faculties exist for the sake of a self (*ātman*) has not been explicitly stated, the fact of existing for the sake of a self is nonetheless the probandum (*sādhya*), even though it remains unstated.
[412] *te* — omitted. [413] *ca* — omitted. [414] that which has "ādi" as its beginning.
In the same way, regarding what is not stated here in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): although it is not stated,
it is nonetheless not unspoken by virtue of the statement.
Even though it has not been brought directly within the scope of the function of denotation by the word itself,
the particle *tu* serves to illuminate a distinction:
that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) is indeed only [the object] to be proven.
Why is this so? He says: because that [subject], such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which resides in the mind, has been stated by implication (*sāmarthya*).
This is what is meant: in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the object stated is the probandum (*sādhya*);
and "stated" means that which is manifested.
And being manifested occurs both through being the direct object of the operation of denotation and through being the object of implication (*sāmarthya*).
Furthermore, "having been stated" (*uktatā*), which is termed "being manifested," is common to both without distinction.
To the question "Whence is this so?", the author of the Vārttika states the reason as being "stated by implication":
for instance, it was said by the Sāṃkhya— “The self exists.”
That [position] was stated by the Buddhist to be contradictory: "There is no self.

Therefore, the Sāṅkhya, taking the Buddhist doctrine—which contradicts his own doctrine—as the reason (*hetu*), has presented a proof (*sādhana*) for the purpose of refuting the contradictory doctrine and establishing his own doctrine.
Consequently, even though it is not explicitly stated, the fact that the self is the object [of the inference] is the probandum (*sādhya*).
Because that is the basis of the dispute:
for in the case of beds, seats, and so forth—which are the instruments of human enjoyment—the connection with the self as their purpose is not established;
however, the fact of being a composite is established merely by its being for the sake of another.

Therefore, it is said that they are for the sake of others (*parārtha*). [417] — Even though not explicitly stated—[418] that which has the discourse refuting the self (*ātmapratiṣedhavāda*) as its subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*)... [419] — Ṭīkā.
[419] In matters such as beds and so forth, [420] it is well known as being for the sake of another [421] because its purpose is for the benefit of others.

In the phrase "the eyes and so forth for the sake of another," by the inclusion of "and so forth," visual consciousness and the others are also intended to be established as being for the sake of another;
and that which is other than consciousness must be the self itself.
[422] In the view of the Buddhists, since the nature of an atom is consciousness (*jñāna*), it follows that [the eye and so forth] possess a composite nature (*sāṅghātarūpatva*).—

Note [423]— Thinking that by implication the eyes and other [faculties] will be established as having their own benefit (*ātmārthatva*) through the fact that consciousness accomplishes the purpose of another, the term "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*) was employed. [424] Therefore, what was stated does not merely express that which is already accepted or already proven.

Rather, because it is the subject of dispute for the opponent, that which is intended to be established by the proponent— whether explicitly stated or unstated, but understood from the context— is what is called the "probandum" (sādhya).
[423] Of another — om.
[424] The statement of the probandum — [425] by the proponent.

Although the dispute is rooted in that [notion], nevertheless, the object (*artha*) that serves as the locus for the cessation of the operation of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāraviśrāmabhūmi*) is precisely what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Nor is the self (*ātman*) and so forth the subject of the dispute.
Anticipating the objection—"Since such a thing does not exist, how can it be proven?"—he says: "This is what is meant."

That which is the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the locus (*āspada*) of dispute—namely, the mutually contradictory discourse consisting of "this exists" and "this does not exist," concerning the self (*ātman*) and so forth.
Here he states the justification: "since" (*yataḥ*). [He means:
since there is no contradictory discourse, such as "this does not exist," which opposes one's own position.
If that [subject] were not the object for the presentation of reasons intended to remove contradictory assertions, and if it were neither the probandum nor what one wished to make known,

then, under this assumption, what kind of thing— whether restricted by its genus (*jāti*), restricted by the genus of being a probandum, or subject to its class— could possibly be fit to be the probandum?
Because of the use of *kim* in the sense of censure, the meaning "nothing at all" remains established.
Even though it is not explicitly stated— that is, even though it is not the direct object of the operation of denotation—
it [is understood] because it is a composite and possesses multiple forms;
furthermore, this should be regarded as independent of any specific time.

In that sequence, or simultaneously, that [collection] is "combined"; thus, even consciousness (*vijñāna*), which has a combined form, possesses multiple forms sequentially. Therefore, since the state of being a combination is established there as well, that too must be included as the subject (*dharmin*) by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
For this very reason, it will be stated immediately after: "Here, by the word 'etcetera,' consciousness also [is included]."
Otherwise, even if the fact that the eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another— namely, consciousness— is established, the Sāṃkhya's intended point would not be proven;
for this would follow by implication even if it were not explicitly stated.
In some places, however, there is a reading where "for its own sake" (*ātmārthatā*) is not mentioned;
in that case, the connection is made through straightforwardness (*ārjava*).
The sense is that because it has been introduced as the subject matter due to the presentation of the means of proof (*sādhana*), the word "its" (*tasyāḥ*) refers to that [thesis].

The phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth explains this very point. Having made it the cause (*hetu*) and having made it the sign (*nimitta*), the word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the result (*phala*); even though it is not explicitly stated, it should be understood as before.
If this were his intention, then why does he not simply say "for their own sake"? Anticipating this objection, he says "śayanādi" in order to show the specific intention with which he spoke thus.
The particle *hi* has the sense of "because.
[DhPr 182]

"Uncontradicted" (anirākṛta): This is for the purpose of demonstrating that even when a subject possesses these defining characteristics, if the intended object to be proven is contradicted by perception, inference, common consensus, or one's own statement, it is not a valid thesis (pakṣa). III-48 [426] Thesis (pakṣa) — demonstration.
The term "unrefuted" (*anirākṛta*) is to be explained as follows:

although the definition previously introduced— namely, that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*) and so forth— is present here, the inclusion of the word "unrefuted" is made for the purpose of demonstrating and establishing that even when joined with this definition, such a case does not constitute a valid thesis (*pakṣa*).

In order to demonstrate [the point] beginning with "because it is intended as the probandum" (sādhyatveneṣṭatvāt), he states what kind of object is not a *pakṣa*, even if it is intended to be proven: "that object which is intended to be proven..."
Perception, inference, common consensus, and one's own word—by these it is refuted;
that which is contradicted is not a valid thesis.
That which is to be proven by them is not a valid thesis (*pakṣa*) in that case, just like that which is refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣanirākṛta*).

Regarding the statement "sound is inaudible" (III-49), the word *tatra* refers to those four [types of objects] refuted by perception and so forth. What is the nature of that which is refuted by perception? The meaning of the word *yathā* is: "just as this one is refuted by perception, so too should the others be understood."
That which is to be heard is grasped by means of hearing when it has been produced; that which is not to be heard is "unhearable" (*aśrāvaṇa*).
The meaning of the proposition is that "it is not to be grasped by the ear.
The quality of being ungraspable by the ear in the case of sound is contradicted by its being graspable by the ear, which is established through direct perception.

[432] Regarding the phrase "to be grasped by auditory cognition"—is it not the case that the eyes and so forth will be established as having the eye-consciousness and other cognitions as their purpose? How, then, is it established that they have the self as their purpose? To this he says: "The eyes and so forth," and so on.
Nevertheless, he asks, "From where is its establishment? and replies, "And from consciousness" (*vijñānāc ca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) means "because.

Then, having raised the doubt—"If consciousness itself is the subject (*dharmin*), how is the establishment of its being for the sake of a self (*ātmārthatā*) achieved?"—he says "of another" (*parasya*) in order to clarify it.
