Thinking that the fact that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of the self would be established by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the Sāṃkhya made the inclusion of the term "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*); this is understood from the context, or else it is supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

Since it is also possible for them to have the nature of being objects of cognition, one might suspect that their capacity is established as a single [entity]. Anticipating this, the word "of the other" (*parasya*) should be supplied.
It should be understood that cognition (*vijñāna*) also performs a function—that is, it serves a purpose.
The intention of one who says "it will be established" is as follows:

by the word "and so forth" (ādi), when it is to be proven that even consciousness is likewise [of such a nature], the meaning is that consciousness, which acts for the sake of others, will be established.
The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
By this, the capacity of the eyes and other [senses] to establish that they exist for the sake of a self has been demonstrated.

The explanation of the root term "by that" (*tena*) is given by the phrase "by the statement of the means of accomplishing what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanavacanena*), which refers to that which has been made the object of the proponent's desire to prove.
Showing that this [object] is of two kinds, he says: "It is said," and so forth. "Said" means made the object of direct verbal expression; its opposite is "unsaid."
How, then, is that [probandum] established? He says: "by the context" (*prakaraṇa*).

By means of the context—since it is understood as being the subject matter by virtue of being the basis for the presentation of the probandum—it is said that the probandum is precisely that which is to be manifested and revealed.
An example of what is refuted by inference (*anumānanirākṛta*) is as follows: "Sound is eternal" (III-50).
An example of what is refuted by inference is: "Sound is eternal."
The eternality of sound, which has been asserted, is refuted by impermanence established through inference.

[433] The meaning is: "by means of the knowledge arising from the auditory faculty" — Ṭīkā [434] For example: "The moon is not the moon" (acandraḥ śaśī), which is refuted by common experience (pratīti). III-51.

The thesis-meaning—that "the hare-marked one (śaśin) is not denotable by the word 'moon' because it is excluded from being a moon"—is refuted by common consensus (*pratīti*). And this [refutation] is by way of consensus;
for "consensus" refers to an object that is the domain of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*).

"Recognition," "the state of being recognized," and "the meaning of an admission"—this is an explanation of the sense of the phrase "even when conjoined with this definition. That is to say: "even when conjoined with this definition, it is the object."
But is it not the case that [the opponent] holds the view that [an object] is refuted or set aside by perception and the other means of knowledge?
And yet, the function of perception and the rest is not the setting aside of objects, but rather the establishment of the nature of things; thus he says: "contrary" (*viparīta*).
"Śravaṇa" means that by which one hears; it is the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). [The object] is "to be grasped" (*grāhya*) or perceived by that.
Furthermore, because it is graspable by the cognition of that [faculty], it is said to be "graspable by that. He states the compound with the negative particle (*nañ*) as "not" (*na*).

He states the meaning of the whole [verse] as follows: "By the ear," etc. This is its intention: one who asserts that "sound is not audible"—that is, it is not experienced by a cognition born of the ear—is contradicted by that very perception born of the auditory faculty which has sound as its object.
"Because it establishes, by means of that [word], the appearance of what is contrary to the non-appearance inherent in the word.
By this, that which was stated by Uddyotakara is refuted: "He describes the example 'sound is inaudible' as one that contradicts perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*)."
The object is not known through perception, nor through inference.
What is the reason? Because the functions of the sense organs are beyond the reach of the senses.
And audibility is the functioning of a sense faculty;
how could that be perceptible?
Therefore, this is an example of something contradicted by inference.
"Fire is not hot because it is produced"—this is an example of that which contradicts perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*).
See the *Nyāyavārttika*, 1.1.33, p. 113.
For it is not intended that there is an absence of the ear-faculty's activity regarding the object called "sound" when cognition arises through the word "inaudible";
rather, this statement made by the Teacher is refuted by perception, because for that opponent, the activity of the auditory faculty toward the object of sound is contradicted by perception.

If it is asked, "Since the functioning of the senses is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), how can it be perceptible such that this example would be applicable?"—what then? It is with respect to a particular opponent who, due to the power of delusion, asserts that this non-dual form which is apprehended by the ear does not exist; for him, why is this not an example that contradicts perception?
This is what is meant:
for one who says "sound does not exist," there is sublation by perception;
however, the negation of the object alone has many ways of being established.
"Sound does not exist because it is all-pervasive, because it is eternal," and so forth.
In that case, if the word "audible" were absent and everything were being negated, one might suspect a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*).

However, by using the word "audible," it is made known that the contradiction with direct perception occurs only when negating that specific form which is graspable solely through hearing, and not when negating a general property (*sāmānyadharma*).
It is said that [the hare-marked entity] is the object of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*).
Therefore, by means of that conceptual cognition, which consists in the form of apprehension, its status as being denotable by the word "hare-marked moon" is indeed established.
For instance: whatever is apprehended by conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) is capable of being associated with the form of a word;
and whatever is capable of being associated with the form of a word can be expressed by a conventional term.

Therefore, the fact that "non-moon-ness" (*acandratva*) is established as an object of conceptual cognition by way of its nature as a mental construction serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) of its being denotable by the word "moon."
And the logical reason is one of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), namely, cognition.
Since being denotable by a conventional term is invariably concomitant with the mere state of being an object of conceptual construction,
it should be understood that the denotability by the word "moon"— established through this *svabhāvahetu*— is the sublater of [the opponent's] denotability.
By being the object of conceptualizing consciousness;
by being the object of conceptual cognition; by means of conceptualizing consciousness.
[438] That which is conceptual cognition; that which is graspable by cognition,
because the object is designated by means of the subject in the form of conceptual consciousness.
He demonstrates this very point with the word "pratīta" (cognized).

The meaning is that it is called "cognized" because it is so designated in conventional usage; for even in the case of something directly perceived, there is no such conventional designation if there is no determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it as having arisen.
The cognition clearly demonstrates that the property residing in the object has been stated by the subject—that is, "cognized-ness" (pratītatva) as having the nature of being cognized (pratītatva).
By the phrase "by that conceptual cognition," it should be understood as "by way of being the object of conceptual consciousness," [referring to the object] in its form as something cognized.
He establishes this very point with the words "for thus" (tathā hi).
"Let it be that [the universal] possesses the fitness for association with the form of a word;
but how can it be denotable by that word? To this he says: "That which... and so forth, showing that cognition (pratīti) serves as a subverting proof (bādhaka).

Regarding "non-moon-ness," which is the state of not being denotable by the word "moon": [the author] asks, "How is this denotability by the word 'moon' established by the proof? and answers with the words "by its own nature" (*svabhāva*).
Applying the definition of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "Because... (*yasmāt*).
The conclusion is indicated by the words "tataḥ" and so forth.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) should be seen as follows: whatever object is the domain of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) can be expressed by a conventional term (*sāṅketika-śabda*);
for example, an object possessing branches and so on is expressed by the word "tree."
And [the claim] that "the moon is the object of conceptual cognition" would only hold true if,
despite an actual, fixed relationship between a word and its referent, it were impossible for some word to denote something;
however, that [impossibility] has been refuted elsewhere.

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), for an object that has ascended into the nature of cognition, with what could a connection to a word be established—given that it does not merge with that word-form within a single cognition?
Furthermore, since cognition has an indefinite object, an object ascended therein is indeed fit for association with the form of its designating expression.
Therefore, the impossibility of being expressed by that word is pervaded by the fitness for non-association with that [word's] form.
And that fitness for association with the form of its designation is contradictory to its pervader;
and by that [fitness], being the object of conceptual cognition is pervaded.
Thus, because being the object of conceptual cognition is pervaded by that which is contradictory to its pervader, it is also contradicted by that [fitness].
And therefore, since it is pervaded by "cognizability," which is the opposite of that [non-cognizability], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Consequently, being the object of conceptual cognition itself is what is called "cognition," "establishment," and "linguistic usage.
That which is established by means of this cognition—namely, the moon's state of being denotable by the word "moon"—serves as a sublater of its own opposite, namely, its non-denotability.

The ultimate meaning is as follows: because the property characterized by being denotable by a desired word is produced from that cognition—which is characterized by conceptual consciousness—there is a sublation of its non-denotability; thus, it is called "sublation by cognition" (*pratītibādha*). Alternatively, the term "cognition" refers to the very property characterized by being denotable by a desired word that is produced from such a cognition.
[DhPr 185]
An example of what is refuted by one's own words is as follows: "Inference is not a valid means of cognition" (III-52).
One's own words are the verbal expression belonging to the subject of the thesis;
that which is refuted by such words cannot be established as the thesis.
In the statement "inference is not a valid means of cognition," the negation of inference's validity is the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
This is contradicted by the very sentence expressing it— "inference is not a valid means of cognition"—
because the employment of this sentence indicates that the speaker intends the verbal cognition produced by it to have a real object.

For instance: if a speaker were to demonstrate that the comprehension of meaning arising from his words in you is false, he would not utter the sentence at all; for if the meaning of what is spoken must be known by another to be existent, then the speech is purposeless.
Even one who says, "Everything I say is false," utters that very sentence only by showing that this particular sentence possesses a true meaning.
If this statement were shown to have a true meaning, then other statements of one's own would likewise be shown to have false meanings;
however, if only this very one has a true meaning, [then the others must be false].
Otherwise, other true meanings would not be revealed;
consequently, there would be no fruit in utterance at all, and thus one would not utter it.
Therefore, a speaker utters a sentence only by revealing a true meaning through a cognition that arises from the sentence and has the sentence-meaning as its object.
And this being so, one who demonstrates that a word is invariably concomitant with an external object must demonstrate that the cognition produced by the word has a real object.

Therefore, by demonstrating that the cognition arising from a word—which is the effect of an external object—is possessed of a real object, verbal [cognition] is shown to be inference based on an effect as its logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*).
This is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here.
And that inference— [441] verbal cognition— [442] replies, it speaks.
The passage beginning with "etad eva" and ending with "bhavanti" is printed as a sūtra; however,
this is not a sūtra— namely, one characterized by the negation of the life-force of inference— [as indicated by the marginal note (ṭi)].
[445] Just as [446] the one who demonstrates [the point] shows that the object which is established merely through cognition is what constitutes the sublation here.
And this status as a reason based on essential identity (svabhāvahetu) is accepted as conceptualized, not as real,
because the moon's being an object of conceptual cognition is merely a matter of determinative judgment (adhyavasānika).
Otherwise, there would be no separate mention of this [contradiction by perception], as it would already be subsumed under contradiction by inference.

With the intention that, because of the context, the word "own" (*sva*)—meaning "self"—refers to the subject of the thesis (*sādhya*), he says: "belonging to the meaning of the proposition. By this, "it is refuted" should be understood as being refuted by that which establishes it, namely, by the very life-force of the inference.
To the question "How is it refuted?", he says: "the statement."

Since this sentence, when employed, indicates—that is, reveals—the fact that the speaker’s verbal cognition, which originates from words, possesses a real object (*sadarthatva*) or is true in its meaning (*satyārthatva*), even though it has already been answered, [the author] asks how it acts in such a way and says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
He should not utter it; he is not fit to utter it.
"Because it is meaningless" refers to what is present in the mind;
however, by the words "speech" and so forth, he clarifies this very point: not every speech that is employed acts in such a way as the speech, "I speak everything falsely. He says, "even he who...
for (*hi*) means because (*yasmāt*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "If this," etc.:
let it be granted that the cognition which arises from a sentence and has the meaning of the sentence as its object possesses a true referent;

nevertheless, how is the validity of inference established by the verbal statement, such that the negation of the validity of inference would be [refuted] by the validity of inference established by that statement?

Therefore, by one who asserts that "inference is not a means of valid cognition," it is implied that the object of verbal cognition must be apprehended as non-existent; for it is precisely this state of having a non-existent object that is called invalidity, and nothing else.
By virtue of the capacity for the utterance of a word, its own term is shown to be inseparable from its object;

thus, the existing object is demonstrated. Consequently, the existence of the object of verbal cognition—inferred from the word which is the effect of that conceptualized object—subverts the existence being asserted in the thesis.
[447] Since that which is graspable has been stated [to be non-existent], [448] the object [of the word] is non-existent;

[449] from this [statement] "inference is not a means of valid cognition," the object beginning with "not inference" is understood. A word produced by that—such as "not inference"—will not be accepted [as a valid indicator], because it is devoid of reality due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
[450] Superimposed—[451]—the word-sound...
Thus, non-existence being sublated by existence as inferred from one's own statement, it is said to be "sublated by one's own statement"; this is the meaning here.
[452] Others, however, say: the cognition produced from a word that is the effect of an intention has that intention as its object;
the employment of a word occurs by one who desires a real object.
Thinking that his own assertion of invalidity would thus be contradicted,

and that being refuted he would be self-contradicted by his own words, he says: "And this being so"— that is, when there is the manner of uttering the sentence with the intention of establishing that verbal cognition possesses a true object.
The meaning is that by one who demonstrates the inseparability—that is, the necessary concomitance—with an external object, it is proper and possible to demonstrate the true object;
"from this" means for that reason.

The intention is that because there is a distinction [between the two], the state of being inseparable is possible only through the relation of origination (*tadutpatti*) from the effect of the external object.

Because "verbal" (*śābda*) is the subject under discussion, it refers to knowledge produced by the effect-evidence (*kāryaliṅga*), specifically that produced by the effect-evidence which is the form of the word (*śabdarūpa*). Thus, inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is shown—that is, revealed—as being characterized by its causal nature.
He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth.
Now, one might object: it would be more appropriate to say that for inference, the object to be grasped (*grāhya*) is non-existent.
If it is asked, "Then how is it that verbal cognition was mentioned [as being distinct]?"—
this is not a fault;
for even verbal cognition is an inference by virtue of the reasoning already stated.
Furthermore, since this [inference] itself is also sublated by the negation of the validity of all inference,
its presentation is indeed appropriate, because this very inference sublates the meaning of the thesis characterized by the negation of the validity of inference.
If that is so, it is logical to say that invalidity has been stated and that it is being sublated.

To the question, "Why was it stated thus?", he says: "Because its object is non-existent" (*asadarthatvam*). The word "hi" means "because. [Objection: "Let it be that the apprehended object is non-existent; what follows from this? To this he replies: "The word... (*śabda*).
The word "ca" (and) is used either in the sense of a reason or for emphasis.

Since the word has also been shown in that manner, one might ask: "What follows from this? To which he replies: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). This means that when the method of demonstrating that a word is invariably concomitant with an external object is established, the existing object is shown to be the determinable [referent].

That is to say, the definition of validity as having a real object (*sadarthatva*) has been shown. To demonstrate that it possesses such a real object, he asks, "But how is there sublation? and replies with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

By this very inference based on the verbal indicative (*śabda-liṅga*), that object which is to be made known by the verbal cognition and which is characterized by the validity of inference is itself inferred.
The existence (*sattva*) being asserted as the agent obstructs the object (*karman*), which is the non-existent entity characterized by invalidity;

for while one might say it "refutes" (*nirākaroti*), the author says it "obstructs" (*pratibadhnāti*) because, in the ultimate sense, there is no sublation (*bādhā*) since this [existence] is not real, but rather there is a mutual obstruction between the two [terms] presented by this [assertion].
[DhPr 187]
That is incorrect;

for in this context, it is accepted that the cognition [of the subject] functions as a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), while one's own statement functions as a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*).
It is not real;
moreover, the fact that a word has its effect through intention is indeed real,
and therefore that is not what is being grasped here.

Furthermore, what is meant by "real"? Just as one who does not accept inference would not perceive that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire, so too one would not perceive that a word is invariably concomitant with the speaker's intention.
Furthermore, a word is employed for the purpose of making an external object known;
thus, the employment of a word is not preceded by the admission that the word is invariably concomitant with the speaker's intention.
Moreover, a word is not uttered for the sake of communicating one's own intention.
Rather, it is for the purpose of establishing external entities;
therefore, the employment of words is preceded by the admission of their inseparable connection with external objects. Consequently, the previous explanation alone is faultless.
[454] *agnyavya-* [455] Furthermore, the indeclinable *api ca* is used here in the sense of "because. The reading beginning with *api ca* and ending with *śabdaprayogaḥ* does not exist.
[456] Regarding the existence of external objects—
[457] the explanation has already been provided [458].
Thus, four fallacious positions (pakṣābhāsa) are excluded.
And this being the case—by the inclusion of the term "not refuted" (anirākṛta)—the four [cases] mentioned above, which appear as if they were positions, are thereby rejected as fallacious positions.
This being the case,

in order to demonstrate what kind of meaning for the thesis (*pakṣa*) is obtained through the exclusion of those things which are excluded by the words defining the characteristics of the thesis, the objects of exclusion are summarized, and thus the thesis— [460] the thesis— [is presented].

One might object: "Surely the validity of inference contradicts non-existence, but it does not contradict one's own words; so how can this be cited as an example of what is refuted by one's own words?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] shows what kind of meaning is intended by the term "refuted by one's own words" with the words "Thus, in this way.
Here, "in this" refers to that which is refuted by one's own words.

Regarding the point that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [the author] first provides an explanation according to his own intention, and then, with the words "But others... and so forth, he states the following in order to refute the previous explanation.
By using the particle *tu*, he indicates the dissimilarity between his own explanation and the former one.

If this inference were real for one who says "it is not real," then it would not be stated separately from the examples refuted by inference. Furthermore, the word "and" (*kiñ ca*) is used to add another thing to be stated; likewise, the particle "also" (*api*) in the phrase "and for the purpose of making known external objects" (*bāhyavastupratyāyanāya ca*) is also for the purpose of adding another thing to be stated.
Since it is so, therefore:
"one whose prior acceptance [of the word] as being non-deviant from the intention to utter— that is, the desire to speak— one's own [meaning]— is not thus."

By the phrase "previously, for the purpose of making known an external object," although it was stated by implication that [the use of words] is not for the purpose of making known one's own intention, this is now shown explicitly. Furthermore, although it was shown by implication through the statement "the employment of words is preceded by the admission of their inseparable connection with an external object"— rather than being preceded by the admission of their inseparable connection with an intention— this is now demonstrated directly.
The phrase "also for the purpose of showing" (*darśayitum api ca*) is a clarification of the previously mentioned indicator of another point to be stated.

Even where a word is employed to demonstrate non-existence (*asattva*), it is said to be "for the purpose of demonstrating external existence" (*bāhyasattvapratipādanāya*), because it demonstrates another kind of existence that is distinct from the intended [specific] existence.
Alternatively, this is because the mention of "existence" (*sattva*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, regarding that which is established, as well as that which is not yet established but is intended as a means of proof:

When a proponent himself intends to prove something that is not desired [by others], the probandum (*sādhya*) is the opposite of what has been stated and refuted; it is that which is intended by the proponent in its very own form, desired, and unrefuted. Thus, the definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*) is shown to be faultless. III-54
[461] Thus— omitted [462]— the characteristic is blameworthy;
thus— in the sequence just mentioned [463].

The probandum (sādhya) is to be understood by way of the opposite of the established (siddha), that is, by virtue of its being contrary [to it]. The intended meaning is that the object which is the reverse of the established object is the probandum.
And the established (*siddha*) is the opposite of the unestablished (*asiddha*); therefore, the unestablished is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, not every unestablished thing [is to be proven], but rather the opposite of that unestablished thing which is stated as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
That is to say, it is the opposite of the unestablished thing that the proponent himself does not intend to prove.

Likewise, even that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) immediately upon being stated is established by its opposite; likewise, even that which is refuted (*nirākṛta*) is established by its opposite through the unestablished,
as has been explained.

And that object which is devoid of the five exclusions—being unestablished, not a proof for the proponent, intended by the proponent himself to be established, whether stated or unstated, and not refuted by means of valid cognition—is the *sādhya*.
This very thing is what is expressed by these words as "intended by the proponent himself in its own form" and "unrefuted. Furthermore, that which is the *sādhya* is called the *pakṣa*.
The word *iti* has the sense of "thus. Thus, the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is faultless (*anavadya*).
That which has no fault (*avadya*), that is, no defect (*doṣa*), is "faultless."
It has been shown and stated.
[464] Following the words "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth, numerical figures have been provided—saṃ- [465] —"thus" (*iti*). *om*.

Having completed the exposition of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) and having stated the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) as it arose in the course of discussion, the author, desiring to speak of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), introduces them with the words "the three-featured," etc.
Having concluded the exposition of the three-featured logical mark, it was stated that inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) consists of this.
In that regard, if even one of the three forms is not stated, it is a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsa). III-55.
This is what is meant: one who wishes to state a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three forms must state them clearly;
and thus, they have been stated clearly in this manner.
It should also be understood that the statement of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is for the purpose of producing in the external listener the cognition of existence;
in no way can the existence or non-existence of one's own intention be established by the employment of words— this is the reason [stated] by this [passage].
Since this is so, therefore that which was previously explained by me is indeed faultless and free from defect.
Thus, explaining the root text—that these four fallacious positions are thereby refuted—he says: "In this way.
They are "refuted as being [valid] positions" because of the context.
The meaning is that it is called a "pakṣa" (side/position) according to the etymological derivation *vyaktīkriyate* ("it is made manifest").

But has it not already been stated that the subject under discussion is the exposition of the three-featured logical mark? Why then is the exposition of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), which is not the subject at hand, being undertaken?
[DhPr 189]
If that [object] exists,
it is also called its "counterpart" (*tatpratirūpaka*); for when there is knowledge of what is to be abandoned, that which is to be adopted, being distinct from it, becomes well-known.

It was stated previously that "inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics" [3.1]. That which is presented as a semblance [of such a mark] is understood to be a fallacious mark (liṅgābhāsa)— [Note].
[469] Regarding that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be known;
[470] "for the sake of others" means therein, when that exists.
The meaning is that [this occurs] in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), which consists in the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).
This applies when not even one of the three features is stated;
by the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that it also applies when two are not stated.
The meaning is that it resembles a semblance of a proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), not a proof itself;
the deficiency of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) is what is called a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*).
[471] In inference for the sake of others, even when [the reason] has been stated, if it is unestablished or doubtful for either the person to be convinced or the person who convinces—
III-56— not only when it is unstated, but also when it has been stated, if it is unestablished or doubtful;
To whom does it belong? He says: to the respondent (*prativādin*) who is being instructed, and to the proponent (*vādin*) who is instructing; [it refers to] a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Now, when one of the [three] characteristics is unestablished or doubtful, what is the name of that fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? He says: "When one characteristic is unestablished... and "...or when there is doubt regarding one characteristic, the statement is a fallacy of the reason."
When the connection between the subject (*dharmin*) and a single property (*rūpa*) is unestablished or doubtful, the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Anticipating the objection that it is "unestablished" even when there is doubt, he says: "This is what is meant."

Furthermore, the fact that the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) is for the purpose of clear expression is merely an illustration; it should be understood as also being for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions (*vipratipatti*), since one observes such misconceptions regarding defects such as the doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*).

This is an explanation of the meaning as "resembling the means of proof" (*sādhanasya sadṛśam*). As for its etymological derivation: *ābhāsa* means appearing, manifestation, or representation; thus, it is so called because it has a manifestation or representation that is like that of the means of proof.

"Deficiency" (*nyūnatā*) means being less than required or incompleteness. To the question "Of what? he says: "Of the three. Since if one or two are not stated, the three are not fully explained, the meaning is that there is a deficiency of the three.
Now, one might object: "Is deficiency of members (*hīnāṅgatva*) not a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*)?

For even when the three forms [of the syllogism] are present, deficiency is possible if the speaker fails to state two or even one of them. Therefore, how can this be called a fault of the proof rather than a fault of the speaker? If this is asked:
True; however, in this context, by the word "means" (*sādhana*), the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not intended.
What then? It is the sentence that establishes it, and its incompleteness is indeed a fault.
But since the cause for [the sentence's] completeness lies in the fault of the speaker, what is the harm?

Thus, because this [term] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), just as deficiency (*nyūnatā*)—which is a fault of the proof (*sādhana*)—arises from being inferior even by way of any one form [of the reason], so too defeat (*nigraha*) of the proponent (*vādin*) is intended due to the failure to state the reason (*hetūvacana*).
By the words "of the person to be informed" (*pratipādyasya*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of both the word "to be informed" (*pratipādya*) and the word "informing agent" (*pratipādaka*).

However, the Master’s intention is a designation that may be applied either distributively or collectively: namely, "of the person to be informed," "of the informing agent," and "of both the person to be informed and the informing agent."
"Of a single form" means a connection with the subject (*dharmin*); that is, a connection with the locus of properties.
The presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*dharmin*):
if that [presence] is unestablished or doubtful, it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) designated as "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
And precisely because it is unestablished, it is a cause for non-comprehension regarding the subject.
It is not a reason for the thesis, nor for the contradictory, nor for doubt; rather, it is a cause for non-comprehension.
This is because no one would practice [the path] on this basis;
furthermore, this meaning is to be understood precisely from the fact that the designation "unestablished" (asiddha) was employed.
He states an example:
"For instance, when 'sound is impermanent' is the thesis, visibility is unestablished for both [proponent and opponent]" (III-58), beginning with the word "for instance."

When "sound is impermanent" is the thesis to be proven—meaning sound qualified by impermanence—the property of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*), that is, being graspable by the eye, is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent with respect to sound.

[475] Regarding the thesis that "trees possess consciousness" [476] because they are permanent [477] and because death occurs when both [types of trees] have their bark stripped from all sides, this [death] is unestablished for the opponent.

Because death, characterized by the cessation of consciousness, the sense faculties, and vitality, is accepted [by the opponent] through this [definition], and because that [death] is impossible in trees; thus, [the argument] "because of death" is refuted.
III-59 [477] From death—refutation.
[478] By this [reasoning], "trees possess consciousness because they have the desire for death"— when consciousness is to be proven in trees—
*sarvā tvak* means "all bark."
When its [the body's] removal occurs, death—which was proposed by the Digambaras—is unestablished for the Buddhist opponent.
Why is it unestablished? He says: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*), the sense faculty (*indriya*), and life-force (*āyus*)"—this is a dvandva compound.
Among these, consciousness is that which is produced from the eye and the other [senses].
That which is inferred from the arising of the consciousnesses of form and so forth— namely, the form located within the body, situated in the eyeball and other such places—
and the life-force therein; both that form and the life-force are present there.
[480] Born from the eye-consciousness; [481] eye-consciousness and so forth [perceive] form and so forth;
consciousness of the eye and so forth [perceives] form and so forth.

Regarding the question of what kind of cognition this fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), whose nature is fixed at the end of the effect, produces, he says: "Precisely because of its being unestablished" (*asiddhatvāt*).
The particle *ca* has the sense of the word *tu*.
To explain how this is obtained, he says: "And this...
Here, *ca* is used in the sense of "because."
The intention is that [the reason] is stated to be "unestablished" (asiddha) because it is not established as the cause for any practice whatsoever.
"Unestablished for both" means not certain for either the proponent or the opponent.
By this, the "unestablished due to a difference in locus" (vyadhikaraṇāsiddha) should also be understood as being stated.
For example: "This palace belongs to the king."
Regarding the argument "because of the blackness of the crow":
since that blackness is unestablished for both [the subject and the probandum] with respect to the palace,
which is the locus (*dharmin*), it is designated in that way merely because it is presented as residing in the factual locus (*arthadharmin*), even though it is unestablished there.
But is it not observed that even a mark (*liṅga*) residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) can be an indicator?
For example, the sight of a fresh clay bowl serves as an indicator of the state of being a fresh clay bowl for one who is mistaken, and of the state of being a wheel-turner for one who is mistaken;
and because this [latter case] functions as a logical reason (*hetu*).

For it is the very location that is the subject (*dharmin*), and its state of being connected to a nearby potter is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). Of that subject, its connection with a fresh clay bowl and its connection with the [rotating] wheel are indeed properties (*dharma*);
however, the actual existence of the potter as a subject is not what is being proven here.
By that very [means] it is stated;

likewise, the unestablishedness of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the unestablishedness of the qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddha*) should also be understood as expressed by this very [same principle].
For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is non-denotable..."
That sense-faculty is called "vitality" (āyus) in the world; it is referred to as the "life-breaths" (prāṇa).
And it is not appropriate to state here that which is established by scripture;
therefore, in this context, life has the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
and their cessation is their "termination" (*nivṛtti*).
That which has that characteristic as its reality is described as such;
for death of that nature has been acknowledged by this Buddhist. Thus it is said.
[485] Even if it were so, how could it be unestablished? He says: because that which consists of the cessation of consciousness and so forth [486] is impossible in trees;
for cessation is preceded by existence (*sattā*).

And therefore, how could one who would desire the cessation of consciousness in trees not also desire consciousness itself? Consequently, because consciousness is not desired in trees, its cessation is likewise not desired in them,
due to the absence of consciousness in trees.
But is it not the case that withering is also called death, and that is established in trees? True.
In this context, the cause is that death which is pervaded by the mere existence of consciousness;
and the cessation of consciousness is pervaded by its existence, not merely by its drying up.
Therefore, that which is the cause of death is unestablished in trees; however,
that which is established as having the nature of withering is not the cause of existence.
In that regard,
the cause of death is that which...
The Digambara, however, without distinguishing whether death is pervaded or not pervaded by the probandum, stated "death" alone as the reason.
Thus, this proponent did not understand death as being the actual reason;
because of this ignorance, the form of "withering" was established [as the reason].
Since death in the form of withering is observed in trees,
it is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent because he does not know it; however,
when it is known even by the proponent, then according to the rule, it would be unestablished for the proponent as well.
[491] The characteristic of the cessation of consciousness, the faculties, and vitality— ṭīkā—
[492] the characteristic of desiccation [493] is known through its cause.

The definition of cessation as the extinction of consciousness, the sense faculties, and vitality—[this is not valid] because it exists [as a subject], being an object of cognition (*prameya*). [For example:

"Sound is impermanent because, while being an object of cognition, it is non-denotable. In this case, since both the proponent and the opponent lack proof regarding that substratum (*dharmin*) with respect to the form qualified by the two qualifiers, [the reason is unestablished].

It is simply that [the reason] is unestablished (asiddha) there, because the nature of the thing presented as qualified by its qualifiers is not established in that manner; thus it is designated accordingly.

Regarding the term *cetanā*: they are called *cetanās* because they intend (*cetayante*). By the etymological derivation "those whose garment is the directions themselves," the *kṣapaṇakas* (Jainas) are called *digambaras*.
To the question of what kind of sense faculty has been apprehended by them as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "form and so forth."

When other causes are present, the fact that the cognition of form and so forth does not arise while the eye and other faculties are inactive indicates that another cause must be expected for its own production.
However, when the eye and other faculties are directed [toward their objects], the arising [of cognition] makes it known that there exists some cause situated therein.
For this very reason, it is said: "contained within the body" means "supported by the body."

The fact that [consciousness] is dependent on the body has been stated in general. With the intention of referring to specific types of knowledge, he shows its dependence on specific bases by saying "the eye," and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the tongue and so forth are included.
The point is that since clarity and other such qualities also exist, the physical eyeball and so forth alone cannot be the sense organ.
To the question "What is life-force (āyus)?", he says: "By the word 'life-force' (āyus)"—this is the meaning.

In common worldly usage among people, it is the single internal vital breath within the body, which, being the cause for the impelling of the constituents such as nutritional essence (rasa) and waste products (mala), [is designated as such] due to the differentiation of its functions.
It acquires the designations "apāna" and so forth; thus, depending on the intended state, there is the plural form "prāṇāḥ.
[Objection: But in the Āgama it is stated that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is longevity (*āyus*);
why then is it explained in this way? To this he says: "And not... and so on.
The word "co" (ca) is used either for emphasis or to indicate a reason; that is,
because it is so, for this reason,
in this context of demonstrating entities established by valid cognition, it is likewise.
When it is to be proven that pleasure and so forth are insentient, the property of having an origin or impermanence is unestablished for the Sāṃkhya himself, the proponent;
[III-60] [it is] impermanent.
"Regarding the statement 'pleasure and so forth are insentient'— those for which pleasure is the first are 'pleasure and so forth,' namely suffering and the rest.
When their lack of sentience is to be proven, the reason (liṅga) presented is either the state of having an origin or impermanence."
Whatever things are produced or are impermanent are not conscious,
such as form and so forth;
and since pleasure and the like are likewise produced or impermanent, they are therefore non-conscious.
Consciousness (*caitanya*), however, is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the person (*puruṣa*).
In this context, either "having an origin" or "impermanence" serves as the reason, but not both simultaneously;
and both of these are unestablished for the Sāṃkhya proponent.
For the presentation of a reason is for the sake of another;
therefore, that which is established for the other must be stated as the reason. And for the other, there is the arising of what was non-existent, which is the state of having an origin.
Furthermore, it is established that the impermanence of an existent consists in its destruction without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśa*).
Such a twofold [impermanence] is unestablished for the Sāṃkhya;
here too, because impermanence and the possession of origination are being proven, they are unestablished for the proponent (*vādin*).
If, however, the validity of impermanence and having an origin were known by the proponent, then it would be established for the proponent as well;
therefore, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not fully understood, this is unestablished for the proponent.
[495] its own form; [496] for the sake of others, etc., here; [497] the means of valid cognition.
[498] Consciousness [499] at that time— omitted.
To demonstrate that it is "doubtful-unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddha), he says:
Likewise, when there is doubt regarding the reason itself or its locus, it is unestablished (asiddha).

Regarding "itself": when there is doubt concerning the reason's own nature, it is unestablished. Regarding "or its locus": the locus of that reason—what is called the "locus" because the reason is supported therein—is said to be the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), which is distinct from the reason and serves as its substratum.
For in that case, [the phrase] "and of this" refers to the basis (āśraya).
Regarding that very form:

"that which is pervaded by the existence of consciousness" means that at the death in question, that which was necessarily previously possessed of consciousness is said to be pervaded by the existence of consciousness.
And as for that [death], which is characterized by the cessation of breath, warmth, movement, and so forth—how is it established even for a Digambara? To this he says: "Because of ignorance.
That is, because of ignorance of death, which is invariably concomitant with consciousness.

By this he says the following: if death, which is pervaded by that [probandum], were distinguished from mere emaciation—which merely bears the same name as "death"—by him, then it would be established; however, it is said to be so established only out of ignorance. He states this very point with the words: "But when..."
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
"Pleasure" (sukha) is that which is to be experienced as favorable.
By the word "etc. (ādi), desire, aversion, and so forth are included.

The grasping of the self by the *puruṣa* as conceived by the Sāṃkhya school follows from their tenet that "the *puruṣa* perceives, while the intellect (*buddhi*) determines. A Sāṃkhya is so called because he deals with another system—the enumeration of twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*); this term is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*).
It is precisely because it is accepted [by the opponent] that it is so called.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that having an origin (*utpattimattva*) or being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is already established for oneself, and thus should be presented by him? And indeed, it has been presented. So how can it be 'unestablished for the proponent' (*vādyasiddha*)? To this he says: "For it is for the sake of another... (*parārtho hi*).
For this reason:
"for the sake of others" means having the purpose of bringing about understanding in others;
"without continuity" means total annihilation in every respect.
A reason that exists in the present is relied upon as that which makes [the probandum] known;
when there is doubt regarding that reliance, it is "doubtful."
To provide an example of that which is doubted from its own nature, he says:

"Just as a collection of elements, when being doubted in its own nature as being vapor or the like, is taught for the purpose of proving fire, it is 'doubtfully unestablished' (sandigdhāsiddha). (III-62)
[503] The "doubtful-unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddha) — the word *yathā* is omitted. That which has vapor (*bāṣpa*) and so forth as its beginning is "vapor-and-the-rest" (*bāṣpādi*).

By virtue of being that, i.e., by being vapor-and-the-rest, a "collection of elements" (*bhūtasaṃghāta*) is being doubted; this refers to a collection (*saṃghāta*), meaning an aggregate (*samūha*), of the elements (*bhūta*) such as earth and the others.
Regarding the proof of fire: that which is employed for the purpose of proving fire is "unestablished" (asiddha).
This is what is meant: when even smoke is doubted as being vapor or the like, it is then unestablished, because the form of the probans (gamaka) is not ascertained.
Smoke that is ascertained as such is an indicator because it is produced by fire;
however, when it is doubtful, it is not an indicator, and this is the fault known as "unestablished" (asiddha).
Because it is an effect of fire, it is an indicator;
he provides an example of that which is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*): "For instance, there is a peacock in this bower because of the sound of its cry" (III-63).

[505] "As in the case of a bower" (*niguñje yathā*): here, "bower" (*nikuñja*) is the subject (*dharmin*). A bower is a portion of ground covered by the upper part of a mountain that extends outwards horizontally.
"Mayūra" (peacock) is the thesis (*sādhya*); "because of its kekāyita" (because of its cry) is the reason (*hetu*);
*kekāyita* is the sound of a peacock.
But it is not accepted that even that which has perished continues to exist in the form of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The word "even" (*api*) implies that this is not only the case previously.
Regarding the proof—the means of valid cognition—that establishes impermanence and the state of being subject to origination—of that [proof]...
With the words "If [it were] from impermanent knowledge," and so forth, he confirms this very point.
The word "svayam" (by oneself) is understood as having the genitive ending "ātmanaḥ" (of oneself) following it.

And because "hetuḥ" (the reason) is the subject under discussion, he explains it as "hetoh" (of the reason). [The term] "āśraya" means that in which something is resorted to or taken up as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
With the intention that "he who has doubt regarding a self is one whose [perception] is doubted by himself," he says: "doubted by oneself.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), mist and so forth are included.
Now, if this is smoke in the ultimate sense, then why is it not an indicator even when there is doubt? To this he says: "This is what is meant."
"What is that indicative form by which [the fire] is not ascertained? To this he says: "Fire... and so forth.
He clarifies exactly what was stated by the words "But when... and so on.
And the intention of one who says, "In that case, it is not indicative," is that the very basis for its being indicative—namely, its being produced from fire—is at that time unascertained.

By this, the unestablished nature of a doubtful qualifier (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the unestablished nature of a doubtful qualificand (*sandigdhaviśeṣyāsiddha*) should be understood as stated; for example: "This is the sound of a peacock because, while possessing the *ṣaḍja* note and so forth, it is not of the nature of a letter-sound (*avarṇātmaka*)," when there is doubt regarding the existence of the *ṣaḍja* note and so forth; or [when there is doubt regarding the latter]: "while being of the nature of not being a letter-sound..."
[DHPR 194] [506] How is this [reason] unestablished in respect of its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*)? He says: How is the locus—
Regarding the phrase "tadāpātadeśavibhrame" (III-64), it is explained as *tadāpāta*:
the arrival (*āpāta*) of that *kekāyita* (the cry of the peacock); its "place" (*deśa*) is said to be the location from which the *kekāyita* comes.
When there is such confusion or delusion regarding it, this [reason] is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

For instance, when there are many contiguous groves and one is confused as to whether the sound of peacock cries has come from this particular grove or from another— namely, "Has the cry come from this grove,
or from another?"— [the reason remains unestablished].
In that case, this [reason] is unestablished with respect to its locus (āśrayāsiddha).
[507] Its destruction; [508] the arrival; [509] the confusion caused by the flight of the cries of peacocks.
[510] Or rather, "from this":
[511] he provides an example of how there is non-establishment even when the substratum (āśraya) and the property-bearer (dharmin) are unestablished.

It is also unestablished (*asiddha*) when the property itself is unestablished (*dharmyasiddhi*), as for example, when "being perceived everywhere" is cited as the reason to prove that "the self is omnipresent" (III-65). "Omnipresent" (*sarvagata*) means gone to, or situated in, everything; that is to say, all-pervading (*vyāpin*).
When the pervasiveness of the self is to be proven, the mark (liṅga) is the fact that its qualities are perceived everywhere.
This refers to the state or nature of that self whose qualities—such as pleasure, pain, desire, and aversion—are perceived in all locations.
Qualities do not exist apart from the possessor of those qualities.
Because qualities must reside in a substratum that pervades them,
and the self is devoid of action;
therefore, if it were not all-pervasive, how could pleasures and other sensations perceived in the Deccan be perceived in the Middle Country?

Therefore, the self is omnipresent. Since, in this case, even the existence of a self is not established for the Buddhist, how much less could its quality of being perceived everywhere be established? Thus, because [the subject] is unestablished, it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Previously, doubt regarding the locus (*dharmī*) was stated due to doubt concerning the reliance [upon it]; now, however, the locus is stated to be unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus, there is no distinction between these two. [512] Regarding the locus (*dharmi*):
Regarding the non-establishment of the reason, the relation, and the existence [of the subject]— namely, "because it possesses the notes ṣaḍja and so forth"— in both cases,

the form qualified by the qualification is uncertain for both the proponent and the opponent; and because there is doubt regarding the qualification alone, it is unestablished in its form as qualified by that qualification.
Thus it is designated in that manner.
The expressions "by means of the upper part of the mountain" and "extending horizontally" should be understood as figurative indications for any portion of the ground;
however, it is not exclusively such a bower, for the term "bower" (nikuñja) is applied specifically to a secluded, overgrown region within a mountain.

By the grammatical analysis of the statement "from whichever place it comes," he demonstrates that the produced sound generates a series of sounds in the four directions, and that [the final sound], having reached the location of the ear according to the analogy of water waves, is perceived.
In the phrase "from aversion, etc.," the word "etc. includes cognition, effort, and so forth.
They are called *guṇas* because they possess the definition of a quality: "A quality is that which possesses generality and is not an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction.
[They are qualities] because they are inherent through inherence (*samavāya*).

Thus, when a single property connected to the subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished among those [types of reasons] that have been prohibited, it is an unestablished fallacy of the reason (*asiddho hetvābhāsaḥ*).
[513] Even when all [the three forms] are unestablished, one form—the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—is unestablished.

[514] Likewise, when one form—the absence from the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣe 'sattva*)—is unestablished while bound to the subject, it is the inconclusive fallacy of the reason (*anaikāntika hetvābhāsa*). III-66.

Likewise, when there is no proof (*asiddhi*) of the absence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*)— namely, that it does not exist in any single instance of the property to be negated— the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Likewise, in the case of another [reason],
in the counter-instances (*vipakṣa*)— ṭi-
*Eka-anta* means one side, a single point, or certainty. That which has this as its purpose is *aikāntika*;
that which is not *aikāntika* is *anaikāntika*.
For the venerable [author], there is no certainty regarding either the probandum (*sādhya*) or its opposite; rather, it is the contrary, namely doubt (*saṃśaya*).
That which causes doubt concerning both the probandum and its opposite is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
[517] Nor is inherence (samavāya) uncaused,
because it is devoid of activity; and activity resides only in corporeal substances.
And because the self is immortal; such is the established conclusion.
The particle *kim uta* occurs in the sense of "how much more so" (*kim punar*).

Anticipating the question of what distinction there is between the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) and the unestablished property-possessor (*dharmyasiddha*), and demonstrating that distinction, he says: "Previously," etc.

The meaning is as follows: previously, although [the locus] existed in an ultimate sense, it was said to be "unestablished as a property-possessor" because it was not ascertained due to doubt regarding its nature as the substratum of the reason;
however, at present, it is called "unestablished" in the sense that it is entirely non-existent as a property-possessor.
It is said that what is unestablished in terms of its property (*dharmyasiddha*) is precisely what is called "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Therefore, there is no separate variety of fallacy named "unestablished in its locus.
As for the "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*), it is simply not a form of the unestablished at all; thus, its subsumption [under other categories] is not even considered.
For what is the meaning of "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*)? Does it mean established only in another way, or established also in another way?
Surely, if it were established only in another way, [it would not be a valid reason].
In that case, since [the probandum] is already established and proven by the very opposite of what one intends to demonstrate, it is indeed contradictory [to say it is proven] "in this manner.
Alternatively, if it is established in another way as well,
then since it is established by this other manner too, this [reason] would also become [a contradictory reason].
And since it is not the probandum, its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) is doubtful; thus, it is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika).
He states the etymology of the term *anaikāntika*: "one" (*eka*).

By saying "one," he shows that it is both "one" (*eka*) and "end" (*anta*); it is "one" because its object is a single thing characterized as the probandum (*sādhya*), and it is an "end" because it is the cause for the conclusion of the debate, or the cause for the cessation of expectancy. Thus, it is *ekānta*. [The term *anaikāntika* is derived from the negation of this.]
He states the entire word and its meaning: "ekānta" means certainty (*niścaya*).
The sense is that it has as its result the ascertainment of one or the other between the probandum (*sādhya*) and its opposite.
Furthermore, this negative particle (*nañ*) should be understood as having the sense of "contrary to that."
He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "yasmāt" (since).
The ablative case here in "yasmād dhetoḥ" (since [it is] the reason) is used in the sense of the *apādāna* (ablative of separation).

However, it should be understood that [the referent] is the opposite of that—that is, the opposite of certainty—because of the necessary connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.

He asks, "Where is the doubt? and says: "In the probandum" (*sādhye*). Alternatively, he asks, "How does it become inconclusive? and says: "Because" (*yasmāt*), where the ablative case indicates the reason (*hetu-pañcamī*).

With the intention that by the negation of the conclusive (*aikāntika*) another cause for cognition is stated through the negative particle (*nañ*), he says: "It is the cause of doubt" (*saṃśaya-hetuḥ*).
Therefore, there is no consequence of suchness for that which is unestablished.
Alternatively, because it is exclusively determined, "one" (*eka*) and "end" (*anta*) are said to mean certainty (*niścaya*). For indeed, this entire differentiation of categories—

He refutes that [position] as follows: For example, when a property such as impermanence is to be proven of sound, a property such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) exists either entirely or partially in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). (III-67)
By the words "yathā" and so forth:

that which has impermanence as its beginning is "the property beginning with impermanence" (*anityatvādika*); by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), "not being produced immediately after an effort," "being produced immediately after an effort," and "permanence" are included.

That of which "knowability" (prameyatva) is the first is "knowability and so forth" (prameyatvādikah). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), "impermanence" (anityatva) and further "the state of being impermanent" (anityatva) [are included].
And incorporeality is apprehended.
When a property such as impermanence is to be proven of the subject, sound, a property such as knowability (*prameyatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For in all four cases, the absence [of the reason] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
[518] For that which is impermanent— [519] its state of permanence— omitted [520] are apprehended.

[521] For instance—omitted: "For instance"—"Sound is impermanent because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)," [522] like a pot and like space. Here, *prameyatva* pervades both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Because it is an object of cognition... [522] *prameyatvāt*.

"Like space, like a jar"—thus, "sound is not produced immediately after effort because it is impermanent, like lightning, space, and a jar. Here, impermanence exists in only one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); it exists in lightning and so forth, but not in space.
Not in space and so forth; because even in the case of the counter-example (vipakṣa), [the property] exists everywhere in that which follows immediately upon effort. *Note:
The reading from "ita ārambha" up to "nākāśādau" does not exist in the manuscript.*
[525] It is not pervasive because it exists only in that which follows immediately upon effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*).

[526] Regarding impermanence (*anityatva*): "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a pot, and unlike lightning or space"—here, impermanence resides in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); it exists in lightning and so forth, but not in space and so forth.
The pervading [reason] exists everywhere in the similar class (sapakṣa) because it is invariably concomitant with the probandum;
the non-pervading [reason], however, is joined with the probanda one by one throughout the entire similar class. — Note.
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like the atoms of space and like action and a jar.
Here, the property of incorporeality resides in only one part of both [the similar and dissimilar instances]; that is, it exists in one part of each, namely in space and in action.
However, it does not exist in the atom, which is a portion of the similar class (*sapakṣa*), nor in the jar and so forth, which are portions of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*),
because jars, atoms, and the like possess corporeality (*mūrttatva*).
[Regarding] permanence— [note].
However, the Vaiśeṣikas accept that atoms are eternal;
therefore, they are included within the class of similar instances (sapakṣa). This is because they are also accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas.
It abides in one extreme— in the form of being either eternal or non-eternal, and so forth.
That which has this [extreme] as its purpose is "tathā" (thus).
It is not, however, inconclusive in that way.

The absence [of the probans] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not established in all cases; this should be understood. According to the Vaiśeṣika sūtra, "That which exists and is without cause is eternal" (VS 4.1.1), atoms (*paramāṇu*) are held to be eternal because they possess the characteristics of the eternal.
The non-existence of this fourfold property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished;
therefore, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
Likewise: even when there is doubt regarding this very form [of the reason], it is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Just as it is inconclusive when this form is unestablished (asiddha), so too it is inconclusive when there is doubt regarding this very form called "absence in the dissimilar instance" (vipakṣe 'sattva).

[531] For example, when it is to be proven that a certain intended person is not omniscient or possesses passion and so forth, a property such as "being a speaker" has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa). Regarding the term "asārvajña," non-omniscience is the property to be proven (sādhya).

"Someone intended" refers to the person who is the subject (*dharmin*) as intended by the speaker. "Possessing passion and so forth" (*rāgādimān*) means that which has passion (*rāga*) as its first [quality], such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and the like; this is the second thing to be proven (*sādhya*).

The inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of indicating that the possession of passion (*rāga*) and so forth is to be established as a separate probandum. Therefore, when non-omniscience or the possession of passion is the probandum under discussion, the property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*)—where "speaking" refers to the capacity for speech, and "and so forth" refers to such things as the opening and closing of the eyes—is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason. This is what is meant by the term "or."
When "mere existence" is the property to be proven (sādhya),
that whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) is doubtful is described as such.
When "non-omniscience" is the property to be proven, omniscience is the dissimilar instance.
In that case, the existence or non-existence of speech and so forth is doubtful;
therefore, it is not known whether the speaker is omniscient or non-omniscient, and thus "being a speaker" is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).
It is of doubtful nature.
[535] What—[omission]—is the point?

But surely, since no omniscient speaker is perceived, how can the statement regarding an omniscient being be considered doubtful? Precisely for this reason: because a non-perception of the kind "an omniscient speaker is not perceived" has as its object that which is invisible by nature, it serves as a cause for doubt. [536–537] Thus, due to the fact that such a form of non-perception concerns an invisible essence, it is a ground for uncertainty.
[538] Therefore, the exclusion of properties such as being a speaker from the opposite of non-omniscience is doubtful.
III-70 [536] Whether [the omniscient person] exists everywhere or in one place,
[537] there is doubt regarding the reason.
Because a non-perception of this kind—such as "no omniscient speaker is perceived because he does not exist"—is a cause for doubt.

Why is that? He says: it is because its nature is to have an imperceptible self as its object; that is, the state of having an imperceptible self as its object (*adṛśyātmaviṣayatva*), which constitutes its being a cause for doubt.
By the inclusion of the phrase "of that kind" (jātīyakasya) and "of hatred and so forth" (dveṣādeḥ), where the nature [of the object] is invisible, the inclusion of delusion and the rest is intended.
"Therefore, from mere non-perception alone"—thus says the proponent (*siddhāntin*).
Connecting this very point with the root text, he says: "Omniscient.
By that reason of having an invisible object (*adṛśyaviṣayatva*), there is the state of being a cause for doubt; [he states] "because it is a cause for doubt."
He now explains the fifth [member], the cause (*hetu*), with the words "since" (*yataḥ*).

Since the non-perception of imperceptible particulars is a cause for doubt and not a cause for certainty, the exclusion of "speaking" and other such qualities from an omniscient being— which is the counter-example to the non-omniscient— is therefore doubtful.

[541] It is not a cause for doubt because of non-perception; [542] we do not say that speakerhood is absent in an omniscient being, but rather that there is a contradiction between speakerhood and omniscience. This is not so. [543]
[542]—Because of this, it is doubtful regarding the speaker—[543] this is not so—omitted.

Furthermore, because there is no contradiction between being a speaker and being omniscient, even if one does not observe that "whoever is omniscient is not a speaker," the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established due to doubt. 71
The connection [of the argument] is as follows: there is no contradiction between the state of being a speaker and omniscience;
and because of this absence of contradiction, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established.
He demonstrates the negative concomitance that possesses pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words: "He who is omniscient..."

Having restated omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) as the nature of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), the absence of the means of proof (*sādhanābhāva*), namely the state of being a speaker (*vakṛtva*), is enjoined by the statement "he is not a speaker. Therefore, because the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the means of proof, it is said to be pervaded (*vyāpta*) by the absence of the means of proof. Such a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) possessing pervasion would be established provided there exists a contradiction between the state of being a speaker and omniscience.
And there is no contradiction;
therefore, it is not established.
Why? He says: because of doubt.
Since there is an absence of contradiction, there is doubt;
because of this doubt, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished.
He does not become a speaker [of that];
it is established by way of similarity. Why?

How is there an absence of contradiction? For the contradiction between entities is of two kinds; for it is because contradiction is only of these two kinds and no other that [it is so stated]. III-72 [547] Indeed, contradiction between entities is twofold.
Thus, since contradiction is exclusively of two types and nothing else, [there is no contradiction].
Therefore, there is no contradiction between being a speaker and being omniscient.
[547] Here, *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Since there are two kinds [of contradiction], what then are these two kinds of contradiction? He says:
[548][549] "The cognition of contradiction arises because that which exists with its causes unimpaired is absent when another thing is present. (III-73)
Existence; non-existence;
and "non-attainment" refers to that which has its causes unimpaired.
That which has its causes complete and unimpaired is so described.
For that whose non-existence results from a deficiency of causes, there can be no apprehension of contradiction with anything whatsoever;
it is for this purpose that the term "unimpaired causes" is employed.
But surely, even for that which possesses the completeness of its causes, its cessation cannot be brought about by anyone;
so how can there be an apprehension of contradiction?
If this is so, then the apprehension of contradiction arises from the absence of something—even though its causes were complete—due to the deficiency of causes brought about by another.
With the words "of whom," etc., he describes the result of a cause that is not subject to temporal change.
"In that case" (*evaṃ tarhi*) is the response;
"in that case" (*tarhi*) means at that time.
The meaning is that it should be understood in this way.
The word *api* is used in the sense of possibility;
the intended sense is: "By the very force of logic, we conceive of it as being thus."
The "course" (*gati*) of contradiction is its apprehension (*pratipatti*).
And this being so, whatever is contradictory to something must necessarily produce some effect upon it.

For instance: having become the producer of a cold touch, the contradictory [cause] is that which, by obstructing the capacity to produce another cold touch, brings about the cessation of the cold touch.
Therefore, the contradictory cause is that which effects the deficiency of the [opposing] cause; it is the producer of one and the subverter of the other.
And this is the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*).
Therefore, one must avoid the simultaneous existence of two contradictory things even in a single moment.
Furthermore, since contradiction does not exist between things situated at a distance, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator occurs only between those situated in close proximity.
Consequently, that which is the sublater of another can, at the very most, sublate it in the third moment.
In the first moment, upon coming together, it becomes capable of establishing a state of incapacity;
in the second moment, it renders it incapable by means of an opposing factor.
But when the third [moment], being incapable, has ceased, it occupies that same location;
it is capable of remaining,
not incapable of remaining.

In that case, light, which has the nature of motion, gradually pervades a location according to the analogy of a wave upon water; when it produces a moment of light that is continuous with darkness, it then renders the darkness situated near that light incapable.
Consequently, that darkness which has light in its vicinity becomes powerless.
When that which is incapable has ceased, light arises in its place; in this manner, darkness is to be removed by light.
Likewise, the sensation of cold is to be removed by the sensation of heat.
In that location—
[552] While treading upon [553] the agent [554] in the sense of incapacity,

If there is incapacity, what is established by that? To this he says, "And thus," meaning: when there exists the manner of understanding the contradiction that brings about the deficiency of the cause.
He demonstrates that it indeed performs some function with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth.
How it acts as its producer will be clarified immediately hereafter.

Anticipating the objection—namely, whether the contradiction between the two exists through a relationship of the sublated and the sublater occurring after they have been conjoined for several moments, or otherwise—he says "together" (*saha*).
Because of that, for that reason;
the word "also" (api) implies not only in many moments;
"coexistence" (sahāvasthāna) means staying together in one place.
The thought that "proximity must not be avoided" is present [in your mind].
It should be avoided; it should not be accepted.
Since there is no coexistence of those two even for a single moment, how can this be accepted? Precisely for this reason.
Nor has it been established that there is a contradiction between two things existing simultaneously;

for if this were so, light existing in a single location would, by this very same sequence, dispel the darkness situated throughout the three worlds, and thus darkness would never remain anywhere. To this he replies: "between those situated nearby."

The meaning to be understood is this: where a relationship of the ceased and the ceaser is observed, it exists only between those two things that are in close proximity; however, it is not the case that a relationship of the ceased and the ceaser necessarily exists between all things in close proximity.
To the doubt, "How is it that only those two have such a nature?", the phrase "between those situated at a distance" should be applied.
The word *eva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
Since only that which performs some [specific] action possesses the capacity to exclude [others], it is for this reason that [the term] is "supreme" (*param*), meaning most excellent.

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "the first," because it is proximate (*nikaṭībhavan*) due to its constant association (*sanniyata*), as understood from the context of being the "excluder" (*nivarttaka*).
And that moment of darkness which is in an incapable state—incapable of producing the moment of the effect—is "placed," meaning produced;
[the cause] becomes fit or capable for that. The phrase "in the second moment" is understood to follow here.
It renders it contradictory, incapable of darkness, and unable to produce another moment of its own kind;
in the third moment, that [moment] is incapable.

But when light is produced in that very place where darkness was, then from the very moment the moment of light— the producer of light— is born in the place of darkness, at that same moment the darkness has arisen as incapable of producing further darkness.
Therefore, the capacity to produce a state of incapacity is itself the nature of the obstructor.
[556] The moment of production;
[557] the sense of not producing within the interval of darkness; the sense of not producing within the interval of darkness.
[558] Therefore, because of this incapacity—and for this reason, in the third moment after the moment in which it was the producer—it ceases; provided that the contradictory [factor] ceases quickly.
Furthermore, due to the relationship between producer and produced, the contradiction exists between two continua (*saṃtāna*), not between two moments (*kṣaṇa*). [559]
And although that which is called a "continuum" (saṃtāna) is not a real entity, nevertheless the members of the continuum (saṃtānin) are real entities;
therefore, this is the ultimate sense: there is no contradiction between two moments, but rather [a contradiction] among many.
[559] When the two continuities have ceased in the barren moment— having been naturally obstructed— that [subsequent moment] occupies the place, the location, of that inefficient moment;
by implication, it becomes the occupant of that place, meaning it is the displacer.
