In this regard, some illuminating light, as it occupies a particular direction, removes only that which is opposed to it and situated in that very direction, by means of a gradual process of movement. On the other hand, another [kind of light], as soon as it arises in a place occupied by its opposite, instantly removes the opposing object situated in many directions.
In this case, it is not known how each functions as a remover through its specific efficacy; thus, he says "therein" (*tatra*) to introduce the statement.
The meaning is that, while approaching a desired place—that is, becoming that very place—it becomes light;
"uninterrupted by darkness" means not separated from darkness;
and "situated near the light" means situated near the light being produced there.
It produces that which is incapable, namely, that which is unable to generate further darkness;
since this is so, it possesses the quality of being a producer.
Therefore, it should be understood that light, being in close proximity, possesses the property of motion.
And its incapacity with respect to the production of the moment of the [light] to be appropriated is to be understood from the context.
When that [moment of darkness] has ceased— having naturally subsided once it has become contradictory [to light]—
that light arises, being characterized by a location that was previously occupied by a moment of incapable darkness.
Therefore, in this manner—
by the sequence and order just described— the light of the dharma of the destination, gathering for the purpose of entering that place, becomes capable of establishing a state of incapacity;
in the second moment, it produces that which is incapable.
In the third [case], it arises in that location; thus, the sequence just mentioned should be applied by dividing it accordingly.
Teaching this very same sequence elsewhere, he says: "In the same way.
Just as there is a relationship of the removed and the remover between light and darkness, in that manner, by means of the example of hot touch and the property of motion, it is to be understood.
This sequence applies to light that possesses the nature of motion.
As for what the sequence is like for [light] arising in the middle of a space occupied by a contradictory [object], he says "when" (*yadā*).
The particle *tu* is for the purpose of specification.
Since the moment that produces light arises from a [preceding] moment, he asks, "Of what kind of particle of light? and replies, "of darkness" (*andhakāra*).

This means it belongs to a location where darkness was to be removed; thus, he states that for this very reason, the moment of the production of light and the moment of the location of darkness are dependent upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Since the moment that produces light as the cause for illuminating a region of darkness possesses the quality of rendering that darkness barren, it lacks the capacity to produce its own kind; such is the state belonging to that which is connected with darkness.
This is because, according to the context, the very production of that [darkness] is what constitutes the nature of light.
Showing that even here, in the third moment, there is the capacity to exclude [darkness], he says: "And therefore" (*ataś ca*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Here too, in the first moment, the moment that produces the cause of light in a location of darkness arises as something incapable of darkness and capable of generating the cause of light in that location.
[Regarding] moments: because even though cold moments have arisen while the moments of fire exist, they become subject to cessation;
thus, since the contradiction characterized by the relationship between the ceased and the ceaser is established between the two continua, while all atoms exist...
There is no contradiction even in the absence of remaining in one place, because their respective continua do not cease.
Furthermore, light possesses the property of motion; in whichever direction it spreads, it displaces the contrary continua existing in that direction.

Therefore, you have already demonstrated that the contradiction—which is based on the incapacity of the cause—resides solely within the continuum (*santāna*). For instance, the light of a lamp situated in one part of a room does not dispel the darkness even when it is in close proximity to it, because it lacks the capacity to produce a moment of illumination in a direction already pervaded by darkness.
Thus, for you, there is the non-existence of a continuum of cold touch proceeding in a continuous stream when another continuum of heat exists.
[560] Stepping toward the direction—
[561] of those who turn back— [562] when it has been overtaken by darkness.
[563] "It is produced by causes" [564] means that it exists [565] by way of its connection.

[566] Its continuum proceeds as follows: in the second moment, it produces darknesses that are incapable and opposed to the moment that produces light in a region of darkness; in the third moment, however, when those incapable [darknesses] have ceased, it should be understood that light arises in that region.

In the same way, it should also be understood that a cold sensation must be removed by a heat-sensation—which arises in a region overcome by cold and possesses the nature of abiding—just as [the darkness is removed].
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the moment of light, by which the moment of darkness is rendered incapable upon its arrival, does not itself occupy that location?"
That by which something is approached does not produce it if it is incapable;
likewise, that darkness which exists at the time of its encounter is not opposed to it.
Furthermore, that which is incapable yet produced from it is also non-opposed, precisely because it is produced from it.

And as for those [factors] whose nature is non-arising (*anutpattidharman*), since they too are non-existent, how could there be opposition with them? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the relation of producer and produced" (*janyajanakabhāvāt*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis and should be understood immediately after the phrase "of the two continuums" (*santānayoḥ*).

This is the intended meaning: this very relation of producer and produced is precisely the relation of that which is to be removed and that which removes; and one who perceives only the superficial cannot discern the causal relation between two moments.

Rather, having determined the series of moments of darkness within those two continua to be a single unity, one conceives of that which is to be averted as its opposite; and having resolved upon the series of moments of light as a single unity, one directs one's resolve toward that which opposes it. And this is described from the perspective of ultimate reality by way of delineating the moments.
But this is not based on the conventional mode of worldly existence.
If it is argued that there is therefore no contradiction from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [we ask]:
is it that such a specific nature of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) simply does not exist?
Why have you resolved to speak in this manner?
This point shall be examined immediately hereafter.
Now, is it not the case that no distinct entity called a "continuum" (santāna) is possible apart from the members of that continuum (santānin)?
To the question, "How then can a contradiction between two continua be asserted? he says, "Even though... (yady api), [expressing] consent.

Because the possessors of the continua (*santānin*) exist as real entities (*vastubhūta*), for that reason this [contradiction] which is about to be described [is possible]. He states the justification with the words "because" (*yataḥ*).
Because there is an absence of a continuous stream of moments [of existence], it has the nature of cessation;
likewise, because [it is so] even when light is present...
It should be understood that even though they proceed through moments, those moments characterized by darkness possess the nature of cessation;
the meaning of the context is that there is a contradiction with the continuous series of moments such as light.
[567] The reading enclosed within brackets is redundant—saṃ- [DhPr 202].

However, those who say that there is no real contradiction must be addressed as follows: just as when an effect has already been produced, there is no longer any relationship of producer and produced.

If the definition of opposition as non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) applies when one thing does not occupy the same location as another, then since all atoms, being resistant (*sapratigha*), exist by mutually excluding one another's locations, why is this opposition not established for all atoms? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of two continua" (*santānayor*).
The word "co" is used for emphasis.
He states the reason: "itaretara... (mutually).
Since they all continue to flow as a stream even while those [other factors] exist, their non-cessation from the stream follows from that.

Now, one might object: "If light and darkness are in opposition by virtue of being the dispeller and the dispelled, then why is the darkness existing right there on the surface of the jasmine flower near the lamp not dispelled by the light situated in its vicinity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because its nature is to move" (*gatidharma*).
The word *ca* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
It should be understood from the context that this refers only to those situated in that very direction;
for, since light, moving toward a particular direction, removes only those opposing continua situated in the direction it is traversing,
it is for that reason [that the rule applies].
To the question "Why does it not turn back?", he says: "by darkness.

By the phrase "when overcome by darkness," it is not stated that the cause for the inability of the moments of light to arise in succession—which results in the quarters being shrouded in darkness—is [the darkness itself].
What then? A statement of fact has been made;
the meaning is that in whichever direction darkness is seen to pervade, [the object] lacks the capacity to produce a cognition there.
Otherwise, it would not even possess the quality of being pervaded by darkness.
Since it is impossible for darkness to be removed by light situated nearby, how could this [objection] be consistent?
The ultimate truth here is as follows: first, a certain measure of darkness is observed not to be dispelled even by light standing close by;
yet, the destruction of a mass of darkness located in another chamber is also observed.

Therefore, those who contemplate reality postulate that light lacks the capacity to produce another light, whereas it possesses such capacity in other cases, because the nature of dependent origination is inconceivable.

For this very reason, there is no contradiction between two things—such as a lamp and jasmine, or a wick on a surface and the darkness near it, or that same darkness and the light approaching it—insofar as they do not stand in a relationship of producer and produced, nor in a relationship of that which is to be removed and that which removes.
Nevertheless, in common usage, these two are perceived as being in opposition.

For this very reason, it was previously stated that because there is no contradiction between two things situated at a distance, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*nivartya-nivarttaka-bhāva*) exists only between those situated nearby; however, it was not stated that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists *only* between those situated nearby. Furthermore, it has already been explained that while the relationship of the sublated and the sublator may exist between those situated nearby, it does not necessarily exist between those situated nearby.

Now, demonstrating that this contradiction—which is based on the relationship between producer and produced and pertains specifically to the continuum (*santāna*)—has been established by himself and is also intended by the Master (*ācārya*), he says: "By causes" (*kāraṇaiḥ*).

The incapacity of the cause—that which is to be removed, such as a cold touch—to produce its own kind of moment is its lack of power; in that regard, the causality of the remover is "produced by that," meaning it is brought about by that [incapacity].

For this very reason, the meaning is that it is by the Master [Dharmakīrti], who demonstrates—that is, makes manifest—that which culminates in the continuum (*santāna*), meaning that whose finality (*niṣṭhā*) or conclusion lies within the continuum, which is a series of moments (*kṣaṇaprabandha*).

Furthermore, as for those such as Śāntabhadra and others who claim: "There is no contradiction between light and so forth and darkness and so forth produced [by them], because the latter, being past, does not exist."

Nor can it coexist with that which is about to arise, because that too is non-existent due to its future state; nor can it coexist with that which is present, because that is not incompatible with being produced by it.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "contradiction," which would be a relation residing in two entities.
But it is merely conceptual;
for this very reason, the Teacher stated that there is "the perception of contradiction," but not "contradiction" itself.
Having thus explained those [views], he says "But those who... [DhPr 203] in order to refute them by means of a shift in phrasing;
for there exists a [word] that has two meanings (*nāmadviṣṭha*).
The operation of an effect, however, is preceded by its cause;
therefore, it is indeed real.
Likewise, when a thing has ceased to exist, there is no such thing as "opposition" that is based on duality.
The characteristic of burning, however, consists in the incapacity of cold touch to produce its own subsequent moment;
therefore, even this contradiction is indeed real.
[568] It is observed that [569] there is the occurrence of an effect;
[570] something is desired.
Has anything been seen [571] that is not present in another moment?
[572] Therefore...
He states an example:
"Like cold and hot touch" (III-74).
This means like those two touches, namely the cold and the hot.
For the contradiction between the sensations of cold and heat should be applied here as before.
[573] And in order to demonstrate a second contradiction as well, he says:
[574] Or— omitted.

Or, like two existing entities, there is a mutual exclusion (*parihāra*), that is, a mutual abandonment (*parityāga*). That which has as its established characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or nature (*rūpa*) this [exclusion] is the state of having characteristics established through mutual exclusion (*paraparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatā*); by means of that, [they are] mutually [exclusive].

Through mutual exclusion— omitted here: when something is being delimited, that which is excluded from it must be regarded as having a nature established by way of excluding what is not being delimited.
And when blue is being delimited, its deviation from that nature (tādrūpyapracyuti) is also delimited;
for if that were not delimited, it would follow that blue itself could not be delimited.
Therefore, the existence and non-existence of a thing exist as forms established through mutual exclusion.
Any form other than blue is non-deviant from blue.

Since a visible blue object is not perceived when yellow or other colors are being perceived, the occurrence, activity, or existence of that which is intended as the effect is preceded by its cause—that is, it is preceded by the existence of the entity intended as the cause. This is what is meant.
The particle *tu* has the sense of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Since this is so, for that reason [the relation] is real (*vāstava*), that is, ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
The implication is that otherwise, even the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would have to be unreal.
If it is asked: "Is it not the case that even the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is intended to be some kind of relation residing in two [terms], such that this is being said?"—we reply: No;
because the occurrence of the effect preceded by the cause is real (*vāstava*).
In that case, here too, let the incapacity of cold touch and so forth to produce [heat] due to fire and other causes be real as well.
If it is argued that contradiction (*virodha*) is not a relation (*sambandha*), we say no;
for this specific kind of causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is admitted to be distinct from other causal relations.
We too maintain that such a specific causal relation is what is called contradiction; therefore, how could this be unreal?
As before, that is, as previously demonstrated;
because of the ascertainment of non-existence.
And just as blue excludes its own intrinsic nature,
so too does yellow and the like, which are invariably non-existent;
thus, there is a direct contradiction between existence and non-existence.
However, in the case of two entities (*vastu*), there is contradiction because they are invariably concomitant with mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Just as blue is a non-existence,
so too is that [other entity] like a non-existence— [this is the meaning of the *ṭīkā*].
Furthermore,
there are two types of contradiction: what is direct contradiction,
and which one is determined by the absence of another?
It refers to an object that has a determinate form, and not one with an indeterminate form,
such as momentariness and so forth.
For momentariness is the very nature of all things, such as blue and so forth; therefore, they do not possess a fixed form,
because nothing is perceived apart from its momentary nature.
The meaning is this, but not—
[583]— the meaning of "kṣa-[584] ataḥ"; for there is a marginal note in another manuscript stating, "because of which."

[Objection: Is it not the case that every single entity is one and the same in its nature as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; how then can there be a mutual exclusion of their forms? [Response: To this he says, "In this case" (*iha*). That which is excluded is that which is delimited therein;
for exclusion itself consists in the very nature of delimitation.
That which has as its own nature (*svarūpa*) a form (*rūpa*) that remains established by the exclusion of what is being delimited and the exclusion of what is being excluded is "thus" (*tathā*).
To the question, "What, then, is this well-known [object]? he says: "blue" (*nīla*).
The word "and" (*ca*) means "because."
That very form is *tadrūpa*;

that which is of such a form is *tādrūpya*. The departure from that, its non-existence, is of a single nature as it is to be conventionally expressed; it consists of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and has the nature of a void (*tuccha*). He states the justification for this: "the exclusion of that" (*tadvyavaccheda*).
Since this is so, for that reason:
if there were a contradiction between existence and non-existence, then there would not be one between blue and yellow; thus he says, "from blue," and so forth.
The particle *tu* indicates a distinction.
Establishing precisely the non-deviation from non-existence (*abhāvāvyabhicāritva*), he says: "of the blue" (*nīlasya*).
It is indeed thus that there is the non-existence of blue in yellow and so forth.
But that [blue] is not established as existing apart from that [nature]; thus he says "yathā" (just as).
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "because.
Blue, acting as the agent, [possesses its own] nature... [its own] nature.
And since that state of being [the nature] does not deviate from it, it is "thus" (*tathā*).

This being so, he asks what is established [by this] and says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). That is, when there is the manner of directly avoiding its own absence regarding the blue, and when there is the manner of avoiding other objects because of not deviating from that [blue].
But is it not the case that whatever does not deviate from the absence of something else is contradictory to it?
For there is no determination of its absence through its being of that nature, because of the absence of identity (*tādātmya*).
Because another contradiction has already been refuted, [it is not established].
In that case, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) as well—since it is invariably concomitant with the absence of blue and is thus contradicted by blue—would not be of the nature of blue.
That too would be nothing other than the absence of blue; otherwise, momentariness itself would be the very nature of blue.
And thus, bearing in mind that if whatever is momentary were blue, then the entire threefold world would be nothing but blue, he asks, "Of what?
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the particle "tu" (but).
Having posed the question through the mouth of another, he provides the answer with the words "That which... and so forth.
The analysis of the compound should be understood as: "the form" (ākāra) or "essential nature" (svarūpa) of a fixed and specifically determined object.
He expresses this very point by way of contrast with the words "but not," meaning:
"not, however, of that which is undetermined and consists of the essential nature of all objects."
He demonstrates that very point with the words "like momentariness and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of [theories such as] being composed of atoms and the like is intended.
By this, he says the following: even though it does not deviate from non-existence, by means of that [cognition] having a restricted form, [it is established].
There is no contradiction [of this] with an indefinite form; demonstrating that its form is indeed indefinite, he says: "For momentariness...
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because."
The intention is that [the momentary] is invariably concomitant with existence (*sanmātra*).
For this reason,
it is not the case that the meaning is "fixed" (*niyata*) or "specifically determined" (*pratiniyata*).
If that is so, then even non-existence does not have a fixed form;
how, then, can it be said to have a fixed form?
To the extent that there is an imagined non-existence whose form is distinct from the nature of the thing,
one determines that the seen or imagined determinate form is non-existent elsewhere;
it is not indeterminate.
In this same way, even a conceptual construct such as the "demon of permanence" should be seen as having a determinate form;
furthermore, this constitutes a contradiction with being a single essence.
For when two things exist through mutual exclusion, there is an absence of oneness between them.
[585] How is it that non-existence is not determined by a prover? [586] Even in the case of permanence, [the existence of] a piśāca—
That which has a form characterized by oneness of self and mutual non-existence.
For in this way, even momentariness and so forth would possess a determinate form;
that is to say, because they possess a determinate form by virtue of existing as a nature that subsists within an extremely contracted time.
Dharmottara also, when stating that "momentariness indeed constitutes the essential nature of all things such as blue," [affirms its] determinate form.
In this context, he clarifies that this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound; otherwise, one might say that "all [objects] such as blue are the very nature (*svarūpa*) of momentariness.

And thus, even for one who holds [the view of] non-momentariness, there is no determination of the absence [of momentariness] in blue, because that [non-momentariness], being the essence of all things such as blue, would possess an indefinite form.

That by which [an object] is imagined as momentary is not, by that same [cognition], imagined as having the nature of a specific, determinate entity; for this very reason, the perception apprehending blue is indifferent toward momentariness and non-momentariness, and is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to the blue itself.
Thus, it follows by the force of logic that the persistence of the blue—apart from its momentariness—cannot be determined prior to the establishment of momentariness.
And thus, even though Dharmottara has established that there is no contradiction in the nature of their distinction, those such as Dviṣyamānajalpa and Mahodadhi— who,

desiring to avoid the objection regarding contradiction, attempt to exclude the contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion— must explain for whom this determination of non-existence elsewhere [occurs].

It appears that Dharmottara’s text— stating that [the object] has a determinate form and not an indeterminate form, such as momentariness and so forth— has neither been seen nor its meaning correctly understood.
If this is not a valid rebuttal, [then the objection remains].
If it is asked, "What is the resolution to this?"—the manner in which this is resolved has already been set forth by us in the *Viśeṣākhyāna* itself; therefore, it should be sought there.
It is not stated here, however, because it is not relevant to the present subject.

If one abandons an entity of determinate form but not one of indeterminate form, then existence would remain without abandoning non-existence, because that [non-existence] is of an indeterminate form; anticipating this objection, he says, "If it is so.
This means: if this is accepted, then... [the consequence follows].
The word "api" (also) implies that [the reason] is not only momentariness and so forth.
The proponent asks, "How so?
Here, the particle *yāvatā* functions as a synonym for the ablative ending in the third case (*-tas*), carrying the sense of "because."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that whose form (*ākāra*) is devoid of the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*), meaning it is lacking the intrinsic nature of the blue and so forth that are perceived.
By using the term "imagined" (*kalpita*), this is what is being said: there is no such thing as "non-existence" (*abhāva*) established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
rather, it is merely superimposed in that way by a conceptualizing intellect (*buddhi*).

Since this is so, therefore that which is "seen"— meaning cognized through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether it be a conceptual construction based on scripture or otherwise superimposed—
is determined to be "elsewhere," that is, in something other than that [object], such as in blue and so forth;
it is not determined to exist in that very place as having the nature of blue and so forth, while being non-existent there.
Applying this very same principle to another case, he says "in the same way" (*evam*).

Just as existence (*bhāva*) is imagined as having a restricted form (*niyatākāra*) and not an unrestricted form, so too permanence (*nityatva*), characterized by persisting at all times, must likewise have a restricted form.
[DhPr 206]
For this very reason, this contradiction is called "definitional" (*lākṣaṇika*),
because its purpose (*prayojana*) is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), that is, the essential nature (*rūpa*) of things.
For by means of this contradiction, the true reality (*vastutattva*) of things is distinguished and established.

For this very reason, when something is negated while a form is being perceived, that which is negated is negated precisely by having admitted its perceptibility; for instance, even when a non-entity or even a *piśāca* is intended to be negated in relation to what is seen, it must be negated as having a perceptible nature.
Thus, having admitted its perceptibility, the negation occurs solely through the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).
And this being so, when a single form is being delimited, the absence of that [other form] is seen to be excluded;
and that which possesses such an absence has a determinate aspect.
Now, as for that which possesses such an absence... [pī...]
To the question, "How then is that excluded? he says: [It is] imagined, but not [the non-momentariness] of all things such as blue.
Non-momentariness, however, constitutes the very nature of all things such as blue, because everything indeed persists for multiple moments.
Nor is only that which is non-momentary eternal,

for even among existing things that lack a cause— such as space and so forth— only a limited portion possesses that nature. Likewise, even the state of being a *piśāca* is merely a conceptualized form consisting of bones, sinews, needles, mouths, and the like.

Because that [object] also possesses the form of blue and so forth, there is this contradiction with [the claim of] blue and the like. Alternatively, it is "thus" because its nature is a fixed, specific form; by negation, it would then have an unfixed form.

In that case, however, one must state either that [the object] is not of the nature of all blue things and so forth, or that it is of the nature of all blue things and so forth; or else, that it has a determinate form or an indeterminate form.
Therefore, there is no consequence of having a determinate form in regard to momentariness and the like.
Furthermore, the explanation "consisting of the essential nature of all" is to be understood according to the distinction of its meaning.

One might object: "By this contradiction (*virodha*), the coexistence of two contradictory things is negated; whereas by the former [type of contradiction], their existence through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthāna*) is established. How, then, can one be included within the other? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of being of a single nature" (*ekātmatve*).
The word *ca* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).

The contradiction that negates two contradictory things within a single substrate is called "contradiction in a single substrate. To explain how this is so, he says: "Of which two," where the particle *hi* signifies the sense of "because."

Since by this contradiction the identity of two contradictory things is negated, for that very reason—for this cause alone—he says "the definition" (*lakṣaṇam*) in response to the question: "How is such a contradiction denoted by you through a technical term (*lākṣaṇika-śabda*)?
[The definition] is the distinct nature (*vibhakta-svarūpam*), which is the purpose (*prayojanam*) to be established as the probandum (*sādhyam*).
Alternatively, "purpose" (*prayojana*) refers to that by which one is impelled;
having thus analyzed [the term] on these grounds, the phrase "by such an analysis" means precisely this.
To the question "In what way is this the purpose?", he replies: "By way of contradiction."
The word "hi" means "because.

Since it is differentiated by another—that is, because it is differentiated from this [other] through contradiction—the establishment of the distinct form of blue and so forth negates its identity with that other.
For this very reason, for this cause alone.
When a visible form is being perceived—that is, when the essential nature of a thing is being cognized—whatever is negated is negated as having that very visible nature.

Anticipating the objection that "it is logical to negate one visible object only after first admitting the visibility of another visible object, but not an invisible one," he says, "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
The word "also" (*api*) implies that it is not only a positive entity (*bhāva*) [that is negated].
The word "api" (also) implies that it is not merely a non-existence;
rather, as something possessing a visible nature—that is, as having the nature of a visible yellow—it is the object of negation, worthy of being denied:
"This yellow thing currently being perceived is not [yellow]."
The intention is that [the absence] is established through negation, because it does not appear as having that nature—whether it be a non-entity or a piśāca.
The particle *iti* indicates the reason:
the negation of one thing in another by way of identity is based solely on the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).
Now, it might be argued that perception itself effects the conventional usage regarding the absence of yellow-nature in blue.
Why, then, is it said thus?
If it is replied that this has already been stated—that even those things not perceived cannot be made the object of conventional usage by means of the notion of their existence—[we say]: no.
In this case, because identity is negated,
that form is also excluded as being perceptible.
Therefore, just like one's own fall, those things that possess a fall are also excluded; thus, all those whose forms exist through mutual exclusion have their unity negated by this [reasoning].
Even if this contradiction exists, there might still be coexistence;
therefore, the two contradictions have distinct functions.
By one contradiction, the identity of the sensations of cold and heat is precluded;
by another, their coexistence and their distinct objects are precluded.
The contradiction of mutual exclusion applies to all things, whether real or unreal;
the contradiction of non-coexistence applies only to certain real entities.
Therefore, these two have distinct functions and distinct objects.
Therefore, there is no mutual inclusion between these two.

[591] Having different modes of occurrence and different objects, [592] and being incapable of coexistence— neither of these two types of contradiction is possible in the case of the states of being a speaker and being omniscient. III-76
For this principle applies to the negation of that which is to be placed [within a substrate], but not to the negation of the nature of what is being perceived.
This is true;
however, there is no fault, as this was stated for the sake of one who is utterly deluded.

If this is so, what is established? He says: "And thus," that is, when there is the negation of a single self-nature (*ekātmya*), which is the mode of negating everything by way of its being of the nature of the perceptible (*dṛśyātmatayā*). The non-existence of that—namely, the non-existence of that very nature being delimited, such as blue and so forth—is the "non-existence of that" (*tadabhāva*). Being perceptible, that is, having the nature of the perceptible, it is excluded; that is, it is negated through identity (*tādātmyena*). The sense is: "This blue, which is of the nature of the perceptible, is not a non-existence," because it does not appear in the form of a void, that is, in the form of a non-existence; for it is negated precisely by way of its having the nature of the form currently being perceived.

"Let it be that there is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of a perceptible object whose non-existence is being determined; but what is the case regarding the negation of that which is invariably concomitant with it? To this he says, "And that which...
The word *ca* has the sense of the word *api*. That which possesses the absence of that [object] is "so" (*tathā*).

If that which possesses the absence of X is negated through identity with X, then momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) as well—being like the absence of blue according to the previously stated reasoning—would also have to be excluded through identity;
thus he says "having a restricted form" (niyatākāra).
This has already been explained previously.

Since both the absence and that which possesses the absence are negated by virtue of having the nature of being perceived, it follows that there is a negation of only those things that are perceived; therefore, "from that" means from the fact that they are excluded—negated as having identity with [the locus]—just like its own cessation or its own absence.
The inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of demonstrating completeness.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose unity is negated by this contradiction.
In the case of contradiction—characterized by the state of existing through mutual exclusion—there would be "abiding," that is, coexistence in a single location established by worldly consensus;
the particle *api* is used in the sense of possibility.
Because by this contradiction, it is not the coexistence in one place that is negated, but rather their identity as a single essence;

whereas by the former [contradiction], it is coexistence in one place that is negated, not identity as a single essence. For that reason, they are described as having two distinct and non-identical functions.
He clarifies that these two indeed have distinct functions with the words "one [is]... and so forth.
It is not only because of the difference in their functions that these two are presented as distinct;
rather, he says "and they have distinct objects" to show that they are also distinct because of the difference in their objects.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "also," meaning that [the two] are not only distinct in their operations but also distinct in their objects.
Demonstrating this very distinction in their objects, he says: "entire" (sakala).
"Let it be that contradiction is of only two kinds as previously described;

nevertheless, one or the other of these two types of contradiction will apply to the states of being a speaker and being omniscient. To this he says, "And that" (*sa ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) means "because," for this aforementioned twofold contradiction does not exist [in this case].
The word *api* indicates an intensification (*atiśaya*).
Furthermore, this contradiction, though of two kinds, does not exist between the state of being a speaker and omniscience.
For there is no determination of the non-existence of this omniscience on the basis of the absence of the state of being a speaker,
because omniscience is imperceptible;
and the non-existence of that which is imperceptible cannot be ascertained.
Therefore, there is no contradiction here;
for "going" does not mean that omniscience is established by the exclusion of being a speaker.
For wood and the like are excluded from the state of being a speaker,
because it would follow that they too are omniscient;
nor is there speech apart from omniscience.
Otherwise, it would follow that even pieces of wood and the like possess the capacity for speech;
therefore, since there is no contradiction, the prescription of the capacity for speech does not entail the negation of omniscience.
[594] Even one who possesses compassion is a speaker; for even one who possesses compassion is a speaker [595] in the case of a positive injunction, not everyone—

It might be argued: "If there were indeed no contradiction between them, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, then their coexistence might even be observed. However, since their coexistence is not observed, the cognition of contradiction arises; and from that contradiction, the cognition of non-existence follows. Anticipating this objection, he says:

[596]—the perception [of one thing]; however, from non-perception [597], due to contradiction, there is the cognition of non-existence; and [598] even in the case of non-apprehension, the cognition of non-existence does not arise from the affirmation of something non-contradictory. III-77
[598] Nor is there any contradiction; first, he demonstrates the non-existence of the former with the words "na hi" (for not), and so forth.
The word "hi" means "because."
To the question "Why is there no cognition of non-existence?", he says: "For omniscience...
The word "hi" means "because.
To the question "Why is there no cognition of non-existence even for that which is invisible?", he says: "Of that which is unseen..."
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*);
"since it is thus, therefore" (*tatas tasmāt*).
The meaning is that, by virtue of this quality of being a speaker, there is no contradiction with that [quality of] omniscience.
Demonstrating the absence of the second contradiction, he says "na ca" (and not).
The particle "ca" is used for the conjunction of negations.
He states the reasoning with the word "kāṣṭha" (wood).

For this reason—namely, why omniscience does not remain excluded by the exclusion of speakerhood—he says: "because that would entail [the absurdity] of omniscience for even those things such as wood and so forth.
Anticipating the objection, "How could there be such an entailment for them?", one should supply the word "wood and so forth" [to the argument].
For this reason—
since wood and other such things have been excluded or abandoned by virtue of their lack of speakerhood, that is, the capacity for speech—
it is said "nor even" [in the verse], implying that speakerhood itself will be established as being excluded from omniscience.
The word *api* (also/even) serves to conjoin a negation.
Here too, he states that very same reasoning with the word *kāṣṭha* (wood);
it should be understood that here as well, wood and other such things have been excluded from being omniscient.

It might be argued: "Even if there is no contradiction between being a speaker and being omniscient—since they are characterized by mutual exclusion—what harm is there [in their coexistence] such that their negation was made?
For even though they exist through mutual exclusion, let it be that what is speakerhood is not omniscience, or that what is omniscience is not speakerhood."

However, their coexistence in one place is indeed not contradictory; for this very reason it was stated by Dharmottara immediately after that: "Even if such a contradiction exists, their simultaneous presence might still occur.
This [objection] is incorrect.

For those for whom the two properties—being a speaker and being omniscient—are indeed distinct from the subject, this [argument] is appropriate; but it is not so for the Tathāgatas, who maintain the actual non-difference between the property and the subject.
For if being a speaker were excluded from omniscience, [it would follow that the Buddha is not omniscient].

And it is not a case of a contradictory affirmation (*aviruddhavidhi*). Even in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), this is not a contradictory affirmation; for although there is a non-observation of their coexistence, there is nonetheless no contradiction between the two.

This is because contradiction does not arise from mere non-observation of coexistence, but rather from the determination of a relationship of sublated and sublator (*nivartyanivartakabhāva*) between two things that are being apprehended.
Therefore, even in the case of non-apprehension, there is no contradictory affirmation regarding the affirmation of "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*).
Therefore, from this [perception], there is no cognition of the non-existence of anything else.
And even if there is the affirmation of a contradictory property that is incompatible with being a speaker who has attained *nirvāṇa*.
Likewise, the presence of passion and so forth cannot be inferred from the fact of being a speaker;
for if speech and the like were the effect of passion and so forth, then from speech one could infer passion,
and upon the cessation of passion, there would be a cessation of speech.

Nor is it an effect. Why? Because the causal relationship between speech and so forth on the one hand, and passion and so forth on the other, is not established; thus, there is no cessation of speech. (III-78)
Because the causal relationship between passion and the like, and speech and the like, is not established, the effect does not [arise] from the cause;
therefore, there is no understanding [of the self] from this.
Lest it be thought that while speech is not the effect of passion and so forth, it is nonetheless concomitant with them—
and that therefore, when the concomitants such as passion cease, speech also ceases— the author says: "It will cease."
Furthermore, when another entity that is not a cause ceases, there is no cessation of speech and so forth— III-79—
or rather, it is not the case that there is no cessation of speech and so forth merely because of the observation of concomitance when another entity that is not a cause ceases.
Therefore, there would be both the state of being a speaker and the absence of passion and the like.
Or, [the reason] "being a cause" or "not being a cause" is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) with a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), such as speech and so forth.
(III-80) This is an inconclusive reason with a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyāvṛtti*).
In that case, since the state of being a speaker is non-different from the speaker, and omniscience is non-different from the omniscient one,

it would follow that either the speaker alone is not omniscient, or the omniscient one alone is not a speaker; thus, it is logical to demonstrate that these two lack the characteristic of existing through mutual exclusion.
It should be understood that there is indeed no contradiction characterized by non-coexistence;
otherwise, the example of the jar and the cloth would not be applicable.
Furthermore, this point will be made explicit in the conclusion.
Having raised the objection—"It has been stated that the non-observation of coexistence is the reason for contradiction; why then is it said [here] 'even though'?"—he says "yady api" (even though).
This means: even by that manner.
Therefore, for this reason, from the fact of being a speaker, there is no realization of the non-existence of another quality, namely omniscience.

Wishing to demonstrate that just as there is no inference of non-omniscience from the state of being a speaker, so too there is no inference of possessing passion and the like from the state of being a speaker, he says "likewise" (*tathā*).
By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (*ādi*), hatred and so forth are encompassed.
Due to the proximity of the term "passion and the like," it should be understood that [the subject] is accompanied by passion and the like.
Just as the fault of a probans whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful has already been stated previously, it is not stated again here.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of "therefore";
therefore, from the opposite of non-omniscience— that is, from the counter-example which is omniscience— [it follows].
Because the absence of passion and so forth is the reverse of possessing passion and so forth, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of speech and the like is doubtful;
therefore, speech and the like are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Therefore, it is doubtful because of its presence in the counter-example (vipakṣa)— which is the opposite of being non-omniscient and not free from passion— namely, in that which possesses omniscience and freedom from passion and so forth; and it is doubtful because of its presence in the counter-example which is the opposite of being non-omniscient and possessing passion and so forth, namely, in that which possesses omniscience and freedom from passion and so forth.

[608] Having thus explained the defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) regarding doubt concerning the non-establishment of each individual form, such as the word and so forth, [the author] now says [in order] to state the defects of the reason regarding doubt concerning the non-establishment of two forms at a time:
[609] "Desire" (*kāma*).
When two forms are established as the opposite [of what is intended], it is a contradictory [reason].
(III-81) Regarding the phrase "of two": when two forms are established as being the opposite, it is a contradictory [reason].
There are two and three forms;
therefore, in order to clarify this distinction, he says:
[611] Regarding the phrase "of the two," namely knowledge and its object, in verse III-82:
"of the two" means of these two.
He demonstrates the specific characteristics: its presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and its absence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa).

Just as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) are contradictory pseudo-reasons (*viruddho hetvābhāsaḥ*) when proving permanence (*nityatva*), because their presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and absence in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*) are established in the opposite sense; this is the connection [of the verse]. III-83.
"Being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
"being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*).
For by the term "immediately subsequent to effort," both birth immediately following effort and the cognition [of it] immediately following effort are called "immediately subsequent to effort."
Birth is the intrinsic nature of that which is being born;
knowledge is the effect of the object of knowledge.
Here, however, it is knowledge immediately following effort that is apprehended.
By that, there is the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*); thus,
"establishment" refers to the effect-reason.
[614] Having performed [the analysis],
[615] that which apprehends the state of being immediately following effort— ṭi— [616] from that, the [nature of] cause...

Having stated all the inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*), he demonstrates the intention of the Vārttikakāra by means of the passage beginning with "evam" and so forth, while declaring the logical fallacy of the reason known as contradiction (*viruddhatva*).
He uses the plural number in the phrase "the faults of the reason" (*hetudoṣān*) because he intends to express a distinction between individual instances.
He shows two distinct forms [of the reason].
One might raise the objection: "If both are reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), then what is the purpose of stating them as two?
For the contradiction is already demonstrated by a single *svabhāvahetu*. Anticipating this, he provides the justification with the words: "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).

[Objection: But has not "being produced immediately after effort" been shown elsewhere as a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)? Why, then, is it stated here in this way? [The author] says: "Because of effort" (*prayatna*); for (*hi*) means because.
Knowledge that arises immediately— that is, without any interval— after an effort, which is human activity, is said to have that [effort] as its object.
These two reasons are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) that are contradictory (*viruddha*) to the probandum (*sādhya*), namely, permanence.
Why, then, are these two contradictory? He says:
"The establishment of the opposite [of the required properties] for these two is their non-existence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and their existence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa). (III-84)

"Establishment of the contrary" (*viparyayasiddhi*) refers to these two cases: for it is certain that *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced) and *prayatnānantarīyakatva* (the state of following immediately upon effort) are entirely absent from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), namely the eternal;
whereas their presence is certain only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), namely the non-eternal. Thus, there is establishment of the contrary.
[618] Why, then, are these two contradictory even when they establish the opposite of the probandum? He says:
"And these two are contradictory because they prove the opposite of the probandum" (III-85).
And these two establish the opposite of the probandum—namely impermanence—of what is to be proven, which is permanence;
therefore, because they prove the opposite of the probandum, they are contradictory (*viruddha*).
[619] Therefore—
*om*. If these two are contradictory because they prove the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya*),
and it has been stated that the *sādhya* is [the object] in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*),...
But that which is not stated [is not a contradiction]; moreover, what is intended is that which is not stated.
Therefore, showing that the "contradiction of the intended" is distinct from these two, he says:
But is not the third [type of reason] also a contradictory one that subverts what is intended?
Regarding this,
it is indeed stated that the third is also contradictory.
There are two [types of fallacies] that establish the opposite of what was stated.
This third one is the "subverter of the intended" (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*), because it subverts the intended meaning—which has not been explicitly expressed by words—by establishing its opposite.
In the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* and other works— [the commentary on] the sixth verse— [the author] provides an illustration of that formulation:
[622] he cites an example of its application.

"Just as the eyes and so forth are for the sake of another because they are composite, like the parts of a bed or a seat" (III-87). Now, since the term *prayatnānantarīyaka* [being produced immediately after effort] has already been employed, why is the meaning of the term *aprayatnānantarīyaka* [not being produced immediately after effort] stated? To this he says: "Being produced immediately after effort"—by the term *prayatnānantarīyaka*, that too [is expressed].
This means that it is stated "in reality.

Having raised the doubt as to when, by that word, there is the denotation of the pair—the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) or the effect (kārya)—he analyzes this with the words beginning with "birth" (janma).
Since there is also the denotation of cognition, therefore, in this context within the sequence of examples of contradictory [reasons], [it is explained].

Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), however, is not presented separately because it is already included within these two [types of non-existence]. The underlying intention should be inferred as follows: since that [non-apprehension] is easily understood from the very examples cited here, the Teacher’s intent is to show that when there is absence from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), whether by pervasion (*vyāpti*) or non-pervasion, its presence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) constitutes nothing other than a contradictory reason (*viruddha*). Thus, both [types] are mentioned.

Otherwise, if only "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) were shown to be absent from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) while pervading the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), there might arise the doubt that this is a contradictory reason (*viruddha*)— specifically one that pervades the dissimilar instances— rather than being like "that which follows immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*), which pervades the dissimilar instances. Thus, [Dharmottara’s *Pramāṇaviniścayaṭīkā* 212]:
Regarding the word "yathā" (as): "the eye and so forth" is the subject (*dharmin*).

"For the sake of another" (*parārtha*) means that which has another as its purpose (*prayojana*); those things whose purposeful agent (*prayojaka*), object to be refined (*saṃskārya*), or beneficiary (*upakartavya*) is another are "for the sake of another"—this is the proposition to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because of being an aggregate" (*saṃghātatvāt*), meaning because of having a composite nature (*sañcitarūpatvāt*), is the reason (*hetu*).
For the eye and so forth are composed of an accumulation of atoms; therefore, they are said to be of the nature of a composite (*saṃghāta*).

Regarding the phrase "because it establishes the opposite of what is intended by him as being for the sake of another that is non-composite": "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*) with respect to a non-composite object is "being for the sake of another that is non-composite" (*asaṃhatapārārthya*).

That which is intended by the Sāṃkhya proponent is "being for the sake of another that is non-composite" (*tadiṣṭāsaṃhatapārārthya*). Its opposite is called "being for the sake of another that is composite" (*saṃhatapārārthya*).

Because of that proof, it is contradictory. [627]—[This refers to] the undesired state of being for another by an uncombined entity. For whatever is a benefactor of something else is its producer.

"Uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) means not occurring in either the similar instances (sapakṣa) or the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa); the meaning is that it is a property of the very subject (dharmin) under dispute. Furthermore, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is a cause of doubt for two reasons:
because all things are subsumed under the two forms that constitute the objects of doubt.
And because the occurrence of those two pervading modes is not certain even in a single instance,
there is no doubt regarding those two modes by which every object is not subsumed.
For if another alternative mode were possible, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) would be unable to demonstrate the locus as inseparable from one of the two properties.
Therefore, it would not be a cause of doubt. A cause of doubt is that which demonstrates the indeterminate existence of two properties;
however, one that is unable to demonstrate even the indeterminate existence of two [properties] is a cause of non-comprehension.
If one demonstrates a state that is necessarily existent, it would be either a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) or a contradictory reason (*viruddha*).

Therefore, regarding those two categories by which all things are subsumed, if there were no certainty as to their possibility even in a single instance, they would be reasons for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*).
However, if there is certainty of existence, then if there is a certainty of its necessary presence in one instance, it would be either a valid reason or a contradictory reason.
But when there is no certainty regarding the existence of [the reason] in the indefinite cases, it would be a common inconclusive (sādhāraṇānaikāntika) reason;

or it would be one whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances is doubtful (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika); or it would be one with a doubtful non-existence, which is a case of unestablished negative concomitance (asiddhavyatireka).
But even in a single instance, by means of those two— such as a rabbit’s horn and so forth— [the following applies].

The particle *tu* has the sense of a qualification as before, or it means "therefore" (*yasmād evam tasmāt*). "Determined" (*niyata*) means that its certainty regarding existence does not extend to anything else; one who possesses such [certainty] is described as such.

Even a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is indeed a correct reason (*samyag-hetu*) when there is a reversal [of the property to be proven]; thus, it has been stated that if the presence [of the reason] in one [locus] is certain, it would be contradictory.
However, because its occurrence is not certain, it becomes an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*).
Then, in order to demonstrate two reasons for the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of the uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), he says:

"For there is no other category (*rāśi*) apart from those possessing a self (*sātmaka*) and those lacking a self (*nirātmaka*) in which this [reason], such as vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, could subsist" (III-98).
[Those] possessing a self and [those] lacking a self—
