The property (*dharma*) of those two is restricted to one [locus], meaning its existence (*sadbhāva*, i.e., *sattva*) is characterized by the restriction: "This exists only here. It is intended that from another mode—namely, from a different form whose existence is restricted to a different object—it shall turn away, or rather, it has the capacity to turn away.
The meaning is that one should not touch it; and because its occurrence in a single [locus] is uncertain, the intention is that "this is not so.
Since this is the case, [the following occurs].
And this [breath] and so forth are not like that;
for this very reason, the Teacher said. What did he say? He says: "From that which possesses a self," and so on.
The phrase "from everything" (sarvasmāt) must be connected to each [term].
If this is so, then let the positive concomitance (anvaya) between those two be established; to this he says:—
And it does not follow— possessing positive concomitance— with respect to an object there or not there, whether that object possesses a self-nature or lacks a self-nature.
And why is that? He says: because even in the case of a single self, [the reason] is unestablished (asiddhi). (III-104)
Regarding the phrase "even in a single self":
because it is unestablished whether a single self is possessed of a self or devoid of a self,
it is concluded that vital breath and so forth, by virtue of being properties of a real entity, must subsist in one or the other of those two.
But since it does not exist as either possessing a self or being entirely without a self, how can there be certainty regarding positive concomitance (anvaya)?
[674] "Even in a single self" — this is omitted.
[675] "In both together in one place"; first of all, it exists in one place.

But surely, for the opponent, there is nothing that possesses a self (sātmaka); therefore, this reason has neither positive concomitance (anvaya) nor negative concomitance (vyatireka) with respect to that which possesses a self. Thus, there is a certainty regarding the absence of both positive and negative concomitance in what possesses a self, rather than a doubt regarding its existence. Anticipating this objection, he says:
[676] "Following" (anugamana) means existence (sadbhāva)—[Ṭīkā].
[677] "Exclusion" (vyāvṛtti) means non-existence (abhāva)—[Ṭīkā].
Furthermore, there is no ascertainment of its positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka) with respect to that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self—III-105.

[678] One might object: "Is it not observed that breath and so forth arise from many things, both those possessing a self (sātmaka) and those lacking a self (nirātmaka), such as jars and cloths? Therefore, how can it be said that its exclusion [from all things] is unestablished? To this he says: "Breath and so forth.
This is because there is no definitive determination of its exclusion from *all* things—both those with a self and those without a self.

Why? Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established with either that which possesses a self (*sātmaka*) or that which lacks a self (*anātmaka*); this is the intended meaning in all these cases.
Now, why is it said "not from anything at all"?
For surely its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) can be ascertained precisely from that which lacks a self.
If it is argued that this is because the Buddhist accepts that jars and the like are devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*),

then since the Buddhist likewise accepts the living body as being such [devoid of a self], why should it not also be so? Furthermore, for one who distinguishes between things with a self and those without a self based on mere assertion and then states a reason, the claim that this is "inference" (*gamika*) is quite trivial.
The locative case in "tayor" (of those two) denotes the object;
and the word "tasya" (of that), as in "prāṇādeḥ" (of breath, etc.), is to be supplied as the remainder [of the construction].

[Objection: Surely, as a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*), that [property] must necessarily be restricted to some [locus]. So how can there be an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? [Response: He says, "by virtue of being a property of a real entity.
The intended meaning is that what is called positive concomitance is not a determination of an unrestricted occurrence.
[Objection: "Granted that because [the reason] is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), there may be no certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding a selfless entity;
however, let there be certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since breath and so forth are not observed in selfless things such as jars. [Reply: No.
Regarding the possibility of that very body being selfless, because there is no certainty of cessation for all things that are selfless,
and because there is no certainty of an obstacle to such a determination.
Nor is there a determination of the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [breath and so forth] with respect to an entity possessing a self,
nor with respect to one devoid of a self.

Furthermore, the ablative case in the expressions "from that which possesses a self" (sātmakāt) and "from that which lacks a self" (anātmakāt) should be understood as being used in relation to the word "exclusion" (vyatireka).

How is it that there is no certainty regarding the absence of positive and negative concomitance? He says: [679] of the absence of one thing, [680] there is the necessity of the presence of another; [681] of the absence of another, [682] there is the necessity of the presence of the first.

The ascertainment of the absence of either the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is necessarily accompanied by the ascertainment of the presence of the other, the second one; it is non-deviant from that ascertainment of presence.
Its "being" is its very essence (*tattva*);
therefore, because the ascertainment of the absence of one is necessarily accompanied by the ascertainment of the presence of the other.
Therefore, there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of two things in one place.
That very same [reason],
when [the other] exists,
becomes certain; it is a certainty.

But why is the ascertainment of the absence of one thing invariably concomitant with the ascertainment of the presence of the other? He says: because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consist in their mutual exclusion.
Precisely for that reason, due to doubt regarding positive and negative concomitance, [the reasons] are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). (III-107)
[684] For this very reason, [685] because positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) are of the nature of mutual exclusion.
The mutual exclusion [of two things] is non-existence;
that which has this as its nature (rūpa) is "that-ness" (tattva), and for that reason,
positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) are existence and non-existence.
Existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive in nature;
that which is determined through the exclusion of another is established as being distinct from it.
And existence is determined through the exclusion of its own non-existence.
Therefore, existence is established through the exclusion of its own absence;
for non-existence is formless, as it is presented by conceptual thought. And having excluded this formlessness, a thing possessing form is determined as having a specific nature.
And this being the case, the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya) is negative concomitance (vyatireka), and the absence of negative concomitance is positive concomitance.
Therefore, when the absence of positive concomitance is ascertained, negative concomitance becomes ascertained.
And when the absence of positive concomitance (*vyatireka*) is ascertained, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) becomes ascertained.
Now, the passage from "as for the shrine, etc. up to "therefore, for that reason" has a clear meaning; therefore, it is not explained [here].
Anticipating the question, "How is it that positive and negative concomitance consist in the nature of mutual exclusion? he says: "Positive and negative concomitance..."
And the nature of difference as non-existence should be understood as being established by cognition.
To the question, "What follows from those two being of such a nature for you?", he says: "Because [it is] existence and non-existence.
The word "ca" (and) means "because."

"Let it be so; nevertheless, how do those two exist through mutual exclusion? To this he says: "Of which... [yasya]. Now, one might ask: "In this case, by the exclusion of what is what determined, such that it exists by excluding the other? To this he says: "By its own absence... [svābhāva-]. The particle *ca* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
In that case, what is this so-called "non-existence" by the exclusion of which existence [is established]?
Therefore, even if that which possesses a self (*sātmaka*) is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*) and that which lacks a self (*nirātmaka*) is an entity (*vastu*),

nevertheless, there can be no ascertainment of the absence of [the reason], such as vital breath (*prāṇa*), through its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to those two;
for it is contradictory for one entity to simultaneously exist and not exist within another single entity, and thus it is impossible to ascertain their absence.
Nevertheless, there is no single entity for those two—
no single entity.

[689] This is due to the application of certainty, and not out of deference to the opponent; for the entity that exists as a real thing— whether it possesses a self or is selfless— is established in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, both are doubtful;
consequently, there arises a doubt as to whether the possession of breath and so forth exists or does not exist in those two—
[that is,] a lack of certainty regarding its existence or non-existence.
In some cases, there is neither a determination of existence nor a determination of non-existence regarding these very positive and negative concomitances;
for that very reason, there is doubt concerning the positive and negative concomitances. It is not a case of non-existence—

If, however, there were a certainty regarding the absence of even one of the two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—in any instance whatsoever, that itself would constitute a certainty regarding the presence of the second; thus, there would be no doubt at all concerning positive and negative concomitance.
And since there is no certainty regarding the presence or absence [of either] in any case, for that very reason there is doubt regarding positive and negative concomitance.
And because of doubt, it is inconclusive.
[692] In some cases there is positive concomitance (anvaya); [693] however,
[694] he says that it is "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).

He says, "It is delimited" (*paricchidyate*), meaning: when there is a mode of delimitation for form—which possesses a manifest aspect (*ākāra*)—by means of the exclusion of formlessness (*nīrūpatā-vyavacchedena*).
This is because these two consist in the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
[Objection: But surely for the Buddhists, that which is called "possessing a self" (*sātmaka*) does not exist at all; thus, it is a non-entity (*avastu*).
But the mere existence (*sanmātra*) is devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*); therefore, [it is] the real entity (*vastu*).

Fearing that there might be no certainty regarding the absence of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) of the reason within that entity which is devoid of self-nature, [the author], considering how such [certainty] could not possibly exist within a non-entity (*avastu*) that possesses self-nature, says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) by way of a conclusion.

Since the negation of one between an affirmation and a negation is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other, one might wonder: "How can there be no certainty regarding existence [of the object] from that? Anticipating this, he states the justification: "In one case," etc.

Because those two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which consist respectively of existence and non-existence—it is impossible for there to be a certainty of non-existence; thus, such a certainty is untenable.
He asks, "How is there an inconsistency? and replies: "Of one [entity]. He asks, "Why is it not consistent if there is a difference in time? and replies: "Simultaneously.
And this is based on the opponent's own admission regarding that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self.
This was stated while accepting [the position] that it both exists and does not exist;
however, showing that this very [position] is untenable, he says: "And not... The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate another point to be stated.

In this context, due to the specific topic, the opponent is a Buddhist; therefore, in accordance with his position and by virtue of what he accepts or rejects, one should apply the terms "existent" and "non-existent" appropriately—namely, that which possesses a self is non-existent, and that which lacks a self is existent.
For the point is that such an inference would be unreal (*avāstava*), not proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubala*).
If this is so, how indeed could those two [existence and non-existence] not exist? To this he says: "But rather... (*kiṃ tu*).
And this means of valid cognition operates with certainty;
for since the dispute occurs only regarding the self, [the same applies] elsewhere as well—
neither [existence] with a self nor [existence] without a self [is established].
The meaning is that [the distinction] is established.
"Iti" means therefore.
Both [cases], namely being with a self and being without a self.
Since this is so, for that reason, there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self.
When the expectation arises as to whose [existence or non-existence], it is stated: "of that which has a beginning.
[DhPr 222]
Why is it inconclusive? He says: "Because there is, therefore, no certainty regarding either the probandum or its opposite. (III-108)
Because of this— the absence of certainty due to doubtful positive and negative concomitance (*sandigdhānvayavyatireka*)—

neither the probandum (*sādhya*) nor its opposite, the contradictory (*viruddha*), is established when there is doubt regarding the presence or absence [of the reason] in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Furthermore, no category other than those possessing a self (*sātmaka*) and those lacking a self (*anātmaka*) is possible.

Therefore, since there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the self in the subject—the living body—due to its possession of breath and so forth, breath and the like are inconclusive (anaikāntika).

[696] Non-establishment [697]—and since there is doubt regarding the existence [of the reason] following from those two, why does the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) not occur? To this he says: "Because... (*yataḥ*).
"There is no certainty of existence nor certainty of non-existence" should be understood as referring to a single locus that is either endowed with a self (sātman) or devoid of a self (anātman).

He says "yadi tu" in order to demonstrate that doubt regarding positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) arises precisely because there is no certainty as to whether the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth exist or do not exist in that which is either endowed with a self or devoid of a self, and not otherwise;
the particle *tu* indicates this state as being distinct [from the previous].
Concluding what has already been stated, he says: "And because...
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
Therefore, from the context, it follows that the reason known as "possessing breath and so forth" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to doubt.
That whose positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are doubtful is "thus"; this is because there is no certainty regarding either the probandum (*sādhya*) or its opposite.
The passage beginning with "sapakṣa" [74b] provides support for this very point.

For this reason: when there is doubt regarding the presence or absence of the logical reason (*hetu*) in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), which constitute its domain, there can be no establishment—that is, no certainty—of the opposite, namely the contradictory (*viruddha*) probandum (*sādhya*) that one intends to infer.
This was stated with the intention that even a contradictory [reason] might be considered a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) in the case of a reversal [of the intended conclusion].
The portion beginning with "na ca" and ending with "prāṇādiḥ" is easy to understand.
Indeed, some Naiyāyikas have stated that such an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is "unsubsumable" (*anupasaṃhārya*).
Therefore, one must exercise caution upon hearing the word [“unsubsumable”], thinking, “This is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) that is unsubsumable.”

Uddyotakara, however, spoke as follows regarding the uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇahetu*) called audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), which was pointed out by the Master Dignāga: "If this audibility were observed in both the permanent and the impermanent, it would produce doubt regarding those two, just as verticality [produces doubt] regarding a post and a person."
And it is not observed;
therefore, this is not a cause for doubt, but rather a cause for non-comprehension.
Now, if audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) were a real property of an entity (*vastudharma*), [it would be so].
An entity must be either eternal or impermanent, as there is no other alternative;
yet neither of these is observed in a single locus.
Therefore, one forms a doubt regarding these two possibilities.
"In that case, since it is a property of the object itself, the doubt arises from the nature of the thing and not from audibility.

Because the same logic applies here as well, this very [point] regarding the uncommon [reason] has been discussed in such a manner; thus, he rightly said: "How is this doubt and the cause of doubt to be established?"
It is simply that the correct mind was not directed toward the discernment of the form of the mover;
for the fact that audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is a property of the real entity (*vastudharmatva*) is the basis for generating a cognition that touches upon the aspect of permanence.

However, from that very same property of the real entity, a cognition touching upon both aspects does not waver; nor is it the case that if something is a cause for the non-apprehension of a thing, apprehension arises from that very same cause.
But one cannot say "from that" (tasmāt),
because that would entail the absurd conclusion that the cognition of fire arises from that [cognition of smoke] rather than from smoke itself.

Furthermore, in this way, there would be no doubt even regarding [the property of] being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth; for one could say of that too: "The doubt arises because it is observed in both cases, not because of [the property of] being an object of cognition. Now, if it is argued that its observation in both cases is precisely what causes that [doubt], then [we reply]: [that is true].
If this is so, since audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is also a property of the real entity (*vastudharma*), why does it not [lead to the same conclusion] from that?

Furthermore, although verticality (*ūrdhvatva*) is observed in both a post and a person, nevertheless, when the challenge is raised that "it must exist here [in the case of the post] even without [the presence of a person]," this alone must be said:
namely, that what is called verticality is indeed a property of the real entity.
And the rule regarding the object is as follows: "It must necessarily be either a post or a person.
Thus, since the doubt arises solely from the property of the object itself and not from the quality of height, who could refute this undesirable consequence? Enough of this elaboration.

That which is not a constituent part of the proof because it lacks establishment is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), being either unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The statement of that proponent (*vādin*) is also a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it employs what is incapable.

Therefore, the intention of the author of the *Vārttika* in elucidating fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) should be understood as follows: such a fallacious reason—whether it be one where both members are unestablished or where one is employed by another—is necessarily to be pointed out.
It might be argued: there exists a distinction between an incapable qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and an incapable qualified (*viśeṣya*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent because, while being an object of cognition, it is produced.

Here, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) alone is capable of establishing the probandum; "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*), however, is a qualifier that is incapable of such establishment, and is thus an ineffective qualifier.
In this case, because the qualified object itself is considered "fully equipped" (*samratha*), there occurs a reason with an incapable qualification (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇa*); for example:
"Sound is impermanent because it is knowable (*prameyatva*) while being produced (*kṛtakatva*)."

For in this case, it is the qualifier *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced) alone that is capable of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*), whereas the qualificand *prameyatva* (the state of being knowable) is incapable; thus, the qualificand is an ineffective reason.
For when only the qualifier is capable, a reason is termed "one with an ineffective qualificand."
Let the remainder be included within the two types [of reasons].
First, it cannot be "established," because both [the reason and the probandum] are already established in the subject (dharmin).
Nor is it contradictory, because there is no positive concomitance with the opposite;
nor is it inconclusive, because "knowability qualified by being produced" and "being produced qualified by knowability" do not deviate from the probandum.
Therefore, this would result in a distinct type of fallacy of the reason (hetudoṣa) other than "unestablishedness" (asiddhatva) and so forth; however,
this is flawed because it is not a fault of the reason.
For if this employed reason were indeed contradictory,
then its inclusion within these groups of reasons would have to be considered,
or else some other fault of the reason would have to be admitted.

If it is argued that "this [reason] is not applied in this way, but otherwise, because of the [distinction between] the probandum and the probans," and thus the proponent is not defeated, then why is he not defeated?
Because of the statement of what is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).
In both cases, there is the utterance of "knowability" (*prameyatva*), which is neither a member for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) nor capable [of establishing it].
And just as defeat (*nigraha*) is necessarily entailed by the statement of that which is not a member for the establishment of the probandum, so too [is it entailed here].
Or else, there is a fault in not refuting it;

for, according to the *Vādanyāya*, one who speaks in accordance with reason is called a "rational speaker" (*nyāyavādī*), and therefore that [fault] must be taken into account. Consequently, this matter is simply a fault of the speaker and not a fault of the logical reason (*hetudoṣa*).
Thus, even if it is not included [among the fallacies], there is no entailment of it being a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Let this be the course of reasoning for now;
however, what will happen when the proof is one that proves what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?

For a proof that establishes the already established cannot be a valid proof, as it is vitiated by one or another defect such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), since its capacity to prove the probandum has not been lost.
To this it is replied: here a reason is vitiated in two ways;
one by way of incapacity, and the other by way of futility.
In that regard, only the defect of incapacity (*asāmarthya*) has been shown by the author of the *Vārttika* in the threefold manner just described;

it is not the defect characterized by futility (*vaiyarthya*). However, proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is indeed a distinct defect of the reason, characterized by futility, which is intrinsic to the reason itself. Why, then, should one consider its inclusion [within the previously mentioned defects]?
As the Teacher said: "Otherwise, [the reason] would either be undesirable or indeed fruitless;
likewise, it would not be a probandum because of its deficiency," and so forth.
The claim that "this is merely a fault of the speaker" is also a mere rumor;
for the speaker is not at fault, since he has stated the form of the complete proof as appropriate and has not failed to state what is required.
This speaker is one who has ascertained the reason (*hetu*).
Indeed, that which is employed [as a reason] experiences futility; however,
when the three characteristics are unestablished or doubtful, he concludes by demonstrating the defects of the reason, saying:

[698]—Regarding the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt (*saṃdeha*) of the reason (*hetu*): [699] or [700] thus, when one or two of these three characteristics (*rūpa*) are unestablished or doubtful, [701] there are, according to the respective cases, the three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), namely: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
[700] Thus, [701] and "in this way" means by the sequence just mentioned.
Among these, when each individual form is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful (*saṃdigdha*),
or when two [forms] are both unestablished or both doubtful,
then those fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are the unestablished, the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

"According to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) means that whichever fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is applicable when a given [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful (*saṃdigdha*), it is classified as such on account of that non-establishment or doubt; thus, "according to what is appropriate" refers to the specific connection of each particular [fallacy] with its respective [unestablished or doubtful case].
That which is unestablished—
or— omitted—
or— omitted.
[705] Why has that which was stated as a cause for doubt— the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*)— not been mentioned here? III-110
But has not the Teacher also stated that the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is a cause of doubt?
It is called "non-erroneous contradictory" because it is contradictory to what has been established by another reason, yet it does not deviate from that [contradiction].
Or else, it is "contradictory" because it establishes a property contrary to that which was established by another means of proof.
And it is non-deviant because of its non-deviation from its own probandum; thus, it is a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*).
If it is argued that what is contradictory to it does not function [there], and therefore that contradiction is indeed a fault of the speaker arising from himself;

In that case, let contradiction (*viruddhatva*) also be a fault of the speaker, since the logic is the same. For it can be asserted there as well: "This speaker incurs contradiction by employing [the reason] for an unsuitable probandum (*sādhya*) because he establishes the opposite; however, this [reason] is not inherently faulty."
One should consider how there is no fault of futility in that [statement], given that it possesses an inherent capacity to establish the intended meaning.

However, the defeat of such a proponent should be understood as arising from the statement of what is not a constituent of proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*). "Proof" (*siddhi*) is *sādhana*; it is the property (*dharma*) of that object which is the basis of dispute, introduced by the commencement of the debate, namely the reason (*hetu*).

That is a constituent part of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*); for it is on the grounds that one would be stating something irrelevant which does not exist in that way, that everything is perfectly clear. However, some strive to include this [fallacy] within the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Others, however, hold that [the two reasons] are contradictory;

and how their effort [is directed], and how that [term] is a designation not applying [to those things], has already been stated in the investigation of our own school, so it should be sought from that very source.
The passage beginning with "of the three" and ending with "is established" is easy to understand.
The word "yasya" (of which) refers to the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
To include all fallacious reasons, the word "yasya" is repeated; thus, "yena yena" means by whichever fault there is a connection or relation.
And this is an explanation of the meaning;
the analysis (vigraha) should be made as "not transgressing the yoga."
The portion from "nanu ca" up to "ity āha" is easy to understand.
This is true; it was stated by the Teacher.
But I have not stated this here.
Why? He says:
because its object is non-existent.
The object of inference is the three-fold character (trairūpya) established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
for it is from that which the occurrence of inference arises that it is the object of inference.
And since the occurrence of inference arises from the three-fold character established by valid cognition, [it is the object].
Therefore, that alone is the object of inference.
When that [subject] is under consideration, there is no possibility of a "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) reason.
For when the three-fold character (trairūpya) established by valid cognition is being discussed, only that fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) is possible whose nature is established by valid cognition.
Furthermore, there is no form of the non-erroneous contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) that is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, it is not possible.
Because it is impossible, it was not mentioned.
The existence of inference;
the possibility of inference;
the existence of inference.
[711] Therefore, non-existence (*asambhava*) was not mentioned.
Why is it non-existent? He says:

"For there is no possibility (*sambhava*) of the effect (*kārya*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*)—both having the characteristics already described—and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) being contradictory" (III-112). [712]
[712] Or rather, it is not so; for there is no possibility of contradiction between the effect and the essential nature (svabhāva), as these two have been defined above.
Because inference possesses the three characteristics [of the logical mark], its object is that which possesses the three characteristics other than the mark itself;
just as water is the domain of fish. This is precisely what is stated by the words "since" (yataḥ).
The word *hi* here has the sense of "because"; that is, because the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*), which is the object of inference, has been introduced and is currently under discussion.
