This is because both the relation of cause and effect and identity (*tādātmya*) must be known in the kitchen and in a jar, respectively;
therefore, one who demonstrates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing pervasion must show a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), however, is for the purpose of establishing that when the effect is absent due to the absence of its cause, provided that the fact of being its effect is well-known.
For this very reason, it is not necessarily a real entity (*vastu*);
the absence of the effect upon the absence of the cause occurs whether the locus is a real entity or a non-entity (*avastu*).
Therefore, whether such a thing exists or not, it is accepted as a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) for the purpose of illustrating the point to be proven (sādhya).

Therefore, without an example, neither the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason can be demonstrated. Consequently, the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is that which demonstrates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason, precisely by explaining the nature of the reason.
Without the observation of the negative concomitance of the reason, [the pervasion cannot be shown].

Or rather, it is shown that for one who has established the pervasion (*vyāpti*), a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is to be employed by demonstrating the absence of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*). [810] Or it is not possible [to establish it otherwise]; [811] because it is demonstrated that for the prover (*sādhaka*) whose pervasion is well-established, [the dissimilar example is required] by showing the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent. [812–813] Thus it is shown.
[812] – *abhāvadarśa* [813] —
The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only).
Having explained the nature (*svarūpa*) of this definition (*lakṣaṇa*), he says "this is that" (*so 'yam*), demonstrating the impossibility of explaining it exactly as it was shown.
"In that case, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) need not be shown," he says: "by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*).
The particle *tu* indicates that the example by way of dissimilarity is distinct from the example by way of similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*).
And this [is the case] when the formal argument (*prayoga*) is made by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
It should be understood that this is stated with reference to that specific occasion;
however, the presentation of both [reasons] within a single application is not possible,
as this has already been thoroughly examined previously.

Since the fact that something is an effect of another is already established, a dissimilar example (vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta) must be shown for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of the effect when the cause is absent; it is precisely from that very cause [that this follows].
It does not necessarily have to be a real entity (vastu);
the meaning is that even a non-entity can serve as a dissimilar example.
For if the rule of one thing were to be demonstrated by means of the rule of another, then how could that which is non-existent, such as space (gagana), be the substratum of anything?
That demonstration is not established.

However, when the absence of another [factor], namely the pervader (*vyāpaka*), is to be shown in the absence of one [factor], namely the pervaded (*vyāpya*), then the absence of the pervader is perfectly possible in a non-entity (*avastu*).
Otherwise, even in the case of an absence, its presence would be implied.
If it is argued that "that too is not [the case]," the intended meaning is that this very thing is non-existence (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, the mention of the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) should be understood as an illustration for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of one property through the absence of another property; otherwise, in the case of an example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), [it would necessarily be...]
It would follow that the entity is accepted as having a substratum;
and this being so, much that is inconsistent would result.
Since the absence of an effect follows from the absence of a cause—whether in the case of a real entity or a non-entity—for that reason, the entity [in question] is the great lake and so forth.
"Non-entity" refers to space and so forth.
The word "or" (*vā*) conjoins [this] with [the previous case] as being of equal force.
With the words "therefore," and so forth, he concludes the subject under discussion.
It is called "demonstrative" (*darśaka*) because it demonstrates by being the locus of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*).

If this is so, then since it demonstrates the means of valid cognition that establishes the pervasion between the probandum and the probans, only the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) should be employed and not the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). To this he says: "well-known" (*prasiddha*). Having connected [the text] with the phrase "the dissimilar instance should be employed," one should apply the causal term beginning with "well-known" in response to the doubt as to why it should be employed.
Because it demonstrates the absence of the reason (*hetu*) when there is an absence of the probandum (*sādhya*).
The word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to what is present in the mind.

Alternatively, it is so called because the absence of the reason is demonstrated *in* it, or it demonstrates [it], or it is the demonstration of the absence of the reason; thus it is "the demonstration."
The meaning is that because the instruction emphasizes the state (*bhāva*), it demonstrates the absence of a killer.
And when this meaning is demonstrated, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is indeed demonstrated.

Regarding this point—that the demonstration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), as well as the demonstration of the exclusion [of the counter-example], constitutes the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) once this meaning has been shown—he says: "The state (*tattva*) of that which has this much alone as its nature; therefore."
For this alone is the extent of the nature of an example:
namely, that a similar example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) consists in demonstrating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*),
and a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) consists in demonstrating the cessation of the probans (*sādhana*) upon the cessation of the probandum (*sādhya*).
And since this has already been explained by the very exposition of the nature of the reason (*hetu*), what is the use of a definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)?
For one who perceives the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it also demonstrates the path of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
[816] An example has been shown. [817] To the question "Why?", he says:
[818] because it is the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[819] Or [820] "this belongs to the instance of dissimilarity (vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta)"; "vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntasya" is omitted.

[821] Therefore, by the same method previously stated—namely, by this very demonstration of the nature of the example (dṛṣṭānta) through the exposition of the form of the reason (hetu)—the defects of the example are also refuted. [822] By this very demonstration of the nature of the example through the exposition of the form of the reason, the defects of the example are explained. [823] They are thus made known.

For instance: that example which, even when adduced for the sake of establishing what was previously stated, is incapable of accomplishing its own purpose, is called a "defect of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) by virtue of its lack of efficacy;
thus, the defects of the example have been described by way of their refutation—[Note].
[824] Nor is he capable [825]— because of the sense of "not being so"— this has been stated.
Having restated the root text beginning with "And in this," he explains it with the words "He who is this."
The etymology and compound formation of the word *pradarśana* (demonstration) are to be understood as before.
Its meaning should be seen as the demonstration of the absence of the reason (*hetu*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent, provided that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is well-established.
"It is just this much" means it is of such a measure. He says "it is just this much" because there is also another form of it; for "hi" (indeed) signifies that its dimension is exactly this.
By the word "eva" (only/just), the exclusion of anything else from having that nature is firmly established. To the question "What is that nature?", he says: "namely" (yad uta).
This collection of particles has the sense of "that which is this" (yad etad).

Regarding those things employed as examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) in which the fault of incapacity to produce their own effect occurs, they become "pseudo-examples" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) because they appear like examples due to some commonality [with them]. Relying on this principle (*nyāya*), he says: "The faults of the example are called pseudo-examples."

Since those [examples] are stated as pseudo-examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), they are thereby rejected as being true examples; therefore, it should be understood that the root text has been explained by implication.
He begins with the words "For instance" (tathā hi) in order to demonstrate how the statement of pseudo-examples is made through the illustration of the true nature of an example.

That which, even when employed, is incapable of establishing— either for the sake of proving or ascertaining the previously mentioned connection between birth and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)— the characteristic of the possibility of the excellence of the probandum (*sādhya*) given the possibility of accomplishing its own effect,

nor the characteristic of demonstrating the cessation of the means (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum for a reason (*hetu*) whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is already established; [This is the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).]
That faulty example is a defective example; that is to say, it is a pseudo-example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa),
because by implication it lacks the characteristic of being the cause of its own effect.
He provides examples of fallacious illustrations (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa):
for instance, "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal."
"Like karma," "like an atom," and "like a jar"—

these are fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) that are deficient in the property to be proven (sādhya), the proving property (sādhana), or both. For instance, when it is to be proven that "sound is eternal," the reason "because it is formless" is presented.
By way of similarity, these examples—such as "like karma," "like an atom," and "like a jar"—have been presented;
and these are faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), namely:
[the fault of] the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and both.
They are deficient;
the ritual action is deficient in its objective,
because that [objective] is impermanent.
The atom is devoid of proof,
because atoms possess corporeality (*mūrti*).
Corporeality is the dimension of a substance that is not omnipresent.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas assert that atoms are non-pervasive, have the nature of substances, and are eternal;
therefore, [the example] is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
A jar, however, is devoid of both [properties],
because a jar is impermanent and possesses form.
[826] "Just as" refers to being eternal;
[827] thus, when eternity is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) for sound, [828] and because it is formless (*amūrta*), by those—
[829] not omnipresent;
[830] the examples are deficient in the probandum;
[831] of a jar.
Likewise, there are cases where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and so forth are doubtful, as for example:
"This person possesses passion and the like because he speaks, like a man on the street";
or, "This person is subject to death because he possesses passion and the like, like a man on the street."
"This person is not omniscient because he possesses passion and so forth, like a man in the street" (III-125).
Likewise, that in which the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is doubtful is called "one whose property to be proven is doubtful" (*sandigdhasādhyadharma*).
Those [reasons] of which this is the first are described as such.
The one whose property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is doubtful;
the one whose property to be proven is doubtful; and the one where both are doubtful—likewise.
The section beginning with "the nature of fear" and ending with "of atoms" is easy to understand.
To explain how atoms lack the property of the probans (*sādhanavikala*) but do not lack the property of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), he says: "not all," etc.
Dimension is the cause for the conventional usage of measurement;
and because it is a quality (*guṇatva*), it resides in a substance (*dravyāśrayin*).
By the mention of "substance," its actual ontological nature (*vāstavam rūpam*) is restated.

In this context, if "form" (*mūrti*) were defined merely as the measurement (*parimāṇa*) of a substance, then since even space (*ākāśa*) and other substances possess a measurement known as "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattva*), they would consequently be considered "formed" (*mūrta*). Therefore, to exclude them, the qualification "non-pervasive" (*asarvagata*) is applied to the substance. Demonstrating that an atom is a non-pervasive substance, he says: "And those which are non-pervasive."
Substance is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), or else it is that which possesses qualities; thus, by virtue of possessing the definition of substance, it is of the nature of substance.
The two "ca" particles conjoin these two [definitions] as having a single referent in relation to what precedes them.
Furthermore, that dimension of the atom is to be known as being designated "spherical" (pārimāṇḍalya).
By this much, the deficiency of the proof (*sādhana*) has been shown.
Showing that there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhya*), he says: "But [they] are eternal.
By the particle *tu*, he distinguishes [them] from the internal meaning.

The Vaiśeṣikas are so called because they conduct their discourse by means of specific categories (*padārtha*) consisting of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence; and by conventional usage, they are said to be precisely those who accept the treatise of Kaṇāda. Alternatively, it is intended that the *Viśeṣa* is the treatise of Kaṇāda, as it is distinguished from other treatises by its exposition of the six categories.

The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that [the suffix -ika] is intended in the sense of "those who know it" or "those who study it. By this mode of expression, he indicates that this is merely their own assertion and that there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it here. For comparison: *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59).
[DhPr 241]
The example is as follows: "He possesses desire and so forth" is the probandum (*sādhya*), i.e., the state of possessing desire and so forth; "because of speech" is the logical reason (*hetu*);
and "like a man on the street" is the illustrative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The state of possessing passion and so forth is doubtful.
That which has death as its nature is "subject to death" (*maraṇadharman*);
the state of being such is "the nature of being subject to death" (*maraṇadharmatva*), which is the probandum (*sādhya*).
"This person" is the subject (*dharmin*). "Because of having a beginning" is the reason (*hetu*).
In the example of a person on the street, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is doubtful.
But the probandum (*sādhya*) is determined to be "the state of being subject to death" and "not being omniscient"; thus,
"not being omniscient" is the probandum.
The reason "because of possessing passion and so forth" is doubtful with respect to both [properties] in the example of the man on the street: namely,
both his lack of omniscience and his possession of passion and so forth.
The example [is fallacious when it is] lacking positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) regarding passion and so forth, or when the positive concomitance is not demonstrated;
for instance: "Whoever has been spoken of is possessed of passion and so forth."
Like a desired person.
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot" (III-126). Likewise—omitted.
Likewise, regarding "lack of positive concomitance" (*ananvaya*):
it refers to a case where, in a given example, only the mere possibility of the presence of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is observed,
but the probans is not pervaded by the probandum.

That [example] is "without positive concomitance" (ananvaya) and "one in which the positive concomitance is not demonstrated" (apradarśitānvaya). An example in which the positive concomitance, though present, has not been demonstrated by the speaker is one in which the positive concomitance is not demonstrated.
He provides an illustration of the "lack of positive concomitance" (ananvaya) as follows: "For example... (yathā).
Having restated the property of being a speaker in the phrase "whoever is said [to speak]," the possession of passion and so forth is predicated;
therefore, there is a necessary concomitance (pratiniyama) between being a speaker and possessing passion and so forth.
By this, pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated:
"as in the case of a person who desires [it].
By the inclusion of the term "desires," both the opponent (*prativādī*) and the proponent (*vādī*) are included.
Therefore, while the mere existence of the properties "being a speaker" and "possessing passion and so forth" is established in the person intended [as the subject],
the pervasion (vyāpti) is not established. Consequently, the example lacks positive concomitance (ananvaya).
When [the suffix] -tva is prescribed [after a word ending in a vowel], as in "sound is impermanent" (*anityaḥ śabdaḥ*), impermanence (*anityatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because it is produced" is the reason (*hetu*).
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), "like a jar," the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been demonstrated.
Regarding this point—
The passage beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "maraṇadharmatvam" is easy to understand.
If it is asked: "But how is his mortality certain, such that the reason itself is said to be doubtful?"—this is true.
It should be understood that this was stated solely by relying on common consensus (*prasiddhi*).
"Being concomitant" (*anvīyamānatva*) refers to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the probans with the probandum;
and that [concomitance] is established through the implication of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
But where that [inseparable connection] does not exist, the intention is that only mere possibility or mere concomitance is observed.
When the probans "being a speaker" is to be proven as possessing passion and so forth, "restriction" (*pratiniyama*)—that is, "specificity"—is stated; this is the remainder of the sense.
By that, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of these two by the necessity of the probandum is stated and demonstrated.
It is said that pervasion is stated because such a restatement of the rule (*vidhi*) is subordinate to the [probandum], since it arises directly from the cognition [of the probandum] in that manner.
However, this [logical connection] does not exist for these two based on their verbal statement;
because both the proponent and the opponent include [the example] as an instance (*dṛṣṭāntatvena*), by that reason it is merely existence, merely possibility, or merely concomitance—so to speak.
He says, "But pervasion (*vyāpti*)," meaning that the mere extraction of the co-occurrence (*sahabhāva*) is not a fault, provided that [pervasion] exists.
The word "tu" (but) distinguishes [the pervasion] from mere existence (*sattvamātra*).
It is not established—that is, it is not ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
the sense is that there is an absence of any means of valid cognition that proves the pervasion between these two.
Illustrating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that has been shown, he says: "It is impermanent.

[DhPr 242] Here, although the word is similar to a pot by virtue of being produced (*kṛtaka*), it cannot nevertheless be understood as being similar [to the pot] by virtue of its impermanence as well, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If, however, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is understood to have the nature of impermanence (*anityasvabhāva*), then from the state of being produced there would indeed be the cognition of impermanence.

Therefore, having stated that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—thereby establishing that being produced is necessarily concomitant with impermanence—an example must be adduced as the object for understanding the meaning of the positive statement (*anvayavākya*) for the sake of proving that necessity; and that [example] is precisely one in which the positive concomitance has been demonstrated.
However, by this [statement], the example has been presented without even stating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
And such an example is functional merely through similarity (*sādharmya*);
yet, the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established by mere similarity alone.
Therefore, the example for the purpose of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and its meaning have not been presented by him;
furthermore, the presentation of the meaning of similarity (*sādharmya*), being useless,
is impossible.
[841] Even that which is to be cooked has been attained— ṭi—
[842] impermanence [843] is known.

[844]— Indeed, by means of the example of the jar, it has been shown that through the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), sound is demonstrated to be similar to that jar as being necessarily impermanent (*anityatvaniyata*). [845]— Is this not so?

And since similarity even by way of impermanence has been shown, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is thereby demonstrated; thus he says: "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in the context of establishing impermanence.
To the question, "Why is it impossible to understand it in that way? he says: "because of over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*).
Because even for those things that possess form,
there is the consequence [of this argument] due to the cognition of similarity.
The intended property (*dharma*) is concluded by the process of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), which is excessive application; therefore [the opponent objects]:
"In that case, then, impermanence could never be understood from the state of being produced. To this he says: "But if... The particle *tu* indicates that this particular situation is exceptional.

If, by means of an affirmation preceded by a restatement of "being produced," the nature of permanence is not understood while there is a difference in meaning, then—provided that [the nature] is apprehended through its own essential nature—there would be an apprehension of impermanence from "being produced.

This is because the apprehension of that [impermanence] arises from the comprehension of the nature of impermanence inherent in "being produced," and not otherwise; therefore, this is due to the logical reason (*hetu*).

The meaning, that is, the intended referent, of the positive concomitance (anvaya) statement is the necessity of the probans (sādhana) with respect to the probandum (sādhya); its purpose is the demonstration of that [necessity], which is the object of comprehension.

He says "And that" [in the verse] because even if the example is the object of comprehension for the meaning of the positive concomitance statement, if the positive concomitance is not demonstrated, then it too is useless; why, then, should it be employed? Thus he speaks.
The word *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
To the question, "How indeed has this [opponent] been addressed by him, such that he is spoken of in this way? he says: "By him.
That is, by this proponent (*vādin*).
The word "tu" has the sense of a distinction (*viśeṣa*).
An *anvaya-vākya* is a sentence that establishes positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
[the phrase means] even without stating such a sentence.
Now, if it is argued that even though [the object] has been thus apprehended, there is no harm if it is subsequently utilized, he says: "And if such...
The word "and" (ca) indicates that this state of its is differentiated.
"Sadharmā" means that which possesses a common property (*sāmāna-dharma*), where "common" (*samāna*) refers, by context, to being similar to a jar.
The state of being that is similarity (*sādharmya*);
that alone is "that-only" (*tanmātra*).
By the inclusion of the term "only" (*mātra*), he excludes a qualified similarity.
By that very word "eva" (only), he confirms the exclusion of [any other] refutation;
the meaning is that this [reason] is useful merely by the demonstration of similarity (*sādharmya*).
Now, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is established even from the similarity shown by this term, then how could it be useless? To this he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
The particle *ca* is used here in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*) or as having the meaning of "because" (*yasmāt*).
The intention of one who speaks thus is this: indeed, similarity (*sādharmya*) must be demonstrated by means of this [reason];
and by demonstrating similarity through the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) alone, this [reason] will have fulfilled its purpose.

Nor can it be asserted that once the similarity of sound to a jar is understood through its being a product (*kṛtakatva*), the understanding of its similarity [to the jar] by way of impermanence (*anityatva*) must necessarily follow;

for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that this [understanding] could not be avoided even when a resemblance is perceived through properties such as corporeality (*mūrttatva*).
Since the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established by mere similarity alone, for that reason—

"Concomitance" (*anvaya*) is the state of being concomitant; "that which has this as its purpose" means that for which the purpose (*artha*) or utility is the connection between the probans and the probandum. This implies that it is not for the sake of merely demonstrating similarity (*sādharmya*).
By this [term], he states that this very meaning of concomitance is what is intended—namely, "and that is its purpose.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*): because that is its purpose.
That which has such a meaning as its concomitant (anvaya) is "tathā";
by this [term], the proponent [is indicated].
To the question, "For what purpose, then, has he employed this? he says: "By way of similarity" (sādharmyeṇa).
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because";
thus, this is a fault of the example arising from a fault of the speaker.
For in this case, the speaker is indeed the one who must establish the subject;
therefore, even if the object itself were not faulty, since the speaker has presented it as faulty, it is indeed faulty.
Likewise, there is the inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*): "Whatever is impermanent is produced" (III-127).
That example in which such an inverted positive concomitance occurs is so described.
He explains that very same [example]: "Whatever is impermanent is produced."
In the example, the fact that being produced is necessarily concomitant with impermanence must be demonstrated;
in this way, there would be a cognition of impermanence from the state of being produced.
However, in this case, it is shown that impermanence is necessarily concomitant with being produced.
But being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is indeed not necessarily concomitant with impermanence (*anityatva*).
Therefore, from such a "being produced" as has been shown here to be non-necessary for impermanence, there is no cognition of impermanence.
For instance, having referred back to impermanence by saying "that which is impermanent," the property of being produced is then predicated of it by saying "it is produced."
Therefore, impermanence is stated to be necessarily concomitant with being produced, but being produced is not necessarily concomitant with impermanence.

Consequently, just as from impermanence— which is not necessarily concomitant— one does not have the cognition of "being produced immediately after an effort," [so too one does not infer the latter from the former].
In the same way, there would be no comprehension of impermanence from the state of being produced,
because the state of being produced is not invariably concomitant with impermanence,
as shown by the example.

[847] However, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is stated to be necessarily concomitant with impermanence (*anityatā*) alone; [848] regarding this impermanence, [849] there is an additional reading here: "Therefore, being produced is necessarily concomitant with impermanence."
The meaning of "similarity" (*sādharmya*) has been demonstrated; since the purpose of establishing similarity has already been taken up, that [objection] is useless.
Or, it refers to the sense of "therefore."
And this word "ca" (and) is to be understood as following after [the word "doṣāt"].
Now, one might object: "In the case of producedness and impermanence, there is indeed a real concomitance (*anvaya*) between them.
So how can that example be defective merely by not being demonstrated in such a way, even though that concomitance exists? To this he says: "Because of a defect in the speaker."
He supports this very point with the words beginning "The speaker," and so forth.

If it is objected: "Surely the speaker alone might be at fault for demonstrating it in such a way; but what fault is there on the part of another poor wretch who serves as the example? [the author replies:]...
The failure to perform its own function is indeed a defect;
that non-performance arises from its own inherent incapacity.
Or let it be that [the example] was shown otherwise by someone else;

what does this matter? It has been well said that "this is a fault of the example because of a fault in the speaker," on the grounds that he did not fail to state that [the concomitance] does not exist at all.

As for the phrase "the positive concomitance is reversed," it is called "reversed" because it was presented in reverse order, but it is not the case that the positive concomitance itself actually exists in a reversed form.

To the question, "What kind of non-erroneous positive concomitance (anvaya) is this, such that it is called 'erroneous'? he says: "namely, being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). To the question, "What is the benefit in demonstrating it in this way? he says: "In this manner.
That is to say, when the necessity of being produced for impermanence has been demonstrated in this way.
Regarding this, he asks: "In this case, what is determined where? He answers: "In this [context]. The particle *tu* indicates that this state is characterized by a specific distinction.

The intention is as follows: because the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is enjoined by way of restating impermanence (*anityatva*), and because that which is being enjoined is the object of the restriction due to its pervasiveness. Furthermore, he asks: "What kind of 'being produced' is shown? and answers: [as follows].
—[Regarding "the state of being produced"]:
the particle *tu* distinguishes the state of being produced from impermanence;
[it refers to] the doctrine of the state of being produced, even though it is restricted to impermanence.
He says "therefore" (tataḥ) to show that one should perceive its permanence: since,
in this sequence of restatement and injunction, the state of being produced is shown to be non-necessary with respect to impermanence,
therefore— in this formal argument (prayoga)— from that [reason].
The phrase "of such a kind" refers to that which is being prescribed.

Previously, the proponent demonstrated that impermanence is necessarily concomitant with being produced, whereas being produced is not necessarily concomitant with permanence; this was stated merely by way of a proposition (*pratijñā*). Now, however, the manner in which that very point is to be demonstrated follows, and he shows it with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth.

Although impermanence and the state of following immediately upon effort— namely, being produced— are in fact invariably concomitant with impermanence according to the nature of things, nevertheless, impermanence has been demonstrated by the speaker.
Therefore, although it is not defective in itself, it becomes defective due to the defect of the speaker; thus,
even so, it is "uncertain," as has been demonstrated.
Therefore, that [inference] is not itself faulty;
rather, due to the fault of the speaker,
even a reversed concomitance results from the speaker's error.
Not in reality;
for in the case of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the fault of the speaker (*vaktṛ*) is also taken into consideration.
And not only does the reason [lack validity], but there are also faults in the example by way of similarity (*sādharmya*). III-128.
The fallacies of the example—
omitting [the point of] similarity— there are nine fallacies of the example.

He says this in order to state the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*) by means of that same observed dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "even the nine observed... [858] ...by which that [is shown], even by that dissimilarity... [859] ...he says: "even the nine observed... [860] ...the faults of the example. [859] ...even the nine observed—

[860] One desiring to speak says, by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) as well: "like an atom, like an action, like space"—these are examples where there is no exclusion (*avyatireka*) of the probandum and so forth.
When the eternality of sound is the probandum and its immateriality is the reason, [861] the atom is an example by dissimilarity that lacks exclusion of the probandum.
Because atoms are eternal;
action is not distinct from its means, because action is formless; and space is not distinct from either [of these].
Because of its permanence and because of its incorporeality;
like an atom,
it is [demonstrated] by way of dissimilarity to the atom.
In the interim, impermanence is observed even in cases such as lightning (*aciraprabhā*).

In that regard, just as there is no cognition of being produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) due to [the presence of] impermanence, so too there ought to be a cognition of impermanence from the fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Now, one might object: let it be that there is no cognition of being produced immediately after effort because, in reality, that [quality] is not invariably concomitant with it; however, being produced is ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*) invariably concomitant with impermanence.
"How is it, then, that there is no cognition of it from that? To this he says: "Even though," and so forth.

The intention of one who speaks thus is as follows: although an axe is in reality of the nature of cutting, when it is raised by someone who, through delusion or otherwise, has turned it away [from its purpose] and lifted it up for the sake of splitting [wood], it is brought down upon a *dhava* tree or the like.

Just as in that case, even though it is itself unimpaired, a cutting cannot be accomplished by it, so too in this case, even though it is itself unimpaired, the cognition of an object beyond the senses cannot be accomplished by it.
"Even though it is itself unimpaired" means: [it is not due to its own defect].

Since this is so, for that reason, even a reversed positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) is a fault of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) due to the error or defect of the speaker—the one who infers—hence it is a "fault.
He says "in the case of inference for others" (*parārtha*) to indicate that it is not only the case of the unshown positive concomitance (*apradarśitānvaya*).
By the word "also" (*api*), he implies that it is not only the fault of the proof (*sādhana*) that is being considered.

That which has no smaller part than itself is an atom (*paramāṇu*). Because it is presented as the object for demonstrating dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), it is called a "dissimilar example" (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
It is described as such because it possesses "non-exclusion from the probandum," which is the absence of cessation (*nivṛttyabhāva*).
[DhPr 245]
Those things whose first member is the *sādhya* (the probandum) are "those beginning with the *sādhya*" (*sādhyādīni*), namely the *sādhya*, the *sādhana* (the probans), and both.
Their non-exclusion (*avyatireka*) is the absence of cessation [from the locus]. Those which possess this are "those not excluded from the *sādhya* and so forth" (*sādhyādyavyatirekiṇaḥ*).
And these have been cited.
"—*reka* is the state of non-occurrence;
*reka* is the state of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
To provide another example, he says:"
Likewise, there are cases where the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*) is doubtful, such as:

"Kapila and others are not omniscient or are not authoritative, because they do not possess a teaching that constitutes a superior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśaya*) serving as a mark for the existence of omniscience or authoritativeness.
Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is: "Whoever is omniscient or authoritative has taught [matters such as] the knowledge of astrology and so forth."

For example—[as in the case of] Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others. In that instance, regarding the two properties to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely non-omniscience and non-authoritativeness (*anāpti*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. This is the illustration by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*). III-130. [863] By way of dissimilarity—
For example,
by the dissimilar instance (vaidharmyodāharaṇa) "such as bulls," [it is shown that] not all— [864] [865] [866].
"So be it. The "absence of the probandum" (*sādhyavyatireka*) is the absence of that which is to be proven.
That in which the absence of the probandum is doubtful is "one in which the absence of the probandum is doubtful" (*saṃdigdhasādhyavyatireka*).
Those of which this is the first are described as such.
He says "as follows" (yathā) in order to provide an example where the exclusion of the probandum is doubtful:
"non-omniscient" is one probandum;
"untrustworthy" and "having undestroyed defects" are the second.

"Kapila and others" is the subject (*dharmin*). "The non-existence of omniscience," and so forth, is the reason (*hetu*). Omniscience and reliability (*āptatā*): the excellence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśaya*) which serves as the mark for these two is the specific kind of valid cognition whose nature is that of a mark (*liṅga*).
That teaching in which there exists no excellence of valid cognition that serves as a mark for the omniscience and reliability [of its author] is described as such.
Those who possess such a teaching are so described;
their state is "reality" (tattva).
Therefore,
what is intended here by the "superiority of authority" is the teaching of astrology (*jyotiḥ-jñāna*).
For if Kapila and others were omniscient or trustworthy authorities, why did they not teach astrology and such subjects?
Nor did they teach it;
therefore, Kapila and others are neither omniscient nor authoritative. — Ṭīkā.
In this proof, there is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*):
whoever is omniscient or authoritative has taught such things as the knowledge of astrology, which serve as marks (*liṅga*) for omniscience and authority;
for example, Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others who were their predecessors, namely the Digambaras.

Based on the context, what is intended here as the definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) is the state of having eliminated all defects; thus, he explains that those who are non-authoritative (*anāpta*) are those whose defects have not been eliminated.
"Kapila" refers to the sage who composed the Sāṃkhya system; the word "etc. includes Gautama and others.

The "teaching" (śāsana) refers to the path; that is to say, it refers to the treatise (śāstra) composed by him. [Objection: But surely, in their teaching as well, there exist many superior means of valid cognition (pramāṇātiśaya) consisting of inferential marks (liṅga). Therefore, how is it that this reason is not unestablished (asiddha)? To this he says: "superiority of the means of valid cognition."
The knowledge of the luminaries—the planets and constellations—is their instruction.
Since "knowledge of the luminaries" (*jyotirjñāna*) is used as an illustration, it should be understood that this refers to the instruction on the knowledge of the luminaries and so forth.

Thus, the collective meaning is this: because they did not teach the knowledge of the luminaries and other forms of supersensuous knowledge within their own doctrine, they are not of such a nature [as those who possess them].
With the words "If indeed," and so forth, he demonstrates this very point:
that the Teacher is both omniscient and authoritative.

Therefore, in this case, based on the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of non-omniscience and unreliability from Ṛṣabha and others— is doubtful.
For what contradiction is there in [the claim] that one might teach astrology and yet be non-omniscient or unreliable?
This knowledge is merely indicative and subject to deviation; it cannot logically infer omniscience.
[868] The Teacher possesses the exclusion of what is to be proven; [869] and all—
by the word "etcetera," other forms of supersensuous knowledge are included.
Ṛṣabha and Vardhamāna are the chosen deities of the Ājīvikas;
by the word "etcetera," Pārśvanātha, Ariṣṭanemi, and others are included.
A teacher is one who teaches what he has himself perceived.

By stating "both omniscient and authoritative," he demonstrates the absence of both of these things to be proven. As Akalaṅka said: "If cognition were not possible regarding a subtle, concealed, or utterly imperceptible object, how then could there be non-contradiction in astrological knowledge?
For even astrological knowledge is indeed set forth by an omniscient being."
From this non-contradictory knowledge of astrology, the existence of an omniscient being is established. As it has been said:
"If the intellect of men does not [reach] an object that is entirely beyond the senses, how then could there be non-contradiction regarding astrological knowledge?
If you say it is because it is heard [in scripture], then another means of proof is required."
[Siddhiviniścaya, p. 413].

Furthermore, how is it that even when there is the teaching of astrology and so forth, the exclusion [of such teaching] from the counter-example, such as Ṛṣabha, who is not omniscient, remains doubtful? To this he says: "Since... (yataḥ).
Here, even if omniscience is not desired, what contradiction or impossibility exists in the teaching of astrology and so forth?

Because of the use of *kimaḥ* (the interrogative pronoun) in the sense of exclusion, the meaning is "none whatsoever. Now, if he were not omniscient, how could his knowledge—by which he might correctly instruct—that "this eclipse and so forth will happen from this cause, and therefore it will happen in such a way" have occurred, so as to be reliable? Anticipating the objection that one must therefore conclude he is indeed omniscient, he says: "This is merely based on omens (*naimittakam*)."
This [knowledge] consisting of light, cognition, and so forth,

is "derived from a cause" (*naimittaka*) because it has come about through the observation of a sign (*nimitta*), which is its indirect cause, and because the subject is designated by means of the object.
For this very reason, the omniscience of its teacher is contradicted.
The intention is this: even in the absence of omniscience, there can be knowledge of supersensuous things—such as planetary influences and so forth—as is the case with contemporary astrologers.
Such knowledge, however, cannot lead to the inference of omniscience; that is, it is not capable of proving it.
[Objection: But surely, by means of such [knowledge], someone has indeed perceived some causal relationship between that [knowledge] and a future object.

If it is argued that if he were not omniscient, how could he teach? We say no; for it is possible for him to teach that [truth] by having learned it from another source, since such a person exists elsewhere.
Furthermore, cyclic existence has no beginning;
for if it did, one could say that this very person was the first omniscient knower, and that he was our Ṛṣabha and the others.

Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "If he were not omniscient, then how could there arise from his instruction—given by one who does not know the relationship between the probandum and the probans—this knowledge of supersensible matters such as [the nature of] attachment and so forth, which is moreover reliable?
Anticipating this, he says: "It is occasional" (*naimittikam*).

The meaning is this: this is a cognition of an effect whose nature is the perception of its cause; and this [cognition] may even occur in the absence of a future object, according to the principle that causes do not necessarily possess their effects.
Furthermore, this erroneous cognition, when being taught, cannot be conceived as leading to the inference that the teacher is omniscient.
If it is argued: "How could he know, and how could he teach, that very same [erroneous] cause's capacity to produce such and such future effects, if he were not omniscient?"—[we reply:]...
For having learned that from another, both the knowledge and the teaching of it become possible.
An example of a doubtful negative concomitance of the probans (*sandigdha-sādhanavyatireka*) is as follows:
"No person intended by [the proponent], even if he be a Brahmin learned in the three Vedas, is one whose word is to be accepted, because he possesses passion and so forth.
Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Those whose words are to be accepted do not possess passion and so forth."

For example, Gautama and others are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras; thus, the exclusion of the probans—namely, the state of possessing passion and so forth—from Gautama and the others is doubtful. III-131 [870] A certain person...
[871] Gotama [872] refers to the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
That in which there is an exclusion of the probans that is doubted is so described.
He explains that [the word "udāra"] means "as follows":
one who knows the three—namely the *ṛc*, *sāman*, and *yajus*—is a "knower of the Trayī" (*trayīvit*).
By this, it is established that he is one whose speech is not characterized by dogmatic grasping (*grāha*).
The subject (*dharmin*) intended is Kapila and others; the reason (*hetu*) is "because of possessing passion and so forth";
[the predicate is] "he knows the Three Vedas."

In this context, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is as follows: an example by way of dissimilarity is where the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is shown to be pervaded by the absence of the probans (*sādhana*). Those for whom the word is to be accepted are "those whose words are to be accepted" (*grāhyavacanāḥ*). Having thus restated the absence of the probandum, the absence of the probans is established by the statement, "they are not possessed of passion and so forth.
Gautama and others are those who are mentioned first; such are Manu and others, the authors of the *dharmaśāstras*, which are the *smṛtis*. These are their authors.

For those who have composed the treatises on Dharma are both those whose words must be accepted by a Brahmin learned in the three Vedas and those who are free from passion; thus, in this context, Gautama and others are the subjects characterized by the property of Dharma (the locus of the probandum).
Consequently, the exclusion of the probans—namely, the possession of passion and so forth—from Gautama and others is doubtful.
Even though those knowers of the Three Vedas are authorities whose words are to be accepted, there remains the doubt as to whether they are still possessed of passion or are free from passion.
Where it is shown that [the subject] is pervaded by the absence of [the probandum], here [it refers to] the locus of properties (dharmin);
thus, "the locus of properties" (dharmī).

Thus, even for one who knows the subject (*dharmin*), there is still a case of "doubtful exclusion from both" (*sandigdhobhayavyatireka*), as for example: "Kapila and others are not free from passion."
"Because of the connection with grasping and non-grasping.
Here is the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya): "He who is free from passion has no grasping or non-grasping;
even for him, [it would arise] from another."
And since saṃsāra is beginningless, how can the omniscience of Vardhamāna be established by this much alone?

The term *trayī* is formed from the word *traya* ending in the suffix *ad*, with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, meaning "that collection which has three members. Anticipating the objection—"What is established here by the restatement of the probandum (*sādhya*) such that the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) is enjoined, whereby this becomes an example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*)?"—he says: "The probandum... Gautama, also known by the name Akṣapāda, was the sage who composed the *Nyāyasūtra*.
"Muni" refers to the author of the Smṛti; by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of Viśvarūpa, Yājñavalkya, Saṃvṛtta, and others is intended. "Iti" means "therefore."

Having stated that [the example] has as its object the exclusion of the property-bearer (dharmin) with the desire to make known merely the state of being a property-bearer, [the author] said "Gautama and others" with the intention of demonstrating a specific instance of that very same [property-bearer].

Just as in the cases of "this knowledge is produced by the sense organ and mental attention" or "this is the king," the meaning of the sentence is therefore: Gautama and others are the dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
And their being "thus" (tathātva) should be understood as being due to their being apprehended as such, but not in an ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ).
Even though they are words denoting objects of apprehension, he asks how there can be doubt regarding their having that nature, and says: "Even if... (*yady api*).
The word "utā" indicates an alternative position.
As in the case of "like Ṛṣabha and others" [DhPr 248]:

in the case of Ṛṣabha and others, because their state of not being free from passion (*avītarāgatva*) and their possession of attachment and aversion (*parigrahāgrahayoga*) are present, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) is doubtful. III-132
[877] Regarding the word *bhādeḥ*: that in which there is a doubt concerning both the positive and negative concomitance (*ṛṣa-sandigdhaubhayavyatireka*) is described as such.
He illustrates it with the words "for example" (*yathā*).
"Not free from passion" means that the state of possessing passion and so forth is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Kapila and others" is the subject (*dharmin*).
"Acquisition" (*parigraha*) is the first instance of taking possession of what is being obtained.
The greed and stinginess that follow after acceptance is "clinging" (*āgraha*).

Because they are joined with both "possessiveness" (*parigraha*) and "clinging," it is understood that Kapila and others possess passion and other such defilements, for they accept what is being obtained and do not relinquish what has been accepted.
In this proof, the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is as follows: where the absence of the probans must be shown in the case of the absence of the probandum.
Having restated the absence of the probandum in the phrase "one who is free from passion," the absence of the probans is established in the phrase "he has neither grasping nor non-grasping."
The example "as in the case of Ṛṣabha and others" is as follows:

based on this example of Ṛṣabha and others, the cessation of both the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the state of not being free from passion, and the probans (*sādhana*), which is the connection with grasping and rejecting, is doubtful.
For, in the case of Ṛṣabha and others, both their connection with grasping and rejecting and their state of being free from passion are themselves doubtful.
Even if it is indeed recited in their established doctrine that they are free from passion and possess no possessions, there remains doubt nonetheless.
The exclusion of the state of being yoga is recited [in the following sequence].
He states another three examples to illustrate those that lack negative concomitance (*avyatireka*): "For example, [an argument] lacking negative concomitance..."
This person is not free from passion because he is a speaker.
As for the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*): wherever there is an absence of being free from passion, one is not a speaker, as in the case of a fragment of stone.

Even though both [properties] are excluded from a piece of stone, nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established by the pervasion that "all those free from passion are not speakers," there is no negative concomitance.
Because of this,
where there is neither *avīta* nor *vīta*, that person is not a speaker.
There is no one who is not a speaker; everyone is excluded by that which is excluded. Everyone is excluded.
Likewise,
because the use of the word *ubhaya* in the dual number is observed, he expresses the meaning "of both" by means of the word *ubha*.
In this context, "miserliness" (*mātsarya*) is intended as a specific attachment— the thought, "This object has been obtained by me; let it not go to anyone other than me"—
and thus one does not relinquish it.
He gives [the example] little by little;

it is in this very form that there is an instance of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-udāharaṇa), and not otherwise. In order to confirm this, he says "where" (yatra), reminding us of what has already been stated.

By the phrase "of those beginning with Ṛṣabha," he shows that there is doubt regarding the exclusion of both the probandum and the probans from Ṛṣabha and the others, based on the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). [An objection: "But in our scripture, they are described as possessing those two qualities; how then can their exclusion from that [scripture] be established? To this he says: "Even if... By the expression "it is recited" (*paṭhyate*), he demonstrates that their connection with those qualities is established merely by way of textual recitation, and not by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For this very reason, he says: "Nevertheless."
"Three" refers to the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*).
That in which the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is absent is "that which lacks negative concomitance" (*avyatireka*).
"Non-free-from-lust" (avītarāga) is the probandum (sādhya), meaning the state of possessing lust and so forth.
"Because of being a speaker" (vaktṛtvāt) is the logical reason (hetu).
Here, he states the negative concomitance (vyatireka): "where there is no state of being non-free-from-lust" is the restatement of the absence of the probandum.
In that case, even the state of being a speaker does not exist—this is the formulation of the absence of the probans (*sādhana*).
By means of that absence of the probans, the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is stated to be pervaded.
The example is, for instance, "a piece of stone."
[887] Regarding this, as for the example of the "broken stone" [888]:
how can there be no negative concomitance (*avyatireka*) when both [the property and the probandum] have ceased from the broken stone? [889] How so? Because both have ceased from the broken stone.
What follows from this?
Even if both passionateness and speakerhood are excluded from a piece of stone,
nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established for that [reason], this is a case of non-exclusion (*avyatireka*).
[889] — even fear is not... [890] if it is perceived... [891] where there is freedom from passion (*vītarāgatva*), there is no capacity for speech (*vaktṛtva*) — ṭi-
[892] What, then, is this pervasion (*vyāpti*) like? He says: "Everyone is free from passion" is the restatement of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*);
"does not speak" is the prescription of the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*).
By that, the absence of the probandum is shown to be necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans;
such is the pervasion (vyāpti).
By means of this, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established.
And to establish this point, there is an example:
it is defective because it does not perform its own function.
[893] In the absence of a means of proof, there is no [proof];
the absence of a means of proof is established [894].
[895] There is [the fallacy] where the negative concomitance is not demonstrated, as for example:
"Sound is impermanent."
"Because it is produced, like space"—this is by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*). [896] By way of dissimilarity—omitted;
[it is] also by way of dissimilarity.
It is not taken as a root text, but rather as found in the commentary (*ṭīkā*); for that reason, this is a sequence of restatements (*anuvāda*).
The term *yāvatā*, which resembles an instrumental case ending, is used here in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
"From a fragment of brick, that is, from a piece of stone;
both [the example and the reason] are the probandum and the probans.
To this, the proponent asks: "What follows from this?"
Therefore, what occurs when both are excluded?
The meaning is: "nothing at all. [Objection:

But has it not already been shown by the example of the stone fragment (*upalakhaṇḍa*), which is a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), that both [properties] are excluded; so why is it said thus? [The author] replies: "Even though... (*yady api*).
By "pervasion" (vyāpti), he means by accepting the state of being produced from all passion;
[he asks] "of what kind is it? in order to inquire generally about that pervasion, because its negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished—that is, uncertain.
The word "punar" (again) signifies a specific distinction. The particle "iti" refers back to the word mentioned immediately prior;
thus, the meaning is "by this word."

The phrase "it should not be stated" here also functions as before; by this sequence of restatement and injunction, he thereby reveals the nature of such pervasion (vyāpti), or [he does so] for the sake of the meaning "because."
This third [type of definition] is characterized by such a nature of dependence (*pratītyasambhūtalakṣaṇatayā*);

the meaning is that the definition is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this kind, according to the principle that in the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*), there is an absence of the probandum (*sādhya*). the word "ca" (and/because) has the sense of "since" or functions as a restriction;

"Sound is impermanent"—here, impermanence is the thesis (*sādhya*). "Because it is produced"—this is the reason (*hetu*). "Like space"—this is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa dṛṣṭāntaḥ*).

if [the example] is characterized by the demonstration of the necessary absence of the probandum when there is an absence of the probans.

Alternatively, just as a reason of this kind becomes defective due to the fault of the speaker, so too does the example; thus, the purpose of the example is to show that the reason [is affected] by the transgression of the speaker.
The demonstration of its fallacious nature has been made; thus everything is clear.

Now, one might object: "Just as sound is perceived as having properties different from space by virtue of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), so too will it have properties different from that [space] by virtue of being impermanent (*anityatva*); why then is it said to be 'inapplicable'? To this he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
The word "eva" (only/just) is used either for emphasis or to indicate a reason.

The intention of one who speaks thus is as follows: if the dissimilarity [of the subject] is apprehended through one property, the apprehension of its dissimilarity through another property is necessarily concomitant.

therefore, by parity of reasoning, with reference to the affirmative statement (anvaya-vākya), it was stated "due to similarity" (sādṛśyāt).
This is because the context implies "due to similarity or due to dissimilarity," meaning [the cognition arises] from examples established through similarity (sādharmya) or dissimilarity (vaidharmya).

It has been stated that by means of the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well, through the manifestation of the restriction (*niyama*) by way of the absence of the probans (*sādhana*), the necessity of the reason (*hetu*) is manifested in the probandum (*sādhya*) alone; thus,
it must be shown that this is established.

In the positive statement (anvaya-vākya), having restated the probans (sādhana), the probandum (sādhya) must be affirmed;

The term *pradarśya* means that which is to be demonstrated—namely, the necessity of the reason (*hetu*) with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*) in the manner already described. He demonstrates this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth; since the procedure is thus one of restatement (*anuvāda*), it is as follows: when there is the manner of speaking of the eternal for that which is uncreated.

Furthermore, this exposition of *jātyuttara* (futile rejoinders) by the Teacher is not for the purpose of formal application (*prayoga*), just like the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
This is as the Naiyāyikas maintain: in a state of utter defeat...

[DHPr 256] "Expositions" (*udbhāvanāni*) refer to the bringing forth of this fault which is non-existent and unreal. They are called "expositions" because they are brought forth (*udbhāvyate*) by these [statements]; thus, they are words.
These are "futile rejoinders" (jāty-uttara); they are called "futile rejoinders" because they are responses based on similarity (jāti).

By whatever stainless merit I have acquired through this brief explanation of a few words and topics from the *Nyāyabindu*, like a ray of the moon— may I, having attained the ageless state of supreme knowledge and Dharma, be one whose activity is solely for the benefit of the world.

The *jāti* (futile rejoinders) and the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) must also be explained. Furthermore, this is for the purpose of clarifying the nature of refutation; for when that which is to be abandoned is known, what is to be adopted becomes easily understood as distinct from it. Thus, [the *jāti*]...

The purpose of clearly knowing the true nature of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is to avoid them in one's own statements and to expose the faults in those employed by others; otherwise, confusion would arise, as has already been largely stated. In that regard, the refutation of a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) is as follows: when it is argued, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," one asks: "Is this quality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) presented as the reason as residing in the sound, or as residing in the jar? If it resides in the sound, then the jar cannot serve as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); because of the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."

*Jāti* consists of counter-objections (*pratyavasthāna*). The Naiyāyikas [hold that it arises] "from similarity" (*sādharmyāt*). However, the intention of the Teacher (*ācārya*) is as follows: ... [omitted] ... For instance, the followers of the *Ekāyana* school...

They say that there is a contradiction between the words of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, as follows: [the proponent] states the reason (*hetu*) as "sound is produced immediately after effort" because of its being produced immediately after effort; yet they offer a refutation by means of that very same [reason], because sound is the subject (*dharmin*).
And this [fallacy] is not a *jāti* (futile rejoinder);
therefore, for whomsoever... these are the *jāty-uttaras* (rejoinders based on futile categories). Here, the word "iti" marks the conclusion of the major sentence.

By me, who has composed such a most extensive commentary as this— a true illuminator of the meaning of this treatise entitled *Nyāyabindu*, written by the venerable teacher Dharmakīrti— some merit whatsoever has been produced.

"By him, having reached such a state, that which was previously accumulated has become a benefit for all sentient beings..."—such is my intention... through the application of practice, this Dharmottara, who has made the performance of the welfare of others his very nature, speaks the verse beginning with "katipaye... and so forth.
This is the summarized meaning of this work:
"Whatever merit has been acquired from this *Nyāyabindu*, may I, through that merit, attain the ageless state of knowledge and the Dharma-superiority, and be engaged solely in benefiting the world."
...is understood.

Or, "words" (*padāni*) are sentences (*vākyāni*), because meanings are stepped upon (*padyante*) or traversed (*gamyante*) by means of them; since these convey a real entity (*vastu*), that which is their expressed form (*abhidheyarūpa*) exists. The remainder is to be understood as follows:
"attained" (*āptam*) means reached; "wholesome" (*kuśalam*) means well-performed (*sukṛtam*).
By doing what? ... merit also becomes wholesome;
just as for another... even that which arises from another.
Therefore, because of the possibility of deviation, there is a qualification: "like a ray of the moon.
Why is it stainless?
Because it is like a ray of the moon.
The rays of the moon are like the beams of the sun;
the sense is that whatever is purified by such a method necessarily becomes equal to this [moon] through its stainlessness. "Pada" means a station, that is to say, a state.
What is it that is destroyed where such [a state] exists? Since "the foremost of old age" is used as an illustration, it should be understood that death (*mṛtyu*) is also included therein.
Therefore, the meaning is: "undecaying and immortal."
Alternatively, by the very mention of old age, the understanding of that which includes its means is intended through the maxim of the staff and the cake (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*).
Furthermore, Dharma is seen to bring about all necessary requisites;
that state wherein these two [Dharma and its means] reach their ultimate limit is thus described.

And the latter [of these two] is superior, because the word *tat* is always understood through its constant connection with *yat*; thus the meaning remains "having attained that. *Upakṛtiḥ* is the assistance or benefit for the world, that is, for the realm of living beings.
That very [consciousness] is the subtle element (*tanmātra*).
Its activity (*vyāpṛti*), its operation (*vyāpāra*), or its state of being active (*vyāpriyamāṇatā*) belongs to me, who am such.

Nor should it be said that, in this context which lacks any basis for inference, the optative suffix is used to express a wish—such as "may I become"—for the purpose of establishing the word's meaning; if you ask why he spoke in this way, the answer is: no.
Because there is an absence of being an object of aspiration;

since such a state is attained through the excellence of merit (*puṇya*) born from performing such practices, and because I myself am performing such actions for that very reason, everything is clear according to the intention: "This is precisely this."

Having approached my preceptor, the conqueror of enemies, who is rich in wisdom, I have indeed composed this most lucid commentary; therefore, O discerning ones, it is fitting for you to examine it well, even out of curiosity.

An ignorant person, even when obtaining a jewel here, thinks it is equal to glass and thus moves with a wavering mind; yet would that not still serve as an ornament for him? Or why would those who are destitute not take it up with care?
By having composed this treatise according to the prescribed rules, may some small measure of merit have been acquired by me;
through that, may sentient beings attain infinite perfect enlightenment even in this very life.
The treatise titled *Dharmottarapratīpa*, composed by the scholar Paṇḍita Durveka Miśra, is completed.

"By that" means:

The author of the Vārttika, or the Root Teacher (mūlācārya), while employing the term "ascertained" (*niścita*), has stated that "where [it is not]" refers to another property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
